TERCENTENARY of the PASSION PLAY
Oberammergau and the British Empire

AN INVITATION
(Extracts from a letter to the Press)

SIR:—

The presentation of the Passion Play at Oberammergau in 1930 made so deep an impression on the Executive Secretary of the National Council of Education of Canada that he was moved by a great desire that when next it was presented the greatest possible number of teachers and students from Canada might share his experience. This desire has gradually taken a wider range. Now, through the National Council of Education of Canada (and the Foreign Students Bureau at Berlin) the Municipality of Oberammergau has invited two thousand Educationists, Teachers and Students (including senior boys and girls of the Secondary schools and Teachers in Training) of the British Empire to attend a special performance of the Passion Play on August 10th, and, moreover, to be the guests of the villagers in their homes. The original invitation was for 5,000, the capacity of the new Auditorium, but at the suggestion of the National Council of Education it is now limited to the number mentioned.

The National Council of Education of Canada which, in conjunction with a special London Committee is undertaking the arrangements for this pilgrimage, proposes to organise a short Conference on "The Teaching of Christ and International Goodwill." The Conference will be preceded by a simple service in the great Auditorium, in which the Passion Play Orchestra and Choir will take part. The hope is that the urgent need of peace and goodwill throughout the world may be realised afresh in the wonderful atmosphere of Oberammergau and in the light of the great memories of Calvary and Easter.

Some words written by the Archbishop of Canterbury in a letter to the Executive Secretary may here be quoted:—"I have been greatly moved by the generous and gracious invitation of the people of Oberammergau which you are now authorised to extend to the teachers and students of the Empire. I cannot doubt that those to whom the invitation is addressed will be eager, so far as they can, to accept it. I hope that a great gathering may assemble at Oberammergau to receive for themselves the deep impression which the Passion Play cannot fail to give and with its inspiration to hasten the time when, forgetting the misunderstandings of the past, the nations may live together in mutual understanding and goodwill."

On behalf of the London Committee:—

Form of Service to be used on August 9th

Hymn.

Tune: St. Anne, by W. Croft.

O God our help in ages past,
    Our hope for years to come,
Our shelter from the stormy blast,
    And our eternal home.

Under the shadow of Thy throne,
    Thy saints have dwelt secure;
Sufficient is Thine arm alone,
    And our defence is sure.

Before the hills in order stood,
    Or earth received her frame,
From everlasting Thou art God,
    To endless years the same.

A thousand ages in Thy sight
    Are like an evening gone,
Short as the watch that ends the night
    Before the rising sun.

Time, like an ever rolling stream
    Bears all its sons away;
They fly forgotten as a dream
    Dies at the opening day.

O God our help in ages past,
    Our hope for years to come,
Be Thou our guard while troubles last,
    And our eternal home.  Amen.

I. WATTS, 1674-1748.

Welcome—
HERR BURGERMEISTER LANG,
The Mayor of Oberammergau.

Acknowledgment—
SIR JAMES IRVINE,
Principal of St. Andrews University.

Short Programme of Music
by the PASSION PLAY CHOIR AND ORCHESTRA
including
"God's Tender Mercy."  By G. F. HANDEL, 1685-1759.

Solo:
God's tender mercy knows no bounds,
    His truth shall ne'er decay;
Then let the willing nations round
    Their grateful tribute pay.

Chorus:
Ye boundless realms of joy,
    Exalt your Maker's fame;
His praise your song employ,
    Above the starry frame.

=== Page 6 ===
Prayers

Let us pray for the Peace of the World.

Almighty God, from whom all thoughts of truth and peace proceed; kindle, we pray Thee, in the hearts of all men the true love of peace; and guide with Thy pure and peaceable wisdom those that take counsel for the nations of the earth; that in tranquillity Thy kingdom may go forward, till the earth is filled with the knowledge of Thy love; through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

Let us pray for Industrial Prosperity in all countries.

O God our Father, who through Thy Son Jesus Christ, has consecrated labour to the welfare of mankind, prosper, we pray Thee, the industries of all lands; bless all those who are engaged therein; shield them in all dangers and temptations, and grant that, receiving the due fruits of their labours, they may praise Thee by living according to Thy will; through the same Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

Let us pray for the Universities and Schools.

Bless, O Lord, the work of all Universities, Colleges and Schools, that they who serve Thee therein, as teachers or learners, may set Thy holy will alway before them, and be led to the knowledge of Thy truth; that both Church and Commonwealth may be bettered by their studies and they themselves become true servants of Thy kingdom; through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

Let us pray for the spread of the Gospel of Christ.

O God, who hast made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on the face of the earth, and didst send Thy blessed Son Jesus Christ to preach peace to them that are afar off and to them that are nigh; grant that all the peoples of the world may feel after Thee and find Thee; and hasten, O Lord, the fulfilment of Thy promise to pour out Thy spirit upon all flesh; through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

Our Father, which art in Heaven, hallowed be Thy name, Thy kingdom come, Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread, and forgive us our trespasses as we forgive them that trespass against us. And lead us not into temptation but deliver us from evil. For thine is the kingdom, the power and the glory, for ever and ever. Amen.

The Grace of our Lord Jesus Christ; the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Ghost be with us evermore. Amen.

Hymn.

Tune: Old 124th. Genevan Psalter.

Turn back, O man, forswear thy foolish ways;
Old now is earth, and none may count her days,
Yet thou, her child, whose head is crowned with flame,
Still wilt not hear thine inner God proclaim,
"Turn back, O man, forswear thy foolish ways."

Earth might be fair and all men glad and wise,
Age after age their tragic empire rise,
Built while they dream, and in that dreaming weep:
Would man but wake from out his haunted sleep,
Earth might be fair and all men glad and wise.

Earth shall be fair, and all her people one:
Nor till that hour shall God's whole will be done.
Now, even now, once more from earth to sky,
Peals forth in joy man's old undaunted cry—
"Earth shall be fair, and all her folk be one."

CLIFFORD BAX, 1896.

Address
by the REV. G. H. WOOLLEY, V.C., M.C., M.A.
Chaplain of Harrow School.

Hymn.
Tune: Rockingham. E. Miller.

When I survey the wondrous Cross,
    On which the Prince of Glory died;
My richest gain I count but loss,
    And pour contempt on all my pride.

Forbid it, Lord, that I should boast,
    Save in the death of Christ my God;
All the vain things that charm me most;
    I sacrifice them to His blood.

See from His head, His hands, His feet,
    Sorrow and Love flow mingled down;
Did e'er such love and sorrow meet,
    Or thorns compose so rich a crown?

His dying crimson like a robe,
    Spreads o'er His body on the tree,
Then am I dead to all the globe,
    And all the globe is dead to me.

To Christ who won for sinners grace
    By bitter grief and anguish sore,
Be praise from all the ransomed race
    For ever and for evermore.

Were the whole realm of nature mine,
    That were an offering far too small:
Love so amazing, so Divine,
    Demands my soul, my life, my all. Amen.

I. WATTS, 1674-1748.

A Prayer of St. Chrysostom

Almighty God who hast given us grace at this time with one accord to make our common supplications unto Thee, and dost promise that when two or three are gathered together in Thy name Thou wilt grant their requests; fulfil now, O Lord, the desires and petitions of Thy people as may be most expedient for them, granting us in this life knowledge of Thy truth and in the world to come life everlasting.

Amen.

The Blessing

The peace of God which passeth all understanding, keep your hearts and minds in the knowledge and love of God and of His Son Jesus Christ our Lord, and the Blessing of God Almighty, the Father, the Son and the Holy Ghost be amongst you and remain with you always. Amen.

"THE TEACHING OF CHRIST and INTERNATIONAL GOODWILL"

Conference to be held in Munich.

Chairman: SIR JAMES IRVINE.

Speakers: PROFESSOR DAVID MORRISON, M.A.
REV. G. H. WOOLLEY, V.C., M.C., M.A.

AUGUST 11th.
Introduction: MAJOR F. J. NEY, M.C., Executive Secretary of the National Council of Education of Canada.

Papers to be read—
1. On what Christian principles does modern Internationalism regard itself as based?
2. How far are these justified by New Testament teaching?

AUGUST 12th.
1. What validity have these conclusions as judgments of value?
2. What strict practical relevance and applicability have these principles to actual modern international conditions?
    The difficulties in the way.

SUMMARY: The Chairman.

The Conference will open and close with the singing of a Hymn.

To open the Conference.

Tune: Mannheim.

Lead us, Heavenly Father, lead us
O'er the world's tempestuous sea,
Guard us, guide us, keep us, feed us,
For we have no help but Thee.
Yet possessing every blessing,
If our God our Father be.

=== Page 9 ===
Saviour, breathe forgiveness o'er us;
All our weakness Thou dost know,
Thou didst tread this earth before us,
Thou didst feel its keenest woe;
Lone and dreary, faint and weary,
Through the desert Thou didst go.

Spirit of our God descending,
Fill our hearts with heavenly joy,
Love with every passion blending,
Pleasure that can never cloy:
Thus provided, pardoned, guided,
Nothing can our peace destroy. Amen.

J. EDMESTON.

Hymn to end the Conference.

Now thank we all our God
    With hearts and hands and voices,
Who wondrous things hath done,
    In whom His world rejoices;
Who from our mother's arms
    Hath blessed us on our way,
With countless gifts of love,
    And still is ours to-day.

O may this bounteous God
    Through all our life be near us,
With ever-joyful hearts
    And blessed peace to cheer us,
And keep us in his grace
    And guide us when perplexed,
And free us from all ills
    In this world and the next.

All praise and thanks to God
    The Father now be given;
The Son, and Him who reigns,
    With them in highest heaven,
The one eternal God,
    Whom earth and heaven adore;
For thus it was, is now,
    And shall be evermore. Amen.

Tune: Nun Danket.

M. RINKART, 1586-1649.

Norddeutscher Lloyd Bremen
D. "Europa" July 30th 34

Sailed about 1 p.m. (49,760 tons)
Band playing on board as we approached in launch.
Nice Cabin (2 berths) (and all to myself too)!!
Passed Isle of Wight as we left Southampton.
2 p.m. Talking pictures in Hall.
Tea and Coffee served at 4 p.m. Orchestra playing in lounge.
Every conceivable convenience on this ship.
Wonderful library.
Instead of the customary blast from a bugle as on P.S.O. - a beautiful morning hymn was played on a trumpet to rouse us this morning.

TERCENTENARY OF THE PASSION PLAY
Oberammergau and the British Empire

AN INVITATION
(Reprinted from the Press)

SIR:—

The presentation of the Passion Play at Oberammergau in 1930 made so deep an impression on the Executive Secretary of the National Council of Education of Canada that he was moved by a great desire that when next it was presented the greatest possible number of teachers and students from Canada might share his experience. This desire has gradually taken a wider range. Now, through the National Council of Education of Canada (and the Foreign Students Bureau at Berlin) the Municipality of Oberammergau has invited two thousand Educationists, Teachers and Students (including senior boys and girls of the Secondary schools and Teachers in Training) of the British Empire to attend a special performance of the Passion Play on August 10th, and, moreover, to be the guests of the villagers in their homes. The original invitation was for 5,000, the capacity of the new Auditorium, but at the suggestion of the National Council of Education it is now limited to the number mentioned.

The unique generosity and significance at the present time of this invitation from the people of Oberammergau will be recognised by all, and those who desire to avail themselves of it are asked to apply at once through their respective organisations or Schools. The number of places reserved for students is limited.

It may be added that the German Railways have offered to each registered member of the company exceptional facilities together with greatly reduced rates. The French Authorities have agreed to collaborate in the arrangements in so far as the French part of the journey to and from Oberammergau is concerned and have accorded the most generous of concessions. It is hoped that the British Railways will co-operate in similar manner. Mr. E. W. Beatty, Chancellor of McGill University and President of the Canadian Pacific Railway will play the part of host to a large number of Oberammergau's guests for the crossing from Southampton to Cherbourg on the "Empress of Britain" on July 28th while the Norddeutscher Lloyd has agreed to the chartering of the S.S. "Stuttgart" for a special crossing from Dover to Bremen on August 5th upon most reasonable conditions. The National Council of Education of Canada which, in conjunction with a special London Committee is undertaking the arrangements for this pilgrimage, proposes to organise a short Conference on "The Teaching of Christ and International Goodwill." The Conference will be preceded by a simple service in the great Auditorium, in which the Passion Play Orchestra and Choir will take part. The hope is that the urgent need of peace and goodwill throughout the world may be realised afresh in the wonderful atmosphere of Oberammergau and in the light of the great memories of Calvary and Easter.

Some words written by the Archbishop of Canterbury in a letter to the Executive Secretary may here be quoted:—"I have been greatly moved by the generous and gracious invitation of the people of Oberammergau which you are now authorised to extend to the teachers and students of the Empire. I cannot doubt that those to whom the invitation is addressed will be eager, so far as they can, to accept it. I hope that a great gathering may assemble at Oberammergau to receive for themselves the deep impression which the Passion Play cannot fail to give and with its inspiration to hasten the time when, forgetting the misunderstandings of the past, the nations may live together in mutual understanding and goodwill."

On behalf of the London Committee:—

Moynihan.
L. S. Amery.
James C. Irvine.
T. Percy Nunn.

M. E. Sadler.
Campbell Stuart.

The INVITATION is extended on the assumption that the great majority of those accepting will prefer to make their own plans for the journey to and fro from OBERAMMERGAU, spending the time en route according to individual preference. For such Members, special trains will be run from Munich to Oberammergau and return upon dates and at times to be announced.

For a limited number (including all OVERSEAS GUESTS, ST. ANDREWS UNIVERSITY and certain SCHOOL and OTHER GROUPS) special arrangements will be made, a general outline of which follows:—

GROUP 1.
AUG. 5th. Leave DOVER for BREMEN by s.s. "Stuttgart" (15,000 tons)—if specially chartered as now planned—or by other special steamer.

AUG. 6th. Arrive BREMEN.
Welcome by the City and short programme of sight-seeing. Leave by special trains for BERLIN.

AUG. 7th. In BERLIN.
Morning: Sightseeing. Afternoon: Free.
Evening: Reception and Music with Address of Welcome.

AUG. 8th. In BERLIN.
Programme arranged by the Deutscher Akademischer Austauschdienst (the Foreign Students Bureau).

AUG. 9th. Morning: Between 7 and 8 a.m. leave by special trains via Augsburg, Weilheim for OBERAMMERGAU.
Arrive: 6 p.m.
8.30 p.m. SERVICE (Broadcast) in the Auditorium conducted by the Bishop of RION and Dr. H. J. CODY, the President of Toronto University. MUSIC by the PASSION PLAY CHOIR and Orchestra, and a Boys' Choir under the direction of Mr. A. FORBES MILNE, M.A., B.Mus.

AUG. 10th. 6 a.m. MASS in the Parish Church for Roman Catholic members of the Conference and Villagers.
5 a.m.—6 a.m. HOLY COMMUNION for Protestant members.
8 a.m.—12 noon. PASSION PLAY.
2 p.m.—5.30 p.m. PASSION PLAY (Continued).
6 p.m. Leave by special trains for MUNICH.

AUG. 11th. MUNICH.
Morning: Free.
2 p.m. OPENING OF SHORT CONFERENCE on "THE TEACHING OF CHRIST and INTERNATIONAL GOODWILL."

AUG. 12th. In MUNICH. Conference continued.

AUG. 13th. Leave by special Trains for PARIS.

AUG. 14th—19th. In PARIS; special programme arranged by the French Authorities.

GROUP 1A. Alternative return for those wishing to spend more time in Germany or extend their Continental Itinerary.

AUG. 18th. By N.D.L. s.s. "Bremen" from BREMEN (or later sailing by either s.s. "Europa" or "Bremen").

GROUP 2.
PUBLIC SCHOOL GROUP—BOYS.
AUG. 5th. Leave DOVER for BREMEN on s.s. "STUTTGART" (15,000 tons), thence to Berlin.

ANALYTICAL NOTES by EDWIN EVANS

Sonata in C minor (posthumous) - Schubert

Allegro
Adagio
Menuetto: Allegro
Allegro

This is the first of three sonatas, all composed in September 1828, the others being in A major and B flat major. The third is dated 26 September, 1828, eight weeks before Schubert's death. Ten years later Diabelli issued them as "Franz Schubert's Allerletzte Composition" with a dedication by the publishers to Robert Schumann.

The Allegro opens with a bold theme, followed by an energetic transition passage leading to the dominant of the relative major key, in which the second subject then makes its appearance. This is of more lyrical quality with a characteristic transient modulation to D flat. It is repeated in varied form, and then again in E flat minor, which extends the exposition beyond the usual length. As if to compensate for this the development section is short, though it introduces a new subsidiary which is to acquire importance later on in the coda. The recapitulation passes through the same stages, in the corresponding keys, as the exposition. The coda is impressive. According to Shedlock "the long descending phrase and the sad repeated minor chords at the close suggest exhaustion after fierce conflict."

The principal theme of the Adagio is intimately suggestive of, and probably inspired by Beethoven. A second subject follows, after which the first returns in slightly modified form. There ensues an episode, of more passionate nature, in the minor key, which is however rhythmically related to the principal theme. It leads back through the second subject to the first, from which is formed a moving coda, full of tenderness and regret.

The Minuet is remarkable for its metrical freedom. It defies the convention of the eight-bar phrase.

Had Schubert's posthumous publishers treated this sonata as they did the one in G, Op. 78, played at the last concert, they might have been

=== Page 4 ===
deceived by its rhythm into calling the Finale a tarantella, for that is the appearance presented by its opening and closing pages. It is one of those flights of imagination characteristic of Schubert, taking him from one key to another until an important middle section finds him in B major. But if phantasy appears to reign here, design is present in the proportions of the movement.

Kinderscenen (Scenes of Childhood)
Op. 15 - Schumann

Of Foreign Countries and People
A Strange Story
Catch me if you can
The Entreating Child
Happiness enough
A great event
Dreaming
At the Fireside
The Knight of the Hobby Horse
Almost too serious
Frightening
Child falling asleep
The Poet Speaks

On March 17th, 1838, Schumann wrote to his future wife, then Clara Wieck, somewhat after this fashion: "Before I forget it, let me tell you what else I have composed. Whether it was an echo of what you once said, 'that sometimes I seemed to you like a child,' I know not, but suddenly I had an inspiration. I felt as if I had wings and dashed off about thirty quaint little things, from which I have chosen twelve and called them Kinderscenen. You will like them, but of course you must forget that you are a virtuoso. They will all explain themselves, and are as easy as possible. I am very proud of them and make a great impression—especially on myself—when I play them." A little later he wrote to her "Play my Kreisleriana sometimes. An out-and-out wild love is to be found in some places, and your life and mine and many of your looks. The Kinderscenen are the opposite—peaceful and tender and happy, like our future." And when, ten years later, he wrote the "Album for the Young" he was careful to point out the difference between the two works: "The Kinderscenen are reminiscences of an old person for old folk, whereas the others are rather fore-shadowings, anticipations for young folk." When they were published, in 1839, Rellstab criticised them rather severely, whereupon Schumann pointed out to a friend that "of course the superscriptions came into existence afterwards and are nothing more than delicate directions for the rendering and understanding of the music."

=== Page 5 ===
Sonata in A major (K. 331) - Mozart

Andante grazioso
Minuetto
Alla Turca

This is the second of three which were composed at Salzburg in the latter half of 1779. These were the first of his piano sonatas to be published, and were issued in Vienna as Op. 6. The A major Sonata illustrates Mozart's remarkable freedom from the conventions of his day, for the sequence of movements evolved by Philip Emanuel Bach and his great disciple, Haydn, does not command his unswerving allegiance, and here we have an early example, possibly the earliest, of a sonata which opens with a set of variations. Add the pseudo-exotic character of the Rondo, which may have caused some shaking of venerable heads at the time, and there remains only the Minuet to stand for the true sonata as then established.

The graceful theme of the first movement is simplicity itself. In the variations it is, of course, elaborated rather than varied, for the contrapuntal variation of Bach was fast fading into musical history, and the revolution which Beethoven was to bring about was still a prospect of the future. Here we have six restatements of the theme in successive stages of adornment, but the ornamentation has all the charm of a period when elegance counted for much.

In the Minuet, however, which Shedlock regards as the gem of the sonata, we have a higher flight of imagination. Within the dimensions adopted for the Minuet of the period he contrives to present or suggest the substance of an ampler movement. Each section seems to have a double allowance of thematic material. Then there is the delightful contrast of the middle section, the Trio, with a touch of romantic tenderness, one of those occasional moments when Mozart seems to foreshadow Schubert.

Of the familiar Rondo alla Turca it is scarcely necessary to write. The Viennese conception of Turkish music was at that time mostly associated with percussion instruments—drums, bells, triangle, and so on—and obviously Mozart's intention was to convey a similar effect by means of the piano. In reality the Rondo is no more Turkish than the famous Interlude in Molière's Le Bourgeois Gentilhomme, but musicians in those days were not preoccupied with ethnological considerations.

Four Impromptus, Op. 142 - Schubert

Allegro moderato
Allegretto
Tema con variazioni
Allegro scherzando

The description "Impromptu" was given to these pieces not by Schubert himself, but by his publishers. This, the second set, appeared in 1838, ten years after the composer's death, with a dedication by the publishers to Liszt—a rather high-handed proceeding in the case of

=== Page 6 ===
the work of a dead composer, but one which, as it happened, was justified in the end, for it was Liszt who long afterwards described Schubert as le musicien le plus poète que jamais.

Schumann suspected here portions of a sonata. This is what he wrote:
"The first is evidently the first movement of a sonata, so perfectly carried out and concluded that no doubt can exist about it. I consider the second impromptu to be the second movement of the same sonata; in key and character it fits it precisely . . . Perhaps the fourth impromptu may be regarded as the finale, yet, if the key be in favour of this supposition, the volatility of the whole plan is opposed to it."

Few will venture to disagree with Schumann concerning the first Impromptu which, he says "seems to have been written during a pensive hour, as if while meditating on the past." It is in F minor, and in sonata-form, though Schubert would not be likely to sacrifice his freedom.

The second Impromptu is in the relative major, A flat. In mood also it corresponds to the preceding movement, so that it may well have belonged to the same projected sonata. It has a Trio in D flat.

The theme of the third Impromptu, in B flat, closely resembles that of one of the entr'actes composed in 1823 for Helmina von Chezy's drama of Rosamunde, Princess of Cyprus, the orchestral parts of which were discovered by Grove and Sullivan in 1867. When the variations were written is not known, but Schumann hints that they may be a work of Schubert's boyhood, in which case this would be the older form of the theme. It is followed by five variations.

The fourth Impromptu, like the first, is in F minor, conceived in a very different vein. As Schumann says, its mood is difficult to comprehend, but it is equally difficult to understand how and at what point it reminded that composer-critic of Beethoven's "Anger over a Lost Penny." It has about it a certain suggestion of Schubert's Hungarian manner.

SCHNABEL WILL PLAY FOR YOU WHENEVER YOU WISH

To those who know only the old style of gramophone record, the excellence of present-day Recorded Music will seem incredible. The delicate apparatus and wonderful technique developed by "His Master's Voice" at their famous studios at St. John's Wood have made it possible for you to reproduce in the quiet and comfort of your own home, among your family and friends, exactly what you hear at an original performance.

Schnabel, universally acclaimed as the greatest Beethoven player in living memory, refused all inducements to record until two years ago when he heard new examples of "His Master's Voice" Recorded Music. Translation.

The years roll by, no comfort bringing,
Spring comes smiling, gay flowers flinging,
The birds' sweet song but makes my heart the sadder pine,
My wounds bleed fresh, my heart cries for joys that once were mine.

Along this silent shore I wander lonely,
My grief God knoweth only, ever, evermore
Lía mourns for her child, the child that once she bore.

    Azaël! Azaël!  Ah! wherefore didst thou leave me?
    On my heart thou art graven; I sorrow for thee;
    Azaël! Azaël!  Ah! wherefore didst thou leave me?

Happy days to my memory start when the elm trees waving o'er us,
Homeward the ruddy oxen bore us,
Weary with toil, but light of heart.

Then as the shadows 'gan to fall,
We all the evening hymn did sing
Thankfully to God, our King,
To God the Lord who giveth all.

Sweetly we slept, and glad uprose,
Youths and pure maidens wandered free,
Plighted vows in sincerity.

Evening shades brought rest and calm repose,
Happy ye parents! when to earth your children bind ye:
How glad your lot appears!

Its joys; its tender fears,
With their lives hath their love entwined ye,
Sadly must I alone drag out the leaden years!
    Azaël! Azaël! Azaël! Azaël!
    Ah! wherefore didst thou leave me?

Se il mio sogno si av verasse!
Un esercito di prodi da me guidato
E la vittoria, e il plauso di Menfi tutta!
E a te, ma dolce Aida,
Tornar di lauri cinto,
Dirti; per te ho pugnato.
Per te ho vinto!
Celeste Aida, forma divina,
Mistico serto di luce e fior.
Del mio pensiero tu sei regina,
Tu di mia vita sei lo splendor.
Il tuo bel cielo vorrei ridarti,
Le dolci brezze del patrio suol,
Un regal serto sul crin posarti,
Ergeti un trono vicino al sol.

English Version.

What if 'tis I am chosen, and my dream be now accomplished!
Of a glorious army I the chosen leader,
Mine glorious victory, by Memphis received in triumph,
To thee returned, Aida, my brow entwined with laurels,
Tell thee, for thee I battled—for thee I conquered.
Heavenly Aida, beauty resplendent,
Radiant flower, blooming and bright,
Queenly thou reignest, o'er me transcendent,
Bathing my spirit in beauty's light.
Would that thy bright skies once more beholding,
Breathing the soft airs of thy native land,
Round thy fair brow a diadem folding,
Thine were a throne next the sun to stand.
Heavenly Aida, etc.

=== Page 6 ===
Songs in French
(a) "Les Cloches" ... Debussy
(b) "Si mes Vers avaient des Ailes" ... Reynaldo Hahn
(c) "Aubade" ("Le Roi d'Ys") ... Lalo
(d) "Nymphes et Sylvains" ... Bemberg

Dame NELLIE MELBA.

(a) "LES CLOCHES."

Les feuilles s'ouvraient sur le bord des branches,
Délicatement,
Les cloches tintaiient, légères et franches,
Dans le ciel clément.

Rythmique et fervent comme une antienne,
Ce lointain appel,
Me remémorait la blancheur chrétienne
Des fleurs de l'autel.

Ces cloches parlaient d'heureuses années,
Et dans le grand bois
Semblaient reverdir les feuilles fanées,
Des jours d'autrefois.

(b) "SI MES VERS AVAIENT DES AILES."

Mes vers fuiraient, doux et frêles,
Vers votre jardin si beau,
Si mes vers avaient des ailes,
Comme l'oiseau.

Ils voleraient étincelles,
Vers votre foyer qui rit,
Si mes vers avaient des ailes,
Comme l'esprit.

Près de vous, purs et fidèles,
Ils accouraient, nuit et jour,
Si mes vers avaient des ailes,
Comme l'amour.

=== Page 7 ===
(c) "LE ROI D'YS."

Puisqu'on ne peut fléchir ces jalouses gardiennes,
Ah laissez-moi conter mes peines
Et mon émoi.
Vainement, ma bien aimée,
On croit me désespérer ;
Près de ta porte fermée,
Je veux encore demeurer !
Les soleils pourront s'éteindre,
Les nuits remplacer les jours,
Sans t'accuser et sans me plaindre,
Là je resterai toujours, toujours.
Je le sais, ton âme est douce,
Et l'heure bientôt viendra,
Où la main qui me repousse,
Vers la mienne se tendra !
Ne sois pas trop tardive
A te laisser attendrir !
Si Rozenn bientôt n'arrive,
Je vais hélas mourir.

(d) NYMPHES ET SYLVAINS.

La nuit sur les bois va s'étendre.
Accourez, nymphes et sylvains !
Venez danser sur l'herbe tendre
Au bruit des joyeux tambourins !
L'air est léger, la brise est pure,
Un frais parfum monte des fleurs,
Le clair ruisseau jase et murmure
Auprès des vieux ormes rêveurs !
Dans l'herbe fraîche et douce,
Sur la naissante mousse,
Dansez
Amoureusement emlacés !
Marquez la danse
Bien en cadence,
Gais tambourins
Des vieux sylvains,
Et vous, naïades,
Faunes, dryades,
Dansez, Tournez, volez !

Chantez dans la nuit languissante
Aux cieux pâlis que vore voix
Monte enivrante
Au sein des bois !
Hâtez-vous, avant que l'aurore
Ne reparaisse à l'orient.
Chantez encore
En tournoyant,
Marquez la danse
Bien en cadence,
Gais tambourins
Des vieux sylvains.
etc.

Le jour revient, l'aube s'éclaire ;
D'ar s un dernier soupir d'amour,
Eloignez-vous de la clairière
Disparaissez, voici le jour !
Ah ! voici le jour.

Violin Soli (a) "Ave Maria" ... Schubert-Wilhelm
(b) "Campanella" ... ... Paganini

M. BRONISLAW HUBERMAN.

Songs in English (a) "A Fallen Leaf" Frank St. Leger
(b) "Good-bye" ... Tosti
(By special request).

Dame NELLIE MELBA.

(a) "A FALLEN LEAF."

A trusting little leaf of green,
A bold audacious frost,
A rendezvous, a kiss or two
And youth for ever lost.
    Ah me! Ah me!
The bitter, bitter cost.

A flaunting patch of vivid red,
That quivers in the sun,
A windy gust, a grave of dust
The little race is run.
    Ah me! Ah me!
Were that the only one.

(b) "GOOD-BYE."

Falling leaf and fading tree,
Lines of white in a sullen sea,
Shadows rising on you and me;
The swallows are making them ready to fly,
Wheeling out on a windy sky,
Good-bye, summer! Good-bye! Good-bye!

Hush! a voice from the far away,
"Listen and learn," it seems to say;
"All the to-morrows shall be as to-day."
The cord is frayed—the cruse is dry,
The link must break, and the lamp must die,
Good-bye to hope! Good-bye! Good-bye!

What are we waiting for? O, my heart,
Kiss me straight on the brow and part,
Again, again, my heart!
What are we waiting for, you and I?
A pleading look—a stifled cry,
Good-bye for ever! Good-bye! Good-bye!

=== Page 10 ===
Songs (a) "A Memory" ... ... ... Goring Thomas
(b) "You" { ACCOMPANIED BY COMPOSER. } Percy Kahn
(c) "Ave Maria"

Mr. TOM BURKE.

(a) "A MEMORY."

O flow'rs, all your sweets and splendour!
'Neath my hand you tremble, you thrill,
You hold in chalices tender,
His voice, softly sounding still.
As on that day, dear past naming,
In that hour of joy divine,
When a kiss, like fire forth flaming,
My love's lips laid on mine;
    O flow'rs, etc.

(b) "YOU."

You were my past, my day by day,
You were my life to be,
You were my thoughts, my words, my dreams,
You were the world to me.

You are my past, an echo now,
That dwells in a ling'ring sigh,
You are a memory hard to crush,
Of a love that has long passed by.

Alan Fenwick.

(c) "AVE MARIA."

Ave Maria Gratia plena
Dominus tecum benedicta tu
In mulieribus et benedictus
Ventris tui Jesus.
Sancta Maria! Sancta Maria! Maria!
Ora pro nobis, nobis peccatoribus,
Nunc, et in hora, in hora, mortis nostrae,
    Amen, Amen.

Duet, "Lovely Maid in the Moonlight"
(BY SPECIAL REQUEST).

(Act I. "La Bohême") ... ... Puccini
(Words by kind permission of Messrs. G. Ricordi & Co.)

Mimi ... ... Dame NELLIE MELBA
Rodolfo ... ... Mr. TOM BURKE.

Rod. O soave fanciulla,
O dolce viso di mite circonfuso alba lunar,
il sogno ch'io vorrei sempre sognar!

Rod. Fre mon gio nel l'anima le dolcezze streme, more!
Fremon nell'anima dolcezze estreme fremon dolcezze estreme,
Nel bacio freme amor!

Mim. Ah! tu sol comandi, amor
Tu sol comandi, amore!
Oh! come dolci scendono le sue lusinghe al core
Tu sol comandi, amor!

Mim. No, per pieta!
Rod. Sei mia!
Mim. V'aspettan gli amici.
Rod. Guai mi mandi via?
Mim. Vorrei dir ma non oso
Rod. Di'
Mim. Se venissi con voi?
Rod. Che? Mimi!
Sarebbe così dolce restar qui
C'è freddo fuori
Mim. Vi staro vicina!
Rod. E al ritorno?
Mim. Curioso!
Rod. Dammi il braccio mia piccina
Mim. Obbedisco, signor!
Rod. Che m'ami di
Mim. Io t'amo!
Rod. & Mim. Amor! Amor! Amor!

=== Page 12 ===
Translation.

Rod. Lovely maid in the moonlight!
Your face entrancing,
Like radiant seraph from on high appears!
The dream that I would ever, ever dream, returns.

Rod. Heart to heart and soul to soul
Love binds us in his fetters.
Love now shall rule our hearts alone,
Life's fairest flower is love!

Mim. Love alone o'er hearts has sway.
Ah Love! to thee do we surrender.
Sweet to my soul the magic voice
Of love its music chanteth,
Life's fairest flower is love!

Mim. No, I pray you!
Rod. My Sweetheart!
Mim. Your comrades await you?
Rod. Do you then dismiss me?
Mim. I should like—no, I dare not!
Rod. Say!
Mim. Could I not come with you?
Rod. What, Mimi?
It would be much more pleasant here to stay.
Outside 'tis chilly!
Mim. To you I'll be neighbour! I'll be always near you.
Rod. On returning?
Mim. Who knows, sir?
Rod. Take my arm, my little maiden!
Mim. I obey you, my lord!
Rod. You love me? Say!
Mim. I love thee!
Rod. & Mim. My love! My love!

At the Piano ... Mr. FRANK ST. LEGER.

Part Song

"For Home and Liberty"

LIEDERTAFEL

Hark, brothers, hark! the trumpet's warning blast!
Arm, brothers, arm! the foe is gather'ring fast;
The dawn of the day's at hand,
Fierce muttering comes,
With tramp of hurrying feet;
And the senses reel
In the tumult's wild,
Where the flashing squadrons meet.

Fight, brothers, fight for home and liberty!
Charge, brothers, charge; the hirelings turn and flee.
Like avalanches they rush,
From the ice-king's world,
With thunderous crash we go;
And the mighty host
Of the Tyrant's boast
Has melted away like snow.

Mourn, brothers, mourn for those who bravely fell:
Pray, brothers, pray for those who fought so well.
In their graves we laid
As they nobly died
With face to the foe, they're laid;
We will carve each name
In the stone of fame.
Their memory shall not fade.

March, brothers, march in sight of home again;
Sing, brothers, sing a loud triumphant strain;
Let our lov'd ones hear
The notes of the new song;
For which they have yearn'd so long;
At each hill and dale,
And each hill and dale,
Resound with the joyful song!

Romanza and Scena

"Voi lo Sapete" (Cavalleria Rusticana)

Signora CUTTICA

PART II.

Cantata

"Festgesang"

LIEDERTAFEL

Let all creation praise the Lord,
Ye nations, bow before Him;
In choral strains with one accord,
Exalt Him and adore Him.
Ye orbs of day that roll in light,
Ye beams of morn from morn to night,
O praise your great Creator!
Angel hosts repeat the song,
Ye prophets clad in glory,
Ye nations, raise your voice prolong.
Repeat the wondrous story;
Ye spirits, who are flames of fire,
Awake and sing, and stirke your lyres,
O praise your great Creator!

Let our theme of praise ascending,
Blest in music's lofty strain,
Soaring through the starry main,
Peal in echoes never ending.
Lovingly did, its light arose;
Thus the sun and moon arise,
Faith and Hope began to banish
Doubt and soul-appealing fear.
Spirits of light, your beams so clear,
Error in their beams will vanish
Mortals roam'd without a guide,
Dread the night and shun the region;
Not a ray could be descried,
All was gloom and desolation,
Till the earth with one accord
Shall adore and praise the Lord.

The Word went forth, the Word was Light;
God spoke, His radiance darted.
Light made chaotic darkness bright,
And night when the light was parted.
In space the starry hosts are sung,
The Universe in music sung
Its great Creator's glory
Still in their courses orbs above,
Hail Him in concert as they move,
His praise in everlasting song
Rings through the vast celestial throng.
Soon may we join the lay,
In His presence, in His praises,
And stand in bright array
To harp and sing our praises.
Where shining Cherubim,
And seraphim blend,
Their hallelujahs blend
In strains that never end.

Signora CUTTICA and Signor CUTTICA

Part Song

"Alpine Night"

LIEDERTAFEL

Night around is gently closing,
As the light of day doth fail
Every sorrow's dispelling:
See the fire in the Alpine vale.
See, the meadows darkly shaded
Bid thee, Wanderer, depart;
Alpine light with thee is hid,
Ah, how beautiful thou art.
Softest winds are idly blowing,
Like elves' music in the trees.
Thou, the silver-clad mountains lowing
Hoodoos amongst the breeze.
Swift the eagle homeward flying,
Stirs the slumbering ev'ning air,
Alpine night, in shadow lying,
Thou art fair, ay, passing fair!

Like grim giants darkly frowning,
Mountains rise, steep and clear.
But the stars in their heights are crowning
And the stars are bright and clear.
And a fitful light is gleaming
On the lake's silvered outset,
Alpine night so full of dreaming,
Thou art passing and fair!

When the pale moon mutely gazes
On the scene so still, so fair,
In the east a bright sight she raises,
Like a pious and reverend pray'r.
From my eyes the tears are flowing,
Rest, oh! rest thou too, my heart!
Alpine night, with beauty glowing,
Ah, how fair thou art!

Quartet

"Un di se ben" (Rigoletto)

Signora CUTTICA, Miss ADA CROSSLEY, Signor CUTTICA, and Signor MELOSSI

Part Song

"Sunrise"

LIEDERTAFEL

The starlight pale is waning,
Ere long will the dawn appear,
The deepest silence is ringing,
From the woods no sound I hear.

What joys and what griefs will be given,
Ere this coming day is done.
Let me raise then my heart to Heaven,
In pray'r from the mountain lone.

Alone on the hilltop I wander,
And watch thro' the chill night air,
In the dark horizon yonder,
The light that will glimmer there.

The sigh of the forest grows stronger;
Morning light suddenly breaks.
The lark's song grows louder and longer,
From night's slumber Earth now awakes.

While here in darkness lonely,
I wait for the coming ray,
One voice I hear, and one only,
'Tis the torrent far away.

LE NOUVEL OPÉRA

Le monument bâti sur les plans de Garnier et inauguré le 5 janvier 1875 passe à juste titre pour un des plus magnifiques palais qui jamais aient été offerts aux arts réunis de la musique, du théâtre et de la danse. Sa masse imposante, mais de proportions harmonieuses, sa façade où les groupes de Carpeaux font vivre et danser la pierre, son escalier de marbre, d'une majesté souveraine, le foyer à l'étage des premières loges, doublé de sa riche loggia, la salle où brillent le pourpre et l'or, la scène qui a 16 mètres en hauteur et largeur d'ouverture, 32 mètres en profondeur d'aspects célèbres et déjà presque légendaires, que tout étranger de passage veut avoir contemplés; on en parle en toutes les langues et leur renom est mondial.

Depuis cette année, un nouvel intérêt s'y ajoute : entièrement remis à neuf, l'Opéra, en son noble édifice, loge un appareillage scénique d'une puissance et d'une perfection sans égales.

=== Page 6 ===

=== Page 7 ===
L'appareil qui distribue sur la scène les lumières diversement colorées et qu'on appelle jeu d'orgues (un souvenir de l'ancien éclairage au gaz et de ses tuyaux juxtaposés) est actuellement le plus grand du monde. Une énergie électrique de 2.400 kw. s'y trouve à volonté répartie sur 300 circuits.

Pour tous les décors de plein air, les toiles de fond, qui s'éclairent mal, font des plis et prennent la poussière, ont été remplacées par un panorama, c'est-à-dire par un demi-cylindre rigide, qui a la forme de l'horizon et procure à s'y méprendre l'illusion du ciel. Construit en tôle d'acier pliée et emboutie, celui-ci pèse 22 tonnes. S'il n'est pas en service, il reste suspendu à trente mètres de hauteur au-dessus de la scène. S'il est en action, on le voit doucement descendre.

La manœuvre est silencieuse et s'accomplit en moins d'une minute.

La surface intérieure de ce cylindre, qui est de 940 mètres carrés, est revêtue d'un enduit d'amiante et de mica, dont le coefficient d'absorption du son est aussi élevé que celui de la toile. Les projecteurs y ré-

cigarettes gros module

RÉGIE FRANÇAISE

=== Page 9 ===
pandent à volonté le calme de l’azur, les rougeurs de l’aurore, les pourpres crépusculaires, comme ils y précipitent la course échevelée des nuées orageuses ou y allument dans une transparence ténébreuse les étoiles nocturnes. Tout peut s’y accomplir.

Si l’on vient à l’Opéra, c’est d’abord, sans aucun doute, pour écouter la musique ; mais il faut que le spectacle l’illustre : telle est la règle du genre ; ni la réforme de Wagner, ni les innovations de la musique moderne ne l’ont abolie. On s’efforce, comme le disait déjà La Bruyère, de « tenir les yeux, l’esprit et les oreilles dans un égal enchantement ». A l’Opéra, les plus récents progrès de la science, employés avec une ampleur et une ingéniosité sans précédent, concourent mieux que jamais à cet effort magique.

La salle et ses annexes, c’est-à-dire la partie du monument accessible au public, ont été également remises en état. On a ravivé l’éclat des fonds éteints, la chaleur des ors, révélant à nouveau le magnifique plafond de Lenepveu dans la salle, les fresques de Baudry dans le grand foyer.

=== Page 10 ===
Ph. Lipnitzki

M. Serge LIFAR
Maître de Ballet

=== Page 11 ===
Les travaux, commencés en juillet dernier, ont duré un peu plus de six mois et exigé le concours de 22 entreprises différentes, employant 700 ouvriers. Les peintures ont couvert une surface de 200.000 mètres carrés et les dorures ont consommé 4 kilos d’or. On a posé plus de 500 kilomètres de câbles et fils électriques, 44 kilomètres de filins métalliques pour les manœuvres, 500 tonnes de charpente métallique et 34 kilomètres de dallage en tôle ondulée pour remplacer sur la scène l’ancien équipement en bois, entièrement enlevé, et dont le volume était de 12.000 stères. On ne sera pas surpris de l’énormité de ces chiffres si l’on songe que dans l’espace occupé derrière le rideau pour la scène de l’Opéra et ses coulisses, depuis le plancher jusqu’au faîte, tiendrait tout l’édifice de la Comédie-Française.

La dépense totale a atteint 24 millions. Elle n’a rien d’exagéré si l’on songe que pour construire un monument pareil à l’Opéra, il faudrait, d’après les évaluations les plus modérées, au moins 400 millions de francs.

LA CHARTREUSE DE PARME

ACTE PREMIER

SUR LA ROUTE DE COME A MILAN, EN 1815

DES gendarmes viennent d’arrêter une calèche où se trouvent Fabrice del Dongo et sa tante, la jeune comtesse Gina. Fabrice, grand admirateur de Napoléon s’est compromis en allant prendre part comme volontaire, à la bataille de Waterloo ; il est en fuite pour Milan. Il se croit arrêté par ordre du gouvernement autrichien. L’arrivée de deux autres prisonniers dévoile un quiproquo. On recherchait le général Conti, grand chambellan du Prince de Parme et sa fille Clelia qui avaient quitté Côme sans passeports. À la vue de Clelia, Fabrice s’éprend pour elle d’un grand amour. Les explications du général avec les gendarmes sont orageuses et menacent de tourner mal. Gina alors offre du vin à la troupe. Tout s’arrange. La calèche peut repartir avec les quatre voyageurs.

UNE LOGE, A LA SCALA DE MILAN

Quelques jours plus tard. Avec des libéraux milanais, Gina recherche les moyens

de soustraire Fabrice aux poursuites de la police. Il doit partir à minuit pour le Piémont. Survient le Comte Mosca, premier ministre du Prince de Parme. Il aime Gina et veut l'entraîner à la Cour où, tout puissant, il peut faire d'elle une Duchesse et sauver Fabrice. Celui-ci qui vient faire ses adieux à sa tante, apprend qu'il ira à Naples étudier la théologie pour devenir peut-être un jour une Eminence... Dans la loge, il retrouve Clelia. Le spectacle interrompt les conversations...

LE TRATTORIA DE THEODOLINDE

Gina a suivi les conseils de Mosca : elle est venue à Parme et a épousé le vieux Duc Sanseverina qui l'a rapidement laissée veuve et fort riche. Elle mène une vie fastueuse et fort enviée. Auprès d'elle veille amoureusement le Comte Mosca, mais elle ne cesse de penser tendrement à Fabrice qu'elle protège de loin. Nous la retrouverons plus tard.

Fabrice, de son côté, est allé à Naples étudier la théologie. Il a déjà reçu le titre de Monsignore qui ne l'empêche pas toutefois de continuer sa vie aventureuse. Le voici, quelques années plus tard, dans une pauvre auberge campagnarde sur le bord du Pô, à la frontière des États autrichiens où il est venu se réfugier. Il a tué le protecteur d'une petite danseuse à laquelle il

=== Page 16 ===
Studio Harcourt

M. Raoul JOBIN
rôle de Fabrice
dans "La Chartreuse de Parme"

=== Page 17 ===
faisait la cour et qui lui cherchait querelle. Il risque maintenant d’être emprisonné pour meurtre. Sa bonne étoile l’a conduit ici, chez Théodolinde dont l’amant est l’ancien cocher de sa tante. L’aventure de la première fuite de Fabrice est évoquée. Il songe à la petite Clélia... Les gendarmes le recherchent de nouveau. Il faut se hâter. On le déguisera en paysan et il pourra, la nuit venue, gagner l’autre rive et s’échapper. Avant de s’enfuir il écrit à Gina pour lui annoncer son prochain retour. À Parme, il la retrouvera et peut-être aussi reverra-t-il Clélia qu’il n’a point oubliée, qu’il aime.

ACTE II

LA COUR DE LA PRISON DE PARME

La nuit. Ronde de sentinelles, inspection du Général Conti, gouverneur de la citadelle. On attend un prisonnier d’importance : c’est Fabrice, qui est amené, menottes aux mains. Les adversaires politiques de Mosca (dont est Conti) triomphent. Voici le protégé de la Duchesse en leur pouvoir. Il se débat et, débarrassé de ses menottes, gifle le terrible Barbone, gardien-chef de la prison. On l’enchaîne de nouveau : il sera enfermé dans le plus haut des cachots, la cellule de l’Obéissance Passive.

Alors que les gardes l’entraînent, Clélia survient en robe de bal. Fabrice ébloui, la

LA PLATE-FORME DE LA CITADELLE

On voit la tour où Fabrice est enfermé, le balcon et la terrasse de Clelia. Elle soigne ses oiseaux. Son père survient et la menace de l'envoyer au couvent si elle persiste à refuser les maris qu'il lui propose. En entendant que la vie du prisonnier est menacée, elle accepte de recevoir les hommages du dernier prétendant : le Marquis Crescenzi. Le général la laisse seule. La nuit tombe. Fabrice est parvenu à retirer les panneaux qui masquent la lucarne de sa cellule. Clelia est terrifiée par son audace. Il lui parle d'amour. Elle le supplie de ne songer qu'à s'enfuir : sa vie est en danger. Il refuse et lui demande un rendez-vous.

LA CELLULE DE L'OBEISSANCE PASSIVE

Fabrice est désespéré. Clelia ne vient plus à son balcon. On entend une sérénade. Le geolier qui apporte son repas lui annonce le prochain mariage de Clelia. Mais soudain Clelia, affolée, fait irruption dans la cellule, jette à terre le repas qui était empoisonné et supplie Fabrice de fuir. Tout est préparé pour

cela : les gardes sont ivres, la Duchesse est en bas avec des hommes et voici une corde pour la terrible descente. Fabrice se débat : il veut rester près de celle qu'il aime. Clélia le menace de s'enfuir pour toujours au couvent. Il accepte l'évasion. ACTE III

L'ATELIER DE FABRICE, A LOCARNO

Sur le lac Majeur où il est venu retrouver Gina après son évasion. En vain sa tante l'entoure-t-elle de tendres soins. Il ne songe qu'à son cachot et à sa chère Clélia dont il est sans nouvelles. Mosca va lui en apporter. Le prince de Parme est mort. Une insurrection a été soulevée à l'avènement du nouveau prince que Mosca a pu maîtriser. Sa puissance est maintenant extrême. Fabrice et Gina vont pouvoir rentrer à Parme. Mais Clélia est sur le point de se marier. Fabrice s'enfuit pour arriver à temps. Gina se laisse aller à la mélancolie. Mosca lui offre son amour de nouveau. Peut-être enfin l'acceptera-t-elle ?

LE JARDIN DE CLELIA, LA NUIT

Elle a accepté d’entendre Fabrice une dernière fois. En vain celui-ci tente-t-il de l’arracher à son voeu. Sous son voile, pour que « ses yeux ne le voient plus », Clelia demande à Fabrice la permission d’épouser le Marquis : ils ne trouveront le bonheur éternel que par un acte de renoncement...

LE SERMON AUX LUMIERES

Dans la petite Eglise de la Visitation, à Parme, Fabrice, par son austérité, sa modestie, sa piété, son talent de prédicateur, soulève l’enthousiasme des fidèles qui sont venus en foule l’entendre ce soir. La fatigue interrompt son sermon. Pendant la pause, Clelia, maintenant Marquise Crescenzi, vient écouter celui qu’elle continue de chérir. Fabrice est remonté en chaire. Il la voit. Il va décider de se retirer pour toujours à La Chartreuse de Parme. S’approchant de Clelia, il lui dit un dernier adieu.

Armand LUNEL et Henri SAUGUET.

un succès sans précédent!

1.
Symphony No. 1 in C Major ... ... ... ... Beethoven (1770-1827)
    Adagio molto—Allegro con brio.
    Andante cantabile con molto.
    Minuetto e Trio.
    Adagio—Allegro molto e vivace.

It was in the spring of 1795, when Beethoven was studying counterpoint with Albrechtsberger, that he first planned to write a symphony. From the occurrence of sketches among fugal exercises Grove suggests that in the first place it may have been a relief from dry technical work. Originally it was to be in C minor, but presently that key was abandoned in favour of C major. It is not definitely known when it was completed, but probably not long before the first performance, which took place on April 2nd, 1800, at the Burg Theatre. It was Beethoven's first benefit concert, and, in addition to works by Haydn and Mozart, the programme included the Septet and one of the two first Piano Concertos—it is not certain which. The composer also improvised on the theme of Haydn's Emperor's Hymn. Beethoven was thirty at the time. At that age Mozart had written all but the last three of his symphonies, and Schubert seven works in this form, but Brahms was forty-four before he wrote his first symphony.

=== Page 7 ===
It was Beethoven's first work for the orchestra alone. His only previous orchestral writing consisted of one movement of a discarded violin concerto, and the two first Pianoforte Concertos. The work is scored for the usual orchestra, as employed by Mozart. It is dedicated to Baron von Swieten, who had befriended the composer on his first arrival in Vienna. Because of its close affinity with the works of Mozart and Haydn it has been called "the instrumental swan-song of the eighteenth century," but in spite of that the circumstance that it opens out of the key, and with a discord, gravely incensed several critics of the time, notably the Abbé Stadler.

That discord opens a brief introduction, an Adagio lasting twelve bars. The first subject of the Allegro is characteristic of Beethoven's fondness for emphasising the key. The second subject present itself as a dialogue for flute and oboe over a figure in crotchets which can be regarded as derived from the first. This leads to a brief episode in which the oboe—followed by bassoon—has a counter-subject while the basses quietly continue figures derived from the second subject. Nine bars of coda complete the exposition. The working-out is simple and constructed of alternating fragments from the two subjects, with rather more use of imitation than Beethoven employed in later years. The recapitulation differs in orchestration from the opening, but is otherwise normal. The coda is based upon that which concluded the exposition, but here it is combined with the first subject. About half of the coda is devoted to emphasising the key.

The Andante is built round a lyrical theme and its continuation, with a brief middle section derived from them. A remarkable feature is the use of the drums, which foreshadows much that Beethoven was to write later, notably the well-known passage in the Fifth Symphony. This charming movement, with its Mozartian elegance, is universally liked, but some of Beethoven's contemporaries were inclined to belittle it.

The Minuet has all the character of a true Beethoven Scherzo, from its brisk animation to the suggestion of deeper intent underlying the dance-rhythm. In the second portion of the Minuet there is also a bold modulatory passage, equally characteristic. The Trio consists of a kind of antiphon between wind-chords and string-scales.

The Finale, which is preceded by six bars of Adagio, has the merriment of Haydn together with a touch of the more refined playfulness of Mozart, especially that which occasionally shows itself in rapid conversation among several instruments. Its humour is unlike that which was later to be characteristic of Beethoven. It is not a Rondo, as one might have expected after the preceding movements, but in the form of a sonata-allegro, with the usual two subjects—both of great simplicity, and a short development section followed by recapitulation and coda.

2.
Concerto in D major for Flute and Orchestra (K314) ... Mozart
RENÉ LE ROY (1756-1791)

Allegro.
Allegro ma non troppo.
Rondo: Allegro.

During the time which Mozart spent at Mannheim, from October 30th, 1777, to March 14th, 1778, he naturally became friendly with the soloists of what was then considered to be probably the finest orchestra in Europe. One of them was the celebrated flautist, Johann Baptist Wendling (1730-1797), one of the four players for whom he was to compose, during their subsequent visit to Paris, the Sinfonia Concertante for flute, oboe, horn and bassoon. When Mozart failed to find employment with the Elector and it looked as if he might have to curtail his stay in Mannheim, he told Wendling who, according to Jahn, grew red in the face and said "we must find some way of keeping you here, at all events for the two months before we go to Paris together." When Mozart dined with him next day they discussed ways and means. One contributor to these was a Dutchman, De Jean or Dechamps, of independent means, who played the flute and may have been a pupil of Wendling. He offered to pay 200 florins for three concertos and two quartets for the flute. He was nicknamed the Nabob, and in one of his letters Mozart refers to him as that true philanthropist, the Indian Dutchman. But Mozart procrastinated. When his father remonstrated with him by letter he replied, that "one is not always in the humor for writing. I could certainly scribble away the whole day; but when a thing is to go forth bearing my name, I am determined that I will not be ashamed of it." In the end the commission was only partly executed and he received only 96 florins in payment. Of the music that originated thus have survived two concertos and a separate Andante (K313-3) and two quartets for flute and strings (K285 and 928), one of which had to be sent from Paris after his departure.

The concerto opens with the usual tutti in which both the principal subjects are introduced in the main key. At its first entrance the flute comments on the principal theme and continues it with a passage modulating to the dominant for the second subject. The continuation of the first subject supplies most of the material of the working-outs section, which is brief. Recapitulation ensues. The whole movement is transparently clear, and, as Jahn says, lively and cheerful.

The orchestra gives out the first phrase of the slow movement, in G major. The solo flute repeats it and adds an after-phrase modulating temporarily to the dominant, but the digression is not extended, and on repetition the same passage serves to prepare the conclusion.

=== Page 10 ===
The principal theme of the Rondo is a very evident anticipation of Blonde's aria Welche Wonne, welche Lust in the Seraglio, which was composed four years later. It is begun on the solo instrument but soon taken over by the orchestra. The episodes consist chiefly of bravura passages for the flute, which is given little rest in this sprightly movement.

3.
Suite, "Pelléas and Mélisande" ... ... ... Sibelius 1865
(i) At the Castle-gate.
(ii) Mélisande.
(iii) A Spring in the Park.
(iv) The Three Blind Sisters.
(v) Pastorale.
(vi) Mélisande at the Spinning Wheel.
(vii) Entr'acte.
(viii) The Death of Mélisande.

Maeterlinck's play "Pelléas et Mélisande" is remarkable amongst other things for having inspired several famous composers. Even more remarkable is the astonishing diversity of utterance to which they have been inspired. It would be difficult, indeed, to find works more dissimilar than the vague atmospheric music of Debussy's opera, the delicate, clear-cut, neatly-chiselled incidental music of Fauré, and the gigantic and portentous symphonic poem of Schönberg.

Sibelius's music is again very different from all these, though nearer to Fauré's work, in spirit, than that of any of the others. Curiously enough, this music written to a play by a Flemish dramatist is more definitely Finnish in feeling than much that Sibelius has composed to national subjects. It can have been no mere caprice extraneous form of inducement that led him to incorporate the greater part of it, transcribed for the piano, in the volume of selected piano pieces entitled "Sibeliana"; Scenes from the land of a Thousand Lakes," in which, for example, the piece originally called "Mélisande" becomes "Evening by the Woodland Lake," and "The Death of Mélisande" becomes "The Sun Sinks." The latter titles, indeed, strike one as being even more in keeping with the character of the music from the original ones. However that may be, these little pieces rank amongst Sibelius's finest works in in miniature forms. They are scored for a small orchestra consisting of flute, oboe, cor anglais, two clarinets, two bassoons, two horns, strings and percussion. The work was written in 1905.

The first number, "At the Castle-gate," is the prelude to the first scene of the first act of the drama—broad, sonorous, majestic, tragedy-laden, preoccupied throughout its brief course with one single theme.

=== Page 11 ===
"Mélisande" is played as the prelude to the second scene of the first act—a charming little piece, wonderfully evocative of the character in the play. It begins with the cor anglais solo to an accompaniment of muted violins and violas only. The 'cellos echo and vary it, the cor anglais solo to an accompaniment of muted violin and violas only. The 'cellos echo and vary it, the cor anglais takes it up again, but soon makes way for a new line of thought: a wistful little melody for strings replied to by another slightly gayer one for the wood-wind with a pizzicato accompaniment for the strings. This slender but engaging material is repeated and varied.

A gently, easy-flowing melody for strings to an accompaniment of wood-wind and held notes for the horns constitutes the chief thematic substance of number 3, "A Spring in the Park" (which is the prelude to the second act), for the first part of its course. This is succeeded by a short passage of delicate impressionism, then a sudden and unexpected crescendo culminating in a sonorous climax, after which the music dies away with fragmentary allusions to the initial thought.

"The Three Blind Sisters," a transcription of the song in Act III, Scene 2, consists of a short cor anglais solo, first over a roll for kettle-drums, then entirely unaccompanied, followed by a passage for clarinets supported by horns, then by strings pizzicato, then by horns and drums.

The "Pastorale" is the instrument interlude which follows the words "Quelle belle journée" in Act III, Scene 4. Its character is sufficiently indicated by its title, with wood-wind playing the principle role to an accompaniment of strings and horns. This is one of the simplest and most attractive pieces in the suite.

"Mélisande at the Spinning-wheel," which plays as the prelude to the third act, is, on the other hand, one of the most subtle and elaborate numbers, though none the less attractive. It is ingeniously constructed on an unending whirring figure for violas, descriptive of the spinning wheel, which plays unaltered from first bar to last, against which is projected expressive melodic fragments chiefly confided to the wood-wind. A climax is achieved, whereafter the music gradually subsides and dies away.

The "Entr'acte" is played between third and fourth acts. Its character is rather that of a distraction or diversion from the dramatic situation, unlike that of most of the foregoing numbers. It is a brisk, exhilarating and virile piece, employing the full resources of the modest orchestra for which it is scored.

Finally, in striking contrast to the foregoing number, both in character and in its relevance to the drama, is the deeply moving little piece descriptive of "The Death of Mélisande," which is the introduction to Act V, Scene 2. It begins with a passage for muted strings alone. After the wood-wind has intervened momentarily the strings resume their lament and the whole orchestra then participate in a passionate outburst of grief. The piece ends as it began, with muted strings alone.

Note by Cecil Gray for the Sibelius Festival.

4.

Concerto in C for Flute ... ... ... ... Grétry
RENÉ LE ROY 1741-1813

Allegro
Larghetto
Allegro

Grétry and César Franck are the two musical glories of the City of Liége, but they have little in common. Grétry was above all else a composer of popular and melodious operas of which he wrote forty-seven, first for the Opéra Comique and later for the opéra, and of these more than half was successful. His most famous productions are "Le Tableau parlant" (1769), "Zémire et Azore" (1771), "Céphale et Procris" (1773), and "Richard Coeur de Lion" (1784). His other vocal works include an early Mass and some cantatas written for national occasions under the Revolution. His instrumental works are comparatively few in number. They include an early set of six symphonies; two quartets for harpsichord, flute, violin and bass; and some trios and sonatas. From early days he appears to have given attention to the flute. He spent eight years in Rome—1759-1767, and it was a flute concerto—this or another—which provided the occasion and the means for his long desired migration to Paris. There was at that time an English peer who played the flute and was prepared to pay liberally for compositions for that instrument. Grétry's concerto came under his notice and pleased him so well that the outcome was the composer's journey, first to Geneva and then to Paris where he made his name and fortune.

5.

Menuet des Follets ...
Danse des Sylphes ...
Marche Hongroise ...

From "The Damnation of Faust") Berlioz 1803-1869

Danse des Follets.
Danse des Sylphes.
Marche Hongroise.

In 1828 Berlioz came under the spell of Goethe's Faust in Gérard de Nerval's French translation. He records in his Memoirs: "This wonderful book fascinated me straight away; I never left it; I read it constantly at table, at the theatre, in the streets, everywhere. This prose version contained some versified fragments, songs, hymns, etc. I yielded to the temptation to set them to music; and this difficult task was hardly finished before I had the idiocy—without having heard a note of my score—to get it printed at my expense." The passage is given as quoted in W. J. Turner's recent biography. Thus originated the Eight Scenes

MASTER MUSICIANS WHO RECORD FOR COLUMBIA RECORDS

Orchestral and Banj

from Faust which were, however, subsequently withdrawn from circulation, but the composer was far from abandoning the subject. It was frequently in his mind and when, seventeen years later, he was travelling in Central Europe, he reverted, to it, incorporating most of the eight original scenes in a much larger work, the dramatic legend or concert opera known as The Damnation of Faust. In the Memoirs he writes: "While trailing round Germany in my old postchaise, I composed my Damnation of Faust. Each movement is punctuated by memories of the place where it was written. For instance the Peasants' Dance was jotted down by the light of a shop gas-jet one night when I had lost myself in Pesth, and I got up in the middle of the night at Prague to write the song of the angelic choir." Portions were composed at Vienna and on the Danube steamers. He returned to Paris in April, 1846, and arranged to have this work performed. It was given at the Opéra Comique, December 6th, 1846, and repeated on December 20th, both performances being poorly attended.

In the complete work the three excerpts played to-day have their place in reversed order. The Dance of the Will-o'-the-Wisps takes place in the third of its four parts, or acts. The scene is before Marguerite's house, where Mephistopheles calls upon the spirits of caprice to enchant and subdue her soul. It is fantastically scored, and based on two themes, to which is added in the coda a reference to Mephistopheles' Serenade.

Dance of the Sylphs occurs in the lovely scene on the banks of the Elbe. Faust, rejuvenated, has fallen asleep and Mephistopheles, sending him dreams of Marguerite, summons the sylphs to hover over him with promises of bliss to come. It is scored with the most fascinating delicacy.

The story of the Hungarian March is more involved. In the course of the above-mentioned tour in Central Europe Berlioz arrived at Vienna on November 3rd, 1845, and found many friends there, one of whom—possibly Liszt—lent him a collection of Hungarian national airs. Among them was that of the Rakoczy March, which has a curious history. The original tune was somewhat rudimentary, but in 1809, on the eve of the war which was to bring Napoleon's army to Vienna, John Bihari (1769-1827), a well-known Hungarian violinist-composer of those days, based a march upon it which he played on his violin to Nicholas Scholl, the bandmaster of the "Prince Esterhazy" Regiment. The latter saw its possibilities and orchestrated it. When the regiment marched to Raab to join the main body of the army it was played by the regimental band, and became so popular that Scholl promptly had it published as his own composition. Not only did it retain its popularity, but it became intimately associated with Hungarian aspirations towards national independence. This is the tune that attracted Berlioz so much that during his stay in Vienna, he wrote—according to his Memoirs, in one night—his well-known orchestral version of it.

=== Page 17 ===
At that time, in the restless "forties," the atmosphere in Hungary was heavily charged with political electricity. A storm was brewing which was to burst out later. In the circumstances it is not surprising to read in the composer's Memoirs that the first performance of this march in Budapest made a volcanic impression on an audience of patriots. The crescendo which leads to the recapitulation was accompanied by an even more striking crescendo of popular feeling, and the march had to be repeated. The occasion became, in fact, a patriotic demonstration such as few musicians have evoked since Rouget de Lisle wrote the "Marseillaise." The Hungarians asked Berlioz to dedicate the March to them, and he sent them a copy from Breslau, the next stage of his concert tour.

This is the march which Berlioz incorporated in the first part of the Damnation. The scene is a plain in Hungary, over which Hungarian troops are marching. As the composer explains in his Memoirs: "The extraordinary effect it produced at Budapest induced me to introduce it in 'Faust' by taking the liberty of placing my hero in Hungary at the beginning of the action." But Goethe's countrymen did not readily condone that "liberty"!

=== Page 2 ===
Song Cycle—"The Princess."

1. As Thro' the Land.

As thro' the land at eve we went,
    And pluck'd the ripen'd ears,
We fell out—my wife and I—
    O we fell out, I know not why,
        And kiss'd again with tears.
And blessings on the falling out,
    That all the more endears,
When we fall out with those we love.
        And kiss again with tears.
For when we come where lies the child
    We lost in other years,
O there above the little grave
    We kiss'd again with tears.

2. Sweet and Low.

Sweet and low, sweet and low,
    Wind of the western sea,
Low, low, breathe and blow,
    Wind of the western sea.
Over the rolling waters go,
Come from the dying moon and blow,
Blow him again to me.
While my little one, while my pretty one sleeps.
Sleep and rest, sleep and rest.
    Father will come to thee soon;
Rest, rest, on mother's breast,
    Father will come to thee soon.
Father will come to his babe in the nest,
Silver sails all out of the west;
Under the silver moon
Sleep my little one, sleep my pretty one, sleep.

3. The Splendour Falls.

The splendour falls on castle walls,
    And snowy summits old in story,
The long light shakes across the lakes,
    And the wild cataract leaps in glory.
Blow, bugle, blow, set the wild echoes flying,
Blow, bugle, answer, echoes dying.
O hark, O hear! How thin, how clear,
    And thinner, clearer, further going!
O sweet and far from cliff and scar,
    The horns of Elfland faintly blowing!
Blow, let us hear the purple glens replying,
Blow, bugle, answer, echoes dying.
O love, they die in yon rich sky,
    They faint on hill or field or river.
Our echoes roll from soul to soul,
    And grow for ever and for ever.
Blow, bugle, blow, set the wild echoes flying,
And answer, echoes dying, dying.

=== Page 3 ===
Song Cycle—"The Princess."

4. Tears, Idle Tears.

Tears, idle tears; I know not what they mean;
Tears from the depth of some divine despair,
Rise in the heart, and gather to the eyes,
In looking on the happy autumn fields,
And thinking of the days that are no more.

Fresh as the first beam, glitt'ring on the sail,
That brings our friends up from the under world,
Sad as the last which reddens over one
That sinks with all we love below the verge,
So sad, so fresh the days that are no more.

Ah! Sad and strange, as in dark summer dawns,
The earliest pipe of half-awaken'd birds to dying ears,
When unto dying eyes the casement slowly grows a glimm'ring square;
So sad, so strange the days that are no more.

Dear as remember'd kisses after death,
And sweet as those by hopeless fancy feign'd on lips of others:
Deep as love, deep as first love, and wild with all regret;
O Death in Life. The days that are no more.

5. O Swallow, Swallow.

O swallow, swallow, flying, flying south,
Fly to her, and fall upon her gilded eaves,
And tell her what I tell to thee.
O tell her, swallow, that thou knowest each,
That bright, and fierce, and fickle is the south,
And dark, and true, and tender is the north.

O swallow, swallow, if I could follow
And light upon her lattice,
I would pipe and trill, and cheep and twitter
Twenty million loves.

O were I thou that she might take me in,
And lay me on her bosom,
And her heart would rock the snowy cradle till I died.

Why ling'reth she to clothe her heart with love,
Delaying as the tender ash delays to clothe herself,
When all the woods are green.

O tell her, swallow, that thy brood is flown,
Say to her I do not wanton in the south,
But in the north long since my nest is made.
O tell her brief is life, but love is long,
And brief the sun of summer in the north,
And brief the moon of beauty in the south,
Fly to her, and pipe and woo her, and make her mine
And tell her that I follow thee.

=== Page 4 ===
Song Cycle—"The Princess."

6. Thy Voice is Heard.
Thy voice is heard thro' rolling drums
That beat to battle where he stands,
Thy face before his fancy comes
And gives the battle to his hands.
A moment, when the trumpets blow,
He sees his brood upon his knee.
The next, like fire, meets the foe.
And strike him dead for thine and thee.

7. Home they brought her Warrior dead.
Home they brought her warrior dead,
She nor swoon'd nor utter'd cry,
All her maidens, watching, said
"She must weep or she will die."
Then they praised him soft and low,
Called him worthy to be loved;
Truest friend and noblest foe.
Yet she neither spake nor moved.
Stole a maiden from her place,
Lightly to the warrior slept.
Took the facecloth from the face,
Yet she neither moved nor wept.
Rose a nurse of ninety years,
Set his child upon her knee.
Like summer tempest came her tears—
"Sweet, my child, I live for thee."

8. Our Enemies have Fallen.
Our enemies have fall'n!
The seed—the little seed they laughed at in the dark,
Has ris'n and cleft the soil and grown a spanless girth
That lays on every side a thousand arms,
And rushes on the sun.
Our enemies have fall'n!
They came—the leaves were wet with women's tears.
They heard a noise of songs they would not understand;
They marked it with the red cross to the fall,
And would have strown it, but are fall'n themselves.
Our enemies have fall'n!
They came—the woodman with their axes. Lo, the tree!
But we will make it faggots for the hearth,
And shape it plank and beam for roof and floor,
And boats and bridges for the use of men.
Our enemies have fall'n!
They struck—with their own blows they hurt themselves,
Nor knew there dwelt an iron nature in the grain.
The glitt'ring axe was broken in their arms—
Their arms were shatter'd to the shoulder blade.
Our enemies have fall'n!
But this shall grow a night of summer from the heat,
A breath of autumn, dropping fruits of pow'r.
And rolled with music in the growing breeze of time,
The tops shall strike from star to star,
The fangs shall move the stony bases of the world.

=== Page 5 ===
THE ROYAL VICTORIAN LIEDERTAFEL

"Christmas time! That man must be a misanthrope indeed in whose breast something like a jovial feeling is not aroused—in whose mind some pleasant associations are not awakened—by the recurrence of Christmas."—Charles Dickens.

Programme

Acting President: H. M. LEE
Conductor: J. SUTTON CROW    Pianist: LINDSAY BIGGINS

"God Save the King"

Part Song --
Ring Out, Wild Bells    P. E. Fletcher
Presented to the Society by Mr. Charles Miller.

THE ROYAL VICTORIAN LIEDERTAFEL
and
A.B.C. MILITARY BAND

Ring out, wild bells, to the wild sky,
The flying cloud, the frosty light;
The year is dying in the night.
Ring out, wild bells, and let him die.

Ring out the old, ring in the new.
Ring, happy bells, across the snow;
The year is going, let him go.
Ring out the false, ring in the true
Ring out the old, ring in the new.

Ring out the grief that saps the mind,
For those that here we see no more;
Ring out the feud of rich and poor,
Ring in redress to all mankind.

Ring out a slowly dying cause,
And ancient forms of party strife,
Ring in the nobler modes of life.
With sweeter manners, purer laws.

Ring out the old, ring in the new;
Ring, happy bells, across the snow.

The year is going, let him go.
Ring out the false, ring in the true,
Ring out the old, ring in the new.

Ring out false pride in place and blood,
The civic slander and the spite:
Ring in the love of truth and right,
Ring in the common love of good.

Ring out old shapes of foul disease,
Ring out the narrowing lust of gold:
Ring out the thousand wars of old,
Ring in the thousand years of peace;

Ring in the valiant man and free,
The larger heart, the kindlier hand;
Ring out the darkness of the land,
Ring in the Christ that is to be!

Ring out the old, ring in the new,
The year is going, let him go:
Ring out the false, ring in the true,
Ring out the old, ring in the new.

Band Selection --
Euryanthe    Weber
A.B.C. MILITARY BAND
(Conductor, Mr. Harry Shugg)

Carols—
(a) Sleep, Holy Babe
(b) The Manger Throne

THE ROYAL VICTORIAN LIEDERTAFEL
CHOIR OF BOYS and A.B.C. BAND

(a) Sleep, holy Babe, upon Thy Mother's breast.
Great Lord of earth and sea and sky,
How sweet it is to see Thee lie
In such a place of rest.

Sleep, holy Babe; Thine Angels watch around,
All bending low, with folded wings,
Before the incarnate King of Kings,
In reverent awe profound.

Sleep, holy Babe, ah! take Thy brief repose;
Too quickly will Thy slumbers break.
And Thou to lengthened pains awake,
That Death alone shall close.

(b) Like silver lamps in a distant shrine
The stars are sparkling bright;
The bells of the city of God ring out,
For the Son of Mary was born tonight;
The gloom is past, and the morn at last
Is coming with Orient light.

Never fell melodies half so sweet
As those which are filling the skies:
And never a palace shone half so fair
As the manger bed where our Saviour lies;
No night in the year is half so dear
As this which has ended our sighs.

Now a new power has come on earth,
A match for the armies of Hell:
A Child is born who shall conquer the foe,
And all the spirit of wickedness quell;
For Mary's Son is the Mighty One
Whom the prophets of God foretell.

The stars of heaven still shine as at first
They gleamed on this wonderful night:
The bells of the city of God peal out,
And the Angels' song still rings on the height:
And love still turns where the Godhead burns,
Hid in flesh from fleshly sight.

Faith sees no longer the stable floor,
The pavement of sapphire is there:
The clear light of Heaven streams out to the world.
The Angels of God are crowding the air:
And Heaven and earth, through the spotless birth,
Are at peace on this night so fair.
