Thou aid to victory to those laden with ignominy.
To be near to thee and to sit at thy feet.
That cures all harm and injury.
I suffer hard and well-earned punishment.
I am afraid of my eternal sleep.
Do stay with me and lead me through the sea to the haven.

No. 2.
Ah! the eyes of the holy boy appeared so beautiful and clear to me.
And something shines out of them that wins all my heart.
He looks with his sweet eyes to my eyes;
If he would see his face therein he would greet me kindly:
So I surrender myself perfectly to him only to serve his eyes,
For something shines out of them that wins all my heart.

No. 3.
You that float around these palms in night and wind,
You holy angels, calm the tops of the trees.
There slumbers my child;
You palms of Bethlehem in the storm,
How can you blow so furiously to-day?
Do calm the storm.
Be silent and bow softly and gently;
There slumbers my child.
The heaven's child suffers pains;
Ah, how tired he was from grief of earth!
Ah, in his sleep softly passes his torment.
Do calm the storm.
There slumbers my child.
Grim cold strikes down:
With what shall I cover my child's limbs?
Ah, you angels, flying winged through the night.
Do calm the storm;
There slumbers my child.

THE ROYAL VICTORIAN LIEDERTAFEL

(a) It seemed as tho' high heaven
    Had stooped to kiss the earth.
    Awaking countless blossoms
    To new life-giving birth.

    The breeze was gently blowing,
    The rye swayed to and fro.
    The stars were mildly glowing,
    The forests murmured low.

    And my rapt soul its pinions
    Did eagerly outspread.
    As though from earth's dominions
    To higher homes it fled.
        ---Ben Jonson.

(b) Sleep, rest, my love, rest,
    Dieth the moan of the wind in the tree,
    Foldeth her pinions the bird in her nest,
        Sinks the sun to his bed in the sea.
    Sleep, lull'd on my breast
        Tossing and troubled and thinking of me.
    Peace, falleth the night,
        Veiling in shadows her glory for thee.
    Eyes may be darken'd while visions are bright.
        Senses be fetter'd, though fancy is free.
    Peace, peace, slumbering light,
        Longing, and loving and dreaming of me.

=== Page 10 ===
THE ROYAL VICTORIAN LIEDERTAFEL

(c)
I know not why my gladness
Hath passed so soon away.
My soul is filled to sadness
With lil' of olden lay.
The air is dewy and darkling,
And calmly floweth the Rhine.
The crest of the hills is sparkling
In light of even shine.

There sitteth a maid in the gloaming,
A maid divinely fair.
'Mid gleam of her gems is combing
Her curls of golden hair.

From golden comb she is raining
Her tresses, and sings from on high
A passionate, soul enchanting,
Entrancing melody.

The sailor with wild pangs thrilling
Is chained by magic tone,
While breakers his skiff is filling.
He gazes on her alone.
He, with the surge descending,
Is swept along with his boat.
And such is e'er the ending
Of Lorelei's witching note.

Christmas Appeal
The festive season again approaches, and a happy sense of holiday rest and enjoyment fills our hearts, suggesting kindly thoughts and generous acts.

This evening members and their friends will be afforded an opportunity of contributing to the funds of the

Victorian Homes for Aged and Infirm,
Royal Park

"Life is short, and we have never too much time for gladdening the hearts of those who are travelling the dark journey with us. Oh! be swift to love, make haste to be kind."—Amiel.

Dr. Campbell Tobacco Fund
A box will be found at the main entrance for receiving contributions of Tobacco, Cigars, Pipes, etc.

"I began, by idle accident, to associate the Christmas time of year with human interest, and with some inquiry into, and some care for, the lives of those by whom I found myself surrounded. ... A good time: a kind, forgiving, charitable time: the only time I knew of, in the long calendar of the year, when men and women seem by one consent to open their shut-up hearts freely.... And, therefore, tho' it has never put a scrap of gold or silver in my pocket. I believe it HAS done me good, and WILL do me good, and I say, 'God bless it.'"—Chas. Dickens.

H. M. LEE, Acting President.
E. N. HOCKING, Hon. Secretary.

THE ROYAL VICTORIAN LIEDERTAFEL
CHOIR OF BOYS and BAND

List! afar! what Angel voices
Fall upon the winter night!
Earth amid the sound rejoices:
Broods of evil speed their flight.
List, for aye sweet words of gladness
Through the generations roll.
Calming every mourner's sadness,
"Christ is born to save thy soul."
Child Divine, what pow'rs are round Thee.
Health to man Thy presence brings:
Age by age have myriads found Thee
Lord of Lords and King of Kings!

Born to heal what sin hath broken,
Born, its captives to release.
Born, by prophet lips forespoken,
Mighty God and Prince of Peace.
When the passions rage in blindness,
Thou their stormy waves canst still.

Turning by Thy spell of kindness
Hate and malice to goodwill.
Child Divine, who'eer hath known Thee
Hails the joy thy presence brings.
Thine through life in death we own Thee.
Lord of Lords and King of Kings!

Sing, ye hosts, triumphant thronging,
Round the Lamb enthroned in light.
Sing, O man, the hymn prolonging,
Through thy toils of hourly fight.
Sing what grace, what nameless glory
Stoop'd to rescue sons of earth.
Grateful, spread the wondrous story.
Hail the Incarnate Saviour's birth.
Child Divine, all hearts that know Thee
Know the strength Thy presence brings.
Know what debt of love we owe Thee,
Lord of Lords and King of Kings!

Lieder—

(a) Winterweihe

(b) Hymne an die nacht

(c) Wie Sollten wir geheim sie halten

Strauss

MADAME ALICE ORFF-SOLSCHER

(a) A WINTER DEDICATION.
In days of winter dreary,
When all is gloom and night,
Yet knows the heart one blessing,
Each unto each confessing,
What fills his soul with inner light.

The flame of love enkindled
Shall burn eternally;
What soul to soul uniteth
And fire of love igniteth.
Let that our whispered watchword be.

The wheel of time is turning,
Yet heed we not its flight:
The world in vain allureth.
While Love alone endureth:
We vow ourselves to love, by day, by night.

(b) HYMN TO THE NIGHT.

Holy night! Holy night!
Starbounded Heaven's peace!
All is united that the day has separated,
All wounds bleed sweetly in evening glow.

Bjelborg's spear! Bjelborg's spear
Sinks into the depth of the elated earth.
Which dives with happy air to the bosom
of dark lusts.

Holy night! Sweet bride! Sweet bride!
Hide your sweet shame.
When the wedding cup's sweetness descends,
The day enters into the lustful night!

Holy night! etc.

=== Page 13 ===
THE ROYAL VICTORIAN LIEDERTAFEL

(c) WIE SOLLTEN.
(Why Should We Seek to Hide Our Passion?)
Why should we seek to hide our passion—
    The bliss that bids our hearts o'erflow?
Nay, every human creature living
    Our soul's exultant joy shall know!
When two fond hearts with love are beating
    A shout of joy through Nature goes,
And o'er the hours of lovers' meeting
    Soft summer eve its shadow throws
E'en from the oak's decaying trunk,
    That saw a thousand years go by,
A crown of green once more doth blossom—
    It lifts those aged branches high.
Each leaf, each flower, awakes to gladness,
    Their choicest colours they display:
The brooklet murmurs softer music,
    And blossoms' fragrant splendour tell 'tis May!
Why should we seek to hide our passion—
    The bliss that bids our hearts o'erflow?
Nay, every human creature living, all earth,
    Now I am thine, flowe. of all flowers!

THE ROYAL VICTORIAN LIEDERTAFEL

(a)
Love, fear not if sad thy dreaming
    All thro' the night.
Though o'ercast bright stars are gleaming
    All thro' the night.
Joy will come to thee at morning,
    Life with sunny hope adorning.
Tho' sad dreams may give dark warning
    All thro' the night.

Angels watching ever round thee
    All thro' the night.
In thy slumbers close surround thee.
    All thro' the night.
They should of all fears disarm thee;
    No forebodings should alarm thee:
They will let no peril harm thee,
    All thro' the night.

(b) Ev'ry rustling tree is at peace,
    The whisp'ring winds do cease,
And no sound is heard.

The birds are all sunk in slumber:
    Wait-a-while, wait-a-while,
Soon shalt thou, too, rest in peace.
    Wait-a-while, wait-a-while.
Soon shalt thou, too, rest in peace.
    Thou shalt rest in peace.

(c) While moon and stars above us
    Their airy dance renew.
Say, why should sadness move us.
    Or earth-born care pursue?
Behold! the soft beams play, love.
    Come in my bark away, love.

And glide from bondage free,
    Across the dark blue sea.
Now midnight's boding number
    From good Saint Mark's I hear.
And all are hushed in slumber
    Except Thy Gondolier.

(a) Great is Jehovah the Lord!
The heaven and the earth both proclaim
His mighty power.
We hear Him when roareth the storm,
When the wind through the woods rushes along.
Great is Jehovah the Lord!
Mighty in His power.

Thou hear'st it in the green budding boughs of the forest.
Seest it in the cornfields that glow like gold.
In flowers ye may see it in bright varied hues.
And in the stars still His marvellous power behold.

Awful rolls He in thunder on high,
The flame of His lightning darts in terror below,
And each beating heart, every soul feels His wondrous power and might.

We bow to the power dwelling in Him.
The Lord of all, and up to the Father.

Thou to Him look for aid,
In hope to gain His love and grace.
Turning then, we implore His love and grace and protection.
Great is Jehovah the Lord!

(b)
The Heav'ns with praise to the Lord are abounding.
His name to hear afar they rejoice;
The earth, the sea, to His honour are sounding;

Give ear, O man! to Nature's voice.
The stars above us, who is it upholdeth?
Who leadeth from his tent the sun?
He cometh, laughing. His glory unfoldeth.
A giant who His course would run!

Carols—
(a) Good King Wenceslas
(b) Wassail Song

MASTER WALTER DOIG and P. McFARLANE
and
ROYAL VICTORIAN LIEDERTAFEL

(a) Good King Wenceslas look'd out
    On the feast of Stephen,
    When the snow lay round about,
        Deep, and crisp, and even.
    Brightly shone the moon that night,
        Though the frost was cruel,
    When a poor man came in sight,
        Gather'ring winter fuel.

Baritone Solo:
    "Hither, page, and stand by me,
        If thou know'st it, telling,
    Yonder peasant, who is he?
        Where and what his dwelling?"

Treble Solo:
    "Sire, he lives a good league hence,
        Underneath the mountain;
    Right against the forest fence,
        By St. Agnes' fountain."

Baritone Solo:
    "Bring me flesh, and bring me wine,
        Bring me pine-logs hither:
    Thou and I will see him dine
        When we bear them thither."

Chorus:
    Page and monarch forth they went,
        Forth they went together;
    Through the rude wind's wide lament
        And the bitter weather.

Treble Solo:
    "Sire, the night is darker now,
        And the wind blows stronger:
    Fails my heart, I know not how:
        I can go no longer."

Baritone Solo:
    "Mark my footsteps, my good page:
        Tread thou in them boldly;
    Thou shalt find the winter's rage
        Freeze thy blood less coldly."

Chorus:
    In his master's steps he trod,
        Where the snow lay dinted;
    Heat was in the very sod
        Which the saint had printed.
    Therefore, Christian men, be sure,
        Wealth or rank possessing,
    Ye who now will bless the poor
        Shall yourselves find blessing.

(b) Here we come a-wassailing
        Among the leaves so green;
    Here we come a-wandering,
        So fair to be seen.

Chorus:
    Love and joy come to you,
        And to your wassail too:
    And God bless you and send you a Happy New Year.
    And God send you a Happy New Year.

    Our wassail-cup is made
        Of the rosemary tree,
    And so is your beer
        Of the best barley.
    Love and joy, etc.

    Call up the butler of this house,
        Put on his golden ring;
    Let him bring us a glass of beer,
        And the better we shall sing.
    Love and joy, etc.

    Bring us out a table,
        And spread it with a cloth;
    Bring us out amply cheese,
        And some of your Christmas loaf.
    Love and joy, etc.

    God bless the Master of this house,
        Likewise the Mistress, too;
    And all the little children
        That round the table go.
    Love and joy, etc.

PART I.

Part Song—
The Hunter's Joy
Astholz

Royal Victorian Liedertafel

HALLO! hallo! to cover!
Where waves the forest far around,
And thro' the waving branches
I hear the horn resound.
    Tra-ra!

Then sound aloud the hallo
O'er forest, meadow, stream, and crag,
To startle and to follow
And track the bounding stag.

And homeward when returning,
Beneath the moon's effulgent light,
I seek my lady's window,
To sing a soft good night.

Sleep well! O my beloved,
And may no dream thy peace annoy;
My heart is thine for ever,
Thou art the hunter's joy.
    Sleep well!

And then hallo to cover!
Where waves the forest, &c.

Song—
Prince Ivan's Song
Allitsen

Mr. Horace Stevens

Part Songs—

(a) Evening
(b) Serenade

Soloist: Mr. G. T. Morphet

Royal Victorian Liedertafel

(a) Day again his race has run,
And the tranquil night comes on,
Soothingly her pinions waving,
Heated hill and valley laving,
Spreading from her starry chart
    Holy peace to every dwelling,
    Holy peace to every heart.

All who rest in slumber's arm—
Void of trouble, void of harm—
Heavenly angels now are guarding,
Every danger from them warding—
Powers of evil must depart
    Holy peace to every dwelling,
    Holy peace to every heart.

(b) When in thy dreams thou sayest:
    "Who taps the window there?"
    Then shall the wind make answer:
    "I, and a message bear.
    Thy lover e'er for thee doth long.
    I bring thee greeting, kiss and song."
        Slumber soft, slumber soft.

When in thy dreams thou sayest:
    "What shineth there so clear?"
Then shall the moon make answer:
    "I, and a blessing bear.
I come from one who night and day
For thee doth ever watch and pray."
        Slumber soft, slumber soft.

When in thy dream thou sayest:
    "What doth so soft bewail?"
Then shall a bird make answer:
    "I am the nightingale.
Of love and longing sing to thee
Until thine eyes the morning see."
        Slumber soft, slumber soft.

(b) Am Springbrunnen (The Fountain)

=== Page 10 ===
Part Song—
Students' Evening Song Fischer
Royal Victorian Liedertafel
'Neath the vine tree's garlands bending
Spread, dear maid, the festive board.
With thy fair hands on us tending;
Speeds the day with joyous ending.
Thee we'll pledge with glad accord.
Slumber deep is reigning o'er us,
We alone are now astir
Clink the glasses round in chorus,
Gaudiamus igitur.
Each in turn the tale recount then,
Whence his wandering steps have strayed.
From the distant vale and mountain,
By the mossy dell and fountain,
All in nature's best array'd.
All seems dancing now before us.
As the golden wine we pour,
Joining in the merry chorus,
Gaudiamus igitur.
Blessings rich from heav'n descending,
Rest upon the students free.
Loud in song our voices blending,
Beauty's praise on high ascending,
Praise of maidens true like thee.
Long may heav'n's rich blessings flowing
On our hills and valleys pour,
Where the fruitful vine is growing.
Gaudiamus igitur.

Aria—
Mon cœur s'ouvre à ta voix Saint-Saëns
("Softly awakes my Heart.")
(From the Opera Samson and Delilah.)
Madame Agnes Janson
(Translation.)
Softly awakes my heart, as the flowers awaken
To Aurora's tender zephyr!
But say, O well-belov'd, no more I'll be forsaken;
Speak again, O speak for ever!
O say that from Delilah you never will part!
Your burning vows repeat—vows so dear to my heart.
    Ah, once again do I implore thee,
    Ah, once again then say you adore me.
    Ah, I here implore thee,
    See, I implore thee!
E'en as to whis'ring winds sways the waving grain,
    To and fro so gently moving,
So sways my trembling heart, consoling all its pain,
    To thy voice so dear, so loving.
The arrow in its flight is not swifter than I.
When, leaving all behind, to your arms I fly!

=== Page 11 ===
Part Songs—
Songs of the Sea
C. V. Stanford
(Soloist—Mr. Horace Stevens)
Royal Victorian Liedertafel

DRAKE'S DRUM.

Drake, he's in his hammock, and a thousand miles away
(Captain, art thou sleeping there below?)
Slung atween the round shot in Nombre Dios Bay,
And dreaming all the time of Plymouth Hoe.
Yonder lumes the island, yonder lie the ships,
With sailor lads adancing heel-an'-toe.
And the shore-lights flashing, and the night-tide dashing,
He sees it all so plainly as he saw it long ago.

Drake, he was a Devon man, and ruled the Devon seas,
(Captain, art thou sleeping there below?)
Roving tho' his death fell, he went with heart at ease,
And dreaming all the time of Plymouth Hoe.
"Take my drum to England, hang it by the shore,
Strike it when your powder's running low;
If the Dons sight Devon, I'll quit the port of Heaven,
And drum them up the Channel as we drummed them long ago."

Drake, he's in his hammock till the great Armadas come.
(Captain, art thou sleeping there below?)
Slung atween the round shot, list'ning for the drum,
And dreaming all the time of Plymouth Hoe.
Call him on the deep sea, call him up the Sound,
Call him when ye sail to meet the foe;
Where the old trade's plying and the old flag flying,
They shall find him ware and waking, as they found him long ago!

OUTWARD BOUND.

Dear Earth, near Earth, the clay that made us men,
    The land we sowed.
    The heart that glowed,—
O Mother, must we bid farewell to thee?
Fast dawns the last dawn, and what shall comfort then
    The lonely hearts that roam the outer sea?

Gray wakes the daybreak, the shivering sails are set,
    To misty deeps
    The channel sweeps,—
O Mother, think on us who think on thee!
Earth-home, birth-home, with love remember yet
The sons in exile on the eternal sea.

=== Page 13 ===
DEVON, O DEVON, IN WIND AND RAIN.

DRAKE in the North Sea grimly prowling,
    reading his dear Revenge's deck.
Watch'd, with the sea-dogs round him growling,
    Galleons drifting wreck by wreck.
    "Fetter and Faith for England's neck,
    Faggot and Father. Saint and chain,--
Yonder the Devil and all go howling,
    Devon, O Devon, in wind and rain!"

Drake at the last off Nombre lying,
    Knowing the night that toward him crept.
Gave to the sea-dogs round him crying
    This for a sign before he slept:--
    "Pride of the West! what Devon hath kept:
Devon shall keep on tide or main:
Call to the storm and drive them flying,
    Devon, O Devon, in wind and rain!"

Valour of England gaunt and whitening,
    Far in a South-land brought to bay.*
Locked in a death-grip all day tight'ning,
    Waited the end in twilight gray.
Battle and storm and the sea-dog's way!
Drake from his long rest turn'd again.
Victory lit thy steel with lightning.
    Devon, O Devon, in wind and rain!

* Waggon Hill, 6th January. 1900.

HOMeward BOUND.

AFTER long labouring in the windy ways,
    On smooth and shining tides
        Swiftly the great ship glides,
Her storms forgot, her weary watches past!
Northward she glides, and thro' the enchanted haze
    Faint on the verge her far hope dawns at last.

The phantom sky-line of a shadowy down,
    Whose pale white cliffs below,
        Thro' sunny mist aglow.
    Like noonday ghosts of summer moonshine gleam—
Soft as old sorrow, bright as old renown.
There lies the home of all our mortal dream.

=== Page 14 ===
THE "OLD SUPERB."

The wind was rising easterly, the morning sky was blue,
The straits before us opened wide and free;
We look'd towards the Admiral, where high the Peter flew,
And all our hearts were dancing like the sea.
The French are gone to Martinique with four and twenty sail.
The "Old Superb" is old and foul and slow!
But the French are gone to Martinique, and Nelson's on the trail,
And where he goes the "Old Superb" must go.
So Westward ho! for Trinidad, and Eastward ho! for Spain.
And "Ship ahoy!" a hundred times a day;
Round the world if need be, and round the world again,
With a lame duck lagging all the way.

The "Old Superb" was barnacled and green as grass below,
Her sticks were only fit for stirring grog;
The pride of all her midshipmen was silent long ago,
And long ago they ceased to heave the log.
Four year out from home she was, and ne'er a week in port,
And nothing save the guns aboard her bright;
But Captain Keats he knew the game, and swore to share the sport,
For he never yet came in too late to fight.

So Westward ho! &c.

"Now up, my lads," the Captain cried, "for sure the case were hard
If longest out were first to fall behind;
Aloft, aloft with studding-sails, and lash them on the yard,
For night and day the Trades are driving blind."
So all day long and all day long behind the fleet we crept,
And how we fretted none but Nelson guessed:
But ev'ry night the "Old Superb," she sail'd while others slept,
Till we ran the French to earth with all the rest.

O 'twas Westward ho! &c.

INTERVAL.

=== Page 15 ===
PART II.

Double Chorus—Oedipus Mendelssohn

Royal Victorian Liedertafel

Thou comest here to the land, O friend.
Fam'd for fleet-footed steeds and blooming meadows:
Thou standest now in Colonos' grove.
    Where the voices of nightingales
    Resound, floating in dulcet strains
        Thro' their temples of verdure:
    Where the thick-woven ivy clings.
    Spreading over the sacred aisles:
Where, in security, ripens the fruitful vine,
    Unscathed by beam or stormwind.
And here roameth the bounteous god,
Gay and good Dionysos, ever greeted in lays.
    Sung by the nymphs who rear'd him.

    Fair and fragrant at dawn of day.
    See the beautiful heaven-bedewed Narcissus,
The flow'r that shone in the goddesses' crowns,
        Worn by them in the days of old.
    See the Crocus array'd in gold:
        Hear the slumberless waters.
    While they glide in Cephisus' tide.
Still meandering day by day
Over the plains, bearing streams ever pure along,
    Enriching all the bowers
    Embosomed in the favour'd land;
Ever loved by the tuneful choir of Muses,
    And Cythera, whose zone is golden.

    Here, too, bloometh a tree
Crowned with a fruit not found in Asia;
Nor on Dorian plains doth it appear.
Gracing the island where the Pelops
Held sway: yet here it freely springeth:
    Rever'd by friends, and feared by foes,
        In native splendour it blossoms for Athens.
Behold, ours is the rich oil-dropping olive;
    Aged and youthful, noble and peasant,
Never wantonly harm this holy tree,
    Guarded and cherished, it stands secure,
Everheeded by Morian Jove.
    Lov'd and watch'd by Minerva.

    Grateful, let me extol
Heaven's richest gifts deigned to my country:
Presented by the Pow'r making our State
Fam'd for its wealth, honour, and glory:
    Our land and sea steeds, rein and rudder-guided;
    O Chronos' son, by them we stand pre-eminent.

Part Song—
Thou art my Dream
Royal Victorian Liedertafel
The drooping flow'rs their buds are closing,
    The silver stars keep watch above;
The world in tranquil sleep reposing,
    My wakeful bosom yields to love.
While here in hopeless grief I languish,
    Could I behold thy vision bright,
Then would I fondly breathe my anguish,
    Thou art my dream thro' stilly night.
Tho' all unmoved by love's appealing,
    No kindling passion lights thy brow,
No voice of love thy heart revealing,
    Still all the world to me art thou.
Bend softly down, ye golden tresses:
    Beam kindly once, bright orbs of light;
List, lady, list to love's distresses,
    Thou art my dream thro' stilly night.

Songs—
(a) Snow
(b) On the Mountain
Madame Agnes Janson
(a) There is nought on earth so still as the snow!
    Shrouding all the world in silent glamour;
    Muffling ev'ry sound: on the frozen ground
    Hushing ev'ry footfall's noisy clamour.
    There is nought on earth as pure as the snow!
    Swan's down loosed from winter's pions spreading,
    On the hand a flake doth a teardrop make,
    Through the crystal air white thoughts are threading.
    Nought so lulling on the earth as the snow!
    Sinking light as slumber on the weary.
    Till the silence so into sound doth grow
    Fine as silver bells, as music ringing.

=== Page 18 ===
(b) Ah, me! Up here it is bright and gay,
    On the mountain!
The zephyr rippling in sprightly play
    On the mountain!
Our feet are dancing, our eyes are bright,
Our heart rejoicing with new delight,
    On the mountain!
Come up, come up! From the vale ascend
    To the mountain!
Refreshing odours with zephyrs blend
    On the mountain!
The grass is studded with flowers untold,
The sun is shedding her rays of gold
    O'er the mountain!
Ah, dearest boy of mine! come to me
    On the mountain!
Day after day I have longed for thee
    On the mountain!
Come, let us talk till the sun has set,
And in our loving our grief forget
    On the mountain.

Part Song—
The Frog Cantata
    Royal Victorian Liedertafel
    Hennig

In the lakes and flowing rivers
Dwells a race of free good livers;
Always laughing, swimming, croaking;
Always singing, always joking;
And is heard the whole day long,
Loud and clear their ringing song.
    Quack! quack! Reck! eck! eck!

Eyes like diamonds brightly flashing,
Limbs on lake and riplet splashing,
Sporting, playing, chatting, laughing,
Feasting richly, nectar quaffing,
And is heard the whole day long,
Loud and clear their ringing song.
    Quack! quack! Reck! eck! eck;

Programme

"God Save the King"

"FRITHJOF"

The story of Frithjof the Bold and Ingeborg the Fair is told in "Frithjof's Saga," a poem in twenty-four cantos, by Esaias Tegner, published in 1820.

The hero, Frithjof, is son to Thorsten Vikingsson, who, though King Bele's best warrior and chosen friend, is of lowly origin. Frithjof the Strong and Bold dares to love Fair Ingeborg, daughter of his king and descendant of great Odin. Bele looks kindly on young Frithjof's love, but death takes from the youth at once a monarch and a friend. When Frithjof subsequently demands the hand of Ingeborg from Helge, son and successor of Bele, he is rejected with scorn. Later old King Ring, a mighty monarch of the North, would make fair Ingeborg his queen, but Helge, influenced by soothsayers, sends a refusal, accompanied by a taunting message from brother Halfdan to "Old Grey-beard." King Ring, incensed, declares war against the brothers, and Ingeborg is sent for safety to the vale of Baldur, the god of innocence and virtue. While in the sacred grove the maiden receives a visit from her lover, the joy of which is followed by the fear that she has angered the gods by keeping a love-tryst in that holy place. At a council of war, assembled at Bele's cairn, Frithjof again demands from Helge the hand of Ingeborg, in return for which he offers his best aid in the impending battle. Helge again repels him, and forces him to make the fatal admission that he has visited Ingeborg in the sacred grove. He thereupon denounces him as a profaner of temples, and orders him to do penance for his sacrilege by sailing to the Orkneys to wring from fierce Earl Agantyr long-withheld tribute. Frithjof tries to persuade Ingeborg to fly with him, but in vain. Giving her his arm-ring, he departs, promising to return and make her his bride.

Borne through his perilous voyage by his charmed ship "Ellida," Frithjof returns at length to his native land to find his estates laid waste with fire and sword, and the fair Ingeborg given in marriage to victorious King Ring. He learns that at the marriage ceremony the cowardly Helge tore from his sister's arm her lover's ring, and hung it upon the arm of Baldur's image. Frithjof, furious, seeks out the King whilst he is in the act of offering sacrifice at Baldur's pyre. He flings Agantyr's tribute full in Helge's face, and, hastily snatching at the arm-ring, he overturns the huge idol upon the sacred fire. The flames lap it about, and, leaping upward with angry roar, spread to the temple and the sacred grove, which are soon reduced to ashes.

Frithjof is now shunned by all as a perpetrator of sacrilege; he is banished from his country, and, sailing away in the "Ellida," he devotes himself to a life of wild adventure. The hero's troubled life is ultimately crowned with happiness. After many years he returns to his native land, and succeeds in gaining the goodwill of King Ring, who at his death bequeaths him his kingdom and his queen.

INTRODUCTION

Scene I.
Frithjof's Return

Recitative.

How bravely o'er the floods so bright,
Ellida flies to shore now in sight!
Although the king with demon spell
Invoked the horrid goblin brood,
And unloosed the wings of the tempest,
My Northland courage bore me
Through ardent strife
To glory's height;
From mighty Jarl the tribute I obtained:
I greet thee gladly, Baldur's grove,
Where oft by break of night
Hope filled my heart with sweet delight!
My Ingeborg, but where art thou now?
Beloved maiden, art thou true to me?

See, I vie with the winds and their heavenly train.
Ellida, O hasten and fly o'er the main.

Chorus.

Oh, 'tis delight when the land afar appeareth,
And from the hearth of thy home beloved
The smoke curls upwards
And thou art near to childhood's scenes
For ever dear.

Solo—Frithjof.

On the tomb of my father I planted the lime-tree,
Is the delicate stem still alive?
Give, earth, thy growth,
And thou O heaven, send fostering dew.
Oh, 'tis delight!

Ingeborg's Bridal Procession to King Ring.

March—Orchestra

Chorus.
Sadly the Skald walks before the train.
Pale sits the bride on the coal black palfrey:
The angry Norma her arrow darteth:
She rules the mortals,
As their lot is cast.
From thunder-clouds ruin falls at last.

Solo, Ingeborg—and Chorus.
My heart, with sorrow overflowing,
Heeds not the flowers entwined with my ringlets:
For ever away from my home I go,
By my brother forced to wed his foe!
And endless woe in my bosom burneth.
But Bele's daughter pity spurneth!
Yet bear to Frithjof greetings from Ingeborg!
Great is my grief, but I do not hate.
    All-father judges
    I bear my fate.

Scene III.

Frithjof's Revenge—Temple in Flames—Curse

Chorus of Priests.
Midnight sun on the mountain burns,
    Red like blood appearing,
And through the strange mysterious light
    Helge's train is nearing.
Lo, he comes, while the glare is spread,
Splendid crown adorns his head,
    Helge, mighty monarch!

Recitative—Frithjof.
Go to Hela's dark abode.
    Seek ye there the mighty rover:
Slain upon the horse he rode,
    Helge's life is over!

Chorus.
Woe! Oh! wicked deed!

Frithjof.
Hush, wretched priests with gory knives.
    Moonlight's pallid princes!
Hush! or tremble for your lives,
    Long our blades have thirsted!
Where my father rests,
Where my childhood passed,
Nought save a ruin I found aghast!
And sold to the foe my beloved bride.
    The armlet which to her I left,
Behold, now the God wears it proudly,
    And she is bereft!
Ah, Baldur! is this thy valiant deed?
By theft this armlet was given to thee!
Thou must, O Baldur, restore it to me!
How dar'st thou hold this ring in thy keeping.
Which once my Ingeborg blessed with weeping?
    No longer on thine arm it shall rest!
My hope, my joy, thou could'st destroy,
But, mind! not me shall thou decoy!

Chorus—Priests and People.
Woe! he rags with all his might at the ring
    —O fright!
Ah! the God, now filled with wrath,
    'Midst the flames is rushing,
And the consecrated hearth
    By his weight is crushing.
    Fane in flames!
    Pour water on!
The waves of the sea bring either!
    Lo! clouds of smoke are bursting forth.
Morning winds blow from the North!
    How the flames are glaring!
What availeth human might!
Now from branch to branch they spring
    Through the combat daring!
Blazing flames in the grove abound.
    Onward like rivers flowing,
Sunlight smileth,
    But fiend and sound
Blood-red with fire are glowing.
    Woe! Woe! Woe!

Priests.
Mischief bringer! malediction on thy head!
accurs'd!

People and Priests.
Mount, smoke, and upwards to heaven ascending.
    Valhalla enter, Valhalla enter.
Cry to the Gods, who o'er earth are bending.
And thou, O flame, the deed proclaim.
Fly, and proclaim to the Gods the accursed deed!

Frithjof's Followers
Ashes our temple soon will be:
Frithjof from his home must flee!
Happy he who departs not for ever!

THE ROYAL VICTORIAN LIEDERTAFEL

Scene IV.
Frithjof Goes Into Exile

Solo—Quartette
Sun in the sky
Now mounteth high.
The winds are blowing
And gently flowing,
The waves advance
In joyful dance.

Chorus.
Sadly Frithjof goes his way;
See, he weepeth, while morning gloweth!

Solo—Frithjof and Chorus.
World's grandest region thou mighty North,
From thy dominions I'm driven forth.
Within thy borders I lov'd to dwell!
Midsummer sun, fare thee well!
My love is foiled, my rooftree rent!
With honour soiled, in exile sent!
Cheerless is my soul within me.
Hopeless, I must bear my lot.
Ye rugged mountains where heroes dwell,
And Thor commandeth clouds and winds:
Ye azure lakes that I love so well.
Ye woods and brakes, fare ye well!

Scene V.
Ingeborg's Lament

Solo—Ingeborg.
Storms wildly roar!
Billows break madly upon the shore.
Would 'neath the sod I were lying,
Winds o'er me sighing!
Sad and oppress,
Thee I did watch, flying sail in the west!
Onward with Frithjof thou glidest,
With him abidest.
Falcon, beloved! thee he left here;
Falcon for his sake to me thou art dear.
Shake not thy pinions, stay near me,
O, why should'st thou fear me?
Here on his hand,
Worker on the canvas, thou proudly shall stand,
Silver thy pinions unfolden;
Thy claws shall be golden.
Thou darling bird!
Sit on my shoulder, and list to my word!
When I'm no more
He will come hither, and his heart will be sore:
Greet from me Frithjof.
Who loves me, and never forgets me.

Scene VI.
Frithjof On the Sea

Chorus—Frithjof's Followers.
Now he crossed the floods of the salt desert waste.
Far off like a falcon he flew!
But for warriors on board he wrote maxims and rules!
List to the laws of his crew!

Frithjof and Chorus.
On this deck raise no tent,
And ashore do not sleep:
Within houses the foe lurks for thee!

On thy shield sleep, Viking.
Thy sword in thy hand:
Let the heavens thy canopy be.
Now hold high your lances—
Your lances hold high—
Our banners unfold ye,
The triumph is nigh.
To climes of the south we shall wander.
When hurricanes rage,
Hoist the canvas on high!
Let them come as they may:
He who flinches must die.
Rise, rise, unfold ye our banners!

(a) Holy night, oh soothe my breast
With thy solemn tranquil calm:
Give the weary wand'rer rest,
O'er his sorrows shed thy balm.
Stars brightly o'er me gleaming,
From azure fields are beaming,
They set my soul a-dreaming
Of rest above.
Hallowed sounds fall on my ear,
Wafted on the nightwind's sighs:
Murmurings from some blissful sphere.
Echoes from love's paradise.
On high my glances turning,
Where heaven's stars are burning,
I dream with fervent yearning
Of peace and love.

away

moor.

But come with thy naked feet.
We shall have to pass thro' the dewy

Yes, weekly from Southampton,
Great steamers, white and gold,
Go rolling down to Rio,
And I'd like to roll to Rio

I'd like to roll to Rio
Some day before I'm old!

Some day before I'm old!
I'd love to roll to Rio
Some day before I'm old!

Operatic Chorus—
Bandit's Chorus
From "Ernani"
with
A.B.C. ORCHESTRA
THE ROYAL VICTORIAN LIEDERTAFEL

All welcome the bowl!
A full flowing soul.
Unfathomed by care!
What boots it the bandit.
If hunted and branded,
So wine be his share!
To play, sirs!

Treasure is merely a pleasure
That flies soon as come!
And play hath a duty.
It charmeth when beauty
Inconstant may roam.

Thrice welcome the bowl!
Whose glorious soul
Doth bleed at our call!
The bowl, the bowl,
Whose glorious soul, sirs,
Doth bleed at our call.

Hernani, still pensive?
Quick thought grows apprehensive
To view his cheek so 'blanch'd
Where's life's tide hath motion.
On Death's shoreless ocean
Our one bark is launched.

To give, then, thy willing
Immediate fulfilling.
Ere will'd we prepare.
The hawk's speed 'e'en tarries
In hitting her quarries
If ours ye compare.

Come, welcome the bowl.
Whose glorious soul
Can drown all thy care!

Now homeward hie, and take your rest
With conscience clear and sins confess'd.
We bid you all Good Night!

■クロス・トーク3（3月）には、次のような作曲家の作品を演奏する予定です。
石井真木、松平頼暁、佐藤慶次郎、ポール・チハラ、ヘンリー・カウエル、ラリー・オースチン。

■12月31日午前11時から、アメリカ文化センター・ホールで〈クロス・トーク〉特別演奏会として、エリック・サティのピアノ曲（ヴェクサシオン）の日本初演を行いました。この作品は全曲1分ほどの長さのピアノ曲ですが、840回繰り返えして演奏せよ——という指定をもっています。黛敏郎、入野義朗、戸田邦雄、一柳慧、笠間春子、湯浅譲二、石井真木、松平頼暁、レイノルズ夫妻ら15人が参加して、実に13時間38分かかって、1967年1月1日午前2時半、ついに全曲を完奏しました。

=== Page 14 ===
〈地の口は速い〉について

この作品は1964〜65年にかけて作曲された室内オーケストラのための作品である。題名の Quick are the mouths of Earth はいささか奇妙だが、これはアメリカの小説家トマス・ウルフから引用されたのだという。「大地の口はすべて貧欲である」とも訳されるほか、さまざまな意味がふくまれているらしいが、ここでは作曲者の意向によって、むしろ直訳的に〈地の口は速い〉としておく。

18分ほどの作品だが、6つの部分にわかれている。そしてそれぞれのパートは、さらに6つの部分に分割できる。また各部分の楽器の音のうごきも、それぞれ6つの要素にわけられる。つまりここでは〈6〉のプロポーションで曲が構成されているといえる。このような構成方法は、かれはすでに2度とこころみないだろうといっていいる。それはそのご時間に関するつここんだ追求の結果、新しい時間構造への方向をあゆみだしているからだという。心理学によれば、人間は時間のプロポーションというものは知覚できないらしい。心理学上では、人間には最大5秒程度の時間のプロポーションしかわからないことになっている。つまり、それは時間というよりは、むしろ多くの小さな瞬間（あるいはモメント）の集合としてうけとっているというべきだろう。

しかしこの曲での構造の特色は、むしろ時間的なプロポーションよりも、このような小さなモメントの集合構造にあるといえるようにおもわれる。音のテクスチュアは、つねにすばやく変化しつづけているものと、あまり変化しないものとが濃密にくみあわされている。聴衆は、こうした激しい変化とうごきの複雑なテクスチュアの中に、つねに新しい要素を発見していく。

楽器のグループのうえからみると、大きくわけて3つの群に分割されている。そして①多くの異った音が星座のように散らばる各群間のとびかうような交錯。②まったく同じではないが、同質といえる音色の対比。③同じ音の前後の関係——といった音のインタープレイがみられる。

またこの曲の特色のひとつは、こうした各群の音のインタープレーのなかからうまれてくる音の空間的なうごきということだ。つまり空間におけるさまざまな音のうごきのパターンの可能性をこころみているともいえる。そしておなじような音の空間的なうごきをきいていると、いつのまにか、それはひとつの音のうごきのモティーフのように感じられてくる。

またここではオーボーがかなり重要な存在である。しかし主演役者の、独奏的的には、けしてうかびあがらない。この曲では名人芸的な演奏や個人的な表現はおさえられている。それぞれの楽器の音色や、音のうごきが織りなしていく複雑なテクスチュアズの構造とその展開こそを重んじているからだ。

この作品では即興性はもちいられていないが楽器の奏法と記譜法のうえで、不確定性の要素がとりいれられている。たとえばチェロのA弦に弓をあてて、しっかりと押さえる。そしてたえずむらのない緊張度で、徐々に弓をひくと、不規則な震動をおこし、予想できないときに、ぽつんと、きしる音がでたり、あるいは継続的な音がでる。このような奏法上の不確定性はずいしょにみられる。

また第2部の冒頭（スコアの8〜9頁）では、チェロのパートはグラフによって記譜されている。このグラフの音のパターンは、ついて通常のリズムの音価で示され、やがてこの部分の終りのほうでは、さらに確定的な記譜法で指示されている。こうした記譜法や指定の変化をもちこみながら、演奏における多様な可能性がこころみられているのだ。

ロジャー・レイノルズ

1934年生れ。ミシガン大学で物理工学と作曲を学ぶ。ロス・リー・フィニー、ロベルト・ジェルハルトらに師事。アン・アルボールでアシュレーらと〈ワンス〉グループを組織。1962年にフルブライト計画によって、ドイツで電子工学の計画に参加。1963年には、パリで現代音楽の演奏会をつづけ、64年以後グッゲンハイム財団、ロックフェラー財団の奨学金で欧州各地で活躍。1966年暮以来現代世界事情研究所の資金により、フルート奏者のカレン夫人と日本に滞在中。

かれの作品の多くは、C．F．ビータースから出版されており、フルート曲〈アンバージュ〉が日本ビクターからLＰででている。

なおレイノルズの音楽の考え方や方法論については、かれ自身がかいた論文〈不確定性——試論〉「音楽芸術」誌1967年12月号に、かなりくわしくのべられている。

=== Page 18 ===
15.
〈バラード〉についてのノート

この作品は1966年に作曲されたが、まだ未完である。つまり現在もつぎつぎに書きたして、作曲が進行中の作品だからである。今回の演奏では、つぎの3つのパートがつづけて演奏されていく。

I  too（あまりにすぎる）
II  メドレー
III  ブルース

記符は図形楽譜を用いているが、ブルースの部分は音符でかかれ、ピッチは確定的にしるされている。ここでもかれの特色があきらかで歌手がうたうブルースは、ジャズメンたちだったら、だれでも知っているいずれも有名なスタンダード・ナンバーである（部分的に変えてはいるが……）。

こうしたブルース調の声楽パートが素朴で美しい旋律線をうかびあがらせ、器楽の不確定な要素が、繊細な音色をそれにからませていくのである。しかしこの場合、器楽はたんなる伴奏ではないし、またリズミック、ハーモニックなパターンで旋律的な要素に組みあわさるのでもない。指揮者は旋律のうごきをきき、コントロールしながら、器楽パートの音響を旋律に〈おいて〉いくのである。

楽器による音は、かなり複雑であり、トリプル・ストップ、ダブル・ストップ、クラスターなどの2つまたは3つの音を、ひとつの楽器で同時に演奏したり（フルート、テナー・サックスなど）、かなり演奏技術のうえでも至難なところもある。

「奏者は、つぎのような点で、この作品を理解したのちは、自由と解放をこころみてほしい。ひびき、音程の微細な波動運動、ヴィブラートの多様性、ミュートの使用、音の幅の微妙な変化、アタックの多様性 etc…。ともかく音を〈きく〉こと」（作曲者）

この作品は自由なブルースのインプロヴィゼーションのフィーリングと、繊細な音色の要素をミックスしているというスタイルによってすでにのべたように、マルティラーノの特色がいかにもいきいきとあらわれているユニークな作品である。

それと同時に、これはいかにもアメリカの新しいうごきを感じさせる新鮮な興味ぶかい作品といえるだろう。ポピュラー音楽イコールたのしく・やさしい音楽。現代音楽イコール難解で頭の痛くなる音楽。ここではこうしたこれまでの公式をやぶりすてている。そうした偏見をぼくらの環境から払拭してしまおうといった自然で、新鮮な態度がみられる。だいいち、ブルースの旋律がなんと美しく、また器楽の音色がなんと繊細にそのポピュラーな旋律線をつつみこんでしまっているだろう。それは木に竹をついだような実験作品とはちがう。かれ自身の音への感受性と尖鋭な意識が、そこにゆたかなひとつの音の世界をひろげているのである。

最近アメリカの若い世代の作曲家たちのなかには、こうしたポピュラー、あるいはジャズのフィーリングと現代音楽の実験的な技法をとアッケラカンとミックスして、独自な方向をきりひらいているうごきがみられる。ことに20代の作曲家たちには、このような傾向があきらかになっているようだ。楽音の世界と卑俗な騒音の世界との境界線は、すでにとりはらわれてしまった。そうした現代の音楽の世界と卑俗（？）とされてきたポピュラーの世界のあいだの扉だって、自由に開閉できる状態をつくっておくのはすこしもふしぎではないだろう。

なおノーティション（記譜法）のうえでも、かなり興味ぶかいこころみがみられる。たとえばここでは器楽パートのほとんどは図形楽譜として記符されているが、アイヴスの場合のように、ことばによる説明もある。

=== Page 19 ===
(REYNOLDS)
make use of some notational and performance techniques that are inherently indeterminate. Thus, on repeated hearings, although the overall effect remains, the details vary greatly. Integrated into the fabric of the work are numerous instances of flexible (permissive) materials gradually coming under more and more precise control. The most clear example occurs at the beginning of the second section where the performers relate very delicate piano-string pizzicati and cello noise-rasps to graphically represented rhythmic patterns. The same patterns recur several times, notated with increasing precision and performed with increasingly dependable instrumental techniques. As they become more definite (more regular and predictable) their function becomes less important (for example, accompanimental). This tendency is more pronounced in my recent music, where unpredictable and unrepeatable events are primary; and where stable, conventionally notated sounds become standards of comparison.

ROGER REYNOLDS was born in 1934 and received degrees in engineering physics and music from the University of Michigan. His principal teacher was Ross Lee Finney, and he also studied with Roberto Gerhard. In Ann Arbor, Reynolds was a co-founder of the ONCE group (cf., Ashley notes), and later organized concerts in Paris. He was a Guggenheim Fellow in 1964, received a Rockefeller grant the following year, and is now living in Japan as a Fellow of the Institute of Current World Affairs. His compositions are published by C. F. Peters Corporation (*), and recorded on Victor (Japan). Articles by him have appeared in Perspectives of New Music, Arts in Society, The Musical Quarterly, and Ongaku Geijutsu. His compositions include: *The Emperor of Ice Cream (1962) (theater work for 8 voices, percussion, piano, and contrabass); *Fantasy for Pianist (1964); *Gathering (1964) (woodwind quintet); *Graffiti (1964) (orchestra); *Ambages (1965) (solo flute); *Blind Men (1966) (mixed voices, brass, piano, percussion, and projections), commissioned by the Fromm Foundation; Threshold (1967) (divided orchestra with solo groups); piece for divided chamber orchestra, tape, modulators (in progress), commissioned by Hope College; Ping (in progress) (dancer, voice (live and taped), flute, piano, contrabass, percussion, lighting, signal generators, modulators, and closed circuit TV).

QUICK ARE THE MOUTHS OF EARTH (1964-65) is approximately 18 minutes long. Each of its 6 sections is divided into 6 parts, and these are in turn divided according to a fixed system of time proportions. I no longer use this procedure, however, having learned that there is no psychological basis for expecting that one can accurately experience time proportions. Temporal experience is rather made up of a succession of brief moments (The "present" has a maximum length of about 5 seconds.), and there are inevitable shifts of attention between them. In Quick Are The Mouths Of Earth, I try to take this into account. The sound textures are always in one of two states: rapidly changing (keeping pace with the changing psychological "present") or very slowly evolving (providing relief and serving as a foil to the general quickness). There is no middle ground.

The ensemble is divided into three groups, and this permits three types of spatial interplay: constellations of stressed entrances across the entire span of the ensemble; the passing of similar materials from group to group; and the continuous flow of a matched sound (a particular pitch, noise, cluster) from left to right, right to center to right, and so on. The patterns of these movements in space are systematized so as to emerge, after repeated hearings, as "motivic" in themselves. This spatial use of sound is intended as a further development of the antiphonal effects traditionally used for dramatic purposes.

A second purpose of the spatial separation of groups is the clarification in performance of the complex and ornamented texture. Only the oboe (a protagonist who is earnest but - inevitably - ineffectual) emerges occasionally as a soloist. The general avoidance of expressivity and display in the traditional senses, however, is certainly not meant to make the music uncommunicative. On the contrary, I hope that each listener will have his own responses, and I have tried to avoid restricting or predetermining them. The complex aural texture relates, in my mind, to the patterns of events in contemporary life. They are rarely simple.

Quick Are The Mouths Of Earth does not involve improvisation, but does

サルバトーレ・マルティラーノ

1927年、ニューヨーク州ヨンカーズに生れた。オーベリン音楽院、イーストマン音楽大学を卒業後、イタリーのフローレンスにあるケルビーニ音楽院で、ルイジ・ダラビッコラに師事。そのごローマ大賞、グゲンハイム奨学金、フォード財団奨学金、ブランダイス大学クリエーティブ・アート賞をはじめ、多くを受賞。

マルティラーノは、現在イリノイ大学の助教授である。イリノイ大学は、コンピューター音楽の先駆的なスタジオをもち、ヒラーを中心にこの方面的実験、研究で有名だが、現代音楽の活動がかなり盛んでアメリカでは注目される重要な存在となっている。マルティラーノはここで指揮者として、また若い実験的な音楽家たちのオーガナイザーとして欠くことのできない存在である。

マルティラーノの音楽の特色は、つねにふたつの要素が混淆していることであろう。たとえば、それを新しい論理的な音の構造と、ジャズ的な自由な要素を同存させているといいかえてもいい。

その一例として、最近作の〈地下の世界〉をとりだしてみても、あきらかだ。ここでは図形楽譜と電子音楽、俳優を使って、声を素材とした奇妙な空間をうみだしている。まるで演劇のように、四人のアクターは夫、妻、息子、むすめとそれぞれ性格があたえられ、イエス、ノーサイ笑声、泣き声、など対比する単純な4つのカテゴリーのことばを用いている。これらのシラブルが毎回ちがった組みあわせとなってあらわれるが、それはそのまま心理劇のように、あるときはエディプス・コンプレックスのドラマのようにうかびあがったり、あるいはマザー・コンプレックスの会話のひと駒をおもわせたりする。おまけにアクションも加わるから、ストーリーのないドラマそのものである。そしてそこにジャズのインプロヴィゼイションのようなひびきがくわわっていくのである。

ともかく、かれの音楽ではジャズの要素と現代音楽の新しい技法が、たくみにミックスされているのだ。ぼくらは日ごろ、ジャズやポピュラー音楽をたのしんでいる。しかしひとたび現代音楽の問題を論じたり、作曲したりするとなると、ぴしゃりと扉をとじて、これらの要素を別なものとして追いだしてしまう。マルティラーノの音楽は、こうした今日の状況のなかでの〈音楽〉の奇妙な別居状態へのひとつの批評だ。

SALVATORE MARTIRANO was born in 1927, in Yonkers, New York. After earning degrees at the Oberlin Conservatory and the Eastman School of Music, he studied with Luigi Dallapiccola at the Cherubini Conservatory in Florence, Italy. He has received, among other awards, a Prix de Rome, a Guggenheim Fellowship, a Ford Foundation Grant, and a Brandeis Creative Arts Award. Martirano is now an Associate Professor of Composition at the University of Illinois, where he is active as a conductor and as an organizer of the University's many contemporary music projects. His music is published by MCA Music (*) and Schott Edition (**), and is available on records through Advance, CRI, and Heliodor. His works include: A Cappella Mass (mixed double chorus) (1952-55); Contrasto for Orchestra (1954); Chansons Innocents (soprano and piano) (1957); **0,0,0,0, That Shakespeherian Rag (mixed chorus and instruments) (1958), commissioned by the League of Composers - I.S.C.M.; *Cocktail Music (piano) (1962); Octet (1963), commissioned by the Koussevitsky Music Foundation; Underworld (4 actors, 4 percussionists, 2 contrabasses, tenor sax, and 2-channel tape) (1964-65), commissioned by the Fromm Foundation.

Martirano includes tightly rationalized structures (serial and otherwise) and freely felt, jazz-inspired improvisation in a style that sounds completely natural. For example, he has recently used graphic notation, electronic sound, and actors in Underworld. The text needs no translation. Four actors represent a man, wife, son, and daughter, while the vocal materials consist of four categories (affirmative, negative, laughing, crying), each of which, in turn, has six divisions (yes, yeah, yep, uh huh, ...; no, nope, nah, ...; ha, he, ho, ...; etc.). These syllables, in constantly permuting and carefully planned combinations (questioning laughter, sorrowful affirmatives, etc.) are intoned by the actors, implying an exhaustive array of psychological tensions through words and movements. Gestures and actions are prescribed for the actors, and driving jazz improvisations rise easily out of the notated materials.

BALLAD (1966 - ) is a work in progress. Basically reflective, it now consists of three sections played continuously: too, medley, and blues. The notation is graphic, with space more or less equal to time, except in the blues section. The work is generated by a sequence of segments from jazz standards and blues vocal lines. Though the melodic materials are definitely pitched, the accompanying sounds are not rhythmic or harmonic in any obvious sense. They are placed in time along the vocal line by the conductor who refers to their relative graphic position in the score.

Ballad is a cooperative venture, and in the score the composer encourages liberties "with timbre, microtonal fluctuations of pitch, variety of vibratos, use of mutes, subtle changes in amplitude, a variety of attacks, etc. - once the piece is understood. Listen!!" The instrumental sounds are frequently complex (requiring double and triple-stops from the flute and saxophone) and awkward to notate by traditional means. Martirano's graphic method shows what actions the players must perform in order to produce the appropriate sound (this in contrast to normal notation which indicates the desired sound and says nothing about how it is to be achieved). Occasional Ivesian asides in the score help to further clarify the spirit of the work and that of the

アピアランスに関するノート
Appearance は、私のライヴ・エレクトロニック・ミュージック（電子音楽の生演奏）としての第3作にあたる。
したがって、これは電子音楽といっても、テープレコーダーは一際使用されない。私には、電子音楽はこれからの音楽として、もっとも大きな可能性をもった分野におもわれる。これまでの電子音楽のように、スタジオにこもって製作し、それをテープに定着してしまうような方法は、もはや電子音楽のごくひとつの在り方にしかすぎなくなりつつある。
この〈アピアランス〉のように、演奏者が参加して、電子装置をつかっての生演奏を行うもの、さらに光やイメージなどをつかったさまざまなかたちでの視覚的・空間的な要素との結合、演奏者のみならず観賞者も参加でき、かつ包みこまれるような音環境デザイン、そしてコンピューターとの結合などは、いずれもエレクトロニクスの力を抜きにしては考えられないことである。
その点で電子音楽の可能性は、はかりしれなく、大きく拡がっているといえるだろう。私はこれから、これらの可能性を着実に具現してゆく機会をつくってゆきたいとおもっている。そしていまさまざまなプランを練っているところである。
〈アピアランス〉を音楽としてと同時に、そのような観点から観賞していただければ幸いである。（一柳 慧）

この〈アピアランス〉は、作曲者のいうように、テープを使わない電子音楽、つまりライヴ・エレクトロニック・ミュージックの作品である。いうならば電子音楽をステージで生演奏しながらうみだしていく方法である。3つの楽器のほか、2台のオッシレーター、2台のリング変調器といった電子装置を楽器のように使い、演奏しながら、新しい音響世界の生き生きとした状態をうみだしていくわけである。楽器の生ま音は、たえず電子変調器によって変質されるそして異質な音響として空間に出現するのだ。
この作品は1967年2月に、ニューヨーク滞在中に作曲され、同年3月30日にカリフォルニア大学で、デービド・テュードア、ラリー・オースティンらによって初演された。そのごアルヴィン・ルシェ、テュードア、作曲者らによってブランダイス大学のローズ美術館で演奏されたほか、たびたび演奏されている。なおこの図形楽譜は、アメリカの前衛音楽雑誌〈Source〉2号に掲載され、Composer Performer Edition から出版されている。

一柳 慧

1933年生れ。作曲を平尾貴四男、池内友次郎に、ピアノを原智恵子に師事。1949年以来毎日コンクール作曲部門に3度入賞。1952年渡米して、ニューヨークのジュリアード音楽院、ニュー・スクールなどで学び、1959年以後ジョン・ケージに師事した。そしてケージの不確定性の音楽の思想の影響を深くうけた。ニューヨークその他で作曲活動をつづけたのち、1961年帰国。草月会館で作品発表会をひらいたり、20世紀音楽研究所、ニューディレクションのメンバーとして、活発な音楽活動をつづけた。

1966年5月には、武満徹と組んで、〈オーケストラ・スペース〉第1回現代音楽演奏会をひらいた。1966年11月、再度渡米。これまでの不確定性の音楽の追求を、さらにエレクトロニックスの可能性と結びつけて、ライヴ・エレクトロニック・ミュージックの方法による作品をこころみはじめた。アメリカ各地やケルンなどで演奏活動をつづけたのち、昨1967年12月に帰国。

一柳慧の音楽は、つねにけしてかれの小さな自我やミクロコスモスを定着したものではない。逆に変化してやまない現実の環境のなかで自己の音への行為が緊張にたえてうみだしていく音のひとつの状況なのだ。そこではどのような音のイベントがうまれるか。それをかれは予測できない未知への賭けのように、たえず緊迫した自己と現実との状態としておくのである。そこには音楽をたんなる美的な〈作品〉として構築することを拒否してしまった新しい音の環境への精神の構えとでもいった態度がみられる。

(ICHYANAGI)
electronic work, Appearance makes no use of a tape recorder. Sounds fixed on tape in a studio are now only one dimension of the electronic music field. In live electronic music, performers participate in a live situation by means of electronic equipment; disparate elements including light, electronic transformation of sounds, visual images, spatial movement of sound, etc., can be readily combined during performance; not only performers, but members of the audience can contribute to the design of sound environments; electronic sound devices can also be integrated with computers in performance situations.

These only begin to suggest the power of the live electronic idea. The scope is unlimited. Appearance deals with a specific and limited part of this unlimited field, and, in future works, I plan to continue a systematic exploration of it. I hope that the listener will keep in mind not only the music itself, but the point of view.

The score is graphic and indicates only general characteristics of each sound, the exact nature of which is up to the performer. (A sound might be, for example, middle range, weak, and long.) But the score also requires each player to be constantly aware of what the other performers are doing. This may take the form of altering his sounds to coincide with the ways in which they are being transformed by the operators of the signal generators and ring modulators, or it may involve relating his sounds to those of another instrumentalist whose materials serve as a reference. (For example, a sound might be higher than the sound of the reference performer, stronger, and shorter.) The patterns of action for the operator of the ring modulators are assigned definite durations, but this does not influence the total duration of the work, which is indeterminate. ROBERT ASHLEY, born in 1930, graduated from the Manhattan School of Music and the University of Michigan. He, with George Cacioppo, Gordon Mumma, Roger Reynolds, and Donald Scavarda, co-founded the ONCE organization (1960) based in Ann Arbor, Michigan; and, with Gordon Mumma, he in co-director of The Cooperative Studio for Electronic Music. As a composer, musical director and coordinator, Ashley has been active widely in the United States, and in Europe where he first appeared as a participant in the 1963 Venice Festival. Most recently, Ashley has worked with the Sonic Arts Group (which also includes David Behrman, Alvin Lucier, and Gordon Mumma). This organization specializes in live electronic music. Several of Ashley's works are published by CPE (*), and Source magazine has included some of his provocative opinions. His music is available on Advance, ESP, and Columbia records. His works include: Public Opinion Descends Upon The Demonstrators (1961) (4 channels of electronic sound under the control of one performer); Detail for Two Pianists (1962); * in memoriam (1964-65) (a series of graphically and verbally described situations involving musicians and non-musicians); Wolfman (1964) (theater piece for amplified voice and tape); Combination Wedding and Funeral (1965) (theater piece); Frogs (1967), one section of a larger work entitled That Morning Thing (dancers and electronically altered voices); She Was A Visitor (divided chorus).

As early as 1961 Ashley speculated about the possibility "that the entire metaphor of music could change to such an extent that time being uppermost as a definition of music - the ultimate result would be a music that wouldn't necessarily involve anything but the presence of people. If our awareness of time increased to such a degree that it didn't require that we be informed of time through the medium of sound - if our awareness of time became enlarged or changed to a really radical degree - then it's conceivable that we could do away with sound." "Music," he continued, might become "markedly more subjective and particularly involved with a sort of indefinable sense of where (one's) time information was coming from."

Since then his own works have steadily moved in this direction, continually defining new patterns of interaction between performers. Ashley requires less of what is usually called musical skill from performers, more in the way of attentiveness and social skills. The straightforward task of following a detailed score is replaced by the broader demands of responding appropriately to a fluid situation, the details of which can never be accurately predicted. The performer cannot plan his actions or rehearse their sequence; he can only - through thought and practice - become more familiar with the terrain of each individual situation as the composer poses it.

Ashley stresses that there are very beautiful and important things that cannot be put on paper, and he now prefers compositions that are generated through discussion and practice by a group of interested persons. As he said in a recent issue of Source magazine, "We have to create ensemble situations that allow those things that only happen once...that are not dimensions but just moments. They are as much social as they are musical. They are very mysterious. ... You can (listen to) a piece and say that this is a very beautiful moment, but there is no way to recreate that moment. The moment is the result of this peculiar ensemble situation that you're listening to. As a composer I feel, naturally, that I must try to create these social relationships that make music. In Esteban Gómez I try to bring those four guys together in such a way that it's comparable to a rock and roll recording session. It's a social event. It's an ensemble event."

ロバート・アシュレー

1930年生れのアメリカの作曲家。マンハッタン音楽学校とミシガン大学を卒業してのち、かれは1960年にミシガン州のアン・アルボールで前衛音楽グループ〈ワンス〉を組織。ジョージ・カチオポ、ゴードン・ムンマ、ロジャー・レイノルズ、ドナルド・スカバルダらが中核メンバーだった。

そのごはゴードン・ムンマと電子音楽のための〈コーポレイティヴ・スタジオ〉の音楽監督として活動。またいっぽうでは〈ソニック・アート〉グループをデヴィッド・バーマン、アルヴィン・ルシェ、ゴードン・ムンマと組織、もっぱらライヴ・エレクトロニック・ミュージックをうみだしている。

アシュラーの名は、われわれにはまだあまりなじみがないかもしれないが、アメリカやヨーロッパでは、すでに若い実験的な作曲家として注目されているひとりである。かれはケージ以後の新しい音楽観をつねにつきつけている。ライヴ・エレクトロニック・ミュージックのまったくユニークなその作品のうちには、はっきりとかれの新しい思想がうかがえる。

ことに音楽における古典的な時間の観念を徹底的に拒否して、ひとびとの「現在＝瞬間の体験」の重要さを強調しつづけている。音楽では、つねに時間構造だけがとくに発達してきたということがいえるかもしれない。調性音楽はコードの時間的順序の上になりたった理論であり、セリエール音楽にしても、時間上に展開される。もしわれわれが、こうした時間の概念にとりつかれれば、とりつかれるほど、音の問題は遠くおいやられることになりかねない。そこでアシュラーは、瞬間瞬間の音と人間との生き生きとした直接の結びつき、体験を強調するわけである。

「音楽とは、もっときわだって内的なものになるべきである。そしてとりわけ、その場での名づけがたい感覚といったようなもので包みこんでしまうようなものであるはずだ」

「音楽的というよりも、もっと社会的なアンサンブルの状況を創造すること。作曲家はこのような社会的なリレーションシップを創造すべきであろうし、それが音楽を生みだすことなのだ」

「わたしはこのような方向を、この作品では４人の人たちを一緒にすることでこころみた。」とアシュラーはいっている。

この〈エステバン・ゴメツ＝四重奏曲〉は、〈イン・メモリアム〉の一部にあたる作品で、他の〈クレージー・ホース〉（ジョン・スミス）〈キット・カーソン〉と組みあわさって一組をなす。1964年に作曲された作品だが、音符はまったく使われていない。円形が描かれた図形楽譜とインストラクションだけによる。奏者は円周に沿って、一定の時間を定めて円形楽譜を読んでいく。そして各４円にそれぞれ音の高さ、強弱、音色、密度をあてはめ、自分のきめた配列にしたがって演奏していく。演奏はまず各楽器の特性や音色がきわだたないような、ひとつの融けあったクラスター（音響母体）として奏される。つまり基礎音色といってもよい。そのご、この基礎音色から離れて演奏したものに気づいた場合は、すでにきめた音要素の自分の配列をずらさなければならない。こうした相互のリレーションによって、この音楽は変化しひとつのアンサンブルをうみだしていく。

なお四重奏曲とはいえ、４人の奏者の楽器は指定されていない。各奏者の選択にまかされているのだ。

作曲者は、この作品をかなりテンポの速い作品だとしている。しかしテンポといっても、従来の音楽的な時間的速度ではなく、各奏者が円周のパルスを数える行為によってきまってくるものだ。つまり作曲者は各奏者ができるかぎり最少単位（それ以上には分割できないように感じられる個人の自発的な最少単位と楽譜に指定されている）で、つぎつぎと物事をうみだしていくのを意図しているのである。だから各奏者のすばやい反応や演奏にしたがって、生みだされていくものも、多くなる。「これこそが、いい演奏によって“伝達される”ものというべきものだ」とアシュラーはいっている。「この意味で、この作品はまた、ソフトな作品、静かな作品」であるともいっている。

なおついでながら、この題名のエステバン・ゴメツとは、ゴードン・ムンマによれば、ポルトガルの有名な地図製作家であるという。かれの右にでる製図家はいなかったほどだというがまた想像上の道を描きこんだりしたニセ地図を製作したかなり奇怪な男だったといわれる。

=== Page 31 ===
(ASHLEY, ICHIYANAGI)

ESTEBAN GÓMEZ (quartet) (1964) is one of a set, in memoriam, that also includes Crazy Horse (symphony), John Smith (concerto), and Kit Carson (opera). Although none of the traditional means for writing music are used, they are all notated lucidly and economically. Esteban Gómez is concerned with very subtle and gradual deviations from a "reference sonority, within which the individual instruments are not distinguishable." There are four areas in which deviation may occur: pitch, intensity (loudness), timbre (tonal color), and density (the mixing and combining of tonal ingredients).

The work begins with the reference sonority. At any time one of the players may begin a slow and systematic departure from his contribution to the reference sonority. As soon as this deviation is noticed by another player, that player's pattern of responses changes. All action and reaction is strictly individual with no clues or cues deliberately given. For the listener as well as for the performer, everything depends on attentiveness, on experiencing the subtle shifts between unanimity and dissent. The composer writes that Esteban Gómez is "a fairly 'fast' piece. That is, in the only realm that counts, things happen fairly quickly around the player's decisions, and a lot of things are going on for him. This seems to be 'communicated' in a good performance. It is also, for obvious reasons, usually a soft (pp) piece...."

Gordon Mumma writes that "Esteban Gómez was a Portuguese cartographer. His fame in history was that he made the best maps of his time, for anyone who would pay for them. And he was particularly good at making fake maps, when properly reimbursed, in order to slow up the explorations of rival countries."

TOSHI ICHIYANAGI was born in Kobe, Japan, in 1933. He studied composition with Chieko Hara and Tomojiro Ikenouchi in Japan, and with John Cage during a long period of residence in the United States (1956-61). Ichiyanagi has been active as a performer (piano) and as an organizer of concerts including "New Directions" (begun in 1963), and, with Toru Takemitsu, the "Orchestral Space" festival (begun in 1966). His compositions cover a wide variety including solo piano pieces, chamber works for traditional Japanese instruments, tape music, live electronic music, film scores, sound environments, etc. Widely performed, Ichiyanagi's music is regularly included on programs and festivals of new music throughout the world. C. F. Peters Corporation (*) and CPE publish his compositions, some of which are recorded on Columbia and Victor (Japan). Chamber music works: * Extended Voices (chorus) (1967); * Nagaoka (string quartet) (1964); * Pratyahara (7 performers) (1963); * Sapporo (15 performers and 1 conductor) (1962); * Space (biwa and piano) (1967). Live electronic works: * Activities (live electronic ensemble) (1967); * Situation (biwa, koto, violin, doublebass, piano and multiplier) (1966). Orchestra works: * Activities (live electronic ensemble and orchestra) (1967); * The Field (shakuhachi and orchestra) (1966); * Life Music (orchestra, magnetic tape and electronic sound breaker) (1964-66). Piano works include * Music for Piano #2 - #7 (1959-61), and theater works include * Music for Electric Metronomes (1960).

APPEARANCE was composed in New York City during February of 1967, and was first performed under the direction of Larry Austin and David Tudor at Davis, California on March 30 of the same year. THE ROYAL VICTORIAN LIEDERTAFEL

And it was Olav Trygvason,
Sailing on the north sea wide,
Bearing the hope to found a kingdom,
Far on the other side.
Yonder the cliffs appearing,
Like a battlement loom their dark crests rearing.
And it was Olav Trygvason,
Found he ne'er a spot of land,
E'en like the waves, the royal desire
Shattered upon the strand.
"See!" cried the bard upleaping,
"Yonder snow-covered peaks o'er cloud bands peeping."

And it was Olav Trygvason,
Suddenly he seemed to sight
Towering temples, domes and spires,
Glist'ning in virgin white.
Then vowed the king undaunted,
With his followers to tread that land enchanted.

Onward he went; the rushing streams
Heralded the coming spring.
Swayed in the stormy wind, the forest strangely was murmuring
Sounds as of churchbells chiming.
And then spake the king,
Spake as tho' dreaming;
"Here the spot to found our kingdom!
Hell! these temple walls defy thee!
Hearts are swelling, souls are yearning,
God, to thee alone be glory.

"Be my faith as yonder mountains,
Root as deeply, shine as purely;
And as these my faith strive upwards.
On to Him, the All Creator,
Olav's prayer be ours to utter,
As we near the throne of mercy.
Hearts are swelling, souls are yearning
God, to thee alone be glory.
    On to God! On to God!"

DRAKE'S DRUM

Drake, he's in his hammock, and a thousand miles away
(Captain, art thou sleeping there below?)
Slung atween the round shot in Nombre Dios Bay,
And dreaming all the time of Plymouth Hoe.
Yonder lumes the island, yonder lie the ships.
With sailor lads advancing heel-an'-toe,
And the shore-lights flashing, and the night-tide dashing,
He sees it all so plainly as he saw it long ago.

Drake, he was a Devon man, and ruled the Devon seas
(Captain, art thou sleeping there below?)
Roving tho' his death fell, he went with heart at ease,
And dreaming all the time of Plymouth Hoe.
"Take my drum to England, hang it by the shore,
Strike it when your powder's running low;
If the Dons sight Devon, I'll quit the port of Heaven,
And drum them up the Channel as we drummed them long ago."

Drake, he's in his hammock till the great Armada's come
(Captain, art thou sleeping there below?)
Slung atween the round shot, list'ning for the drum,
And dreaming all the time of Plymouth Hoe.

Call him on the deep sea, call him up the Sound,
Call him when ye sail to meet the foe;
Where the old trade's plying and the old flag's flying,
They shall find him ware and waking, as they found him long ago!

OUTWARD BOUND

Dear Earth, near Earth, the clay that made us men.
The land we sowed,
The heart that glowed.—
O Mother, must we bid farewell to thee?
Fast dawns the last dawn, and what shall comfort then
The lonely hearts that roam the outer sea?

Gray wakes the daybreak, the shivering sails are set,
To misty deeps
The channel sweeps,—
O Mother, think on us who think on thee!
Earth-home, birth-home, with love remember yet
The sons in exile on the eternal sea.

DEVON, O DEVON, IN WIND AND RAIN

Drake, in the North Sea grimly prowling,
Treading his dear Revenge's deck.
Watch'd, with the sea-dogs round him growling,
Galleons drifting wreck by wreck.

"Fetter and Faith for England's neck,

Yonder the Devil and all go howling,
  Devon, O Devon, in wind and rain!"
Drake at the last off Nombre lying,
  Knowing the night that towards him crept,
Gave to the sea-dogs around him crying
  This for a sign before he slept:—
"Pride of the West! what Devon hath kept
  Devon shall keep on tide or main:
Call to the storm and drive them flying,

Volour of England gaunt and whitening,

HOMEWARD BOUND

After long labouring in the windy ways,
  On smooth and shining tides,
Swiftly the great ship glides,
  Her storms forgot, her weary watches past!
Northward she glides, and thro' the enchanted haze
  Faint on the verge her far hope dawns at least,
The phantom skyline of a shadowy down
  Whose pale white cliffs below,
Thro' sunny mists aglow,
  Like noonday ghosts of summer moonshine gleam—
Soft as old sorrow, bright as old renown,
  There lies the home of all our mortal dream.

THE OLD SUPERB

The wind was rising easterly, the morning sky was blue,
  The straits before us opened wide and free;
We looked towards the Admiral, where high the Peter flew,
  And all our hearts were dancing like the sea.
The foe are gone to Martinique with four and twenty sail,
  The "Old Superb" is old and foul and slow!
But the foe are gone to Martinique, and Nelson's on the trail,
  And where he goes the "Old Superb" must go.

So Westward ho! for Trinidad, and Eastward ho! for Spain,
  And "Ship ahoy!" a hundred times a day;
Round the world if need be, and round the world again,
  With a lame duck lagging all the way.
The "Old Superb" was barnacled and green as grass below,
  Her sticks were only fit for stirring grog;
The pride of all her midshipmen was silent long ago,
  And long ago they ceased to heave the log.
Four years out from home she was, and ne'er a week in port,
  And nothing save the guns aboard her bright;
But Captain Keats he knew the game, and swore to share the sport,
  For he never yet come in too late to fight.
  So Westward ho; etc.

"Now up, my lads," the Captain cried,
  "For sure the case were hard,
If longest out were first to fall behind;
  Aloft, aloft with studding-sails, and lash them on the yard,
For night and day the Trades are driving blind."
So all day long and all day long behind the fleet we crept,
  And how we fretted none but Nelson guessed;
But ev'ry night the "Old Superb," she sail'd while others slept,
  Till we ran the foe to earth with all the rest.
  O 'twas Westward ho! etc.
