THE Musical Society of Victoria

ANNUAL REPORT
FOR YEAR 1907-8.

THE Council have much pleasure in presenting their Annual Report and Balance-Sheet for 1907-8. Perusal of the transactions of the Society, both on the artistic and financial sides, will show that the year has been one of the most successful yet recorded. The programmes have not only maintained their high-class character, but have also been up-to-date as regards modern music. Owing to the large increase in the attendance the question of a larger hall will have to be considered in the near future.

NEW MEMBERS.—During the year thirty-nine new members were elected.

EXAMINATIONS.—The Examinations conducted by the Society are without doubt a distinct advantage to the community. In studying for these Examinations, students have an aim and purpose. They go into detail more minutely, their attention is more concentrated, and both teacher and pupil know that they cannot ensure success unless they are thoroughly conscientious, determined and whole-souled in their work. The Council would therefore strongly urge all members to prepare students for the Society's Examinations.

The Julius Siede Prize (Preparatory section) was won by Ethel L. Harder and Jean E. Spence (equal) at the November Examination, 1907; and by Foster Nutting, at the May Examination, 1908.

The Special Prize for highest aggregate, with credit, in the Elementary section, at the November Examination, 1907, was awarded to Clarice E. Freeman. The Bronze Medal, for highest aggregate, with credit, in the Intermediate section, at the November Examination, 1907, to Daisy Clarice Purvis (Piano) and Gertrude Carruthers (Violin) equal; and at the May Examination, 1908, to Margaret E. Inglis, Kyneton.

GENERAL MEETINGS.—Ten general meetings and musical evenings have been held, the programme at the June meeting,

=== Page 5 ===
1907, consisting of items by candidates who had gained the highest marks in their respective sections at the previous Examination. The At Home, which was held at Glen's, on February 15th, 1908, was well attended, and a very pleasant evening was spent.

The BALANCE-SHEET shows the Society's finances are in a very satisfactory condition, after paying all expenses the credit balance standing at £228 5s. 4d.

THE LIBRARY.—The additions to the Library during the year were ten operas, in vocal score, presented by Mr. E. H. Hanstein. "Counterpoint, Canon and Fugue," Ousley; "Harmony," Ousley; "Counterpoint" 2 vols., Chernubini, presented by Mr. J. H. Hammond. "The Art of Singing," Henderson; "Quintet, Op. 77," (strings) Dvorak.

COUNCIL MEETINGS.—Fifteen Council Meetings were held, the attendances being as follows: W. H. Heathcote 15, G. Peake 14, H. Curtis 14, S. Lamble 14, Gregor Wood 12, W. Hunter 12, T. J. Lamble 12, M. Greer 12, G. H. Davies 10, A. Zelman 8, E. H. Hanstein 6 (resigned Nov. 1907), H. J. Inge 4, (elected Feb. 1908).

During the year Mr. Gregor Wood and Mr. E. H. Hanstein resigned the offices of Vice-President and Treasurer respectively. The vacancies were filled by the appointment of Mr. Inge as Vice-President and Mr. Gregor Wood as Hon. Treasurer.

The thanks of the Society are due to Messrs. W. H. Glen and Co. for the gratuitous use of their premises as the office of the Society, and to Mr. F. L. Wilson, F.C.P.A., for professional services as auditor.

OBITUARY.—Mr. J. C. W. Nicholson, of the well-known music firm, an honorary member of the Society, passed away in September, 1907. Although living in Sydney, Mr. Nicholson was noted for his liberal gifts to Musical Societies of Melbourne, and his unfailing kindness to musicians generally. It is to be hoped that his generous spirit and practical interest in this and other Musical Societies of Melbourne will inspire others in like position to emulate his example.

To the incoming Council, and to all members of the M.S.V., we would seriously urge that vigilant attention be given to the administration of the Registration of Teachers Act.

GEORGE PEAKE, PRESIDENT.
W. H. HEATHCOTE, SECRETARY.
31st May, 1908.

=== Page 6 ===
PRESIDENT'S ADDRESS,
at the Annual Meeting, 20th June, 1908.

LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,--

At the Annual Meeting it is the President's privilege to inflict you with an address, and this evening I desire to speak briefly on the aim and objects of this Society. I have selected this subject as there is evidence that some of the members have no clear idea of the advantage of belonging to it. Unless we have a very real and sincere conviction that the objects of the Society are worthy of our membership, we certainly shall not be able to maintain that energy and enthusiasm of the immediate past, which have done so much to increase our list of members, and strengthen our individual attachment.

In the April issue of The Musical Times, we learn that a new organisation has just been formed, under the title of the Musical League, with Sir Edward Elgar as President, and Sir A. C. Mackenzie, H. J. Wood, Granville Bantock, Percy Pitt, F. Delius, Dr. Brodsky and Dr. McNaught as Members of Committee. Its objects are:

I. To foster the cause of music in England, and to promote the development of musical life and culture throughout the country.
II. By holding an Annual Festival, introducing new compositions, and also older works whose merits entitle them to more frequent performance.
III. By affording opportunity for exchange of ideas upon questions of interest to musicians.
IV. By watching every proposed legislation that may affect them.
V. By taking steps, when necessary, to promote or prevent such legislation.
VI. To assist necessitous musicians of merit in cases of sickness or undeserved misfortune.

I have quoted the above because with the exception of the Annual Festival those objects are identical with the objects of the Musical Society of Victoria. Reference to past transactions will show that the Society has endeavoured to encourage local composers, with the result that original string quartets, a piano and string trio, violin solos and songs, by various local composers, have been introduced from time to time in the Society's programmes. The Society also offered prizes for the best string quartet, part-song or glee, and I am sure I voice the opinion of the whole Society when I say they would be delighted to hear meritorious works by Australian composers more frequently at our meetings.

=== Page 7 ===
In introducing other new works, and "older works whose merits entitle them to more frequent performance," this Society has a splendid record, and one that any Society may well be proud of. Let it be remembered that for many years there would have been no opportunity of hearing the so-called chamber classics but for the existence of the M.S.V. We do not forget the efforts of private enterprise in the sixties, the popular concerts of the late Mr. T. H. Guenett, or those splendid quartet concerts of the last two years given by the Melbourne String Quartet, but in the long interregnum between these efforts, and throughout the whole period, the M.S.V. kept the flag flying, largely by the untiring and unselfish work of its then members, who, without fee or reward, gave us month after month and year after year of their best.

As regards watching proposed legislation that may affect the profession, it may be pointed out that the M.S.V. were mainly instrumental in securing for the individual teacher's pupils the favored treatment as regards train fares, which the Railway Department had given to the pupils of colleges and corporate bodies only. The Society also initiated the movement whereby the whole profession received some recognition of their work by the Registration Board, and here let me say that unless members of the musical profession are content to be placed at the mercy of one set of individuals, one school of thought, and to be deprived of that freedom which is the very life blood of artistic existence and of skilful teaching, they will require to give vigilant attention to the administration of the Registration of Teachers' Act. I may here also express my opinion that in view of the enormous sums by which distinguished visiting artists reduce the spending power of the community, they ought not to demand full price from the members of the musical profession for admission to their concerts. It is reported that the Clara Butt tour realised £51,000, and Madame Melba's few concerts £10,000, yet the musical profession, who, by their teaching, practically create the constituency which these visitors exploit, receive no consideration or concession when attending the concerts.

Another object of the Society is "to assist necessitous musicians of merit in cases of sickness or undeserved misfortune," for which purpose a substantial Benevolent Fund exists. The foregoing facts are sufficient to show that the M.S.V. has anticipated many of the objects for which Sir Edward Elgar, Sir A. C. Mackenzie and others in England now consider it necessary to form a Musical League.

So much for the objects of the Society. Now for the practical advantages offered to members. In the past we have had members resign, not because they could not afford to pay the subscription, but because they could not see that they obtained

=== Page 8 ===
any advantage in belonging to the Society. I have already named some of the advantages which the Society has secured, not alone for its members, but for the whole profession, and have also indicated that in the future the profession will need a strong Society to protect it from legislative injustice, unfair competition, and iniquitous taxation. But apart from these, members who can see no advantage in belonging to such a Society must be ignorant of the influence of environment. Musical environment is absolutely necessary to the development of a musical mind. In a Society like the M.S.V., consisting of professional musicians, members have an environment which the public can never supply. The members encourage performers to produce the highest and purest forms of musical art, but not so the general public. A well-known public singer was once privately taken to task by an eminent musical critic in England for not always singing high-class music. The reply of the singer was, "If I sing nothing but high-class music I must starve, for unless I sing some of the popular stuff I get no applause, if I get no applause I get no engagements, and if I get no engagements I must starve; I have therefore determined to sing one high-class number for my reputation's sake, and then any 'tommy rot' the public requires." Now, ladies and gentlemen, the environment supplied by this Society will never induce the performer to produce 'tommy rot' —to use that inelegant expression.

I venture to state that no musician not affected by the blindness of conceit or overweening egotism could attend the Society's meetings regularly without deriving very great advantage, that is, if he has got the breadth of mind and the capacity to receive it. An instrumentalist must profit by hearing a good vocalist, and vice versa; the opportunity of hearing new works before we purchase and study them ourselves is a great advantage, and a large acquaintance with the classics, whether for voice, violin, piano, or any combination of instruments, must widen conception and re-act favourably on artistic effort.

It has been contended that members should be paid for their services at our meetings, but as members of this Society are all professionals, it would be scarcely gracious to ask our professional brother to pay us for an occasional performance. Moreover, directly you introduce the practice of paying the members for their services at the monthly meetings you create a spirit that will eventually lead to competition for fees, and so probably destroy the fine spirit which should and does now permeate the whole Society. Surely, ladies and gentlemen, the twentieth century members of the Society are not going to be less unselfish, less interested in musical talent and the musical art of their country than were the nineteenth century members? You may be quite sure that Sir Edward Elgar and Sir A. C. Mackenzie,

=== Page 9 ===
whose names are famous throughout the musical world, are not launching the Musical League for any selfish motives, and if we allow the fair name of the M.S.V. to become tarnished by the breath of selfishness, we shall deserve and probably receive the condemnation of the whole profession. To me it is most inspiring and most gratifying to remember that in every effort in connection with this Society's meetings the members are working unselfishly and in the spirit of true brotherhood for each other and the community.

Ruskin has said, "You may be, after you have made your money, misers and usurers; you may be, after you have got your fame, jealous, proud, wretched and base; but yet, as long as you won't spoil your work, you are artists." Without disputing the dictum of Ruskin, I may be permitted to express the opinion that an artist who allows himself to be jealous, proud, wretched, base, or miserly has spoilt his character as a man, is devoid of gratitude to his Maker, and has lost all nobility, sympathy, dignity and true spirit of manhood, and, believe me, his work will lack sincerity whenever he seeks to portray those qualities.

All honour be given to those members, past and present, who most generously have acknowledged the gratitude they owe to their country and fellow citizens, and who, when opportunity offered, were ever willing, without fee or hope of reward, to do what they could for the uplift and advance of musical art or the welfare of the whole musical profession. Let us remember that all that we are and all that we have gained is due to the gift with which we are endowed, to the environment, and to the great musicians whom we shall never be able to repay. As far as fame, position and wealth are concerned, do we not owe it all, or nearly all, to our country or countrymen? By becoming members of this Society we can stimulate each other to greater exertion in the cause of art, can keep the community in some degree in touch with the most advanced musical thought, protect the musical profession from legislative injustice, and the selfish designs of grasping and greedy tyranny, and in this manner pay back some of the debt we owe to our country, and show our sincere gratitude for those heavenly compositions which the great masters have left us to use and enjoy. Unless a member is touched by some such influence, his membership is not likely to do himself or the Society much good, and unless some of the white heat of enthusiasm is to be found in our midst the Society must become decadent and moribund.

In conclusion, I trust that all members will live up to the dignity of their membership, and in the spirit of true brotherhood, not alone for what they can get out of the Society, but also for what they can do for each other, and for the art whereby they live and have their being.

THE ROYAL VICTORIAN LIEDERTAFEL

Programme

President: E. LIONEL WILSON.

Conductor: FREDERIC EARP.

Accompanist: ERIC FOX.

Harmony whose magic art
Voice to kindred voice unites,
Here thy choicest gifts impart;
Come and bless our festive rites.

PART I.

Part Song Setting of God Save the King
ROYAL VICTORIAN LIEDERTAFEL

Arr. Elgar

Ballet Madrigals—

(a) My Bonny Lass, She Smileth
(b) Now is the Month of Maying

ROYAL VICTORIAN LIEDERTAFEL

(a)
My bonny lass, she smileth,
When she my heart beguileth,
Fa, la, la!
Smiles less, dear love, therefore,
And you shall love me more,
Fa, la, la!
When she her bright eye turneth,
O, how my heart it burneth,
Fa, la, la!
Dear love, call in their light,
Or else you burn me quite.
Fa, la, la!

(b)
Now is the month of Maying,
When merry lads are playing,
Fa, la, la.
Each with his bonny lass,
A-dancing on the grass,
Fa, la, la.
The spring, clad all in gladness,
Doth laugh at winter's sadness,
And to the bagpipes' sound
The nymphs tread out the ground,
Fie, then, why sit we musing?
Youth's sweer delight refusing?
Say, dainty nymphs, and speak,
Shall we play barley-break?

These famous Madrigals are, of course, well known to mixed-voice choirs, but are rarely sung by men's choirs. We are indebted to Dr. Davison, the Conductor of the Harvard University Glee Club, for arranging them for male voices.

Songs of Historic Interest—

(a) Sumer is Icumen In Attributed to John Fornsette, a Monk of Reading Abbey, Circa. 1240.
(13th Century Round for Six Men)

Sumer is icumen in. Bude sing cuccu. Groweth sed and blometh.
Perspicie riviola que digna cacao. celicis agrico.
med and springt he rede nu. Sing cuccu Ave bletrep after la.
pro incil vico. filio — non parenti expoli.
lomb thou pastre callue cu — allue sterrep. bucke vertep.
it. morcis exicio — un captuq seminuos.
ajurie sing cuau. Cuccu cucui Wel singes pu cucui ne swik a suplicacio.
Vice donav et feanni aonat in ae.
link rotam cincare possint quattuor so ch. Apaono.
ribus autem qui a tribus ut talreem duobus no debeu.
dia pret es qui diate pedem. Cunte aut sic. Sacen.
by nauer nu. to li o.
in meam naram post enue. incheav alius. Sic de cetero.
singhi repauserit ad paulamens sfera.
nalihi: siao unum longe nore.
Voc repetit un quoscent opett.
sing cuau nu. Sing cuccu haecent paulamens in fine.
Pct.
hoc dictat: paulamens in modo tu m
sing cuau. Sing cuccu nu kine. Si immediate repetit pricipu.

(Reduced reproduction of original MS. in British Museum.)

THE ROYAL VICTORIAN LIEDERTAFEL

GRACE SIMPSON, Sydney's Brilliant Young Coloratura Soprano.

=== Page 8 ===
THE ROYAL VICTORIAN LIEDERTAFEL

(b) Agincourt
(A Song of Victory to welcome King Henry V. on his return to London, 1415)
Arr. Frederic Earp

(c) Pastime With Good Company
(Composed by King Henry VIII.) Arr. Frederic Earp

ROYAL VICTORIAN LIEDERTAFEL

(a)
Summer is a-coming in,
Loud now sing cuckoo,
Groweth seed and bloweth mead,
And spring the woods anew.
Ewe now bleateth after lamb,
Loweth after calf the cow,
Bullock starteth, buck now darteth,
Merry sing cuckoo.

Cuckoo, cuckoo, well singest thou, cuckoo,
Nor cease thou never now.

(b)
Owre Kynge went forth to normandie,
with grace and myght of chyvalrie
ther God for him wrought mervulously
wher fore englande may calle and cry
Deo gracias.

* * * *
Than went owre Kynge with alle his oste
thorwe fraunce for alle the frenshe hoste
he spared no drede of lest ne moste
tyl he come to agincourt coste
Deo gracias.

* * * *
Ther dukys and erlys lorde and barone
wer take and slayne and that wel sone
and summe wer ladde unto Lundone
with joye and merthe and grete renone
Deo gracias.
Now gracius God he save owre Kynge
his peple and alle his wel wyllynge
gef him gode lyf and gode endyng
that we with merth mowe savely synge
Deo Gracias.

(c)
Pastymye with good companye
I love, and schall untyl I dye
Gruche who lust but none denye,
So God be plesyd thus leve wyll I.
For my pastance, hunt, syng, and daunce;
My hart is sett,
At goodly sport
For my comfort,
Who schal me let?

Companye with honeste
Is vertu, vices to fle.
Companye is good or ill, but evry man hath
hys fre wyll.
The best ensen,
The worst eschew.
My mynde schal be
Vertu to use,

THE ROYAL VICTORIAN LIEDERTAFEL

Folk Songs—

(a) Bushes and Briars (Essex) Arr. Vaughan Williams
(b) Ca' Hawkie Thro' the Watter (Northumberland) Arr. W. G. Whittaker
(Presented by Mr. A. Valentine Soul)
(c) The British Grenadiers (17th Century) Arr. Percy Fletcher

ROYAL VICTORIAN LIEDERTAFEL

(a)
Through bushes and through briars
I lately took my way,
All for to hear the small birds sing
And the lambs to skip and play.
I overheard my own true love,
Her voice it was so clear:
"Long time I have been waiting
For the coming of my dear.
Sometimes I am uneasy and troubled in my mind,
Sometimes I think I'll go to my love,
And tell to him my mind,
And if I should go to my love,
My love, he will say nay;
If I show to him my boldness,
He'll ne'er love me again.
If I show my boldness he'll ne'er love me again."

(b)
Ca' Hawkie, through the watter,
Hawkie is a sweir beast,
And Hawkie winna wade the watter,
Hawkie is a bonnie coo!
Tho' she's loath to wade the watter,
While she waits the work'll stand,
So ca' Hawkie through the watter,
Hawkie winna wade the watter,
Hawkie is a prettier coo!
All the children do adore her,
For she gives them all the milk,
There is none they prize before her!
Girls, be not too nice or coy,
If you swear a man to marry;
Ne'er say nay, but quickly comply,
As 'tis hazardous to tarry.
Now, young maids, my counsel take,
Since that it can be no better:
Cast off baith your hose and shoon,
And safely drive her through the watter.

GLOSSARY FOR CA' HAWKIE.
Ca—Call.
Watter—Water.
Sweir—Unwilling.
Baith—Both.

Shoon—Shoes.
Winna—Will not.
Coo—Cow.

(c)
Some talk of Alexander, and some of Hercules;
Of Hector and Lysander, and such great names as these;
But of all the world's brave heroes there's none that can compare
With a tow row row row row row row
To the British Grenadiers.

Those heroes of antiquity ne'er saw a cannon ball,
Or knew the force of powder to slay their foes withal;
But our brave boys do know it, and banish all their fears;
Sing tow row row row row row row,
For the British Grenadiers.

When e'er we are commanded to storm the palisades,
Our leaders march with fuses, and we with hand grenades;
We throw them from the glacis about the enemies' ears;
Sing tow row row row row row row
For the British Grenadiers.

And when the siege is over, we to the town repair,
The townsman cry, "Hurra, boys! here comes a Grenadier."
Here come the Grenadiers, my boys, who know no doubts or fears,
Then sing tow row row row row row row
For the British Grenadiers.

Then let us fill a bumper and drink a health to those
Who carry caps and pouches and wear the louped clothes;
May they and their commanders live happy all their years,
With a tow row row row row row row
For the British Grenadiers.

PART II.

Let brother to brother good fellowship proffer:
    Apollo invites us, come bow at his shrine.
The glee and the catch are the incense we offer,
    The bond that unites us is music divine.

Chorus, Introduction to Act I., "Ernani"—
    The Bandit                Verdi

ROYAL VICTORIAN LIEDERTAFEL

All welcome the bowl!
A full flowing soul,
    Unfathomed by care!
What boots it the bandit,
If hunted and branded,
    So wine be his share!

    To play, sirs!
Treasure is merely a pleasure
    That flies soon as come!
And play hath a duty,
It charmeth when beauty
    Inconstant may roam.

Thrice welcome the bowl!
Whose glorious soul
    Doth bleed at our call!
The bowl, the bowl,
Whose glorious soul, sirs,
    Doth bleed at our call.

Ernani, still pensive?
    Quick thought grows apprehensive
        To view his cheek so blanch'd
    Where life's tide hath motion,
On Death's shoreless ocean
    Our one bark is launched.

    To give, then thy willing
Immediate fulfilling,
    Ere will'd we prepare.
The hawk's speed 'gan tarries
In hitting her quarries,
    If ours ye compare.

    Come, welcome the bowl,
Whose glorious soul
    Can drown all thy care!

LESLIE McCALLUM. Baritone and Flautist.

I May No Longer Dream Armstrong Gibbs
(Presented by Mr. E. Casper)

ROYAL VICTORIAN LIEDERTAFEL

I may no longer dream
Here by the solitary tulip-tree
That Leirion waits for me;
Nor in the cool
Shade of the sombre cypress look to see
Narcissus, bowed above the marble rim,
Blurring with crystal tears his image in the pool.

I may no more esp'y
By yonder mouldering plinth,
Lord Eros, veiled, with lanthorn lifted high,
Guiding his virgin train,
Hippolytus, Adonis, Hyacinth,
Hylas and Agathon—
Lilies new-blown and clear of earthly stain—
Home to the unguessed heights of his serene domain.
Ah me! ah me!
Must I go mourn for earth-born phantoms fled,
And those Uranian summers lived in vain?
Nay, fond, inveterate lover!

Now, now at last lift up a joyful head!
Thy perilous day is done,
The blessed night draws on—
Love is no dream, as thou wilt prove tomorrow,
When thou shalt wake to find Him standing at thy side.
See where the quiet garden waits for thee!
The sheltering boughs their evening balm have shed;
Dear memories, undefiled;
Gather like dew; closer the shadows creep.
Beneath thy chosen Leirion-haunted tree
Make thou thy lonely bed;
Lie down and rest, by no false dreams beguiled;
With folded hands pray God thy soul to keep,
Even as a little child,
Weary, and very glad because of coming sleep.

—Paul England.

LESLIE McCALLUM

"Young Dietrich"—Words after the German of Felix Dahn.
Defeated and slain with half of his host,
Was Theodemerus, King of the Goths.
The Huns were shouting with fiendish mirth,
The vultures hastened down to earth:
The moon was bright, the wind was cold,
The wolves were howling in distant wold.
Three men were riding through heather and field,
Their helmets battered, and broken their shield.
The first one bore in his saddle sling
The broken spear of his murdered King;
The second, he bore the King's crown, Oh, woe!
Split straight in two, by the axe of a foe.
The third, he hid in faithful arm
A secret veiled in his mantle warm,
A veiled secret!
And when they the river Iser espied,
The first one rested his horse and cried:
"Save a battered crown and a broken spear,
Of the Gothic Kingdom is naught to fear"!

=== Page 12 ===
THE ROYAL VICTORIAN LIEDERTAFEL

And the second, he said, "In those waters deep,
Let us bury our treasure for ever to sleep,
Then follow ourselves, by a leap from the sand;
Why tarry, Master Hildebrand?"
"Ye carry the King's own crown and spear:
My faithful companions, far more have I here."

Thus saying, he opened his cloak so warm;
"I carry the hope of the Goths in my arm.
Ye saved crown and spear, 'twas bravely done;
I—I have rescued the King's own son!
Awake now, my boy, see how homage I bring.
I greet thee Young Dietrich, the Goths' new King."

=== Page 2 ===
Dear Sir or Madam,

As announced at the last Concert of the Melbourne Liedertafel, it is the intention of the Society to tender the Conductor, Mr. August Siede, a Complimentary Concert on the eve of his departure for Europe, and I trust that you will accord this movement your patronage, and the loyal support which it merits.

This will be the first time in the musical annals of Australasia that an Australian Composer and Conductor has been sent to the artistic centres of the Old World to develop those natural gifts which it is acknowledged Mr. Siede possesses: and I am pleased to state that our distinguished visitor, Madame Melba, has shown her interest in this project by assuring us of her heartiest support, and has also signified her intention of being present at the Concert.

The programme, which will be compiled on popular lines, will be contributed by a number of our leading artists, and the full Choir and Orchestra of the Liedertafel; and considering the short notice that is necessarily given to the public, I beg to emphasise my appeal that you will kindly spare no effort to ensure the success of the undertaking.

I am,
Yours faithfully,
JOHN ADCOCK,
Hon. Sec.

Programme.

Under the Baton of
Mr. August Siede.

Part 1.

BALLAD—

"Lord Ullin's Daughter"

Hamish MacCunn

Liedertafel,
Associated Ladies' Choir,
and Orchestra.

A CHIEFTAIN to the highlands bound
Cries "Boatman, do not tarry!
And I'll give thee a silver pound
To row us o'er the ferry."

"Now who be ye would cross Lochgyle
This dark and stormy water?"
"Oh, I'm the chief of U'vas' Isle,
And this, Lord Ullin's daughter."

And fast before her father's men,
Three days we've fled together,
And should he find us in the glen,
My blood would stain the heather.

His horsemen hard behind us ride;
Should they our steps discover,
Then who will cheer my bonny bride,
When they have slain her lover?

Out spake the hardy highland wight,
"I'll go, my chief, I'm ready!
It is not for your silver bright,
But for your winsome lady.

And by my word, the bonny bird
In danger shall not tarry,
So though the waves are raging white,
I'll row you o'er the ferry."

=== Page 7 ===
By this the storm grew loud apace,
The water wraith was shrieking,
And in the scowl of heaven each face
Grew dark as they were speaking.

But still as wilder blew the wind,
And as the night grew drearer,
Adown the glen rode armed men,
Their tramping sounding nearer.

"Oh haste thee, haste!" the lady cries,
"Though storms around us gather,
I'll meet the raging of the skies,
But not an angry father."

The boat has left the stormy land,
A stormy sea before her,
When, oh, too strong for human hand,
The tempest gather'd o'er her.

And still they rowed amidst the roar
Of waters fast prevailing:
Lord Ullin reached the fatal shore,
His wrath was changed to wailing.

For sore dismayed, thro' storm and shade,
He did his child discover:
One lovely arm she stretched for aid,
And one was round her lover.

"Come back, come back!" he cried in grief
Across the stormy water,
And I'll forgive your Highland chief,
My daughter! oh, my daughter!"

'Twas vain: the loud waves lashed the shore,
Return or aid preventing,
The waters wild went o'er his child,
And he was left lamenting.

"Oberon"

Weber

The Orchestra.

=== Page 8 ===
"ELEGY"

Specially Composed for and Dedicated to the Melbourne Liedertafel

By August Siede

(Conducted by the Composer.)

MR. SIEDE'S composition is for full chorus and orchestra, and is entitled "Elegy," the words being selected from the three last wonderful stanzas of Shelley's "Adonais." This work bears few or no traces of the novice, its technique is mastery, both in the severe grip of form and in the polyphonic style of the part writing. It is above all fermented by vivid poetic feeling from first to last. Its deep sadness shows never a touch of morbidity, but is permeated by a certain objective grandeur, which at times is imposing.

WHY linger, why turn back, why shrink, my heart?
Thy hopes are gone before: from all things here
They have departed; thou should'st now depart!

The soft sky smiles, the low wind whispers near;
'Tis Adonais calls! Oh, hasten thither,
No more let Life divide what Death can join together.

That Light whose smile kindles the universe,
That Beauty in which all things work and move,
That Benediction, which the eclipsing Curse
Of birth can quench not,
Now beams on me
Consuming the last clouds of cold mortality.

The breath whose might I have invoked in song,
Decends on me: my spirit's bark is driven
Far from the shore, far from the trembling throng
Whose sails were never to the tempest given;
The massy earth and spher'd skies are riven!
I am borne darkly, fearfully, afar;
Whilst burning through the inmost veil of Heaven
The soul of Adonias, like a star,
Beacons from the abode where the Eternal are.

=== Page 9 ===
Part 2.

"Siegfried Idyll" Wagner
The Orchestra.

Scenes from...
OLAV TRYGVASON
(BJÖRNSTERNE BJÖNSON)
For Solo Voices, Choir and Orchestra.
By Edvard Grieg
Op. 50.

OLAV TRYGVASON, a descendent of Harold Haarfager (the first king of Norway), was brought up at the court of Gardarikke (Russia), and was baptised in England while on a Viking raid. When he learned that Norway was dissatisfied with her king (a scion of an older branch of the same race), he resolved upon conquering the kingdom and converting the people to Christianity. Richly endowed by nature, he was superior of all his contemporaries in bodily and spiritual gifts, and so comely to behold that none had seen his like; he was revered in the middle ages as the noblest example of the Norman race; he conquered more by his personality than by his sword. He commenced his struggle in the Drontheim district, and the beginning of this conflict is depicted in the scenes of the drama here set to music.

The action takes place in an ancient Norman temple in the Drontheim district, at the time of Olaf Trygvason's appearance. Period—End of the tenth century.

The Volva              Mr. E. A. Ure
A Sacrificer

Liedertafel.
Associated Ladies' Choir,
and Orchestra.

A Sacrificer—
THOU to whom fancy lends many titles,
    Giver of runes and of magic!
Working before the world's beginning,
Thou who outgazeth from Lidskialf.

Men—
Hear us!

A Woman—
Tender mother Frigga, sorrowing for Balder;
Bearing in thy bosom all worldly woe;
Comforter of Odin, nourisher of nature,
Drawing all life and care into Fensal.

Women—
Hear us!

The Sacrificer—
Trudyang's Hlorrida, Bilskirner's Yireflame,
Thou of the strength-belt and hammer,
Shield of the Aesir and of the Northmen,
Ever the dread of the giants.

Men—
Hear us;

The Woman—
Beauteous weeping goddess, silent widow Vannadis
Love's dis-tress thine own loss taught unto thee!
Let our tears of sorrow with thine own be mingled;
Thou who dost govern half of the living.

Women—
Hear us!

The Sacrificer—
Horn-beating Heindal, Ull in Ydaler,
Nyord, mighty north-dweller, hear us!
Algenheim's joy, Landvida's sorrow,
Long-bearded minstrel, and thou Tyr.

=== Page 11 ===
Men—
Hear us!

The Woman—
Ever-youthful Idun, Sif of golden harvests,
Saga of the streamlet, Skada of the hills,
All ye mighty Aesir, Vanir and Valkyrie,
Here our complaining, earthward oh hasten!

Women—
Here us!

Men and women—
Other gods are now arising,
Gods of power, gods of battle:
Help us, Mitgard trembles,
Gods alone with gods can wrestle!

(All kneeling.)
Ye who from the Urdar fountains pour life-strength
into our bosoms,
Ye alone who know his will, the Father in gold-caped Gimle;
Ye in Odin's ear who whisper softly as each day
awakens,
Ye who were ere world's beginning,
Ye who will be when 'tis wasted,
Show our fates the way to him, the god so long
awaited—
Hear us!

The Volva—
(From an elevation in the foreground)—

'Tis not enough that ye invoke Nornir and Aesir,
Runes must be graven duly
Evil to disperse from the pathway which to the gods
doth lead.
There, see the gathered hosts
Upon their horns howling, to hide our voices,
That the gods never may hear us!

Men and women—
O prophetess mighty, rise in thy magic!
Fill heaven and earth with Odin's word!

The Volva—
(Raises herself so that she stands high above all the others)—

Spirits base, basely mastered, ye who come from the
southland,
With Hel soon shall feast be holden!
Plague shall gnaw, serpents send through your veins
deadly venom!
Let Hel's hounds awake, howling and foaming,
Monsters filled with madness, for your blood thirsting
blindly!
For Hel no fitter food can afford them!

=== Page 12 ===
With Hel! spirits base, basely mastered, ye who come from the southland,
With Hel, here in the north, your feast is.

Men and women—
O prophetess mighty, rise in thy magic!
Fill heaven and earth with Odin's word!

The Volva—
(Who has been carving runes now continues to cut eagerly)
Spirits base, basely mastered, ye who come from the southland,
To Hel soon shall your way be wended!
Evil ones away! the Thunderer's weapon awaits ye!
Runes I wrote on a staff I rent from the altar of Odin.
To Hel straightway its charm consigns ye.
To Hel! Runes will lead Lokis lot unto the doors of his daughters,
With Hel ye shall devour that writing.

(She casts the Rune-staff on the holy fire, which immediately bursts into flames that ascend to the roof of the Temple. A horrible din, accompanied by thunder in the distance, shakes the Temple.)

Men and women—
(Kneeling in terror)-
Wondrous word of Odin goes
To black abyss, to heaven's height,
Aweful, returneth the answer.

The Volva—
Answer came from Hel, from high gods;
All fear it, yet not I.
Now let us kneel to them!
Every path is free!
So I will pray them first.
Gods, ye holy, eternal gods!
Are ye here? Then heed me!
Where find we the fiat which governs our fate?
Where bends your balance, ordering all?
Show, ah! show to me, ye mighty ones,
Where ye will strike the evil Olaf?
Gods all-governing, endless, omnipotent Aesir; I pray;
Devoted to Odin from my youth.
By the grey wolf's heart, by the raven's tongue,
By my sacrifice in sleepness nights, I pray you!
Show me, mighty ones, where ye will strike the evil Olaf.

(A crash of thunder and the back of the Temple is shattered. The Temple is seen in the distance enclosed in flames and smoke. Thunder continually heard until the Temple becomes invisible.)

The Volva, men and women—
Here! here! hasten the holy ones!
Here! here! strikes him the vengeance of heaven!

=== Page 13 ===
In our hall he must enter,
Let him go in, ne'er to come forth again.

(With Mockery.)
Let this be told to him—
We will believe if he comes safely forth.
Let his god go in to our gods!
If he safely come forth, we will believe.

All— (Turning towards the gods)—
Thanks for the token, solace it sends to us.
Thanks for the token, faith it confirms!
Choice of thy children, come then, oh king, to us;
Come to thy children, strife will be short!
Now will the gods themselves go on their gladsome way,
Now will the gods themselves grant us their grace!
Lit from our land by fire, lo, he shall leave us;
Loki shall lighten him hence unto Hel!

(Assembling round the images of the gods.)
Three nights besought we, suing like son to sire,
Three nights we pleaded, heard is our prayer.

The Sacrificer and Elders having procured horns form a circle round the three "Holy Firs," afterwards advancing and seating themselves at the sides. The Sacrificer, having made the "hammer sign" over the horns, proceeds to render the following song.

The Sacrificer—
Raise high the horn, great host-father, Odin's horn,
Raise high the horn, upheave it for him.
High altar fires, and Akethor's hammer-sign.
High altar fires have hallowed it.

Men and women—
Gladly we join in
Games for the gracious god,
Gladly we join in
Outbursts of joy!

(Preparations are made by the people for a dance. The men leap over the "Holy Fire," lifting the women over on both sides. Then commences a Temple dance in which all join.)

Quartette—
Give to all gods a grace-cup of gratitude,
Give to all gods your greatest of gifts.

Men and women—
Horns fill for Akethor, Drontheimer's deity,
Fill them to Akethor, daring in fight.
    Gladly then, etc.
Fill up to Nyord and Frey, harvest and fish they send,
Fill up to Nyord and Frey, harvest fair, haul of fish,
To freedom, and faith.
    Gaily then, etc.

=== Page 14 ===
Beakers to Braga, bring we with holy vows,
Beakers to Braga, brimming we raise!
Offerings of flesh and blood
To Braga we all freely bring.
    Gaily then, etc.

    Women—
O ye Asynier, honour we offer thee,
All ye Asynier, honour and praise!
Nourish, oh mild ones, men with your mother milk,
Nourish us ye who move us with might!
Young men and maidens, grandsire and grandmother,
Honour for aye the gods ever green?
    Gaily then, etc.

    Men and women—
Glorious Disir, gliding like doves around!
Glorious Disir, death making glad!
Guarding ye, follow friendly our future fate,
Guarding ye, follow us, hail to your flight!
Fortune of fathers, holdeth the hamingja
Fortune of fathers and of the race.

    Women—
O ye Asynia, etc.

    Men and women—
Earthmen and Kobalds, deepening the ground for us
Earthmen and Kobalds, hail to your kind!
Hail to the highest spirit that hides in the hills!
Hail I tiny elves who frolic in flow'rs.
Hail our upholder, guardian of house and halls,
Hail who upholdshest harbour and holm.
    Gaily then, etc.

Faith of our fatherland, love thou dost light in us,
Faith of our fatherland, moving all men.
We will defend thee, fight for our father's faith,
We will defend thee, future be ours,
We will defend thee, source of our weal and woe,
We will defend thee, fount of great deeds.

Three nights besought we suing, like son to sire,
Three nights we prayed, and heard was our prayer
The first night offered we bowls of bloody sacrifice,
On the first offered we oxen with prayer.
Next night guest-offering gave we the gracious gods,
Over their images uttering prayer.
On the third night fair dream faces favoured us,
On the third night we danced and we sang,
Gladly we joined in games to the gracious gods
Gaily we joined in outbursts of joy.

Special Notice

The Council of the Liedertafel has much pleasure in announcing the successful inauguration of the "Siede Fund," which is being raised to enable our Conductor, Mr. August Siede, to pay a twelve months visit to Europe, to there study the latest developments in his art.

Many of Australia's most promising vocalists and instrumentalists have been sent to Europe, some of whom have achieved world-wide fame, but this is the first time that a proposal has been brought forward to send home an Australian composer and conductor, and the cordial co-operation of members and the musical public is invited to assist in bringing this movement to a successful issue.

=== Page 17 ===
The sum of £120 has already been subscribed and the Hon. Secretary will be pleased to receive subscriptions from any lady or gentleman desirous of furthering the movement.

will be tendered to
Mr. Siede, in the
Melbourne Town Hall
on
Monday evening, 24th November next,
which
Madame Melba
has most kindly promised to attend,
the date having been fixed at her special request.

JOHN ADCOCK,
Hon. Secretary.

During the winter of 1968-69, CROSS TALK will sponsor the first festival of live electronic music in Japan. Several guest composer/engineers from the United States are expected. In addition, general demonstrations for the public; special work sessions on basic technical resources (e.g., ring modulators, photo cells, computer applications, etc.); open rehearsals; experimental presentations; and public events are planned.

Later in the spring of 1969, several days of intermedia events will be held, including performances of IANNIS XENAKIS' Terretektorn for 88 players seated among a circularly arranged audience; JOHN CAGE's as yet incomplete HPSCHD for fifty computer-derived tapes and harpsichord soloist; and the premiere of Flight-Operatic by TORU TAKEMITSU, for orchestra, mime, dancers, film, tape, and so on.

Various other events on a smaller scale will be presented from time to time, as announced.

=== Page 8 ===
Distributions（分布）へのノート

1966～67年にかけて作曲。前方から弦楽四重奏が、そして後方からは四重奏中の2パートをリング変調した音響がきこえてくる。
次の諸要素から成る。
O：弦楽器の調弦を模した短かい部分でAとCを内包している。
A：やや長い持続のクラスター。徐々にDに近づく。
B：アルペジオ音型。複雑化されたCとDに似た性格をおびる。
C：グリッサンド。Dに接近する。
D：騒音、極端な状態では事実上Eに等しい。聴覚の分解能力を考えるならば、極度に複雑なものは、かえって単純なものとし
て理解されるからである。
E：間（ま）
各要素は、その持続や出現順序に関してポアソン分布や正規分布などのような分布に従っている。全体的には単純→複雑という傾向に配列されているが、この複雑化の過程で各要素はまったく逆の性質をもったものに変質してしまう（例：A→D、B→C &D、C→DそしてD→E）。最後は最も複雑な要素がおかれているので、聴覚的には単純→複雑→単純という形式をもつようにきこえる。
（松平頼曉）

アルヴィン・ルシエ
1931年、ニューハンプシャーのナシュア生れのアメリカの作曲家。エール大学、ブランダイス大学に学んだのち、フルブライト奨学金によりローマに留学。現在はブランダイス大学の室内合唱団および電子音楽スタジオのディレクターである。
かれは1967年春、ソニック・アーツ・グループのメンバーとして欧州各地をまわり、ライヴ・エレクトロニック・ミュージックを紹介したほか、アメリカ各地でも活動をつづけている。いっぽうブランダイス大学室内合唱団の指揮者としても、ブラウン、ケージ、一柳慧、シュトックハウゼンなどの作品を積極的に初演。こうした作品が米オデッセイ（コロムビア）からLPでだされている。
＜ピアノのアクション・ミュージック＞ 1962
＜ソリストのための音楽＞ 1965
　　脳波（アルファ・リズム）の増幅
＜ホイッスラー＞ 1966
＜北米タイム・キャプセル＞ 1967

=== Page 13 ===
飯村隆彦

1937年生れの実験映画作家。1960年に慶応大学を卒業後、映画の制作に専心。1964年のブリュッセル実験映画祭では、日本の若い一群の作家たちの作品がそろって受賞したが、そのなかには、かれの〈オナン〉も含まれていた。同年、フィルム・アンデパンダンを組織し、日本のアンダー・グラウンド・フィルムの活動をつづけた。1966年、ハーバード大学の国際セミナーに招かれて渡米。

代表作としては、〈オナン〉〈ラヴ〉〈デリバット王国の舞踏会〉などがある。

〈シェルター9999〉について

この作品はアルヴィン・ルシエと渡米中の飯村隆彦の近作の共同作品。4つの要素が同時的にパフォーマンスされていく。その4要素とはまず35分の黒白フィルム。それにループになった4本のエンドレスの黒白フィルム。これには戦術的な意味でパンチがいれられて穴があけられている。さらにこの他にアクチュアルな問題をとらえて撮影した12枚のカラー・スライドが併映される。そしてこれらの映像にたいして、4チャンネルの音響がかみあわされていくが、これはかならずしも映像とシンクロナイズする意図があたえられてはいない。

これらの映像は指定にしたがって上映されていくが、それぞれがほとんど同時にダブって映写されていく。そしてその場合、色彩フィルターとレンズによって、これらの映像が変形されつづける。

テープの音は、3次元の方向性をもつ物体の振動のうちで、とくに一方向の振動についてのみ敏感にキャッチし、とりだした音によっている。こうしてさまざまな視覚的、聴覚的な繰り返しがおこなわれていくのだが、その組み合わせがいつも変化していくことによって、強烈な印象とサイケデリックな効果がうみだされていくのである。

(AUSTIN, BABBITT)

LARRY AUSTIN was born in Oklahoma in 1930. He studied composition with Darius Milhaud, Andrew Imbrie, and Seymour Shifrin while at North Texas State University and the University of California, at Berkeley. Since 1958, he has taught at the University of California, Davis, and formed the New Music Ensemble (NME) with his colleagues there. This group of composer/performers is particularly devoted to evolving new concepts of group improvisation. Mr. Austin has also been instrumental in organizing a music publishing service "Composer/Performer Edition" (CPE) and edits the unique avant garde music magazine, Source. His works include: Improvisations for Orchestra and Jazz Soloists (1963); The Maze for three percussionists, dancer, tape, machines, and projections (1966); Changes for trombone and tape (1966); Accidents for electronically prepared piano, tape, mirrors, actions, and projections (1967); and Bass, a theater piece in open style for contrabass, tape, and film (1967). Mr. Austin's compositions are published by MJQ Music, Inc. and by CPE, and are recorded on Columbia and NME Records.

BRASS was commissioned by the American Brass Quintet with the aid of a research grant from the University of California, Davis. It was filmed in New York City during September of 1967 at the Merce Cunningham Foundation dance studio. Brass is dedicated to my instrument, the trumpet. It was conceived as a silent movie with live electronic sound. Rather than hearing a prerecorded sound track, the movie-goer hears, in actual performance, live electronic music created by the cast (the American Brass Quintet) at the same time the movie is being shown. The sounds are produced by means of special electronically amplified mutes, which make it possible for the audience to hear instrumental sounds that would normally be inaudible beyond a few feet. These "micro-sounds" are electronically modified and finally amplified through speakers in the hall. The players "play" the movie and the slides. They receive some information about what to play from their own images on the screen (density, articulation, texture, timing, instrumentation, timbre, etc.) and the remainder (frequency, intensity, envelope, rhythm, event sequence, etc.) from the color slides of brass tablatures superimposed over the film. Except for the first and last, the slides are faded in and out at random intervals in any order.

The stereophonic tape used at this concert was taken from the November 6, 1967 performance by the American Brass Quintet, and sound modification was achieved by means of Buchla Associates Electronic Modular System equipment. There should be no attempt to synchronize the tape and film.

-Larry Austin

MILTON BABBITT was born in Philadelphia in 1916, and entered New York University in 1931 as a student of mathematics and logic. The impact of Schoenberg and Webern redirected his interest towards music, however, and he began study in composition with Marion Bauer and Philip James in New York. Later he worked with Roger Sessions at Princeton, obtaining his MA in 1942. Mr. Babbitt has taught both mathematics and music at Princeton, where he has been on the faculty since 1938. He is co-director of the Columbia-Princeton Center for Electronic Music. As the leading American theoretician for the post-Webern school, he has written numerous technical articles on serial procedures. His compositions include: Composition for Twelve Instruments (1948); two string quartets (1948 and 1954); Composition for Tenor and Six Instruments (1958-60); Composition for Synthesizer, generated on the RCA Electronic Sound Synthesizer (1961); Ensembles for Synthesizer (1961-63); and Philomel for soprano, recorded soprano, and synthesized sound (1963). A number of Mr. Babbitt's works are available from Associated Music Publishers, and his music is recorded on Columbia and Composers Recordings Incorporated.

(BABBITT, CHIHARA)

COMPOSITION FOR FOUR INSTRUMENTS was composed in 1947-48 and is the second of six works entitled "compositions" extending over a fifteen-year period (the first was Three Compositions for Piano, 1946-47). I chose this term not only to avoid titles with historical or formal connotations, and to suggest (in order to prepare the listener for) a certain degree of abstractness and formalism, but primarily to provide information about the musical "language" employed and specific characteristics of the individual work. In the former case, the term "composition" is associated with the operations on permutations corresponding to a familiar representation of the customary transformations of the twelve-tone system; while in the latter case the term is applied to partitions in which the order of parts is significant, corresponding musically to the registral and timbral partitioning of the twelve-tone aggregate: the unit of ensemble progression, whose "parts" are always segments of a twelve-tone set, and, therefore an ordered pitch collection.

Composition for Four Instruments is the second work I completed after a war-enforced, six-year respite from composition. Before and during this period I was engrossed in the compositional extension and generalization of the Schoenbergian principle of "combinationality," and the Webernian technique of set construction by derivation. In this piece, the twelve-tone set is never presented in an explicit manner. The sets that constitute the pitch material of the individual instruments are all "derived" (by the three operations of the twelve-tone system) from the four discrete hexachords of the work's set, and share a common hexachordal combinationality with each other and with the set of the work. The opening clarinet solo begins by exposing an all-interval set, which functions thereafter as a foreground thematic set. It is produced by a registral delineation of the compositional set's opening trichord and three transformations that form, together, the first of the eight aggregates making up this section. From an awareness of this aspect of the work's structure, its most immediate design characteristic - the fifteen instrumentally defined sections - is observed to function as a large-scale analogue to that disposition of trichords.

Composition for Four Instruments is also the second of my completed works in which the temporal dimension is structured in terms of the formation and transformational principles of the twelve-tone pitch-class system. Thus, it is not just serialized but twelve-tone serialized. It embodies not just a contextual analogy, but a compositional definition of the temporal elements of attack point and metrical organization. Time perception is scaled "intervallically" (with duration functioning as temporal interval) and, thereby, invariants under the operations of the system assume an empirical status in the time domain, one that is closely comparable to their position in the pitch domain.

- Milton Babbitt

PAUL CHIHARA was born in Seattle in 1938. He studied at Cornell University, earning a BA in English and a DMA in music. Later he worked privately with Nadia Boulanger in Paris, under a Cornell travel grant; at the Hochschule für Musik in West Berlin, with a Fulbright Fellowship; and for two summers at Tanglewood, once as a student of Gunther Schuller. Mr. Chihara's Four Pieces for Orchestra won the "Lili Boulanger Memorial Award" in 1963, and his Concerto for Viola and Orchestra was presented by the Baltimore Symphony in 1965. He is now an Assistant Professor in the music department at UCLA. Various instrumental and choral works of Mr. Chihara's are published by Wimbledon Music, NYC, and the Summy-Birchard Company.

ポール・チハラ（千原ポール・清弘）

1938年シアトル生れの日系二世の作曲家。コーネル大学で英文学を学び、BAとDMAを受けた。のちコーネル大学奨学金をうけてパリでナディア・ブーランジェに師事。またベルリン音楽学校に学んだ。1963年には〈オーケストラのための４つの小品〉により、リリー・ブーランジェ記念賞を受賞、また〈ヴィオラとオーケストラのための協奏曲〉が、第１次ロックフェラー財団計画によって、ポルティモア交響楽団により演奏された。のちにタンブルウッドでガンサーシュラーに師事。現在はカリフォルニア大学（ロスアンジェルス）の音楽部助教授、活潑な前衛音楽のコンサート活動もおこなっている。

〈プランチズ〉（枝の曲）は、かれの木を扱った音画連作の第２作。３つのヴィオラと３つのトロンボーンのための〈木の曲〉1965年、ヴィオラと打楽器のための〈レッド・ウッド〉1966年、オーケストラのための〈森の曲〉などと一連の作品である。これらの音画はすべて同族セリエールの技法をもちいており、空間と時間の相互作用がこころみられている。つまり音の空間的な記譜法と、実際的な音の位置づけといった関係が示めされているといえる。

この〈プランチズ〉では、ピッチの異なるドラム群（G、A、B、C♯、D、D♯、E、F）が行動をおこし、曲の高低をえがきだしていく。そして２つのバスーンは、まるで風に吹かれた枝のような音をだしながら、そのドラム群を追っていくのだ。初演は1966年タンブルウッド音楽祭でやられたが、そのご西独のカッセルのほか、シアトル、クリーヴランド、そしてロスアンジェルスでひらかれたI・S・C・M音楽祭でも演奏された。

(CHIHARA, IIMURA-LUCIER)

BRANCHES is the second in a series of tone pictures dealing with trees (The others are Tree Music, for three violas and three trombones; Redwood, for viola and percussion; and Forest Music, for orchestra.). These tone pictures - all of which use the same family of tone rows, grow out of the interaction of time with space; they are reflections on spatial notation and its relationship to the physical placement of sound. In Branches, the principal sound source is a set of chromatically tuned tenor drums (pitched in G, A, B, C#, D, D#, E, and F) that initiates the action and shapes the contour of the piece. The two bassoons, like branches blown by the wind, follow and react to the motion of the drum sound.

- Paul Chihara

TAKAHIKO IIMURA was born in 1937 and graduated from Keio University in 1960, His first one-man show was in Tokyo in 1963, and one year later his Onan won a special prize at the 3rd International Experimental Film Festival in Brussels. On his return to Japan in 1964 Iimura founded "Film Independent" as a result of interest in experimental cinema. He was invited to Harvard University's International Seminar, and his films have been shown at the Cannes Film Festival, The Museum of Modern Art, Lincoln Center, and many universities. His works include: Onan, Love, and Dance Party in Delipat Kingdom.

ALVIN LUCIER was born in Nashua, New Hampshire in 1931, and studied at Yale University, Brandeis University, and in Rome on a Fulbright Fellowship. He is presently on the faculty of Brandeis, where he directs the University Chamber Chorus and the University Electronic Music Studio. During the past several years, he has toured in Europe and America as a member of the Sonic Arts Group. His works include: Action Music for Piano, aural and theatrical (1962); Music for Solo Performer, for a performer's amplified brain-waves, assistant, and differential amplifier-low pass filter (1965); Whistlers, sounds created by the spinning electromagnetic particles that track between the poles of the magnetic field above the earth (1966); North American Time Capsule for voices using materials representative of the current state of the world, modified by the Sylvania Electronics Systems' vocoder (1967).

SHELTER 9999 is a collaboration between Alvin Lucier and film maker Takahiko Iimura. The visual materials consist of one 35-minute exposed length of film, the emulsion of which has been variously scratched; 4 film loops - also black and white - in which holes have been strategically punched; and a set of 12 topical colored slides. All of these materials are superimposed on the same screen by 3 movie projectors and one slide projector according to a specified plan. The images from the slides and loops are altered by two performers using colored gels, lenses, and magnifying glasses.

〈アンダー・グラウンドからの手記〉は、構造的な方法として不確定性をもちいているかれの一連の作品のひとつ。この作品の音は、明確な音から不確定な音にいたるまでが使われ、また音声も明確に識別できるものから曖昧な音までがもちいられている。

作曲者はこう書いている。「歴史的にいって、音楽についての興味とは、つねに予見できるものと予見できないものとのかねあいにあったといえる。即興演奏では、演奏者は自からの演奏がそのままフィード・バックになって働く。ところが紀元600年から1950年に至るまでの音楽は、書かれた楽譜をそのまま演奏するといったことによって、ともすれば単なる機械へと堕してきた。この場合は、即興演奏がおこなわれているときとちがって、作曲家は自分が作曲している時以外には、自分の音楽をもはやきけないのである。

最近10年間の作曲家の問題は、作曲をやめずにどのようにして自分の音楽を聴くかということにしばられているのだ。

この作品では、なかば空間的な記譜法をとっているので、各時間を指定されている各セクションの時間が長ければ、それにしたがって記譜された断片は、不確定的な要素がふえてくる。〈サギタ67〉以来、わたしはこうした考えのもとで、作曲してきた。記譜された音楽であろうと　テープ音楽であろうと、そこに提出されたものはスタティックな確定の点である。演奏者はそこから出発して、自由な解釈をひろげるべきなのだ。私がここでもくろんだのも、こうした確定的な点をふみこえてしまわずに、予見できない要素をできるかぎり多く提供したいとこころみることだった。」

（作曲者）

武田明倫

1937年金沢生れ。1962年に東京芸大音楽学部楽理科を卒業。同年小杉武久らと〈グループ・音楽〉を組織して、作曲やハプニングをつづけた。1965年以来、武蔵野音楽大学で音楽史の講座をうけもっている。また現在〈音楽芸術〉誌上に、柴田南雄ら4人のグループ・ワーク〈音と思考〉を連載執筆している。作品としては、弦楽器のための〈変化〉1963、〈パッセージ〉1964、テープ作品〈開けた音〉1965　などがあるが、寡作である。しかしイヴェントやハプニングの奏者として、これまでに多くの作家の作品に参加したり、ケージの来日した際の演奏者として加わるなど、活動をつづけてきた。

=== Page 26 ===
(IIMURA - LUCIER, MATSUDAIRA)

4 channels of tape sound run concurrently with the visual materials, though no effort is made to achieve synchronization. The sounds originate with polarized vibrational pick-ups. These devices selectively "analyze" aural (or vibrational) phenomena because they are relatively more sensitive to vibration along one axis than along the others (e.g., more sensitive to the y-axis of an x-y-z coordinate system). The 4 channels of sound, formed of two 2-channel stereo tapes also use loop techniques. Familiar aural and visual elements incessantly recur, but in rapidly, constantly changing superpositions. The effect is powerful, sometimes psychedelic.

YORI-AKI MATSUDAIRA was born in 1931 in Tokyo, and is self-educated in piano and composition. He graduated from Tokyo Metropolitan University with a PhD in biology from the faculty of science, and now teaches in the Saint Paul University biophysics department. In 1967, Configuration was done at the ISCM Festival in Prague. During 1965 and 66, Mr. Matsudaira visited and worked in Europe and the United States. He was, at that time, the Japanese delegate to the ISCM. His works include Variations for violin, cello, and piano (1957); Configuration for chamber orchestra (1961-63); Transients '64, electronic sound; Rhymes for Gazzelloni for flute (1965-66); What's next? for soprano and 2 noise makers (1967); and Alternation for combo (1967). Variations, Configuration, and Rhymes for Gazzelloni are published by Edizioni Suvini Zerboni, Milano, Italy.

DISTRIBUTIONS was composed during 1966 and 67. In the foreground is a string quartet, while from the rear, speakers emit sounds that are the modulated product of two portions of the quartet's live sound. The composition is made up of material in the following conditions:
O) one short portion in imitation of the tuning of the instruments (This segment also employs A and C.)
A) a cluster of relatively long duration, gradually approaching the condition D
B) an arpeggiated gesture that gradually approaches the status of C or D
C) glissandi that gradually approach the condition D

D) an extremely complex spectrum (noise) (Considering the analytic capabilities of our ears - they have limited powers of resolution - extreme complexity is interpreted as undifferentiated chaos. For this reason, one may say that D approaches E.)
E) inaction
When seen in terms of its duration and order of appearance, each "condition" complies strictly with some type of mathematical distribution: Poisson's distribution, normal distribution, etc.

=== Page 27 ===
2人の奏者のための〈場〉について

シェーンベルクの12音技法から、ミュージック・セリエルや電子音楽を発展させた、ヨーロッパ近代文化を「正統」とする立場から、今日いわば、正統的前衛主義者と考えられている作家達の「思考」、すなわち「作曲技法」においては、一般的傾向として、「音」は実在的な「音」である前に、抽象的な「音高」として、「音価」として、「強弱」として、あるいは「音色」として在らねばならなかった。そして更に、このような「パラメーター」の総体として観念的に規定された「音」は、それ自体、自立的に存在し得るのではなく、より上位の構造を構成するための「素材」としてしか在ることができなかった。勿論、「技法」が一種の「便法」である以上、このことのみを取り上げてこれらの作家達の行き方を全面的に否定するつもりは全くない。しかし、私自身が求める「音」は、主として数理的な思考と操作によってその存在の場を保証されて在るような「音」ではない。あたかも自ら息づきつつその実在の瞬間を、深く埋めて在るような「音」なのだ「2人の奏者のための〈場〉」で、私は「音」がそのような「在り方」をする〈場〉を構成しようと意図した。

このことを実現するため、この作品では「音」に極度に執着し、表裏一体の関係として、その「音」が感性豊かな「人間」によって発せられるものであることに執着した。そしてこの作品において「音」は、「音高」・「音価」・「強弱」、あるいは（厳密にはすべてを総合したものとしてのみ認識される）「音色」などの、個々の「価」としての量的な制約を持たない。当然のことながら、記譜法は伝統的な5線記譜法ではない方法をとっている。「楽譜」は奏者に「奏法」と「2奏者間における呼吸の合一」とについては厳格な指定を与え、「音」の音の次元における形態に関しては、多分にあいまいでありながら、作者の主観的な希望についての情報を与える役をしている。演奏に用いられる楽器は、ヴァイオリン属の弓奏弦楽器であれば何でもよい。なお、この作品にとりいれられた「不確定性」は、ケージの「偶然性」とは異質なものである。（武田明倫）

ミルトン・バビット

1916年フィラデルフィア生れ。今日ではアメリカ作曲界の大御所的な存在であり、セリエル音楽の指導者格でもある。1940年以来、ポスト・ウェーベルン派として、かれはアメリカでおそらく最初に厳格なセリエル技法を適用した作曲家といってよいだろう。

1931年にニューヨーク大学に入って数学・論理学を専攻。そのごシェーンベルクとウェーベルンに強い刺激をうけて、音楽をはじめるようになった。そしてM・バウアー、F・ジェームス、ロジャー・セッションズらについて学び、1942年プリンストン大学を卒業。1938年以来、母校プリンストン大学で数学と音楽を教えた。戦後シンセサイザーを備えたプリンストン電子音楽スタジオを創設、ディレクターとなって現在に及んでいる。

(MATSUDAIRA, MORRIS)
Further, each condition, if the collection of all of its appearances is viewed as a whole, is arrayed from simpler to more complex forms. In the process of gradual complication, each element is converted, assuming the nature of an opposite (for example, A→D, B→C, B→D, C→D, and D→E). Since the most complex section occurs at the very end of the piece, the aural experience should effectively go from simple to complex and back to simple (due to the psychological equivalence of D to E). - Yori-Aki Matsudaira

ROBERT MORRIS was born in Cheltenham, England in 1943. He received his BM from the Eastman School of Music and an MM from the University of Michigan. Presently completing his Doctorate in Composition and Ethnomusicology at the University of Michigan where he is a teaching fellow, he has studied with Ross Lee Finney, Leslie Bassett, Niccolo Castiglioni, and Eugene Kurtz. At the Berkshire Music Center (Tanglewood) as a Margaret Lee Crofts Fellow, he worked with Gunther Schuller, and in 1965, the University of Syracuse commissioned him to write music for Max Frisch's Biederman and the Firebugs. He also participated in the Rockefeller Foundation's program for orchestral readings by the Baltimore Symphony Orchestra. In conjunction with Russell Peck, William Albright, and David Andrew, Mr. Morris co-founded The Great Society, a theater group in Ann Arbor. His works include: Frondescence 65 for flute and piano; Sangita 67 for any number of flutes, strings, and percussion; Dark Halo for Orchestra; Night Crawlers for tape and dancers; Denkmaeler, theater event; Forgotten Vibrations for ten instruments and soprano; and Capricorn 68 for nine to infinity players, with at least three conductors.

In the history of art music, the listener's interest within some understood set of rules, traditions, proprieties, forms, etc., is what will happen, that is, the relationship of predictable to unpredictable elements in a piece of music. If the music is improvised (instead of notated descriptively or in any way), the performer also becomes involved as a listener. His perception of what he is playing acts as a feedback governing how or what he will play next.

In Western Music from 1600-1950 there has been the figure of the composer as an autonomous personality who structures the whole musical situation so that the players become ultimately mere machines translating a notational system into an aural one. In such a position the composer can never become a listener except when he is actually composing, since once the piece is completed, he "knows" it (in the sense that he has totally determined it).

The nearer we get to the present the more crucial the problem becomes, and it seems to me that the composer's problem in the last ten years has been how to become a listener again without giving up composition.

NOTES FROM THE UNDERGROUND (1966) is one of a series of pieces that employs indeterminacy as a structural device. The sounds used are arranged in a continuum from clearly recognizable pitches to ambiant noises. The vocal elements are likewise disposed from purely phonetic sounds to an almost phonemic section based on the permutation of the letters of a five-letter word. A semi-spacial notation is used, placing events within sections of various lengths. The result will be progressively more unpredictable the longer the section.

I continued this train of thought in subsequent works (Sangita 67, Next to Last Rites, and Capricorn 68) where notation or a prerecorded tape serves as a static, determinant element from which the performers can interpret/improvise. I hoped to bring to these pieces that special quality of the unforeseen, without trespassing the boundaries I had originally conceived.

- Robert Morris

〈4つの楽器のための作品〉へのノート
この作品は1947～48年にかけて作曲したもので、1946～47年の〈ピアノのための3つの作品〉を最初としてはじまった15年間にわたる〈作品（コンポジション）〉と名づけられた6つの作品の第2番目にあたるものだ。

〈コンポジション（作品）＝つまりコンポジチオ〉の名をえらんだ理由は、歴史的、または楽曲形式による名前によってうまれる無用な連想をさけながら、同時に、聴衆にある程度の抽象性と形式性を意識させることである。そればかりでなく、それは私のもちいる音楽言語の性質と作品そのものの特性について、あらかじめ情報を提供するということにほかならない。
つまりコンポジチオという名称は、12音組織の一般的な変形法の慣習的なやり方である音の順列組みあわせ操作——セリエルの音列技法を意味する。またこの名称は、12音の総体を、音高と音色によって区分し、その区分の順序、およびその部分がつねに12音の音高のセットからなる全体の時間的な推移を重要視するものと考えられているはずだからである。
この〈4つの楽器のための作品〉は、戦争によって中断された6年間の休息ののちにできあがった第2の作品である。この前後の時期に、私はシェーンベルクの〈結合の原理〉の拡張とその一般化、およびウェーベルンの〈派生法〉によるセリー構成の技法に熱中した。その結果この両者は私の考えのなかで、切り離しがたく合体し、相関した。
この作品のなかでは、12音のセットは、ふつうの意味では明白には示されない。個々の楽器の音高素材を形成するセットは、すべて作品のセットをなす6音から（12音組織の3つの基本

Milton Babbitt ミルトン・バビット

=== Page 30 ===
AKIMICHI TAKEDA was born in 1937, and graduated in musicology from Tokyo University of the Arts in 1962. Beginning at this time, he participated with Takehisa Kosugi, Shuko Mizuno, Yasunao Tone, and Chieko Shiomi in the "Group Ongaku" (Music Group). He has been teaching music history at the Musashino Music Academy since 1965, and is presently working on a collective article "Sound and Thought" carried in installments by the Japanese magazine Ongaku Geijutsu. His compositions include: Changes for string instruments (1963); Passages for unspecified performer(s) (1964); and Open Sounds for tape (1965).

If one views the development of modern European music from Schoenberg through serialism and electronic music as legitimate, one can say that, for Europeans, tone is above all an abstract entity characterized by pitch, duration, intensity, and tone color. There is another European supposition: that the overall tonal form is a result of relationships between these parameters, and that sound itself can only be thought of as raw material by means of which a structure on a higher plane can be achieved. Because this viewpoint and technique itself are only conventions, I do not intend to detract from them. On the other hand, the world of tone that I envisage is not the kind of world in which existences can be guaranteed by mathematical thinking. I rather propose a world of tonal existence in which each moment is interred with a vital, self-breathing tonal event.

In A FIELD, I have tried to construct a situation in which tones are given such a mode of being. In order to realize my design, the work is carefully restricted to the use of "tone" itself. It is vital, therefore, that the sounds be performed by persons with rich sensibilities: the tone and its producer should be inseparable. In my composition, "tone" is not thought of quantitatively in the European manner (Tone color can only be perceived as a complex of factors, but even it is broken down, quantified, by the Europeans.).

As a matter of course, I have used a non-traditional manner of notation. It gives strictly directive information concerning playing method and also about the way in which rapport between the players may be attained and developed. Information on the specific characteristics of the tones themselves, however, is quite ambiguous, conveying only the subjective wishes of the composer. Any instruments from the string (violin) family may be used in performance. It should be noted that the indeterminacy used in this composition is not in agreement with John Cage's approach. I always envisage a total structure (or product), and try to transmit this to the performer and listener as accurately as possible.

- Akimichi Takeda

Akimichi Takeda 武田明倫

操作によって）、すべて〈派生〉したものである。そして共有する6音の結合と相互に関係し、かつ作品全体としても連関する。

冒頭のクラリネットのソロは、全音程のセットを呈示し、これが終りまで、前景をなす主題的なセットとして働く。それは、最初の3音と3つの基本的な変形の音高により描かれ、このセクションを形成する8個の部分の第1の部分となる。作品構造のこの局面の意識から、15の楽器によって区分されたセクションが、直接的にあらわれるデザインの特性として生まれ、最初の3音の性向の巨視的な類比物として作用する。

〈4つの楽器のための作品〉は、時間または持続の領域が、12音システムの形成原理ならびに変形原理によって構成されている私の作品の第2番目のものである。したがって、この音楽はたんに〈セリー化（音列化）〉された作品であるだけでなく、〈12音的にセリー化〉されたものといわれなければならない。言いかえれば、ここでは音楽の時間的な要素は、文脈的類似性にしたがって並べられるといっただけではない。各音の開始点と、すべての音のリズム的組織そのものが、コンポジチオの定義によって規定されているのである。時間の知覚は、〈音程的に〉（持続を時間的音程とみなして）スケール化されているのだ。

このようにして、作品の組織の操作における恒数的なものが、音の高低の領域でと同様、時間の領域における経験の土台となるのである。（ミルトン・バビット）

松平 賢 晓

1931年東京生れ。1957年東京都立大学大学院理学研究科を修了。この間独学で作曲とピアノを学んでいたが、かれの父上は作曲家の松平賢則氏である。かれ自身によれば、父上からはいちども教わらなかったという。

1957年に、父上の弟子であった江崎健次郎、下山一二三、遠藤亮らと〈グループ・20.5〉を組織。たびたび演奏会をひらいた。いっぽうかれの作品〈V. VC. Pのためのヴァリエーション〉が1958年の世界音楽祭に入選。1967年にも再度〈室内オーケストラのためのコンフィギュレーション〉が入選した。また1967年第1回ロッシュ音楽奨励賞を受賞している。

1965～66年にかけて欧米各地に滞在。この間にフィラデルフィア作曲家フォーラムの名誉会員に推挙された。現在、立教大学理学部・生物物理学研究室の助教授。

■1967～68年のシーズンに、〈クロス・トーク〉は下記の作曲家および映画作家の作品を、世界初演、または日本初演をふくめてとりあげました。
アシュレー、オースティン、バビット、バーマン、ケージ、千原、フルンド、一柳慧、飯村隆彦、アイヴス、小杉武久、ルシエ、マルティラーノ、松平顕隆、水野修孝、モリス、ムンマ、ネルソン、サティ、シリング、スポットニック、ライヒ、レイノルズ、高橋悠治、武田明倫、武満徹、湯浅譲二（5月に予定されている作品を含む）

■〈クロス・トーク〉では、1969年の春にライヴ・エレクトロニック・ミュージックの音楽祭を計画、進行中です。
アメリカから、数人の作曲家と技師を招待して、さまざまなデモンストレーションやコンサートをおこなう予定です。それと同時に、日本の若い作曲家や技術者のために、電子音響機械（リング・モデュレーター、フォト・セル、コムピューター、変調器その他）を使用するゼミナールを行います。電子工学と芸術との新しい結びつきや、その可能性が活発にこころみはじめられている今日、こうしたエンジニアリングへの新しい視野をひろげることは意味のあることでしょう。

■1969年春以降の予定としては、目下さまざまな構想を検討中ですが、次のような、いわゆるインター・メディアともいうべき動向をうかびあがらせるコンサートを計画しています。
88人の奏者と聴衆を参加させるイアニス・クセナキスの〈テレテクトール〉1966、ジョン・ケージが目下イリノイ大学のコムピューターを使って作曲中の〈HPSCHD〉（これは50チャンネルにわけられたテープとハープシコード奏者による作品）、さらにアメリカから帰国した武満徹がオペラティックな作品として構想中の〈フライト〉（オーケストラ、マイム、舞踊、映画、テープその他を使用）などを予定しています。

■このほか、特別コンサートと、定期的なコンサートも継続しておこなう予定ですが、いずれ詳細は追ってお知らせします。

Programme

German Requiem
FOR
SOLI, CHORUS, AND ORCHESTRA.

JOHANNES BRAHMS,
(Op. 45).

Royal Victorian Liedertafel,
Associated Ladies' Choir, and Orchestra

Soprano Solo—Miss LILIAN REID.
Baritone Solo—Mr. G. THEXTON MORPHET.

The following notes are principally taken from Masters of German Music, by Mr. J. A. Fuller Maitland.

The Requiem, which was finished in 1868, and first produced, in a complete form, at Bremen, on Good Friday in that year, was the first work which established Brahms' fame, and has been described as "the greatest achievement of modern sacred music in Germany." It is not a "Requiem" in the ordinary acceptation of the term. It is in reality a Sacred Cantata, composed to words selected from the Holy Scripture, in illustration of the joys of the blessed and the glories of the life to come. It exhibits throughout a striking originality. In his desire to shadow forth the glories of a higher state of existence, the composer has availed himself of the latest resources of modern music, including the most complicated orchestral effects, and choral passages of almost unconquerable difficulty.

The first chorus (I.) opens with the calm utterance of the words "Blessed are they that mourn"; succeeded by the promise "They

=== Page 13 ===
that sow in tears shall reap in joy," set to music of the most consolatory character. In this movement an indescribable richness of tone is produced by the skilful management of the stringed band, from which the violins are altogether excluded.

The next number (II.) opens with a Funeral March. The idea is that of the whole human race marching in solemn procession to the grave, and this idea has inspired Brahms to the composition of a march unlike all marches that were ever written. It is in triple-time—the measured tramp of no ordinary host. The effect is heightened by the employment of unison in the vocal parts at the words "Behold all flesh is as the grass." The imagery of these words, perhaps connected with the "sowing in tears" of the preceding chorus, suggests the passage from the Epistle of St. James, "The husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth"; and this leads to the beautiful fugal setting of the words "The redeemed of the Lord shall return." The repetition of the words "joy everlasting," with which the chorus closes, is a most striking contrast to the gloom of the beginning.

The third number (III.) starts with a Baritone Solo, "Lord make me to know," melodious, expressive, and pre-eminently vocal. The Chorus then repeat the same words, as also in the next section, "Verily mankind walketh in a vain show." At the words "Now, Lord, O what do I wait for," the voice parts become more involved and the music more agitated, leading up to a very fine climax at the words "My hope is in Thee." Here the four sections of the choir enter successively from the lowest register of the bass to the high soprano, suggesting the idea of a hope built upon a sure foundation, and leading into the splendid fugue "But the righteous souls are in the hand of God," in which the same impression of stability and permanence is conveyed, and is indeed accentuated by its being constructed throughout one continuing Pedal note.

After the assurance as to the destiny of the "righteous souls," it is natural to turn to the joys of their abode, and in the next number (IV.) "How lovely is thy dwelling place!" the perfect peace of heaven is reflected. Attention may be drawn to the fine fugal treatment of the words "They praise Thy Name evermore," towards the end of this movement.

The subject of the next number (V.) is that of comfort to mourners, based on the happy state of the holy dead. The loss of the composer's mother is said to have determined its form, which is that of a soprano solo, accompanied by a quiet chorus, which repeats the words "As one whom his own mother comforteth, so will I comfort you."

The sixth chorus (VI.) begins with a passage of simple four-part harmony, "Here we have no continuing place," and the baritone solo entering at the words "Lo! I unfold unto you a mystery," the thoughts are led on to the change from mortality to immortality, on which the burial service lays stress. To English ears the re-setting of "For the trumpet shall sound," &c., may seem almost sacrilegious; but it must be remembered that the Messiah is far less familiar in Germany than here. The dramatic passages descriptive of the "mystery" serve as a preparation for the calm dignity and devotional grandeur of the double fugue, "Lord, Thou art worthy."

I.

CHORUS.

Blessed are they that mourn, for they shall have comfort. They that sow in tears shall reap in joy. Who goeth forth and weepeth, and beareth precious seed, shall doubtless return with rejoicing and bring his sheaves with him.

II.

CHORUS.

Behold all flesh is as the grass, and all the goodliness of man is as the flower of grass: for lo! the grass withereth, and the flower thereof decayeth. Now therefore be patient. O my brethren, unto the coming of Christ. See how the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth, and hath long patience for it, until he receive the early rain, and the latter rain. So be ye patient. Behold all flesh is as the grass, &c.

Albeit the Lord's word endureth for evermore. The redeemed of the Lord shall return again, and come rejoicing unto Zion; gladness, joy everlasting, joy upon their heads shall be; joy and gladness, these shall be their portion, and tears and sighing shall flee from them.

III.

BARITONE SOLO and CHORUS.

Lord, make me to know the measure of my days on earth, to consider my frailty, that I must perish. Surely all my days here are as an hand-breadth to Thee, and my lifetime is as nought to Thee.

BARITONE SOLO.

Verily mankind walketh in a vain show, and his best state is vanity. He passeth away like a shadow, he is disquieted in vain, he heapeth up riches, and cannot tell who shall gather them.

CHORUS.

Verily mankind walketh in a vain show, and his best state is altogether vanity.

BARITONE SOLO and CHORUS.

Now, Lord, O what do I wait for? My hope is in Thee.
But the righteous souls are in the hand of God, nor pain nor grief shall nigh them come.

IV.

CHORUS.

How lovely is Thy dwelling place, O Lord of Hosts!
For my soul it longeth, yea fainteth for the courts of the Lord; my soul and body crieth out, yea for the living God.
Blest are they, O blest are they that dwell within Thy house. They praise Thy name evermore; they praise Thee.

V.

SOPRANO SOLO.

Ye now are sorrowful, howbeit ye shall again behold Me, and your heart shall be joyful, and your joy no man taketh from you.

CHORUS.

Yea I will comfort you, as one whom his own mother comforteth.

SOPRANO SOLO.

Look upon me! Ye know that for a little time labour and sorrow were mine, but at the last I have found comfort.

CHORUS.

Yea I will comfort you.

VI.

CHORUS.

Here on earth have we no continuing place: howbeit we seek one to come.

Lo, I unfold unto you a mystery. We shall not all sleep when he cometh, but we shall all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the sound of the trumpet. For the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and all we shall be changed.

BARITONE SOLO.

Then what of old was written, the same shall be brought to pass:—

CHORUS.

CHORUS.

Worthy art Thou to be praised, Lord of honour and might, for thou hast earth and heaven created, and for Thy good pleasure all things have their being, and are and were created.

VII.

CHORUS.

Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord, from henceforth; saith the Spirit; that they rest from their labours, and that their works follow after them.

RHAPSODIE.
(FRAGMENT AUS GETHE'S "HARZREISE IM WINTER.")
FOR
CONTRALTO SOLO, CHORUS OF MEN'S VOICES, AND ORCHESTRA.

BY JOHANNES BRAHMS (Op. 53)

Royal Victorian Liedertafel and Orchestra
SOLOIST—MADAME AGNES JANSON.

The deep majestic expression which the greatest musical classic of our time has given to the words of Goethe, establishes the work under notice as one of the highest manifestations of lofty subjectivity and profound contemplation that we worship in art. The Solo voice is responsible for the text throughout. The entry of Tenors and Basses—each in two parts—is made at the words, "But if from thy Psalter."

JOHANNES BRAHMS, born 1833 at Hamburg; as a boy excited great attention both by compositions and pianoforte playing. In 1874, he was made a member of the Academy of Arts at Berlin. Excepting opera, Brahms cultivated nearly every branch of musical composition. Powerful, original and versatile, Brahms, more than any other, sums up in his strongly-marked individuality the varying elements: classical as well as romantic, of contemporaneous culture. His imagination, to which he at first allowed too free a scope (about to Op. 10), he bridled by severe study and rigid self-criticism; and although reflection plays a large part in his compositions, he produced abundance of music of a thoroughly spontaneous and inspired character. His melodies possess inexhaustible variety, ranging from naive simplicity and a dreamy poetical tenderness peculiar to himself, to stirring pathos, striking force, and glowing passion; always remaining pregnant and concise. His harmony, often surprisingly bold and original, is subordinated to the dictates of a high artistic idea, which permeates and controls the formal construction of his works, in which an admirable mastery of contrapuntal art is often exhibited. His songs extend from the simplest specimens of popular melody to the richest and most complicated forms of art.

But who goes there apart? In the brake his pathway is lost;
Close behind clash the branches together, the grass rises again, the desert engulfs him.
Who can comfort his anguish?
Who, if balsam be deathly,
If the hate of men from the fulness of love be drained.
He that was scorned turned to scorner, lonely now devours all he hath of worth in a barren self-seeking.

But if from Thy Psalter, all-loving Father, one strain can but come to his hearing,
Oh! enlighten his heart!
Lift up his o'er-clouded eyes where are the fountains hard by the thirsty one in the desert.
But if from Thy Psalter, all-loving Father, one strain can but come to his hearing,
Oh! enlighten his heart. enlighten his heart.

GOD SAVE THE KING.
