=== Page 9 ===
The whole of this Music has been generously donated to the Liedertafel by the President, the Hon. F. S. GRIMWADE.

THE DREAM OF GERONTIUS.

By SIR EDWARD ELGAR.

Characters Represented:

PART I.

<table>
  <tr>
    <th>Gerontius</th>
    <th>Mr. Gregor Wood.</th>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <th>Assistants</th>
    <th>THE LIEDERTAFEL.</th>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <th>The Priest</th>
    <th>Mr. Horace Stevens.</th>
  </tr>
</table>

ARGUMENT.

Gerontius, lying at the point of death, sees in a dream the passing of his soul from earth towards the judgment seat of the Almighty.

Part I. of the Poem is descriptive of the last moments on earth of the departing spirit. Gerontius, surrounded by his friends, feels that he is being called away, and prays for the sustaining presence of the Almighty in his extremity. A sense of impending ruin disquiets his thoughts from time to time, but supported by the intercessory prayers of the priests and his friends, he repeats the Creed and gradually falls into a sleep ending in death.

In Part II. the disembodied soul of Gerontius awakens to consciousness and feels itself being borne onward by unseen hands. The song of the Guardian Angel is heard, rejoicing in the completion of his work, and that the child of clay confided to his care is saved. The Soul questions the Angel, and learns that it is being carried towards the Throne of God. On the way they encounter a cloud of Demons, hungry and wild to gather souls for hell, who mock and jeer at the heavenly aspirations of "low-born clods of brute earth." On approaching nearer to and passing through the gateway of the House of Judgment they are met by a Choir of Angelicals singing praises and thanksgiving. Then, as the veiled presence of God is reached, echoes are heard of the earthly voices of the friends of Gerontius, and the priests reciting the "Subvenite," while the Angel of the Agony pleads before the Throne of Grace for the dying and the dead. The soul is then tenderly consigned to the penal waters by the Guardian Angel, who promises to return, after the night of trial, and awaken the Soul to a glad to-morrow. The voices of the Angelicals are again faintly heard singing the hymn, "Praise to the Holiest," and the work closes with a beautiful seven-fold Amen.

=== Page 11 ===
GERONTIUS.

JESU, MARIA—I am near to death.
And Thou art calling me; I know it now.
Not by the token of this faltering breath,
This chill at heart, this dampness on my brow.

(Jesu, have mercy! Mary, pray for me!)
'Tis this new feeling, never felt before,
(Be with me, Lord, in my extremity!)
That I am going, that I am no more.
'Tis this strange innermost abandonment.
(Lover of souls! great God! I look to Thee.)
This emptying out of each constituent
And natural force, by which I come to be.
Pray for me, O my friends; a visitant
Is knocking his dire summons at my door,
The like of whom, to scare me and to daunt,
Has never, never come to me before:

So pray for me, my friends, who have not strength to pray.

ASSISTANTS.
Kyrie eleison, Christe eleison, Kyrie eleison.
Holy Mary, pray for him.
All holy Angels, pray for him.
Choirs of the righteous, pray for him.
All Apostles, all Evangelists, pray for him.
All holy Disciples of the Lord, pray for him.
All holy innocents, pray for him.
All holy martyrs, all holy Confessors,
All holy Hermits, all holy Virgins,
All ye Saints of God, pray for him.

GERONTIUS.

Rouse ye, my fainting soul, and play the man;
And through such waning span
Of life and thought as still has to be trod,
Prepare to meet thy God.
And while the storm of that bewilderment
Is for a season spent,
And, ere afresh the ruin on me fall,
Use well the interval.

ASSISTANTS.
Be merciful, be gracious; spare him, Lord.
Be merciful, be gracious; Lord, deliver him.
From the sins that are past,
From thy drown and Thine ire;
From the perils of dying;
From any complying
With sin, or denying
His God, or relying
On self, at the last;
From the nethermost fire;
From all that is evil;
From power of the devil;
Thy servant deliver,
For once and for ever.
By Thy birth, and by Thy Cross,
Rescue him from endless loss;
By Thy death and burial,
Save him from a final fall;
By Thy rising from the tomb,
By Thy mounting up above,
By the Spirit's gracious love,
Save him in the day of doom.

GEBONTIUS.

Sanctus fortis, Sanctus Deus,
De profundis oro te,
Miserere, Judex meus,
Parce mihi, Domine.

Firmly I believe, and truly
God is Three, and God is One:
And I next acknowledge duly
Manhood taken by the Son.
And I trust and hope most fully
In that Manhood crucified;
And each thought and deed unruly
Do to death, as He has died.
Simply to His grace and wholly
Light and life and strength belong
And I love, supremely, solely,
Him the holy, Him the strong.
Sanctus fortis, Sanctus Deus,
De profundis oro te,
Miserere, Judex meus,
Parce mihi, Domine.

And I hold in veneration,
For the love of Him alone.
Holy Church, as His creation,
And her teachings, as His own.
And I take with joy whatever
Now besets me, pain or fear,
And with a strong will I sever
All the ties which bind me here.
Adoration aye be given.
With and through the angelic host.
To the God of earth and heaven,
Father, Son, and Holy Ghost.
Sanctus fortis, Sanctus Deus,
De profundis oro te,
Miserere, Judex meus,
Moruis in discrimine.

I can no more; for now it comes again,
That sense of ruin, which is worse than pain,
That masterful negation and collapse
Of all that makes me man.

And, crueller still,
A fierce and restless fright begins to fill
The mansion of my soul. And, worse and worse,
Some bodily form of ill
Floats on the wind, with many a loathsome curse
Tainting the hallowed air, and laughs, and haps
Its hideous wings,
And makes me wild with horror and dismay
O Jesu, help! pray for me, Mary, pray!
Some Angel, Jesu! such as came to Thee
In Thine own agony—
Mary, pray for me. Joseph, pray for me.
Mary, pray for me.

ASSISTANTS.
Rescue him, O Lord, in this his evil hour,
As of old so many by Thy gracious power—
Now from the waters in a saving home:
(Amen.)
Job from all his multiform and fell distress; (Amen).

=== Page 15 ===
SOUL.
I would have nothing but to speak with thee
For speaking's sake. I wish to hold with thee
Conscious communion; though I fain would know
A maze of things, were it but meet to ask,
And not a curiousness.

ANGEL.
You cannot now
Cherish a wish which ought not to be wished.

SOUL.
Then I will speak. I ever had believed
That on the moment when the struggling soul
Quitted its mortal case, forthwith it fell
Under the awful Presence of its God,
There to be judged and sent to its own place.
What lets me now from going to my Lord?

ANGEL.
Thou art not let; but with extremest speed
Art hurrying to the Just and Holy Judge.

SOUL.
Dear Angel, say,
Why have I now no fear at meeting Him?
Along my earthly life, the thought of death
And judgment was to me most terrible.

ANGEL.
It is because
Then thou didst fear, that now thou dost not fear.
Thou hast forestalled the agony, and so
For thee the bitterness of death is passed.
Also, because already in thy soul
The judgment is begun.

ANGEL.
A message falls upon thee, as a ray
Straight from the Judge, expressive of thy lot.
That calm and joy uprising in thy soul
Is first-fruit to thee of thy recompense,
And heaven begun.

SOUL.
Now that the hour is come, my fear is fled;
And at this balance of my destiny,
Now close upon me, I can forward look
With a serenest joy.

But hark! upon my sense
Comes a fierce hubbub, which would make me fear
Could I be frighted.

ANGEL.
We are now arrived
Close on the judgment-court; that sullen howl
Is from the demons who assemble there.
Hungry and wild, to claim their property,
And gather souls for hell. Hist to their cry.

SOUL.
How sour and how uncoutn a dissonance!

DEMONS.
Low-born clods
Of brute earth,
They aspire
To become gods,
By a new birth.
And an extra grace,
And a score of merits,
As if aught
Could stand in place
Of the high thought,
And the glance of fire
Of the great spirits,
The powers blest,
The lords by right,
The primal owners,
Of the proud dwelling
And realm of light.—
Dispossessed,
Aside thrust.
Chucked down,
By the sheer might
Of a despot's will,
Of a tyrant's frown,
Who after expelling
Their hosts gave.
Triumphant still,
And still unjust,
Each forfeit crown
To psalm-droners,
And canting groaners,
To every slave,
And pious cheat,
And crawling knave,
And licked the dust
Under his feet.

ANGEL.
It is the restless panting of their being:
Like beasts of prey, who, caged within their bars,
In a deep hideous purring have their life,
And an incessant pacing to and fro.

DEMONS.
The mind bold
And independent.
The purpose free,
So we are told.
Must not think
To have the ascendant.
What's a saint?
One whose breath
Doth the air taint
Before his death;
A bundle of bones,
Which fools adore.
Ha! ha!
When life is o'er.

=== Page 16 ===
By Appointment to His Excellency the Governor, Sir REGINALD TALBOT, K.C.B.

145-147 COLLINS STREET, MELBOURNE (Opposite Scots' Church),
For Spectacles and Eyeglasses.
Oculists' work our Speciality. Maker of the New "Toric Periscopic" Lens
'Phone 2684. The Lens for comfort and elegance.

Percy Lindsay

=== Page 17 ===
Virtue and vice,
A knave's pretence,
'Tis all the same;
Ha! ha!
    Dread of bell-fire,
Of the venomous flame.
    A coward's plea.
Give him his price,
Saint though he be.
Ha! ha!
    From shrewd good sense
    He'll slave for hire.
Ha! ha!
    And does but aspire
To the heaven above
    With sordid aim,
And not from love.
    Ha! ha!

SOUL.
I see not those false spirits: shall I see
My dearest Master, when I reach His throne?

ANGEL.
Yes,—for one moment thou shalt see thy Lord.
One moment; but thou knowest not, my child,
What thou doth ask: that sight of the Most Fair
Will gladden thee, but it will pierce thee too.

SOUL.
Thou speakest darkly, Angel! and an awe
Falls on me, and a fear lest I be rash.

ANGEL.
There was a mortal, who is now above
In the mid glory: he, when near to die,
Was given communion with the Crucified,—
Such, that the Master's very wounds were stamped
Upon his flesh, and, from the agony
Which thrilled through body and soul in that embrace,
Learn that the flame of the Everlasting Love
Doth burn ere it transform.

CHOIR OF ANGELICALS.
Praise to the Holiest in the height,
And in the depth be praise:

ANGEL.
    . . . . Hark to those sounds!
They come of tender beings angelical,
Least and most childlike of the sons of God.

CHOIR OF ANGELICALS.
Praise to the Holiest in the height,
And in the depth be praise:
In all His words most wonderful;
Most sure in all His ways!

To us His elder race He gave
To battle and to win,
Without the chastisement of pain.
Without the soil of sin.
The younger son He willed to be
A marvel in His birth;
Spirit and flesh His parents were:
His home was heaven and earth.
The Eternal blessed His child, and armed,
And sent Him hence afar,
To serve as champion in the field
Of elemental war.
To be His Viceroy in the world
Of matter, and of sense;
Upon the frontier, towards the foe.
A resolute defence.

ANGEL.
We now have passed the gate, and are within
The House of Judgment. . . .

SOUL.
The sound is like the rushing of the wind—
The summer wind—among the lofty pines.

CHOIR OF ANGELICALS.
Glory to Him, who evermore
By truth and justice reigns:
Who tears the soul from out its case.
And burns away its stains!

ANGEL.
They sing of thy approaching agony,
Which thou so eagerly didst question of.

SOUL.
My soul is in my hand: I have no fear,—
But hark! a grand mysterious harmony:
It floods me, like the deep and solemn sound
Of many waters.

ANGEL.
And now the threshold, as we traverse it,
Utters aloud its glad responsive chant.

CHOIR OF ANGELICALS.
Praise to the Holiest in the height.
And in the depth be praise:
In all His words most wonderful;
Most sure in all His ways!
O loving wisdom of our God!
When all was sin and shame.
A second Adam to the fight
And to the rescue came.
O wisest love! that flesh and blood
Which did in Adam fail,
Should strive afresh against the foe.
Should strive and should prevail:
And that a higher gift than grace
Should flesh and blood refine,
God's Presence and his very Self,
And Essence all divine.

=== Page 18 ===
O generous love! that He who smote
In man for man the foe,
The double agony in man
For man should undergo.

And in the garden secretly,
And on the cross on high,
Should teach His brethren and inspire
To suffer and to die.

Praise to the Holiest in the height,
And in the depth be praise:
In all His words most wonderful;
Most sure in all His ways!

ANGEL.
Thy judgment now is near, for we are come
Into the veiled presence of our God.

SOUL.
I hear the voices that I left on earth.

ANGEL.
It is the voice of friends around thy bed.
Who say the "Subvenite" with the priest.
Hither the echoes come; before the Throne
Stands the Great Angel of the Agony.
The same who strengthened Him, what time He knelt
Lone in the garden shade, bedewed with blood.
That Angel best can plead with Him for all
Tormented souls, the dying and the dead.

ANGEL OF THE AGONY.
Jesu! by that shuddering dread which fell on Thee;
Jesu! by that cold dismay which sickened Thee;
Jesu! by that pang of heart which thrilled in Thee;
Jesu! by that mount of sins which crippled Thee;
Jesu! by that sense of guilt which stifled Thee;
Jesu! by that innocence which girdled Thee;
Jesu! by that sanctity which reigned in Thee;
Jesu! by that Godhead which was one with Thee;
Jesu! spare these souls which are so dear to Thee,
Souls, who in prison, calm and patient, wait for Thee;
Hasten, Lord, their hour, and bid them come to Thee,
To that glorious home, where they shall ever gaze on Thee.

SOUL.
I go before my Judge.

VOICES ON EARTH.
Be merciful, be gracious; spare him, Lord.
Be merciful, be gracious, Lord, deliver him.

ANGEL.
Praise to His name!
O happy, suffering soul! for it is safe,
Consumed, yet quickened, by the glance of God

SOUL.
Take me away, and in the lowest deep
There let me be,
And there in hope the lone night-watches keep,
Told out for me.
There motionless and happy in my pain.
Lone, not forlorn,—
There will I sing my sad perpetual strain,
Until the morn,
There will I sing, and soothe my stricken breast,
Which ne'er can cease
To throb, and pine, and languish, till possess
Of its Sole Peace.
There will I sing my absent Lord and Love:—
Take me away.
That sooner I may rise, and go above,
And see Him in the truth of everlasting day.

SOULS IN PURGATORY.
Lord, Thou hast been our refuge: in every generation;
Before the hills were born, and the world was: from age to age Thou art God.
Bring us not, Lord, very low: for Thou hast said, Come back again, ye sons of Adam.
Come back, O Lord! how long: and be entreated for Thy servants.

ANGEL.
Softly and gently, dearly-ransomed soul,
In my most loving arms I now enfold thee.
And, o'er the penal waters, as they roll,
I poise thee, and I lower thee, and hold thee.
And carefully I dip thee in the lake,
And thou, without a sob or a resistance,
Dost through the flood thy rapid passage take,
Sinking deep, deeper, into the dim distance.
Angels, to whom the willing task is given,
Shall tend, and nurse, and lull thee, as thou liest;
And Masses on the earth, and prayers in heaven,
Shall aid thee at the Throne of the Most Highest.
Farewell, but not for ever, brother dear,
Be brave and patient on thy bed of sorrow:
Swiftly shall pass thy night of trial here,
And I will come and wake thee on the morrow.

SOULS.
Lord, Thou hast been our refuge, &c.
Amen.

CHOIR OF ANGELICALS.
Praise to the Holiest, &c. Amen.

CARDINAL NEWMAN.

Part Song—
Champagnerlied
Hofmann
Solo, Mr. G. J. Johnson

Royal Victorian Liedertafel

Pour the libation in fizzing champagne,
Leaping in silvery, swirling cascades;
Pour the libation in fizzing champagne,
Gushing in tremulous, prancing, proud courses,
Flowing in boiling and high foaming ardours,
Like to the olden-time streamlets and sources
    Deeply in Ida's dun thickets concealed.

Mould there thy pearl drops from silvery foam;
Seething they climb from their specular home.
    Mould there thy pearl drops from silvery foam.
There in the sharp infundibular goblets,
Sparkling and glistening light bubbling fountains,
Pour from the mouth of the broken sealed magnum
    Swaying and dancing on odorous pinions.

Swaying and sinking in aureate room,
Clink now the glasses with resonant swing;
Rolling and swelling like zephyrs in spring time.
There, in the fragrant recesses, in the delicate depths of the vessel
Dance frolicsome spirits, the lighthearted genii of champagne;
Backward and forward enlacing, departing,
Glistening, vanishing, lost in the crystal vase;
    Brief as the day of youth's gay effervescence.

=== Page 9 ===
Song—
The Windmill
Mr. Horace E. Stevens

Carol—
Child Divine
Choir of Boys and Royal Victorian Liedertafel

List! afar! what Angel voices
Fall upon the winter night!
Earth amid the sound rejoices:
Broods of evil speed their flight.
List, for aye sweet words of gladness
Through the generations roll,
Calming every mourner's sadness,
"Christ is born to save thy soul,"
Child Divine, what pow'rs are round Thee!
Health to man Thy presence brings:
Age by age have myriads found Thee,
Lord of lords and King of kings!

Born to heal what sin hath broken,
Born, its captives to release,
Born, by prophet lips forespoken,
Mighty God and Prince of Peace.
When the passions rage in blindness,
Thou their stormy waves canst still,
Turning by Thy spell of kindness
Hate and malice to good will.
Child Divine, who'er hath known Thee,
Hails the joy Thy presence brings,
Thine through life, in death we own Thee
Lord of lords and King of kings!

Sing, ye hosts, triumphant thronging
Round the lamb enthroned in light;
Sing, O man, the hymn prolonging,
Through thy toils of hourly fight.
Sing what grace, what nameless glory,
Stoop'd to rescue sons of earth,
Grateful spread the wondrous story,
Hail the Incarnate Saviour's birth,
Child Divine, all hearts that know Thee
Know the strength Thy presence brings,
Know what debt of love we owe Thee,
Lord of lords and King of kings!

Part Song—
Gondolier's Serenade
Royal Victorian Liedertafel
Schubert

WHILE moon and stars above us
Their airy dance renew,
Say, why should sadness move us,
Or earth-born care pursue?

Behold! the soft beams play, love.
Come in my bark away, love,
And glide, from bondage free,
Across the dark blue sea.

Now midnight's boding number
From good Saint Mark's I hear,
And all are hushed in slumber,
Except thy Gondolier.

Choir of Boys and Royal Victorian Liedertafel

(a) SLEEP, holy Babe, upon Thy Mother's breast,
Great Lord of earth and sea and sky,
How sweet it is to see Thee lie
In such a place of rest.
Sleep, holy Babe; Thine Angels watch around,
All bending low with folded wings,
Before the Incarnate King of kings,
In reverent awe profound.
Sleep, holy Babe, ah, take Thy brief repose;
Too quickly will Thy slumbers break,
And Thou to lengthened pains awake,
That Death alone shall close.

=== Page 11 ===
(b) Like silver lamps in a distant shrine
    The stars are sparkling bright;
    The bells of the city of God ring out,
    For the Son of Mary was born to-night;
    The gloom is past, and the morn at last
    Is coming with orient light.

    Never fell melodies half so sweet
    As those which are filling the skies;
    And never a palace shone half so fair
    As the manger bed where our Saviour lies;
    No night in the year is half so dear
    As this which has ended our sighs.

    Now a new power has come on earth,
    A match for the armies of Hell;
    A Child is born who shall conquer the foe,
    And all the spirits of wickedness quell;
    For Mary's Son is the Mighty One
    Whom the prophets of God foretell.

    The stars of heaven still shine as at first
    They gleamed on this wonderful night
    The bells of the city of God peal out,
    And the Angels' song still rings in the height;
    And love still burns where the Godhead burns,
    Hid in Flesh from our daily sight.

    Faith sees no longer the stable floor,
    The pavement of sapphire is there;
    The bright stream of Heaven streams out to the world,
    And Angels of God are crowding the air;
    And Heaven and earth, through the spotless birth,
    Are at peace on this night so fair.

Forty miles off, like a roebuck at bay,
Flouts Castle Brancepeth the Roundheads' array,
Who laughs "Good fellows ere this, by my fay?"
    Boot, saddle, to horse, and away!

Who? My wife Gertrude, that, honest and gay,
Laughs when you talk of surrendering. Nay!
I've better counsellors, what counsel they?
    Boot, saddle, to horse, and away!

(b) King Charles! and who'll do him right now?
King Charles! and who's ripe for the fight now?
    Give a rouse,
Here's in Hell's despite now—
    King Charles.

Who gave me the goods that went since?
Who raised me the house that sank once?
Who helped me to gold I spent since?
Who found me in wine you drank once?
    King Charles.

For whom used my boy George quaff else
By the old fool's side that begot him?
For whom did he cheer and quaff else
While Noll's damn'd troopers shot him?
    King Charles.

(c) Kentish Sir Byng stood for his king,
Bidding the crop-headed Parliament swing,
And pressing a troop, unable to stoop,
And see the rogues flourish and honest men droop.
Marched them along, fifty score strong,
Great-hearted gentlemen singing this song.

God for King Charles! Pym and such carles
To the devil that prompts their treasonous parles!
Cavaliers up! lips from the cup!
Hands from the pastry, nor bite take or sup,
    Till your marching along, fifty score strong,
    Great-hearted gentlemen singing this song.

Hampden to hell, and his obsequies knell,
Serve Hazelrig Fiennes and young Harry as well.
England good cheer. Rupert is near,
Kentish and loyalists keep we not here.
    Marching along, &c.

Royal Victorian Liedertafel

GLORY and love to the men of old.
Their sons may copy their virtues bold:
Courage in heart and sword in hand,
Ready to fight or ready to die for Fatherland.
Who needs biddig to dare by a trumpet blown?
Who lacks pity to spare when the field is won?
Who would fly from a foe if alone, or last,
And boast he was true, as cowards might do when peril is past?
Now to home again we come, the long and fiery strife of battle over;
Rest is pleasant after toil as hard as ours beneath a stranger sun.
Many a maiden fair is waiting here to greet her truant soldier lover,
And many a heart will fail, and brow grow pale, to hear the tale of cruel peril he has run.

Royal Victorian Liedertafel

(a) Good King Wenceslas look'd out,
    On the feast of Stephen;
    When the snow lay round about,
    Deep, and crisp, and even.
    Brightly shone the moon that night,
    Though the frost was cruel,
    When a poor man came in sight,
    Gath'ring winter fuel.

Tenor Solo. "Hither, page, and stand by me,
    If thou know'st it, telling,
    Yonder peasant, who is he?
    Where and what his dwelling?"

Treble Solo. "Sire, he lives a good league hence
    Underneath the mountain;
    Right against the forest fence,
    By St. Agnes' fountain."

Tenor Solo. "Bring me flesh, and bring me wine,
    Bring me pine-logs hither;
    Thou and I will see him dine,
    When we bear them thither."

Chorus. Page and monarch forth they went,
    Forth they went together;
    Through the rude wind's wild lament
    And the bitter weather.

Treble Solo. "Sire, the night is darker now,
    And the wind blows stronger;
    Fails my heart; I know not how,
    I can go no longer."

Tenor Solo. "Mark my footsteps, my good page
    Tread thou in them boldly;
    Thou shalt find the winter's rage
    Freeze thy blood less coldly."

Chorus. In his master's steps he trod,
    Where the snow lay dinted;
    Heat was in the very sod
    Which the saint had printed.

    Therefore, Christian men, be sure,
    Wealth or rank possessing,
    Ye who now will bless the poor,
    Shall yourselves find blessing.

Programme

Under the Batons of
Mr. MANSLEY GREER and
Mr. J. W. DAWSON.

Overture—
"Coriolan"
L. van Beethoven

The ORCHESTRA.

THANKS to Plutarch's stirring "Life" and Shakespeare's yet more stirring drama, everyone can know how that mighty warrior Caius Marcius, surnamed Coriolanus, delivered Rome repeatedly from the greedy grasp of her foes; and how that, having done so, he was shamefully handled by the ungrateful people he had saved spirited out as though he were a few ignorant and envious mob orators; how that he was banished the city and reviled with nothing vengeance, with a vast and invincible army; how that on the eve of the fulfilment of his just wrath his wife and little son and mother penetrated to the hostile camp and after long entreaty prevailed on him to withdraw his troops, conscious as he was that this course was tantamount to signing his own death-warrant—these several events subsequently proved.

It is this tragic crisis with which Beethoven has dealt in the present powerful tragic overture, how truthfully and well he felt by those who can sympathise with the contending passions which must have torn the warrior's heart during the terrible interval.

Madrigals—
(a) "Now is the Month of Maying"
Thomas Morley (1595)
(b) "Awake! Sweet Love"
John Dowland (1597)

LIEDERTAFEL and ASSOCIATED LADIES' CHOIR.

(a) NOW is the month of Maying, when merry lads are playing,
Fa la la, etc.
Each with his honey lass, a dancing on the greene,
Fa la la, etc.
The Spring clad all in gladness, doth laugh at Winter's sadness,
Fa la la, etc.
And to the Bazpipes' sound, the nymphs tread out their ground.
Fa la la, etc.
Fie then, why sit we 'musing, youth's sweet delights refusing?
Fa la la, etc.
Say, dainty nymphs, and speak, shall we play harley break?
Fa la la, etc.

(b) AWAKE, sweet love! thou art return'd;
My heart, which long in absence mourn'd,
Lives now in perfect joy.
Only herself hath seemed fair,
She only I could love,
She only drove me to despair
When she unkind did prove.

Recit—
"E' Strano!"
Aria—
"Ah, fors' e' lui"
(La Traviata)
Miss CESCA VOLLOGI.

E' STRANO! in coro scolpiti ho quegli Scutia che amore, è il palpit' dell'universo intorno misterioso orvce o delizia alcor!
Saria per me sventura un serio amore?
Che risolvi, turbata anima mia?
Nell'uomo ancora tacendeva,
Oh gioia ch'io non conobbi, esser amata amando!
E sdegnar la poss'io per l'aride follie del viver suo?
Ah, fors'è lui che l'anima solinga ne' tumulti,
goda sovente pingers de' suoi colori oculti!
Lui che, modesto e virile, all'egregio soglio ascese
destandomi all'amor!
A quell'amor che e' palpit' dell'universo, dell'universo intero, misterioso, altero,
crese e alizia al cor mio.
A me fioristi un araldo e tregiolo desira
quest'efficio dolceissimo signor dell'avvenire, quando ne' cieli il raggio di sua belta veda e tutta me paseca de quel divino error.

Follie! follie! delirio vano è questo!
Povera donna, soa, abbandonata in questo pozzoloso deserto che appallano.
Parigi, che spero or più? che far degg'io?
gioire di voluta ne' vorrici, di voluta gioir? gioir! gioir!
Sempre liberi degli' folleggiare di gioia in gioia, via che scorra il viver mio pel seno del passato.
Nasca il giorno o il giorno muoja, sempre lieta ne' ri rovi a diletti sempre nuovi del volare il meo pensier.

Madrigal—
"Matona, Lovely Maiden"
Orlando Lassus (1520-1594)

LIEDERTAFEL and ASSOCIATED LADIES' CHOIR.

MATONA, lovely maiden,
O listen to the song
I sing beneath thy window,
While night clouds roll along.
Dong, dong, derry, derry, etc.

I pray you hear my ditty,
'Tis sweet and not too long,
'Tis pointed, if not witty,
And sharpened like a prong.
Dong, dong, derry, derry, etc.

The words of choicest tissue,
To shoot love's aim, belong,
Then from your window issue,
Or else you do me wrong.
Dong, dong, derry, derry, etc.

You'll say if once you catch them,
And note their fine ding dong
Petrarca could not match them,
They are so sweet and strong.
Dong, dong, derry, derry, etc.

But if you think the more,
Should to all scorn belong,
A more complying treasure,
I'll choose from out the throng.
Dong, dong, derry, derry, etc.

LIEDERTAFEL and ASSOCIATED LADIES' CHOIR.

Here is a Rose unfolken,
Out of a tender shoot;

From Jesse sprung its root.

Interval

Symphony
No. 1 C major
L. van Beethoven

Adagio Molto
Allegro con brio
Andante cantabile con moto
Allegro molto e vivace (Minuetto and Trio)
Adagio
Allegro molto e vivace

The ORCHESTRA.

This the first of the great master's symphonic works, will be especially interesting, owing to the rarity of its performance and the opportunity it affords us of observing the development of the genius of Beethoven.
Throughout the work the influence of Haydn and Mozart is felt, and it has been said that the Andante un rit. even have been written by a Mozart or a Haydn.
The Third Movement, however, clearly prophesies the scherzo of the later symphonies, as do some of the earlier chamber works of the master.
With the last Movement we are carried back to the graceful time of Haydn, with all its quaintness and light-hearted gaiety.

Madrigals

(a) "April is in my Mistress' Face"
Thomas Morley (1594)

(b) "Flora gave me Fairest Flowers"
John Wilbye (1598)

LIEDERTAFEL and ASSOCIATED LADIES' CHOIR.

(a) APRIL is in my Mistress' face,
And July in her eyes hath place,
Within her bosom is September,
But in her heart is cold December.
O were it July all the year,
Then April show'rs I would not fear,
Nor blight that falleth in September,
Nor frost that chills in cold December.

(b) FLORA gave me fairest flowers,
None so fair in Flora's treasure.
These I placed in Phillis' bowers,
She was pleas'd and she's my pleasure.
Smiling meadows seem to say,
Come ye wantons, here to play.

"The Page Song"
(Romeo and Juliet)
Gounod

Miss CESCA VOLLOGI.

SINCE yesterday I've sought in vain my master.
Oh Capulet, perhaps he yet honours thy house!
I'll sing a stave—so the servants will come
Flocking out to repair yesternight's sad disaster.

Gentle dove wherefore art thou clinging
To a wild vulture's nest?
Soon, we trust, thou wilt be a-winging
To a far dearer rest.

Fond shepherdess, thy loves fight and foray,
And to tear and mangle his quarry
Hath beak both sharp and strong.
Unlike thine, soft and true and slender.
Oh may thine bend to lips more tender,
With kisses warm and long.

See you guard her safely,
They that live will know
For your dove may flutter
From her cage and go.

Now, it happ'd, that a ringdove flying
From her woodland so green.
To that eyrie came one eve sighing
For her young love, I ween.
O'er a banquet of prey they'd mangled
In the nest the vulture's brood wrangled.
Hark! rose their cry afar,
But the dove, far away was hearing
Love's own voice in its tones endearing
Beneath the evening star.

See you guard her safely,
They that live will know
For your dove may flutter
From her cage and go.

Madrigal—

"Down in a Flow'ry Vale"
Constantine Festa (1541)

LIEDERTAFEL and ASSOCIATED LADIES' CHOIR.

DOWN in a flow'ry vale, all on a summer morning.
Phillis I spied, fair nature's self adorning:
Swiftly on wings of love, I flew to meet her,
Coldly she welcomed me when I did greet her.

I warbled thus my ditty:
O shepherdess have pity,
And hear a faithful lover, his passion true discover.
Ah! why art thou to me so cruel?
Then straight replied my jewel—
If gold thou hast, fond youth, 'twill speed thy suiting,
But if thy purse be empty, come not to me a wooing.

Soon as I careless strayed, fond youth, with eyes averted,
Phillis I met, by all the swains deserted;
Swift she (tho' late so coy) then flew to meet me,
My lack I turn'd, all drest to her entrance;
She warbled thus her ditty:
O shepherd, now have pity,
And to your faithful lover your passion true discover
Then did I, cold and naughty, view her,
And thus replied unto her—
The love that's won by gold will prove undoing.
So since my purse is empty, I go no more a wooing.

=== Page 2 ===
La la la la la la!
We come in melodious measure,
O lady fair thy praise to sing:
'Twere us to a gladness to bring
Unto thy soul one thrill of pleasure.

What tho' with guarded door thou meet us,
If only thy heart open be?
'Tis all we are asking of thee
That thy rosy lips smile to greet us.

Song

Cello Solo

Cantata

Recit. and Aria

Part Song

Song

Cello Solo

Part Song

Bacchus: Ye lords, whose vicious treasure
Should mankind's woes allay,
I've called you in displeasure
Before my hook to-day.
The world more melancholy
And tedious daily grows,
And more than all, the folly
That from the winecup flows.
The people drudge and labour,
Debited as they are,
The sword rules and sabre,—
'Tis pity to behold!
Such misuse and detraction,
By Stry Thine eyes no more!
Look to our gay subjection
The world we must restore.
And therefore, children of the berry,
Ye wine both wise and merry, all take heed—
A King we'll choose both wise and merry,
So haste, approach, and to the poll proceed!

Chorus of Wines: Great Bacchus, hail!
Thy plan is wise, it cannot fail.
Our faith we plight by red and white,
The best of wines, wherever grown,
We loyally as king shall own.

Bacchus: See Don Sherry then, Spain's redoubtable knight,
He first appears your kind votes to invite;
By churchmen and laymen he e'er was beloved,
By the King of Prussia, All England's lord,
And e'en Isabella, the fond-hearted queen,
Regarded our knight with affectionate mien.
Where to sound of castanet
Gave the King of Wines his title
Where the sun doth never set,
Choose ye there the King of Wines?

The cold blast of winter why heed we,
If only thy bright face be near,
And with thy smile, what cheer?
Here standing at thy door what need we?
Of the brightness that springtime bringeth
Thine abode at all times can tell,
And fair lady, where thou dost dwell
Ever the nightingale singeth.
And to know is thy bosom longing
What gleam of light these may be.

"My Life for Thee"

Mr. H. M. Lee

Andante from B minor Concerto

Herr Theo. Liebe

"To the Sons of Art"

Soli, Messrs. T. Jack, S. Friff, S. J. Bruce and A. E. Johns.

Liedertafel

O Sons of Art, man's dignity to you is given:
Preserve it man!
It falls with you, with you ascends to heaven!
The hallowed themes of Magian dreams,
Founded in woman's vast creation,
Gliding like rivers find their ocean,
That great harmonious plan.

Eternal truth tho' oft rejected,
Exists not ever unprotected;
She finds a refuge with a truthful throng,
She turns to them for all her glory,
Mighty when veil'd in mystic story;
She wakes the lay of lofty voices,
And over all her foes rejoices,
Her vengeance flashing, peals in song.

"The Pilgrim of Love"

Mr. Armes Beaumont

"The Beleaguered"

Liedertafel

Fling wide the gates! come out!
Dauntless and true;
Brothers, of heart be stout,
We must not go,
Bring from the battlements
Our flag again;
Tho' by the leaguer rent
It hath no stain.

Mothers and wives to pray'r,
From this eve,
The Lord of Hosts will care
For all we leave.
Plead that we sought not fight,
Nor chose the field;
But ev'ry free heart's right
We dare not yield.

"I Fear no Foe"

Mr. Gladstone Wright

(a) Melody in F
(b) Gavotte in D

Herr Theo. Liebe

"Bacchanalian Election"

Solo by Mr. Gladstone Wright.

Liedertafel

Chorus: Oh no, no, no!
A Philistine and bigot he,
Our king Don Sherry cannot be!

Bacchus: Preferreth then Tokay, the valiant Magyar,
Who has off prov'd his mettle in love and in war;
The spirit of fortune auxiliarily bold,
Carried by the best of the young and the old.
Marianas—a many his honey have sipp'd,
And sturdy young Wenceles he many has tripp'd.
He drinks the wine of the strays,
Fiddling his fantastic lays,
Spurs the nut-brown maidens wear—
Will ye choose your monarch there?

Chorus: Oh no, no, no!
The Baron of Grünberg by far is he—
Tokay our king can never be!

Bacchus: The Baron of Grünberg now comes to view,
Whoever molesteth him, his boldness shall rue;
A cion of old and august name,
His "vinegar aspect" belies not his fame.
No enemy yet could against him prevail—
He drank, made grimaces, and so quickly turned tail.
That if a monarch you select
This candidate sardonically
Your stoutest foes you may defy,
They'll conquer, taste, and conquer'd fly!
Ye, then, O King, a king elect,
Will prove a bitter toad.

Chorus: No, no, no, no!
This is a false deceitful wine,
He never shall be king of mine!

Bacchus: Behold then the Freischutz! Pretender
In chivalry!
The lord of Champagne is, in all men's belief.
The elements four as his sponsors have stood,
And lavished their gifts in a generous mood.

"GOD SAVE THE QUEEN"

That come to say good-night to thee
And beneath thy window are thronging.
List then to what our song discovers:
With the dusk that closely hide,
Thus join the lovers we desire,
We are rovers, yes, gallant rovers,
For our gentle courtesy noted,
Two deities ruling our hearts,
To woman not to man devoted.
La la la la la! Ah! la la la!

Stephen Adams

To your free mother homage render,—
Boldly to gain her height aspire;
Enthroned she dwells in radiant splendour
No other throne her lustre desert.
While you her thousand paths are tracing
Press onward, keeping Truth in sight;
Come altogether, stand embracing
Before the Throne where paths unite!

Bishop

Mother and wives, to prayer
Relief is nigh,
For you each man will dare
Deeds not do die.
For sure as fire doth blaze,
Or foaming wine, you
Yield well-to-night upraise
Songs of the free.

Pinsuti

Kässmayer

From Fire he had the fervid glow
That animates his flow;
And Water gave the beads that swim
Like pearls on goblet's rim.
The air the fragrant, golden dress,
The garb of joyousness;
And Air gave him the spirit free,
That he may sing and be.
Piff, paff! see the froth
Mounting in the cup, sir!
Piff, paff! be not loth,
Quickly fill, quicky fill, sir!
Fill again, drink again,
Sparkling vintage of Champagne—
Crown him king and let him reign
O'er all the world, sir!

Chorus: No! 'tis an uproarious wine,
A bragart and vain-glorious wine!
Howe er he fume and rave.
He fills your glass to half, the knave!
A knave who will conquer's bent,
But whose élan is quickly spent.
No, no! Champagne
As King of Wines shall never reign!

Bacchus: Then lo! by the Rhine-river's beautiful
Behold the vine of Rauenthal grow!
From pure Teutonic blood 'tis sprung,
Make glad the heart, the spirit young—
The noble Rhine's vines,
Shall be as King have sway!

Chorus: In crystal green the golden wine,
The heart's blood of dear Father Rhine,
Yes, sent the strain of land and sea
This shall be King! O, our joy be!
All joyous hearts in concord sing,
The glorious Rhine-wine shall be King!

Free translation by H.W.P.

Chas. D. Dixon, Hon. Secretary.

Programme

The Orchestra. Mozart.

SONG—
"The Bedouin Love Song"
Mr. W. E. Lewis. Pinsuti.

PART SONG—
"Indian Love Song"
The Liedertafel and Orchestra. Zollner.

ONAWAY, awake, beloved,
Thou wild flower of the forest,
Thou the wild bird of the prairie,
Thou with eyes so soft and brown!
If thou only lookest at me,
I am happy, I am happy!
As the lilies of the prairie,
When they dew upon them feel!

=== Page 5 ===
Sweet thy breath is as the fragrance of the flowers in the morn.
As their fragrance is at evening, in the Moon when leaves do fall.
Does not all the blood within me leap to meet thee, Onaway.
As the springs to meet the sunshine in the Moon when nights are bright?
    Onaway!

    Onaway! my heart sings to thee,
    Sings with joy, when thou art near,
    As the sighing, singing branches
    In the pleasant Springtime Moon.
    When thou art not pleased, beloved,
    Then my heart is sad and dark,
    As the shining river darkens
    When the clouds on it throw shade.

    When thou smilest, my beloved,
    Then my troubled heart is brightened,
    As in sunshine gleam the ripples,
    That cold winds in rivers make.

    Smiles the earth, and smile the waters,
    Smile the cloudless skies above,
    But I lose the way of smiling
    When thou art no longer near.
    Onaway! I myself, behold me!
    Blood of my beating heart, behold!
    O awake, awake, beloved,
    Onaway! beloved awake,
    Onaway! Onaway! Onaway, wake,
    Awake! loved one, Onaway!

Mr. H. J. Robinson.

"Departure of the Caravan"
The Liedertafel and Orchestra.

AGAIN our march we resume, going on
Across the weary wastes alone,
The depths of the desert beholding,
We forward press throughout the day,
Though days are long, and long the way,
Life no joys unfolding:
And as we go, we yearn to know
How Fate our course is moulding.
We take our way, with a song we march,
With full delight, we onward fare,
Beneath this blue overhanging arch
We freely breathe in ample air.
We sing, we march

=== Page 7 ===
Allah, Allah, to Thee I render homage,
Allah, Allah, of Thine eternity, of Thine immensity,
I am the created image.
    Allah, Allah!
To Thee be praise, Thou ruler of creation,
That dwellest in eternity.
The solitude of the desert
Thou fillest with Thy majesty,
    Allah, Allah!

O Sanctissima! O Piissima!
Dulcis Virgo, Maria,
Mater amata intemerata;
Ora, ora pro nobis!

HAL-LOH! Hal loh! Hal-loh!
Hal-loh! o'er hill and dale we go,
Thro' smiling forest bounding,
No fear of danger can we know,
While loud the hunter's horn we blow,
The woods and craigs resounding
Echo as we go.

Tra-ra.

The sunbeams fill our hearts with glee,
With rapture now our souls are free,
All dangers then we laugh to scorn,
While merry sounds the twanging horn,
All dangers then we laugh to scorn,
While merry sounds the horn.

Tra-ra.

=== Page 8 ===
The eager chase to follow,
O'er hill thro' break and hollow.
And when the nimble deer we spy,
With ecstasy our hearts beat high,
All dangers laugh to scorn,
While merry sounds the horn,
    Tra-ra.

Our homeward way now wending,
We pause awhile at even's close,
Beneath some dear one's window,
And wish her sweet repose,
We pause beneath her window,
And sing at even's close.
Repose thou dearest maiden,
May heav'nly angels guard thy rest,
For thou with joy and beauty,
The hunter's life has blest.
Beneath thy chamber window,
The happy day we close,
Repose! Repose!
Hal-loh! Hal-loh! etc.

=== Page 9 ===
PART SONG—

"Happy Hours"

J. Siede.

The Liedertafel and Orchestra.

HAIL, O Night!
    Calm and bright;
    From care all hearts set free:
    Peace restoring,
    Come in thy majesty!
Shine brightly on us with thy mild beaming eye,
From thy glad presence all sorrow shall fly,
    As with the merry dance and song,
    The happy hours will pass along
        In harmony and revelry.

While pleasure reigning holds her radiant sway,
And hearts unfeigning glad homage pay,
While joy and beauty on life's pathway shine,
Why should we sorrow, why then repine?
Youth, happy youth, is life's richest prize!
Then love, then young love, beams in beauty's
    bright eyes
Banish maiden, all thoughts of sorrow,
Cares that sudden thee leave till morrow;
    And lightly as thy twinkling feet,
    Light my fond heart doth beat;
    Thy fond glance I meet,
        When thou art near.
    List to the beeze, love.
    Softly whisp'ring through the trees, love,
While the moon in her splendour sheds her rays
    from above;
Gently, so gently, on zephyrs borne, love stealing,
Softly in whispers, two fond hearts appealing;
Thine's my heart, dearest maiden,
    With love's bliss ever laden;
Thine are my thoughts, ever thine.

Hark! Hark! 'tis the midnight chime,
Wafted on the sweet wing of time;
    It sighs farewell, with parting knell.
Farewell, fair maiden, we shall meet again;
Joy's in the future though parting is pain;
Parting is brief, joy shall remain.
Fare thee well!

Notice to Members

Choir Rehearsals are held on Monday and Orchestral Rehearsals on Tuesday evenings, at 8 p.m., at the Society's Rooms, Independent Hall, Russell St.

Ladies and Gentlemen wishing to join the Society, either as Subscribing or Performing Members, will please communicate with the Hon. Secretary, c/o Messrs. Glen & Co., Collins St., who will be pleased to forward all information required.

Programme

Under the Baton of the Hon. Conductor,
Professor Marshall-Hall.

Part I.

Madrigals—

(a) Now is the month of Maying
THOMAS MORLEY
(1595)

(b) Awake! Sweet Love
JOHN DOWLAND
(1597)

Liedertafel and Associated Ladies' Choir.

(a) Now is the month of Maying, when merry lads are playing,
    Fa la la, etc.
Each with his bonny lass, a dancing on the grass.
    Fa la la, etc.
The Spring clad all in gladness, doth laugh at Winter's sadness,
    Fa la la, etc.
And to the Bagpipes sound, the nymphs tread out their ground.
    Fa la la, etc.
Fie then, why sit we musing, youth's sweet delight refusing?
    Fa la la, etc.
Say, dainty nymphs, and speak, shall we play barley break?
    Fa la la, etc.

(b) Awake, sweet love! thou art return'd;
    My heart, which long in absence mourn'd,
    Lives now in perfect joy.
Only herself hath seemed fair,
    She only I could love,
She only drove me to despair
    When she unkind did prove.

=== Page 6 ===
Arias—
(a) Tre Giorni
GIOVANNI B. PERGOLESE
(1710)
(b) Caro Mio Ben
GIUSEPPE GIORDANI
(1743)
Miss Elva Rogers.

Madrigal—
Matona, Lovely Maiden
ORLANDO LASSUS
(1520-1594)

Liedertafel and Associated Ladies' Choir.

MATONA, lovely maiden,
O listen to the song
I sing beneath thy window,
    While night clouds roll along,
        Dong, dong, derry, derry, etc.,

I pray you hear my ditty,
    'Tis sweet and not too long,
    'Tis pointed, if not witty,
        And sharpen'd like a prong.
        Dong, dong, derry, derry, etc.

The words of choicest tissue,
    To shoot love's aim, belong,
Then from your window issue,
    Or else you do me wrong.
        Dong, dong, derry, derry, etc.

You'll say if once you catch them,
    And note their fine ding dong,
Petrarcha could not match them,
    They are so sweet and strong.
        Dong, dong, derry, derry, etc.

But if you think the measure,
    Should to all scorn belong,
A more complying treasure
    I'll choose from out the throng.
        Dong, dong, derry derry, etc.

Sonata for Violin and Pianoforte—
NICOLO PORPORA (1686-1767)
GRAVE SOSTENUTO.
FUGA (ALLEGRO).

ALLEGRETTO MODERATO.

Mr. A. Zeiman, jun.

Part Song—Marienlied
MICHAEL PRAETORIUS (1571-1621)

Liedertafel and Associated Ladies' Choir.
(Translated from the German, for the Liedertafel, by Herr H. W. Puttman).

THERE is a Rose unfolded,
    Out of a tender shoot;
As sung to us of olden,
    From Jesse sprung its root.
It bloom'd for our delight
    All 'mid the frosts of winter,
Nigh on the noon of night.

That Roselet blest of Heaven,
    Isaiah did forshow,
By Mary to us given,
    The virgin pure as snow.
She, thro' God's holy might
    Gave birth unto an infant,
Nigh on the noon of night.

Duetto—Dall tuo Soglio Luminoso
LEONARDO LEO (1694)

JOHANN SEBASTIAN BACH

Part II.

Madrigal—
Flora gave me Fairest Flowers
JOHN WILBYE (1598)

Liedertafel and Associated Ladies' Choir.

FLORA gave me fairest flowers,
None so fair in Flora's treasure.
These I placed in Phillis' bowers,

Madrigal—
Down in a Flow'ry Vale
CONSTANTINE FESTA
(1541)
Liedertafel and Associated Ladies' Choir.

DOWN in a flow'ry vale, all on a summer morning,
Phillis I spied, fair nature's self adorning;
Swiftly on wings of love, I flew to meet her,
Coldly she welcomed me when I did greet her.

I warbled thus my ditty:
O shepherdess have pity,
And hear a faithful lover, his passion true discover;
Ah! why art thou to me so cruel?
Then straight replied my jewel—
If gold thou hast, fond youth, 'twill speed thy suing,
But if thy purse be empty, come not to me a wooing.

=== Page 10 ===
Soon as I careless stray'd, fond youth, with eyes averted,
Phillis I met, by all the swains deserted;
Swift she (tho' late so coy) then flew to meet me,
My back I turn'd, all deal to her entreaty;

She warbled thus her ditty:
O shepherd, now have pity,
And to your faithful lover your passion true discover.
Then did I, cold and haughty view her,
And thus replied unto her—
The love that's won by gold will prove undoing;
So since my purse is empty, I go no more a wooing.

=== Page 5 ===
PRÉFACE

La Fête fédérale de chant qui aura lieu à Lausanne au mois de juillet 1928 réunira environ quatorze mille chanteurs. C'est-à-dire que ce sera une manifestation musicale très importante. Or, selon la coutume, les sociétés lausannoises offriront à nos confédérés un concert, dit « de réception ». L'œuvre qui sera interprétée à cette occasion sera la Messe en fa mineur de Bruckner, qui, outre ses qualités de style et d'expression dont le public jugera, aura cet avantage de convenir à l'immense hall de Beaulieu où auront lieu les concerts et dans lequel des œuvres plus délicates ne feraient aucun effet. La Messe en fa mineur de Bruckner est une partition où trouvent leur emploi les qualités de simplicité et de grandeur que l'on s'accorde à reconnaître au maître autrichien ; c'est une fresque sonore, et, pour en saisir la beauté, il convient de faire abstraction du détail pour considérer l'ensemble de la composition. Elle n'est pas longue, mais elle est traitée dans un style large qui répondra, nous l'espérons, à l'ampleur de la salle. Il eut été imprudent de ne pas tenir compte de cette question de convenance.

Les organisateurs du « concert de réception » ont pensé bien faire en offrant au public de la Suisse romande une audition de la Messe en fa mineur de Bruckner quelques semaines avant la Fête fédérale. Le concert du mois de mars servira ainsi de prélude aux manifestations du mois de juillet.

Les sociétés suivantes prendront part à l'exécution de la Messe en fa mineur de Bruckner :
Chœur du Conservatoire de Lausanne (dir. M. Ch. Troyon); Union Chorale de Lausanne (dir. M. H. Lang); Chorale de la Pontaise (dir. M. N. Rochat).

Le Chœur du Conservatoire de Lausanne est renforcé, pour la circonstance, par un groupe important de dames de Lausanne et de Vevey.

L'Orchestre de la Suisse romande prête son concours. Et M. Hermann Lang, dont l'éloge n'est plus à faire, a été chargé de la direction du concert.

=== Page 6 ===
HERMANN LANG
Chef des auditions de la Messe en fa mineur.

L'antique Credo du 1er concile de Nicée (325) complété par le concile de Constantinople (381) affirme la foi du chrétien. Les formules musicales en sont énergiques et éclatantes :

Allegro
Credo, credo, unum Deum.

Au moment où le texte énonce le mystère de l'Incarnation une modulation amène une tonalité claire (d'ut, on passe en mi) et le ténor solo chante, sur un fond composé par les bois, et accompagné par des phrases alternées du violon solo et de l'alto solo :

![Musical notation for the Sanctus movement](page_180_232_1012_120.png)

La tonalité s'assombrit pour le Crucifixus et s'éclaire de nouveau pour un Et resurrexit éclatant suivi d'un judicare dramatique.

Ce Credo est le centre de l'œuvre, les autres morceaux semblent en découler par voie de conséquence et avoir été groupés autour de lui.

L’Agnus Dei reprend les implorations du Kyrie, et l’on retrouve le ton (fa mineur) et l’atmosphère du premier morceau :

![Musical notation for Agnus Dei](page_180_1400_1047_180.png)

=== Page 14 ===
puis le mode mineur fait place au majeur et l'appel dona nobis pacem, qui commence piano et parvient au fortissimo, retombe dans la douceur et remonte dans la force, finit par mourir dans une atmosphère de sérénité, comme si l'âme croyante sentait que sa prière est exaucée.

Les thèmes importants de l'œuvre semblent s'être donné rendez-vous à la page finale, comme pour appliquer un principe du cyclisme, cher à César Franck : le thème du Kyrie reparaît et domine les dernières phrases, il chante au hautbois solo au moment de la conclusion ; il est accompagné du thème de la fugue du Gloria, exposé par le chœur, et du thème initial du Credo, donné par les hautbois.

=== Page 15 ===
ANTON BRUCKNER

Fils et petit-fils de maîtres d'école, Anton Bruckner naquit à Ansfelden, village situé au sud de Linz, en Autriche, le 4 septembre 1824.

Parti à la conquête de son art, il connut les angoisses de l'autodidacte, qui tâtonne et qui doute. Et son œuvre fut un fruit tardif, puisque le compositeur avait déjà quarante ans quand il écrivit sa Messe en ré mineur qui fut sa première composition. Mais il était devenu un bon organiste et un solide contrapontiste. Il avait trouvé les conseillers qu'il cherchait. Le fameux théoricien et pédagogue Sechter, puis Otto Kitzler, étaient devenus ses maîtres.

Il avait appris le rudiment de son art au couvent de Saint-Florian, où il avait été admis comme enfant de chœur, à la mort de son père. Il y reçut des leçons de violon, de piano et d'orgue. Quand il eut terminé ses études, il fut nommé instituteur-adjoint à Windhag, près de Freistadt, où il fut aussi chef de chœur et sacristain. Mais il s'entendit mal avec ses supérieurs : il fut déplacé. On l'envoya dans un petit village, Kronstorf, où il fut assez heureux pour trouver un paysan qui possédait un piano et qui eut la générosité de le lui prêter. En 1845, Bruckner passa son examen final et fut appelé au poste d'instituteur de Saint-Florian, où il retrouva un milieu qu'il aimait beaucoup et dont il garda toujours le meilleur souvenir. Il fut bientôt nommé organiste du couvent. Enfin, le poste d'organiste de la cathédrale de Linz étant vacant, Bruckner se présenta et fut nommé après un concours où il avait montré un grand talent et beaucoup d'acquis. Il avait alors trente-deux ans. L'archevêque de Linz devint son protecteur et c'est grâce à sa bienveillance que le futur compositeur put obtenir des congés pour se rendre à Vienne, où vivait le professeur Sechter, qui lui enseigna la composition, et où Otto Kitzler l'initia aux principes de l'orchestration.

Douze ans plus tard, Bruckner s'installait à Vienne ; il avait été nommé professeur de composition au Conservatoire. Il fut bientôt chargé de tenir l'orgue de la chapelle impériale, il fit un cours à l'Université, sa musique commença à être jouée. Mais il n'eut que rarement l'occasion de s'entendre. L'estime de quelques-uns et la notoriété qu'il avait acquise ne suffisaient pas à rendre sa musique populaire. Aussi les exécutions de ses œuvres furent-elles rares. Et c'est la plus méchante aventure qui puisse arriver à un compositeur, car il perd ainsi l'occasion de se juger et de se corriger. On peut sans hésiter attribuer à cette cause certaines gaucheries dont Bruckner ne se défit jamais. Plusieurs de ses grandes compositions ne furent jouées qu'après sa mort ; d'autres ne furent présentées au public que longtemps après avoir été écrites. Et ses œuvres qui étaient jouées dans les concerts n'y obtenaient qu'un médiocre succès.

=== Page 16 ===
Mais voici que deux grands chefs d'orchestre s'emparent de cette musique et la révèlent avec éclat au public autrichien et allemand. Arthur Nikisch et Herman Levi eurent en effet le très grand mérite de défendre une cause qui semblait perdue. Mais la gloire de Bruckner n'a pas encore franchi certaines frontières : les pays latins ne l'ont point fêtée, jusqu'à ce jour. C'est que sa musique a des qualités et des défauts qui sont pour plaire aux publics de l'Europe centrale. Les musicographes français sont sévères pour lui. Ils lui reprochent « une emphase, une affectation de grandeur qui communiquent à ses œuvres une lourdeur toute germanique » (Woollett)¹ ; ils sont rebutés par « ces constructions immenses et bizarres » qui donnent « l'impression d'un effort un peu désordonné qui manque bien souvent son but » (Landormy)² ; mais certains d'entre eux s'efforcent de le comprendre et de l'aimer ; M. Camille Mauclair, par exemple, qui s'exprime ainsi : « Il est majestueux sans morgue et sans austérité ni emphase, avec une bonne foi persuasive et touchante qui, sans atteindre à la suavité subtile de Franck, la rappelle parfois. Anton Bruckner est de ceux, parmi les grands étrangers, que le public français devra apprendre tôt ou tard à connaître et à vénérer pour la beauté de son œuvre et pour la haute dignité de sa vie, semblable à celle des créateurs croyants du XIVe siècle »³.

Anton Bruckner a écrit trois messes, neuf symphonies, un Te Deum et un Psaume CL.

Il eut une vie difficile, et même à Vienne, où il avait une situation importante, il ne put jamais se soustraire aux soucis d'une activité intense.

Il forma des élèves dont plusieurs devinrent célèbres : Mahler, Hugo Wolf, Nikisch, Mottl, Klose.

La réputation lui étant venue, il reçut le titre de docteur honoraire de l'Université et la bourgeoisie d'honneur de la ville de Vienne.

Il était très pieux et sa musique n'a point d'autre objet que sa foi. Sentant sa fin venir, il dédia sa dernière symphonie « Au Bon Dieu », et, voyant qu'il n'arriverait pas à la terminer, il désigna son Te Deum comme devant lui servir de finale.

Il mourut le 11 octobre 1896.

Il était resté jusqu'à la fin de sa vie d'une simplicité et d'une naïveté touchantes. On raconte ce trait qui le peint à merveille : il avait déjà écrit des partitions compliquées, et prouvé sa valeur comme compositeur, qu'il ignorait encore tout de la pratique de l'orchestre, et comme Hans Richter lui offrait la baguette, au cours d'une répétition, pour diriger l'une de ses œuvres, on vit le pauvre homme debout, les bras ballants, dans une attitude de gaucherie et de timidité extrêmes... qui attendait, pour battre la mesure, que l'orchestre partît. Et comme personne ne bougeait, on l'entendit articuler, d'une voix étranglée par la peur : « Eh ! bien, Messieurs, quand il vous plaira ! »

¹ Histoire de la musique, 4e vol. p. 8.
² Histoire de la musique, nouvelle édition, p. 259.
³ Histoire de la musique européenne (1850-1914) p. 192.

=== Page 17 ===
M. Carl Næf remarque que les musiciens de l'époque romantique étaient Allemands du nord, et que Leipzig était leur foyer, mais que durant la deuxième moitié du XIXe siècle, le centre de gravité fait retour progressivement vers le sud1. Reger et Strauss sont Bavarois, Bruckner et son continuateur Mahler sont Autrichiens. Vienne, qui avait attiré Beethoven, reprend son rôle de capitale musicale des pays germaniques, qui lui fut contesté pendant la période romantique.

Mais le romantisme avait triomphé, et Wagner, continuant et dépassant le romantisme, avait fait une révolution dont toute la musique subit l'influence. Une réaction, cependant, s'était dessinée, et Brahms en avait été le chef. Bruckner avait pris parti pour Wagner. Aussi les noms de Bruckner et de Brahms furent-ils comme les drapeaux des deux camps ennemis, dont les querelles furent chaudes.

Bruckner introduit le style de Wagner dans la symphonie et dans la musique d'église. Son orchestre n'est plus celui de Beethoven et de Brahms, il accueille, dans la symphonie, des instruments et des procédés wagnériens. Toutefois cette influence de Wagner sur Bruckner ne doit pas nous tromper, il importe de distinguer : l'inspiration de Bruckner a d'autres sources que celle de son modèle. Le musicien autrichien emprunte à Wagner certains procédés, mais son milieu, sa nature, sa religion, donnent à sa musique une couleur et une signification qui ne sont pas wagnériennes. En effet, Bruckner chante sa foi chrétienne et ne connaît point d'autre thème. Sa musique symphonique elle-même n'est qu'un cantique instrumental. Et cela pourrait bien être la cause des faiblesses que l'on y trouve. Mais ceci demande à être expliqué.

Comme on le sait, l'ancienne „suite de danses“ des Français est la mère de la musique instrumentale moderne. L'esprit des gavottes, des bourrées, des menuets et des gigue n'a pas entièrement disparu à l'époque de la symphonie classique des Viennois, et, comme pour en témoigner, les compositeurs de ce temps conservent le menuet poitevin. Et, après, la musique symphonique remonte souvent à la source de l'art instrumental, en marquant une prédilection pour les formes rythmiques qui semblent accompagner des danses imaginaires, La VIIe symphonie de Beethoven, par exemple, n'a-t-elle pas mérité d'être appelée par Wagner «l'apothéose de la danse»?

D'essence profane, la musique symphonique s'inspire du rythme du geste. N'était-il pas dangereux de l'oublier? N'était-ce pas une folle gageure que de confier à l'orchestre ce que les voix expriment par les moyens d'une technique basée sur le rythme de la parole? En d'autres termes: la musique religieuse peut-elle impunément renier le verbe?

Bruckner ne fut pas le premier qui demanda à l'orchestre de se substituer aux voix, mais plus que les autres ses symphonies ont mérité le reproche

1 Carl Næf, Histoire de la Musique, p. 352.

=== Page 18 ===
que M. Louis Laloy fait à la musique moderne qui, ayant abandonné le théâtre pour le concert, a abandonné ainsi toute prétention à être matériellement réalisée, et où l'on a vu — dit-il — «s'y dilater ces andantes contemplatifs, ces largos extasiés, et y prédominer finalement l'amorphe «mélodie infinie», tandis que les scherzos saisis de vertige y précipitaient follement des ébats impossibles» ¹.

Le public lausannois a eu l'occasion d'apprécier récemment une symphonie de Bruckner. Nous ne serions pas surpris que l'audition de la Messe en fa mineur ne lui procurât l'occasion de constater que ce musicien y est beaucoup plus parfait que dans sa musique symphonique. C'est que là, il est dans son élément. Pour chanter la louange du Créateur rien ne vaut la voix humaine. Et la convenance des moyens à la destination de l'œuvre, la règle que lui impose le texte, l'appui d'une tradition bien établie, tout cela soutient et endigue l'imagination de Bruckner.

Le résultat est surprenant : celui qui écrit des symphonies dont le plan est parfois un peu flasque et qui paraissent bien longues, malgré leurs réelles beautés, réussit à mettre sur pied des messes bien composées, de vaste dimension, il est vrai — comme celles de Bach et de Beethoven, — mais dont les proportions sont bonnes et dont on peut dire qu'elles sont bien venues.

Le voeu de M. Camille Mauclair de voir se répandre la musique de Bruckner dans les pays de langue française pourrait être exaucé si l'on commençait par la musique religieuse du compositeur autrichien.

La Messe en fa mineur qui est exécutée aujourd'hui est faite pour initier l'auditeur à l'art d'un maître dont la vie et l'œuvre imposent le respect.

Aloys FORNEROD.

¹ Rameau, p. 194.

In fear of the Gods shall ye dwell, sons of men!
So the empire they hold in their hands everlasting
And wield at their pleasure the lightnings of fate.

He doubly shall tremble whom they have exalted!
On turrets of cloudland enthroned they banquet,
Pour golden libations.

But are they offended, they hurl forth the guest,
To dishonour and ruin, where shadows are deepest.
There vainly he waiteth, in darkness and bondage,
For justice and judgment.

But they hold, the Immortals, eternal carousals,
Pour golden libations.
They stride over height unto height thro' the heavens.

=== Page 11 ===
In fear of the Gods shall ye dwell, sons of men!
So 'le empire they hold in their hands everlasting
And wield at their pleasure the lightnings of fate.

He doubly shall tremble whom they have exalted!
On turrets of cloudland enthroned they banquet,
Pour golden libations.

But are they offended, they hurl forth the guest,
To dishonour and ruin, where shadows are deepest.
There vainly he waiteth, in darkness and bondage,
For justice and judgment.

But they hold, th' Immortals, eternal carousals,
Pour golden libations.
They stride over height unto height thro' the heavens,
From earthy abysses arises the groaning
Of long smother'd Titans,
A fragrant oblation, faint cloud on the azure.

The all-ruling Gods shut the gates of their blessings
On whole generations,
Avoiding the once cherish'd, still speaking features
Of Grandsire in far distant and blameless sons.

Thus chanted the Sisters; below, 'mong the Shadows
The Exil'd one hearken'd the Fates' dread foreboding
He thinks on his children, all darkness and doubt.

Ah! Rendimi Quel Core

Francesco Rossi
MISS LOVIE MULLER.

NOTE.—Those desiring to leave the Hall before the end of the Programme are requested to do so now, as the doors will not again be opened until conclusion of Concert.

THE BIRTH OF HERCULES,
FROM THE LYRIC DRAMA
ARISTODEMUS.
G. W. L. Marshall-Hall.

THE LIEDERTAFEL
AND ORCHESTRA.

THE lineal descendants of Hercules, the Messenians, have, by pestilence and their foes, been driven to their last stronghold, the citadel of Ithome. There they await the oracle of the god, which shall determine their fate, and in worship to Zeus recall the ancient splendid legend of the birth of their ancestor Hercules, and of the wrath of Hèrè (Juno), to whom they ascribe all their misfortunes. They implore Zeus to remember his erewhile love towards his offspring, and to avert from them "the wrath and the doom." The music is an attempt to realize something of the dignity and splendour with which the Greeks surrounded their gods, in whom they embodied the most vital characteristics of their race. There is nothing in the wonderful symbolism of their mythology more inspired than the conception that their Heroes were the offspring of the intercourse of gods with mortal beings. Thus alone did it seem to them, could the pre-eminence of certain of the greatest among men be accounted for.

Programme.

Under the Baton of
Mr. August Siede.

Part I.

OVERTURE—
"Fidelio"
The Orchestra. Beethoven.

"The Migration of the Normans"
Max Bruch.
Soloist—Signor A. Rebottaro.

Liedertafel and Orchestra.

THE evening approaches and the autumnal breeze is blowing;
Hoarfrost encircles the firs;
O crosier and book and monks prayer;
We must all leave here (go away from here).

The native country is getting dark, dusky and cold;
The holy springs are running turbidly.
Already the axe is flashing to fell thee
Thou green forest, round which the gods are hovering.

And we depart silently, a beaten army;
Extinguished are our stars;
O Iceland, icy rock of the sea,
Rise up in mighty distance!

Rise up and receive our equipped race!
The old gods, the old right,
The old Normans
Upon rostrate ships come swimming.

Where the volcano is blazing embers are falling,
Stormy waves surround the shores with foam;
Upon thee, thou defying extremity of the world
We will dream away the winter night.

=== Page 7 ===
ARIA—
"Und ob die Wolke sie ver-hülle"
(DER FREISCHUTZ) Weber.
Miss Hesketh Jones.

"NÄNIE"
(SCHILLER) Johannes Brahms.
Op. 82.
For Chorus of Mixed Voices and Orchestra.
Liedertafel,
Associated Ladies' Choir and Orchestra.

AND the beautiful too, must die!
    Even the beautiful die,
What men and gods has conquered, melts not the iron heart,
Melts not the stygian Jove.
Only once, for love! the Monarch of Shadows relented,
But at the threshold called back.
    Called he back his gift!
Aphrodite staunches not the wound,
Which in the lovely body, the Cruel Boar has torn.
Nor could mother immortal save the godly hero falling at the gate of Troy,
    Falling, his fate fulfilled!
But from the sea she arises, with the daughters of Nereus,
And in loud lamenting, mourns for the son now glorified.
    See, how mourn the gods!
    See, how mourn the goddesses all!
That the beautiful Fades!
Mourn that the Highest dies!
And a song of lament from heart of the loved is glorious!
    Ah! to go songless and silent to Orcus dark reign!
And a song of lament from heart of the loved is glorious!

=== Page 8 ===
Part 2.

Symphony. No. 2 in D.
Beethoven,
Adagio Molto—Allegro con brio—Larghetto—
Scherzo (Allegro)—Finale (Allegro molto).
The Orchestra.

THE CATHEDRAL SCENE
from "FAUST"
Schumann.
(Service, Organ and Singing. Gretchen amongst the crowd. Evil Spirit behind Gretchen.)
Miss Hesketh Jones (Gretchen),
Signor A. Rebottaro (Evil Spirit),
Liedertafel,
Associated Ladies' Choir and Orchestra.

Evil Spirit—
How diff'rent, Gretchen, was it
When thou cam'st with pure heart
Here to the altar,
Thy well thumb'd little book didst clasp,
Thy pray'r's soft lisping;
Thy thoughts half playful,
Half turned to Heaven.
Gretchen,
Where now thy thoughts?
And in thy bosom
What misdeed hast thou?
Ist for thy mother's soul thou'rt praying,
Who through thee, to never ending pain,
Slept on and on?
Upon the threshold, whose the blood?
What stirs beneath thy heart?
Hath it not dawning Life
That scares itself and thee
With its forboding presence!

=== Page 9 ===
Gretchen—
Woe! Woe!
Could I from the thoughts escape,
That pierce through my being
And, accusing me,
Haunt me still!

Chorus—
Dies irae, dies illa,
Solvent sæculum in favilla.

Evil Spirit—
Tremble thou!
For the trumpet sounds!
The graves are quaking!
And from its ashy rest,
Thy heart,
For flaming tortures
Afresh created,
Starts forth;

Gretchen—
Would I were hence!
'Twould seem as though the organ's tone
Could hinder my breathing;
The singing
Thrills my heart with torture!

Chorus—
Judex ergo cum sedebit,
Quidquid latet ad parebit,
Nil inultum remanebit.

Gretchen—
Oppress'd I feel!
The cluster'd pillars
Imprison me,
And the groined roof
Whelms me—Air!

Evil Spirit—
Ah, hide thee! Sin and shame
Are never hidden.
Air? Light?
Woe's thee.

Chorus—
Quid sum miser tunc dicturus?
Quem prætonum rogaturus,
Cum vix justus sit securus?

Evil Spirit—
Their faces from thee
The blessed turn away,
The pure from thee withhold
Their hands with shudd'ring!
Woe!

Chorus—
Quid sum miser tunc dicturus?

Gretchen—
Friend your help!
Or I faint.

=== Page 6 ===
Programme

Under the Batons of
Messrs. MANSLEY GREER
and JOHN W. DAWSON.

Accompanist:
Mr. H. S. ELVINS.

"Salutations and greeting to you all."

"The hour's now come,
The very moment bids thee ope thine ear."
—Shakespeare.

Part I.

Overture—
"Il Flauto Magico"
Mozart

The ORCHESTRA.

Part Songs—

(a) "Evening"
(Solo: Mr. F. S. WHITEHEAD)
Albt

(b) "Die Post"
(Cornet Solo by Mr. A. HAIGH)
Schafer

The LIEDERTAFEL.

=== Page 7 ===
"It is a beauteous evening, calm and free,
The holy time is quiet as a nun
Breathless with adoration." —Wordsworth.

(a) DAY again his race has run,
    And the tranquill night comes on,
    Soothingly her pinions waving,
    Heated hill and valley laving,
    Spreading from her starry chart.
        Holy peace to every dwelling,
        Holy peace to ev'ry heart.

    All who rest in slumber's arm,
    Void of trouble, void of harm,
    Heavn'ly angels now are guarding,
    Ev'ry danger from them warding,
    Pow'rs of evil must depart—
        Holy peace to every dwelling,
        Holy peace to ev'ry heart.

(b) THRO' forest deep at dead of night,
    The mail is slowly borne;
    While sleep the weary travellers,
    The post-boy winds his horn.

    The forest-ranger's dwelling
    Within the wood is seen,
    The horn a tale is telling—
    What can its echoes mean?

    It's tunes so soft and sweetly flow,
    The winds, in passing by,
    Pause at an open window,
    And mingling with them fly.

    Where sleeps the forest maiden,
    While beams the moon above;
    With love her dreams are laden—
    With melody and love.

    "The horn sounds, and produces a general bustle. . . . As the coach rattles through the village, everyone runs to the window, and you have glances on every side of fresh country faces, and blooming, giggling girls." —Washington Irving.

Bass Solo—

"The Wanderer" Schubert

Mr. EDWIN A. URE.

=== Page 8 ===
Tenor Solo—
"Onaway, awake beloved"
(Hiawatha's Wedding Feast)
Coleridge Taylor
Mr. JAMES W. WADE.

"You shall hear
How the gentle Chibiabas
Sang his songs of love and longing."
—"Legend of Hiawatha"—Longfellow.

Cello Solo—
(with Orchestral Accompaniment)
"Kol Nidrei"
Max Bruch
Op. 47.
Herr LOUIS HATTENBACH.

Recit and Aria—
"Non Mi Dir"
(Don Giovanni)
Mozart
Miss ELSIE DAVIES.

=== Page 9 ===
Part Songs—

(a) "O Sanctissima"

(b) "Warrior's Prayer" Lachner

The LIEDERTAFEL.

(a) Sanctissima! O Piissima!
    Dulcis Virgo, Maria,
    Mater amata Intemerata;
    Ora, ora pro nobis!

(b) Thou art, O Lord, my star by night,
    By day my sun above me;
    Thou art my confidence and might,
    That onward ever move me;
    With Thee o'er deserts do I go,
    And brave in trust no terror know.

    Give me the power my sword to wield,
    And steel my blade to serve me,
    That ere my purpose I shall yield,
    No foe may e'er unnerve me;
    Aid me when I oppose the foe,
    And guide my eye to strike the blow.

    On mountain's height wher'er I stray
    From faltering horse protect me,
    And let Thy angel on my way
    Thro' wood and wild direct me;
    And when upon the trackless sand,
    Be Thou my ever-guiding hand.

    The balmy breeze upon me send,
    To cooling shade convey me,
    E'er head and heart in conflict end,
    And foot and eye betray me;
    And fill me into quiet rest,
    In dreams of home afar caressed.

    Thou art, O Lord, my star by night,
    By day my sun above me.

"Here pause we gentle, for a space;
    And if our tale hath won your grace
    Grant us brief passage, and again
    We will renew the Minstrel strain."
    —Scott.

=== Page 10 ===
Special Notice.

One of the Greatest Musical Events of the Year will take place with the presentation early in July next of Mozart's "Requiem," by the Liedertafel, under the baton of the Hon. Conductor, Professor Marshall-Hall. This Immortal work has been in rehearsal for some time past, and every effort will be made to ensure a performance worthy of the best traditions of the Society.

=== Page 11 ===
Part II.

"Masters, play here; I will content your pains,—
Something that's brief."
—Othello, Act III., Scene I.

Overture—
"Oberon" Weber
Adagio. Allegro con fuoco.

The ORCHESTRA.

SINCE the creation of Shakespere's "Midsummer Night Dream," no such delightfully picturesque suggestion of the world of sprites, elves and fairies has been given to us as is contained in this romantic Overture. From the mysterious horn call, with which the introduction opens, and the gradual awakening of the drowsy little hamsters of the woodland, to the brilliant and lively theme of the Allegro, and the delightful suggestion of sweet melodies which follow, everything is invested with a profound sympathy with Nature, whose myriad life seems here informed with soul understanding. As we listen to this deeply penetrating poet, the line of demarcation between higher and lower organisms fades away, and their hidden secrets, the unity of life, is disclosed. It is this highly beautiful revelation which causes us to experience such aesthetic pleasure, unmixed with any feeling of incongruity.
—G. W. L. M. H.

"Marcia Aria e Coro dei Sacerdoti" (Il Flauto Magico) Mozart
Mr. EDWIN A. URE,
LIEDERTAFEL and ORCHESTRA.
"A mellifluous voice, as I am a true knight;"
Twelfth Night. Act II., Scene III.

Part Song—
"The Image of the Rose" Reichardt
Solo: Miss ELSIE DAVIES.
The LIEDERTAFEL.
WHILE through a valley I was straying,
A rose fresh blooming met my sight,
Such ample store of charm displaying,
My bosom felt unknown delight.

=== Page 12 ===
With fragrant moss around it swelling,
Appeared the gem of lustre mild;
Oh, ne'er from out a fairer dwelling;
The angel face of virtue smiled.
Beautiful form, tarry, oh, tarry with me.

A strange yet pleasing sense came oe'r me,
I felt new life within me bound,
While I beheld the flow'r before me,
Unwonted rapture then I found.
That image fair of heav'nly pleasure,
Upon my heart is deeply traced;
It is my bosom's dearest treasure,
And never can it be o'ersc'd.
Beautiful form, tarry, oh, tarry with me.

When sorrow's clouds are round me low'ring
At once the rose's form appears,
A charm such anguish overpow'ring,
It stills my sighs, it dries my tears.
Oh flow'r that 'mid the darkness springing,
By heav'n's decree upon me shone;
To thee my heart is fondly clinging,
And will not cease till life is gone.
Beautiful form, tarry, oh, tarry with me.

"Ye flowers, . . . . Bright gems of earth, in which,
Perchance, we see
What Eden was—what Paradise may be."
—Anon.

(a) "Abenlied" Schumann

(b) "Weigenlied" Schubert

(c) "Tarantelle" G major Hopper

Herr LOUIS HATTENBACH.

"There is sweet music here, that softer falls
Than petals from blown roses on the grass."
—Tennyson.

Mr. JAMES W. WADE.

=== Page 13 ===
Symphonic Ode—
The Desert
Felicien David

Translated from the French for the Melbourne Liedertafel by Madame Carlotta Tasca.

The LIEDERTAFEL and ORCHESTRA.

"The rosy tints of morning pierce the haze—
The eastern sky illumining with its rays,
From the heav'n above,
The star of day, like a loud hymn of praise,
Fills all the Desert with new light and love.

Part III.
Sleep.
The Rising of the Sun.

The Caravan resumes its progress.

Chorus.
With cheerful heart
On our way let us start,
Toil heeding not, our aim to gain
We roam through the Desert dreary;
Still! on we press nor stay for rest,
Nor stay for rest, though the days are long
And our limbs are weary.
Away we march, ever free and gay,
So pure the air, so bright the day!
We blithely sing as we march along,
Our feet keep time to our rhythmic song.

The Caravan disappears in the distance.

Chorus.
STLLAH! Allah! To Thee I homage render.
Of Thine immensity,
Of Thine eternity,
Image am I, my praise I tender.
Allah!
All praise to Thee; Thy glory is unbounded,
The Sovereign of the world Thou art;
In solitude though I should wander,
Yet Thou art there, in every part.
Allah!

"Sleep dwell upon thine eyes, peace in thy breast."
—Romeo and Juliet. Act II., Scene II.

"A little warmth, a little light
Of loves bestowing, and so, good night."
—Du Maurier.

=== Page 7 ===
Programme

PART I

Cantata—The Viking's Last Voyage
(BARITONE SOLO, MR. HORACE E. STEVENS) CHADWICK

Liedertafel

NORTHWARD from Denmark came Eric and Jorund,
    To Upsal came sailing to win back their own
From Hakon the Sea-king, who, conquering Sweden,
    Their kinsman had slain, and had seized on his throne,

King Hakon of Sweden was strong, brave and fearless,
    And though half his warriors were roaming the sea,
And cruising as vikings from Norway to Bretland,
    As fierce as the tempest, as wild and as free,

Yet fought he the brothers with spirit undaunted,
    Until by his sword-stroke King Eric fell dead;
Until with his forces all broken and scattered,
    Back to his warships King Jorund had fled.

But Hakon, the fearless, was mortally wounded,
    His men, dead and dying, were strewn on the shore,
The tide was fast ebbing and so was his life-blood,
    He knew that by nightfall he'd enter death's door.

=== Page 8 ===
Sadly, yet bravely, he turned his glance seaward,
    He saw his great warship at rest on the strand;
The ship that had borne him through storm and through battle,
    Her helm ever faithful beneath his firm hand.

Then all the old mem'ries came thronging and throbbing:
    Of cruises so many, so long and so far,
Of storms on the ocean, of salt spray a-dashing,
    Of fights in the Baltic, of wounds, and of scar.

Of midnight in summer, the sky flushed with crimson,
    The waters reflecting the northern light's bars.
Of loyal companions, and telling of sagas,
    While sailing on swiftly beneath the bright stars.

"And now a long cruise we shall sail for the last time."
    The dying King said to those gathered near,
"His heroes with Hakon will set out undaunted,
    To death as to battle we go without fear.

"Launch then the warship, her deck pile with dead wood.
    And thereon rest gently my battle-men dead,
Your King place among them all clad in his armour,
    And bright shield untarnished laid under his head.

"Free let the helm be, set all the flags flying,
    The great anchor hang in its place at the rail,
And then fire the death pile, thus passing in glory
    Straight east to Walhalla and Odin we'll sail."

Just as the low sun had gilded with splendour
    The wild rocky islands that bounded the bay,
And then sunk in crimson behind the far mountains,
    The soul of King Hakon from earth passed away.

In the grey gloaming the moorings were severed,
    The fresh wind blew off shore, the fire leaped up red,
In clear flame a-burning between the dark islands,
    Straight eastward to Odin, King Hakon's ship sped.
