曲目解説

●岩井 宏之

「コシ・ファン・トゥッテ」舞台装置図

●モーツァルトとオペラ
ヨーロッパが生んだ最も偉大な旋律作家にして、かつ最も偉大な劇詩人だったW.A.モーツァルト（1756－1791）は、劇音楽の分野で三つのタイプの作品を遺した。イタリア語で歌われ、かつ悲劇的な内容を持つオペラ・セリア、イタリア語で歌われるのだが喜劇的な内容を持つオペラ・ブッファ、ドイツ語で歌われ、かつ喜劇的な要素を強くとどめているジングシュピール——以上がそれぞれある。こんにち、どのタイプのオペラもレパートリーとしてヨーロッパの歌劇場に生き続けているが、モーツァルトの名前をオペラ作曲家として高めているのは、喜劇的な内容を持つオペラ・ブッファとジングシュピールである。そこでは、モーツァルトでなければ生み出せなかったような人物に出会う。手垢にまみれた類型的でない人物、いつの時代であれ、現実に生きていたであろうような人物に出会うのである。たとえば、〈フィガロの結婚〉におけるフィガロ、スザンナ、ケルビーノ、〈ドン・ジョヴァンニ〉におけるレポレロ、〈魔笛〉におけるパバゲーノ、などをあげれば充分であろう。彼らは——そしてここにあげなかった登場人物の多くは——人間であるがゆえの喜びや悲しみ、楽しみや悩みを持っている。いかに考えるなら、彼らはモーツァルトによって血と肉を与えられた存在そのもの、なのである。

〈コシ・ファン・トゥッテ〉は、オペラ・ブッファに属する作品であり、〈フィガロの結婚〉（1786年）、〈ドン・ジョヴァンニ〉（1787年）と並んで、モーツァルトのオペラ・ブッファを代表する三大傑作の一つ、その最後の作品である。

モーツァルトが〈コシ・ファン・トゥッテ〉を書きあげたのは、1790年、亡くなる1年前のことで、当時モーツァルトは34歳だった。まったく奇妙なことだが、あらゆるオペラ作曲家のなかで最も観客を楽しませる技術にすぐれ、しかも芸術的に高い水準でそれを成し得るモーツァルトが、〈コシ・ファン・トゥッテ〉を作曲するころには、2年以上もオペラの注文なしに過ごさなければならなかったのだ。時代を超越するすぐれた作品は、しばしば、それが書かれた時代からは冷たい目で迎えられる。モーツァルトのオペラも——いや、モーツァルトの人生そのものも——その例外ではなかった。

だがしかし、ともかくモーツァルトは〈コシ・ファン・トゥッテ〉を作曲する機会をつかんだ。作曲を注文したのは、啓蒙君主の一人としてヨーロッパ史上にその名をとどめた神聖ローマ皇帝（オーストリア皇帝）フランツ・ヨーゼフ二世である。そして台本作製にあたったのが、〈フィガロの結婚〉〈ドン・ジョヴァンニ〉ですでにモーツァルトと協力し、成果をあげていたロレンツォ・ダ・ボンテ（1749－1838）だった。こうして、モーツァルトとダ・ボンテとの最後の協力が実現することになったのである。

=== Page 6 ===
曲目解説

●ダ・ボンテと《コシ・ファン・トゥッテ》
モーツァルトより7歳年長のダ・ボンテは、本名エムマヌエーレ・コネリアーノ、イタリア生まれのユダヤ人である。14歳のとき、父や弟たちとキリスト教に改宗、ロレンツォ・ダ・ボンテと名乗るようになった。この名前は彼等をキリスト教に改宗させた司教の名前そのままである。ダ・ボンテは神学校に学び、1770年に下級神父となったが、やがて文学と女性に身をゆだね、イタリアから逃げ出る破目にになる。ウィーンで、オペラの台本作者として活躍するようになったのは、1783年のことだった。そして、この年、ダ・ボンテとモーツァルトは知り合い、ダ・ボンテはモーツァルトのためにオペラの台本を書くことを約束した。以後、1790年まで、両者の協力は続くのである。

《コシ・ファン・トゥッテ》のためにダ・ボンテが選んだ題材は、当時、ウィーンの貴族の間で実際に起こった事件だといわれている。2人の若い貴族と皮肉な老人とが絡むした。2人の貴族が、それぞれのファンセを、24時間以内に、たがいに入れ替って誘惑することができるかどうか——これが話の内容である。女性の真顔を信じていなかったダ・ボンテは、さっそくこの題材にとびついた。そしてこれを、2幕のコミックなオペラに仕立てあげた。オペラに出てくる哲学者ドン・アルフォンソは、女性の真顔を頭から否定してかかるが、これはおそらく、ダ・ボンテの本心を代弁したものであろう。

《コシ・ファン・トゥッテ》は、その内容が不真面目であるとして、後世から多くの非難を浴びた。たとえばベートーヴェンは、女性を理想化する傾向が強かったが——オペラ《ウィディオロ》のヒロイン、レオノーレはその典型である——そのベートーヴェンからみれば、《コシ・ファン・トゥッテ》のような題材を、わざわざ舞台にかけること自体が許せない行為であり、音楽としての価値にはかかわらなく、《コシ・ファン・トゥッテ》を排斥した。だが、19世紀および20世紀の舞台芸術のありようを多少とも知っているものにとって、ベートーヴェン的な考え方は、もはや意味がないのは明らかであろう。

●《コシ・ファン・トゥッテ》の登場人物
フェルランド……（テノール）……青年士官
グリエルモ……（バリトン）……青年士官
アルフォンソ……（バス）……哲学者
フィオルディリージ……（ソプラノ）……グリエルモの恋人
ドラベルラ………（ソプラノ）……フェルランドの恋人、フィオルディリージの妹
デスピーナ………（ソプラノ）……フィオルディリージ、ドラベルラ姉妹に仕える女中
（その他、兵士、召使、水夫など）

《コシ・ファン・トゥッテ》の事件進行係は、皮肉な老哲学者ドン・アルフォンソであり、ある意味では彼こそが主役といってもよい。彼を助けるのが、若いに似ず世間を、そして人間の本音を知っている女中のデスピーナである。この2人には、士官とその恋人たちは操られ、あるいは駆使されて動く。青年士官のうち、グリエルモは積極的で向う見ずなところがあり、たちまち友人の恋人を誘惑してしまう。そのグリエルモの本来の恋人は、やや引き込み思案の姉妹フィオルディリージである。これに対して、陽気で気楽な妹妹ドラベルラの本来の恋人は、慎重な、だが多少気が弱いフェルランドである。これら2組の恋人たちは、ドン・アルフォンソの計略のおかげで、それまで意識したこともないような自分たちの精神の内部を覗きみる機会にめぐり合うのである。

これらの登場人物のうち、最も親しみやすく、かつ憎めないのは、デスピーナであろう。抜け目のないちゃっかり屋で、人情の機微に通じ、必要とあれば変装して他の人物になり切るという役柄は、オペラ・ブッファには欠くことができない存在だが、デスピーナは、まさしくそういう役柄として登場する。彼女は、第1幕のフィオルディリージでは、磁石による霊験術法を行なう医者となり、第2幕では、証人になる。こうした小間使役の俳優たちの1人3役は、18世紀のイタリアの舞台ではごく普通のことで、彼らは変身劇のなかで、さまざまな人物を演じわけるのを楽しみ、かつ誇りにしていたのである。それにもしてもデスピーナという人物の、なんというか、いかにも生き生きとした劇的真実性と素晴らしい。これはモーツァルトとダ・ボンテの、とりわけ前者の勝利であり、フィガロ、レオノーレ、スザンナ、ケルビーノなどに匹敵する人物の創出につながっているのである。

モーツァルト研究家として著名なA.アイシュタイインはいう。

「《コシ・ファン・トゥッテ》に近づくには二つの道——いや、（中略）おそらくはもっと多くの道——がある。その一つ——人々は、19、20世紀の〈道徳的〉立場を忘れるのがよい、そして〈あり得ない〉または〈ばかげた〉事件進行に反復しないで微笑するがよい」（浅井真男氏訳）。でなければ、すでに書いたようなベートーヴェンの偏見に陥るのは避けがたいであろう。

以上の登場人物は、アリアよりもむしろアンサンブルによって聴き手を楽しませてくれる。モーツァルトの絶

=== Page 7 ===
妙な声楽のアンサンブルは、他のオペラでも見受けられるものの、＜コシ・ファン・トゥッテ＞を超えるオペラはない。もし命名するなら、＜コシ・ファン・トゥッテ＞はアンサンブル・オペラである。この点で＜コシ・ファン・トゥッテ＞があらゆるオペラの頂点に位置しているのは、ほとんど疑いの余地がないだろう。

●あらすじ
とき：18世紀のなかごろ
ところ：ナポリ
第一幕
カフィーの場
幕があがるとナポリのカフィー。ナポリに住む2人の青年士官フェルランドとグリエルモが、年老いた哲学者のドン・アルフォンソと女性の貞節について論争している。まずフェルランドが、自分は恋人のドラベルラを絶対に信頼しているというと、グリエルモもまけじとばかり自分の恋人フィオルディリージの様をたたえる。2人の青年士官の恋に浮かされた熱っぽい話をきいたドン・アルフォンソは、かつて若いころその道で苦労したことがあるだけに、2人の青年の話がおかしくて仕方がない。そこで彼は、女は移り気なもので、フィオルディリージとドラベルラ姉妹とで例外ではない、と強く主張する。すると2人の士官は立腹してその証拠を出すようにドン・アルフォンソに追り、あげくの果て決斗を挑む。しかしアルフォンソは平然としたもので、2人の青年の人のよさを笑う。ついに青年士官たちと老哲学者の間に奇妙な賭けが成立し、どちらが正しいか決着をつけようということになる。賭することにあたってアルフォンソが出した条件は、2人の士官はこの賭のことを恋人たちに一切秘密にすること、これから24時間、何事も自分の指示に従うこと、というものであった。賭に勝つことをすこしも疑わない2人の青年は、その条件を受け入れ、賭勝って大金がころがり込んだら盛大な宴会を催そうと相談しながら、愛の女神を請えて乾杯する。
ナポリ湾を見下す庭園の場
ここは見晴らしのいいフィオルディリージ、ドラベルラ姉妹の家の庭。フィオルディリージとドラベルラが、お互いの恋人の肖像の描かれているメダルを見ながら、恍惚として恋人のことを考えていると、アルフォンソが、あわてた様子でやってきて、フェルランドとグリエルモの2人がすぐに戦場に行けなくなればならなくなったと告げる。あまり突然のことでぼう然とする姉妹。やがてアルフォンソの招きの声に応じて、出発の準備を整えた2人の士官が姿をみせる。2組の恋人たちは、思いがけない突然の別離を悲しみ合う。いよいよアルフォンソの工作がはじまったのである。
海辺の場
遠くから行進曲が聞こえ、出征する兵士たちを讃える歌が力強く歌われる。頃はよしと、アルフォンソは2人の士官に出発を命ずる。これが計略とは知らないフィオルディリージとドラベルラは、「この胸は張り裂けるばかり……」と歌うが、2人の士官は、この歌に合わせていかにも悲しそうに芝居をしてみせる。そばではアルフォンソが「おかしくて死にそうだ」といしながら、自分の計画がうまく図にあたったことを喜んでいる。やがて2人の士官は出発し、その姿を見送りながら、フィオルディリージ、ドラベルラ姉妹とドン・アルフォンソは、それぞれの気持を三重唱で歌う。
姉妹の家の場
女中のデスピーナがチョコレートを作っている。そこに恋人を見送ったフィオルディリージとドラベルラが入ってくる。ドラベルラはデスピーナが差し出したチョコレートの盆をひっくり返したうえ、恋人と別れた悲しみを歌う。するとデスピーナは、男は他にいくらでもいるし、それに男、とりわけ軍人は浮気であてにならないものであるから、私たち女も負けずに大いに浮気しましょう、と姉妹を元気づける。
さて、姉妹が退場した隙に、ドン・アルフォンソがやってきて、デスピーナに取り入り、自分がつれてきた2人のアルバニアの貴族と姉妹の仲を取り持つことを引き受けさせる。このアルバニアの貴族というのが、実は変装したフェルランドとグリエルモである。アルフォンソがこの奇妙な変装した2人の男をデスピーナに紹介してから身を隠すと、姉妹が部屋に帰ってきて、見知らぬ奇妙な男が2人いるのを見て驚ろく。2人の貴族は、アルフォンソのいいつけ通りに、燃ゆる想いを姉妹に打ち明けるけれど、2人は服を立てて見向きもしない。するとそこにドン・アルフォンソがやってきて、アルバニアの貴族は懐しい旧友であるといって姉妹に紹介する。2人の男はそれに力を得て、さらに恋の言葉を述べ立てるけれど、姉妹はまるで取り合わず、自分たちは恋人がいて、しかも自分たちの愛は絶対に揺がないものである、と歌う。それを聞いて2人の貴族、すなわち変装したフェルランドとグリエルモは勝ち誇って退場する。あとに残ったドン・アルフォンソは新しい計略を思いつき、それをデスピーナに伝える。
庭園の場
ここから第一幕のフィナーレとなる。フィオルディリージとドラベルラが、恋のほかなさを嘆いていると、ア

=== Page 8 ===
曲目解説

ルバニアの貴族に変装したフェルランドとグリエルモが、手に毒薬のピンをもち、いかにも毒薬を飲んだかのようによろめきながら出てくる。それを追ってドン・アルフォンソがあわてた様子でやってくる。突然の騒ぎに姉妹が驚いていると、ドン・アルフォンソは2人の命がないといってデスピーナとともに医者を呼び出てゆく。やがてドン・アルフォンソは医者をつれて帰ってくるがこの医者が実は女中のデスピーナである。彼女は磁石を使って怪しげな治療をほどこし2人の貴族の命をとりとめる。われにかえった2人の若者は、ふたたび恋の芝居をはじめるが、姉妹はまだ心を動かす気配はない。

第二幕
姉妹の家の場

女中の姿に戻ったデスピーナは、手を変え、品を変え、真節などというもののはもう時代遅れのたわ言ですよ、と主人である姉妹に吹きこむので、ついに姉妹は、それでは2人のアルバニア人に会ってみようという気持になる。すかさずデスピーナは、娘は年頃になったら男を御する術を覚えなくてはいけません、と歌って姉妹の気持を焚きつける。アルバニアの貴族の自殺さわぎ以来、かなり気持の動いていた妹のドベルラは、デスピーナの巧妙なワナにかかって、ちょっとした浮気なら構わないだろうと思うようになり、その浮気の相手にグリエルモの変装したアルバニア貴族を選ぶことにする。そして妹にも浮気をすすめるので、フィオルディリージは妹の恋人フェルランドを浮気の相手にすることになる。姉妹が意見の一致を見、恋愛遊戯の楽しさを歌っているところにドン・アルフォンソがやってきて、姉妹を庭園に誘い出す。

ナポリ湾を見下す庭園の場

アルバニア貴族に変装したフェルランドとグリエルモが、姉妹にセレナード、つまり愛の歌を歌ってきさせ、やがて庭に入ってくる。するとデスピーナはドベルラの手をとってグリエルモのそばに連れてゆき、ドン・アルフォンソはフィオルディリージの手をとってフェルランドのそばに連れてゆく。そうしてデスピーナとドン・アルフォンソはわざとその場を外してしまう。

やがて2人のアルバニア貴族は、それぞれ相手に愛の告白をはじめる。まず妹のドベルラが誘惑に負けて、〈恋人を得たいまは死んでも悔いはない〉とグリエルモと二重唱しながら、手に手を取って退場する。いっぽうフィオルディリージは誘惑に負けかかるが、やっとのことで思いとどまる。しかし誘惑に負けかったことを後悔して、〈ああ、許して恋人よ〉とその気持を歌う。誘惑に失敗したフェルランドは、グリエルモから自分の恋人ドベルラが心変わりしたことを聞いて、信頼を裏切られたことを嘆き悲しむ。

姉妹の部屋の場

誘惑に負けたドベルラは、しきりに姉フィオルディリージに恋の楽しさを吹聴する。フィオルディリージは心を動かされながらも、戦地にいるグリエルモのことが気になってなかなかふんざりがつかない。ドベルラは何事も決心が大切だと〈恋は曲者〉と楽しそうに歌って部屋から出ていく。気持の追いつめられたフィオルディリージは、恋人を追って戦地に行こうとするが、そこにフェルランドがやってきて、以前より一層熱烈に恋の想いを打ち明けるので、すさがのフィオルディリージもついに気持が動いて、誘惑に負けてしまう。これをみたドン・アルフォンソは、わが計略成れりとばかり、すぐ結婚したほうがいいと入れ智恵する。そしてフィオルディリージとドベルラ姉妹は、以前の恋人を捨てて、新しい求婚者と結婚する決心をしてしまう。

結婚式の場

第二幕のフィナーレ、大詰めである。

式場の飾りつけがすむと、行進曲に合わせて2組の新郎新婦が登場する。すると公証人に変装したデスピーナが入って来て、結婚契約書を読みあげる。2組の新郎新婦は間違いのないことを確かめたうえで、それに署名する。ところがそのとき、勇ましい合唱が聞こえてくる。何事かと窓際に様子を見に行ったドン・アルフォンソは、一同に、フェルランドとグリエルモが帰ってきたことを知らせるので、2人のアルバニア貴族は急いで別室に逃れ去る。そしてすぐに軍服に着かえて、何喰わぬ顔で驚きあわてる姉妹の前にふたたび姿を現す。2人の士官は、さっさと署名したばかりの結婚契約書を手に入れ、これは一体何なのか、と大いに立腹した振りをする。気の毒なのは2人の姉妹で、彼女たちは〈こんなことなら一息に死んだほうがよい〉と嘆くと、2人の士官はアルバニア貴族に、デスピーナは医者に変装して出てくるので、やっと真相を知った姉妹は、取すかしさに耐えられない。しかし勝ち勝ったドン・アルフォンソが、女だって結局は生身の人間、女だけが悪いのではないと、巧妙なさばきで2組の恋人たちを元どおり円満に伸直りさせ、楽しいアンサンブルのうちに最後の幕が下りる。

=== Page 9 ===
音がとけあう、心が高鳴る。さあ、明日は本番だ。

思いのままに表現できる……その素晴しさがすべての器種で味わえます。

YAMAHA CONCERT GRAND PIANO CF

私たちはCFを「ピアノの芸術品」とあると自信をもっています。そのことは、世界の権舞台でヤマハを選ぶピアニストが、年ごとに増えていることも証明されています。「ピアノは音の響きだけではだめだ。弾く人の嬉しい心、悲しい心まで表現できるものでなければならない。CFには心の感度がある。」鬼才スビヤトスラフ・リヒテルのこの言葉が、CFのすべてをあらわしています。

繊細な「心の感度」をうたいあげます。ときには激しく、またあるときは静かに。

Part I.

OVERTURE—
The Ship o' the Fiend
Hamish MacCunn.
(The Score and Parts kindly lent by Mr. Charles Levy.)

ORCHESTRA.

"O WHERE hae ye been, my long lost lover,
This seven lang years and mair?"
"O I'm come again to seek your love,
An' the vows that ye did swear."

=== Page 8 ===
"Now haud your tongue o' my love and vows,
For they can breed but strife;
Now haud your tongue o' my former vows,
For I am another man's wife."

"O fause are the vows o' womankind,
But fair is their fause bodie;
I wad never hae trodden on Irish ground,
Were it no for the love o' thee."

"Ye may leave your husband to himsel',
And your little son also,
And sail wi' me across the sea,
Sae fair the wind doth blow."

"See ye not seven pretty ships,
The eighth brought me to land,
With merchandise and mariners,
And music on every hand?"

"There's mantles warm to wrap my love,
O' the silk and soft velvet,
And rich attires to deck her head,
And costly shoon for her feet."

"O how do you like the ship?" he said,
"Or how do you like the sea?
And how do you like the bold mariners
That wait upon thee and me?"

"O weel I like the ship," she said,
"And weel I like the sea,
But where are a' your mariners?
I see nane but thee and me."

They hadna sailed a league, a league,
A league, but barely three,
When eerie grew the lift above,
And gurly grew the sea.

She hadna sailed a league, a league,
A league, but barely three,
When she espied the cloven hoof,
And wept right bitterlie.

"O what are yon, yon pleasant hills,
That the sun shines sweetly on?"
"O yon are the hills of heaven," he said
"Where you will never win."

=== Page 9 ===
"O whatna mountain is yon," she said,
"Sae dreary wi' frost and snow?"
"O yon is the mountain o' hell," he cried,
"Where you and I maun go."

The clouds grew black, and the wind grew loud,
And the levin filled her e'e;
And wesome wailed the snow-white sprites,
Out o'er the roaring sea.

He struck the mainmast wi' his hand,
The foremast wi' his knee;
He split the gallant ship in twain,
And sank her in the sea.

CHORAL ODE—

From Goethe's "Helena"

(Faust, Part 2, Act 3.)

G. W. L. Marshall-Hall.

(Composed specially for and dedicated to the Melbourne Liedertafel.)

THE LIEDERTAFEL, LADIES' CHOIR
AND ORCHESTRA.

ALTO SOLO—MISS SPENCE.

Life presented itself to the Greek mind as a series of manifestations of Power Omnipotent, irresistible, irrevocable, first in the order of forces, loom'd Fate, then the gods, the ancestral heroes, and the pre-eminent men of the times. Each State, surrounded by enemies, depended for its safety on the courage and power of its citizens, whom a reverse of war would convert into slaves with their wives and children. The actual experience of the Power and Tragedy of human existence, which to our modern comfortable plebian semi-vegetable life are almost unintelligible, lent an intensity to the moment which we can but faintly imagine. Power and its limitation were equally displayed in the sudden plunge from the height of prosperity to the depth of woe, and to find expression in the never equalled strength and restraint of Greek art, imparting a reverential solemnity even to its most joyous utterances. This is the key note of their art, energetic power, and fate:

Fate, whose horizons, narrowing from afar
Within their blind abysmal night immerse
Both gods and men, and all things else that be
In irremediable catastrophe.

In the following ode from Goethe's masterpiece, these qualities are passionately felt by one who was himself a Greek at heart though born in a barbarian age. The music is an endeavour to complete and enforce the poet's intention. The serenity, not untinged with a certain noble sadness, of the first stanza, is contrasted with those following, in which the power and majesty and terrible presence of the gods is imaged, to which succeeds the picture of limited fettered humanity.

SCENE: Before the Palace of Menelaus at Sparta.

=== Page 14 ===
Part II.

ORGAN SOLO—
Passacaglia
J. S. Bach.
MR. AUGUST SIEDE.

In the Passacaglia we see, from a single idea by a development gradual, but resistless as fate, the growth of a huge superstructure almost overpowering in its nobility and grandeur, suggesting the unfolding of some mighty work of nature herself.
When the watery ear-tickling organ music of the present age will have vanished into oblivion, such works as this will stand as the eternal monument to the imperishable glory of Bach.

ARIA
Honor and Arms
(Sampson)
Handel.
MR. W. G. BARKER.

Hungarian Dances
J. Brahms.
No. 1—Allegro molto.
No. 2—Allegretto.
ORCHESTRA.

In the wonderfully expressive and characteristic music of the Hungarians we find preserved the nobler and more significant phases of the Dance, before it had been corrupted by civilised larrkinism, and whilst it still remained among the people at large the one means through which their natural feelings and instincts found expression.

=== Page 15 ===
Not only at one time was the Dance a religious rite, but also it fulfilled the present office of the drama, and became an artistic representation of human passion and action. In the course of the various figures through which the dancers went, the joy and woe, love and hate, hope and despair, of mankind were represented. Youths would woo and maidens would play the coquette.

In Brahms' music we find not only those poetical moods which it once was the object of the dance to portray, but a delightful suggestion of the picturesque character of the people, and the free, wild naive aspect of Nature, which nowhere assumes a more beautiful or striking aspect than in the country of the Maygars.

ARIA—

Kommt ein Schlauher Bursch
(Der Freischutz)
Weber.

MISS ADELAIDE DONOVAN.

If a youth should meet a maiden,
    Need she run away with fright;
If his looks should win her favour,
    Sure the girl may use her sight.
Tho' she must, in maiden manner,
    Seem her glances to conceal;
Where's the harm, if she, unnoticed,
    Strive a sidelong look to steal.
Should perchance their eyes encounter,
    I no guilt therein can find;
Tho' her cheeks may blush a little,
    Yet it will not strike her blind.
Looking hither, looking thither,
    Looks are followed soon by sighs;
He sighs fairest, she smiles dearest,
    Soon a marriage we will see.
Come around me, dear companions,
    Would you like to see me bride?
Am I not a pretty maiden,
    And he is a smart young boy.

=== Page 16 ===
BALLAD—

Lord Ullin's Daughter
Hamish MacCunn.

THE LIEDERTAFEL, LADIES CHOIR
AND ORCHESTRA.

A CHIEFTAIN to the highlands bound
    Cries "Boatman, do not tarry!
And I'll give thee a silver pound
    To row us o'er the ferry."

"Now who be ye would cross Lochgyle
    This dark and stormy water?"
"Oh, I'm the chief of Ulvas' Isle,
    And this, Lord Ullin's daughter."

And fast before her father's men,
    Three days we've fled together,
And should he find us in the glen,
    My blood would stain the heather.

His horsemen hard behind us ride;
    Should they our steps discover,
Then who will cheer my bonny bride,
    When they have slain her lover?

Out spake the hardy highland wight,
    "I'll go, my chief, I'm ready!
It is not for your silver bright,
    But for your winsome lady.

And by my word, the bonny bird
    In danger shall not tarry,
So though the waves are raging white,
    I'll row you o'er the ferry."

By this the storm grew loud apace,
    The water wraith was shrieking,
And in the scowl of heaven each face
    Grew dark as they were speaking.

But still as wilder blew the wind,
    And as the night grew drearer,
Adown the glen rode armed men,
    Their tramping sounded nearer.

=== Page 17 ===
"Oh haste thee, haste!" the lady cries,
    "Though storms around us gather,
I'll meet the raging of the skies,
    But not an angry father."

The boat has left the stormy land,
    A stormy sea before her,
When, oh, too strong for human hand,
    The tempest gather'd o'er her.

And still they rowed amidst the roar
    Of waters fast prevailing:
Lord Ullin reached the fatal shore,
    His wrath was changed to wailing.

For sore dismayed, thro' storm and shade,
    He did his child discover:
One lovely arm she stretched for aid,
    And one was round her lover.

"Come back, come back!" he cried in grief
    Across the stormy water,
And I'll forgive your Highland chief,
    My daughter! oh, my daughter!"

'Twas vain: the loud waves lashed the shore,
    Return or aid preventing,
The waters wild went o'er his child,
    And he was left lamenting.

Programme

PART I.

Ungarische Tänze Johannes Brahms
The Melbourne Orchestral Society

Solo—
"O Star of Eve" Wagner
(Tannhäuser)
Mr. Horace Stevens

Double Choruses from Oedipus at Colonos.
MUSIC BY FELIX MENDELSSOHN-BARTHOLDY
(WITH ORCHESTRAL ACCOMPANIMENT)
The Royal Victorian Liedertafel and Orchestra
The Chorus sing the praises of Colonos.

THOU comest here to the land, O friend,
Fam'd for fleet-footed steeds and blooming meadows;
Thou standest now in Colonos' grove,
Where the voices of nightingales
Resound, floating in dulcet strains
Thro' their temples of verdure;
Where the thick-woven ivy clings,
Spreading over the sacred aisles;
Where, in security, ripens the fruitful vine,
Unscath'd by beam or stormwind.
And here roameth the bounteous god
Gay and good Dionysos, ever greeted in lays,
Sung by the nymphs who rear'd him.

=== Page 10 ===
Fair and fragrant at dawn of day
See the beautiful heaven-bedewed Narcissus,
The flow'r that shone in the goddesses' crowns,
Worn by them in the days of old.
See the Crocus array'd in gold:
    Hear the slumberless waters,
While they glide in Cephisus' tide.
Still meandering day by day
Over the plains, bearing streams ever pure along,
    Enriching all the bowers
Embosomed in the favour'd land;
Ever loved by the tuneful choir of Muses,
    And Cythera, whose zone is golden.

Here, too, bloometh a tree
Crowned with a fruit not found in Asia;
Nor on Dorian plains doth it appear,
Gracing the island where the Pelops
Held sway; yet here it freely springeth;
    Rever'd by friends; and fear'd by foes,
    In native splendour it blossoms for Athens.
Behold ours is the rich oil-dropping olive!
    Aged and youthful, noble and peasant,
Never wantonly harm this holy tree.
    Guarded and cherished, it stands secure,
Ever heeded by Morian Jove.
    Lov'd and watch'd by Minerva,

Grateful, let me extol
Heaven's richest gifts designed to my country;
Presented by the Pow'r making our State
Fam'd for its wealth, honour, and glory:
    Our land and sea steeds, rein and rudder guided;
    O Chronos' son, by them we stand pre-eminent.
    Mighty god Poseidon,
Thou didst give us the rein form'd for the courser;
Guided thus, or curbed, he yields obedience.
Through the billows we dash, stemming the deep,
    Speeded along by the oar and helm,
    Bounding on with the dancing nymphs—
Nereus' hundred-footed daughters.

The Athenians are successful, and Thesens returns with Antigone and Ismene. Oedipus expresses his gratitude to the King, who announces the arrival of Polynices seeking an interview with his father. The chorus describes the sorrows of life, and the blessing of death when old age has come.

When the health and the strength are gone
He that still would be lingering here,
Borne down by a load of care,
Is, I consider, devoid of wisdom
Old age bringeth disease and pain,
Grief, anguish and regret remain.

=== Page 11 ===
For youth's bloom and its fleeting joys
Never, never return again.
Life's varied journeys lead to death;
Smooth or rugged, all its pathways,
Even its wishes, end in Hades.
Love hymeneal, revels, dances, strains of music
    Cease, when the Foe appeareth!

Better not to exist;
Or, if born, in early childhood to die,
And escape all the cares and pains.
They, living longest, endure the longest.
Youth and Folly and Sorrow roam
Hand in hand to their destined home:
For none liveth devoid of care;
None escapeth what all must bear.
Envy, Sedition, Murder, Strife,
Fear and Rage hover around us:
And, in conclusion, feeble, helpless,
Old and friendless, all these ills together meeting
    Crush their devoted victim.

On man, poor mourner, all these evils fall.
Fall as billows rushing beat the north strand,
Dashing onward, urged by the blast of winter.
Thus, then, storms of affliction, never-ending, assail us.
    Thus lowering sorrows around us gather;
    Whether from Helios' western bound,
        Or from his eastern gate,
        Or where his rays beam brightest,
        Or down from the home of Arcturus.

Theseus, followed by the citizens of Athens, again appears, and learning what Creon has done, sends for soldiers and renews his promises of protection to Oedipus, declaring that his daughters shall be restored to him, and that Creon shall not be allowed to bring such a disgrace upon Athens. The chorus describes the contest, and invokes the aid of the Gods in favour of Theseus and his followers.

    Ah, were I on yonder plain,
    Where now our undaunted sons
        Stand arm'd for the hostile fray;
    There, where the shrine of Phoebus gleams,
        And torches are burning;
    Where Mortals bow down to the awe-inspiring pair,
        Whose hallowed rites are mystic deeds,
        Wrought by Eumolpidan priests,
        And never breath'd to mortal ear.
    There, glowing with ardour,
        Panting to rush agains the foe,
        See, see all our legions,
    With Theseus they wave their swords, and cry.
        Rescue the sisters!

Into the silence of the monotonous Steppes of Middle Asia come the first echoes of a peaceful Russian song. In the distance sound the trampling of horses and camels and the strange cries of the Orient. Under the protection of the Russian flag it moves safely on its weary journey through the immeasurable waste. It recedes further and further. The songs of Russia and the wild notes of the East merge into the solemn harmony of nature, slowly sinking into the echoes of the eternal Steppes.

INTERVAL.

=== Page 14 ===
"FRITHJOF."

The story of Frithjof the Bold and Ingeborg the Fair is told in "Frithjof's Saga," a poem in twenty-four cantos, by Esaias Tegner, published in 1820.

The hero, Frithjof, is son to Thorsten Vikingsson, who, though King Bele's best warrior and chosen friend, is of lowly origin. Frithjof the Strong and Bold dares to love Fair Ingeborg, daughter of his king and descendant of great Odin. Bele looks kindly on young Frithjof's love, but death takes from the youth at once a monarch and a friend. When Frithjof subsequently demands the hand of Ingeborg from Helge, son and successor of Bele, he is rejected with scorn. Later, old King Ring, a mighty monarch of the North, would make fair Ingeborg his queen, but Helge, influenced by soothsayers, sends a refusal, accompanied by a taunting message from brother Halfdan, to "Old Grey-beard." King Ring incensed, declares war against the brothers, and Ingeborg is sent for safety to the vale of Baldur, the god of innocence and virtue. While in the sacred grove, the maiden receives a visit from her lover, the joy of which is followed by the fear that she has angered the gods by keeping a love-tryst in that holy place. At a council of war assembled at Bele's cairn, Frithjof again demands from Helge the hand of Ingeborg, in return for which he offers his best aid in the impending battle. Helge again repels him, and forces him to make the fatal admission that he has visited Ingeborg in the sacred grove. He thereupon denounces him as a profaner of temples, and orders him to do penance for his sacrilege by sailing to the Orkneys to wring from fierce Earl Agantyr long-withheld tribute. Frithjof tries to persuade Ingeborg to fly with him, but in vain. Giving her his arm-ring, he departs, promising to return and make her his bride.

Borne through his perilous voyage by his charmed ship "Ellida," Frithjof returns at length to his native land to find his estates laid waste with fire and sword, and the fair Ingeborg given in marriage to victorious King Ring. He learns that at the marriage ceremony the cowardly Helge tore from his sister's arm her lover's ring, and hung it upon the arm of Baldur's image. Frithjof, furious, seeks out the King whilst he is in the act of offering sacrifice at Baldur's pyre. He flings Agantyr's tribute full in Helge's face, and, hastily snatching at the arm ring, he overturns the huge idol upon the sacred fire. The flames lap it about, and, leaping upward with angry roar, spread to the temple and the sacred grove, which are soon reduced to ashes.

Frithjof is now shunned by all as a perpetrator of sacrilege; he is banished from his country, and, sailing away in the "Ellida," he devotes himself to a life of wild adventure. The hero's troubled life is ultimately crowned with happiness. After many years he returns to his native land, and succeeds in gaining the goodwill of King Ring, who at his death bequeaths him his kingdom and his queen.

=== Page 15 ===
Bruch, Max, musical composer, born at Cologne 6th January, 1838, received his first musical instruction from his mother (nee Almenrider), who was a highly-esteemed teacher of music, and who often in her young days sang at the Rhenish musical festivals. At the age of eleven Bruch, then a pupil of Karl Breidenstein, attempted compositions on a large scale, and at the age of fourteen he had already brought out a Symphony at Cologne. From 1853 to 1857 he held the Mozart Scholarship at Cologne, and in that capacity he was a special pupil of Ferdinand Hiller in the theory of music and composition; and of Karl Reinecke (till 1854), and of Ferdinand Breunung in playing the piano. After a short stay in Leipzig, he resided from 1858 to 1861 as musical teacher at Cologne, and was very assiduous in composing. On the death of his father, in 1861 he set out on an extensive tour of study, which, after brief stays at Berlin, Leipzig, Vienna, Dresden, and Munich, ended at Mannheim, where his opera "Lorelei" (after the text written by Geibel for Mendelssohn) was produced in 1863. At Mannheim also, between 1862 and 1864, he wrote the chorus-works, "Frithjof," "Römischer Triumphgesang," "Gesang der heiligen drei Könige," and "Flucht der heiligen Familie." In 1864-65 he was again on his travels, visiting Hamburg, Hanover, Dresden, Breslau, Munich, Brussels, and Paris. Then he brought out his "Frithjof" with extraordinary success at Aix-la-Chapelle, Leipzig, and Vienna. From 1865 to 1867 he was musical director at Coblenz, and from 1867 to 1870 director of the court choir at Sonderhausen. At Coblenz he wrote, among other things, his well-known first concerto for the violin, and at Sonderhausen two symphonies and portions of a Mass. The opera "Hermione," which was produced in 1872 at Berlin, where Bruch resided from 1871 to 1873, had only a succès d'estime. The chorus "Odysseus" likewise belongs to the period of the composer's residence at Berlin. After he had been five years (1873-78) at Bonn, devoting his time exclusively to composing "Arminius," "The Song of the Bell," and his second concerto for the violin, and after he had paid two visits to England for the purpose of producing some of his works, he became in 1878, on the resignation of Hockhausen, Director of Stern's Singing Academy at Berlin; and in 1880 he was nominated to succeed Sir Julius Benedict as Director of the Philharmonic Society at Liverpool.

MELBOURNE LIEDERTAFEL.

ANNOUNCEMENTS.—The Council has to express its deep regret, that, owing to the continued ill health of Herr Julius Siede (the Society's Life Conductor), it will not be possible to carry out the promise made that he would conduct part of the "Scheme" this afternoon.

The Liedertafel—and the musical public generally—is indebted to MR. H. J. KING, the Conductor, for the whole of the music set down for performance this afternoon.

THE SCHEME.

PARSIFAL
A Festival Drama
By RICHARD WAGNER.

=== Page 8 ===
WAGNER was sixty-five years old when he began the music of "Parsifal"—the poem of which he had published in 1877. This Festival Drama occupied him until April 1879, while the instrumentation was finished at Palermo, January 15th, 1882. "Parsifal" was first produced in July 1882. Wagner has certainly in "Parsifal" succeeded in giving the most exquisite expressions to the deepest religious feeling—for Parsifal is really an allegorical personification of Christ—and, if we consider religious feeling the most exalted of all emotions, we must agree that Wagner in "Parsifal" struck finer chords than in any other of his works. The "Forspiel" is based on three of the most deeply religious motives in the entire work. It opens with the Motive of the Sacrament. Through this motive we gain insight into the office of the Knights of the Grail, who from time to time strengthen themselves for their spiritual duties by partaking of the Communion, on which occasions the Grail itself is uncovered. The Second Motive is indicative of the Grail, and the trumpets announce the third—the Motive of Faith.

The plot of "Parsifal" is briefly as follows:—Amfortas, as King of the Knights of the Holy Grail, who dwell in the castle of Montsalvat among the mountains of Gothic Spain, is enticed by Kundry, a lovely woman under the sway of Klingsor, an evil magician on the southern slope of the same mountains, supposed to be facing Arabian Spain, into Klingsor's magic garden. While in her arms Amfortas drops the holy spear, which is at once seized by Klingsor, who wounds the King therewith, and carries it off. Amfortas cannot recover from the wound until it has been touched by the spear, which can be wrested from Klingsor only by "the guileless fool," one who has been all his life ignorant of sin, who through deep sympathy with the anguish of Amfortas becomes conscious of the King's sin, and can resist temptation though it come to him ever so enticingly. Such an one is Parsifal. By resisting Kundry's charms he regains the spear, destroys Klingsor, and thus frees Kundry from his evil sway, heals the wound of Amfortas, and is proclaimed King of the Knighthood. The plot is allegorical. Parsifal is the personification of Christianity, and the triumph of Parsifal over Klingsor is the triumph of Christianity over Paganism.

=== Page 9 ===
The performance this afternoon will—after the Vorspiel—begin at a point in Act I, where the Knights of the Grail are to celebrate the Love Feast or Communion that day. Gurnemanz—an old but vigorous knight—bids the youthful Parsifal accompany him to the castle. Then occurs a change of scene which, in itself is highly effective dramatically. Long sustained trombone notes softly swell; approaching peals of bells are heard. At last Gurnemanz and Parsifal arrive at a mighty hall, which looms itself overhead in a high vaulted dome, down from which alone the light streams in. The change of scene is ushered in by the solemn BELL MOTIVE, which is the basis of the powerful Orchestral Interlude accompanying the Panorama, and also of the scene in the hall of the Grail Castle. King Amfortas gives way to violent grief and the MOTIVE OF CONTRITION graphically portrays his spiritual suffering. The MOTIVE OF THE SACRAMENT (followed by the BELL MOTIVE and the sonorous and powerful GRAIL MOTIVE) is succeeded by the Knights intoning the chorus, "To the last love feast," while the Orchestra plays a solemn processional based on the Bell Motive. Amfortas is borne in preceded by pages who bear the covered Grail. A chorus based upon the Motive of Contrition and then the Motive of Faith floats down from the dome in ethereal beauty as it sung by angel voices. Tortured by contrition the King refuses Titurel's summons to uncover the Grail. Comforting voices chant the prophecy of Amfortas' redemption through the Guileless Fool. The Grail is uncovered and the voices chant the chorus, "Take of my body, take of my blood, to the Sacrament Motive. Amfortas is bowed in prayer. Through the dusk a ray of brilliant light darts upon the Grail; Amfortas raises the Grail and blesses the wine and bread, all kneeling, while voices in the dome chant a chorus based on the Sacrament Motive. When it has been repeated, one-half of the Knights intone a chant, the Bell Motive solemnly accompanying it in the Orchestra, the other half chorus repeats the chant, and then the entire chorus takes up the Grail Motive. To the Faith Motive the congregation prepares to go. Amfortas bows his head and touches his wound, his action being accompanied by the Motive of Contrition in union with the Bell Motive. Parsifal presses his hand to his heart. We again hear the Motive of the Prophecy. The Grail and Bell Motives lead once more to the Prophecy, and the Act closes amid the spiritual harmonies of the Prophecy of the Guileless Fool and of the Grail Motive.

Richard Wagner was born May 22, 1813, and died February 13, 1883.
—From Gustav Kobbé on "Wagner."

A. Vorspiel for Orchestra alone.

B. Verwandlungs—Musik und Schluss-Scene des 1ten Aktes.

First production in Australia of the latter.

RHAPSODIE
(Fragment aus Goethe's Harzreise im Winter),

FOR
Contralto Solo, Chorus of Men's Voices and Orchestra.

BY JOHANNES BRAHMS.
Op. 53.

LIEDERTAFEL AND ORCHESTRA.

SOLOIST - Miss ADA CROSSLEY.

The deep majestic expression which the greatest musical classic of our time has given to the Words of Gustle, establishes the work under notice as one of the highest manifestations of lofty subjectivity and profound contemplation that we worship in art. The Solo voice is responsible for the text throughout. The entry of Tenors and Basses—each in two parts—is made at the words, "But if thy Psalter."

JOHANNES BRAHMS, born 1833 at Hamburg; as a boy excited great attention both by compositions and pianoforte playing. In 1874 he was made a member of the Academy of Arts at Berlin. Excepting opera, Brahms has cultivated nearly every branch of musical composition. Powerful, original and versatile, Brahms, more than any other, sums up in his strongly-marked individuality the varying elements, classical as well as romantic, of contemporaneous culture. His imagination, to which he at first allowed too free a scope (about to Op. 10), he has briddled by severe study and rigid self-criticism; and although reflection plays a large part in his compositions, he has produced abundance of music of a thoroughly spontaneous and inspired character. His melodies possess inexhaustible variety, ranging from naïve simplicity and a dreamy poetical tenderness peculiar to himself, to stirring pathos, striking force, and glowing passion, always remaining pregnant and concise. His harmony, often surprisingly bold and original, is subordinated to the dictates of a high artistic idea, which permeates and controls the formal construction of his works, in which an admirable mastery of contrapuntal art is often exhibited. His songs extend from the simplest specimens of popular melody to the richest and most complicated forms of art.

BUT who goes there apart? In the brake his pathway is lost,
Close behind clash the branches together, the grass rises again,
the desert engulphs him.
Who can comfort his anguish?
Who, if balsam be deathly,
If the hate of men from the fulness of love be drained?

=== Page 13 ===
He that was scorned turned to scorner, lonely now devours all he hath of worth in a barren self-seeking.
But if from Thy Psalter all-loving Father one strain can but come to his hearing,
Oh! enlighten his heart!
Lift up his o'er-clouded eyes where are the fountains hard by the thirsty one in the desert.
But if from Thy Psalter, all-loving Father, one strain can but come to his hearing,
Oh! enlighten his heart, enlighten his heart.

"LANDERKENNUNG"

(LAND SIGHTING)

For Baritone Solo, Chorus of Men's voices, Organ and Orchestra.

By EDWARD GRIEG.
Op. 31.

(First performance in this city.)

LIEDERTAFEL AND ORCHESTRA.

SOLOIST - HERR R. NITSCHKE.

EDWARD GRIEG was born in 1843. His melodic inventiveness and original power of expression places him in the front rank of contemporary composers. The presentation of Landerkennung in Melbourne will doubtless be acceptable as a tribute to his genius.

AND it was Olav Trygvason,
    Sailing on the north sea wide,
Bearing the hope to found a kingdom,
    Far on the other side.
Yonder the cliffs appearing,
Like a battlement loom their dark crest rearing,
And it was Olav Trygvason,
Found he ne'er a spot to land.
E'en like the waves the royal desire,
Shattered upon the strand.
"See!" cried the bard upleaping.
Yonder snow covered peaks o'er cloud bands peeping.

And it was Olav Trygvason,
    Suddenly he seemed to sight,
Towering temples, domes and spires,
    Glist'ning in virgin white.
Then vow'd the king undaunted,
With his followers to tread that land enchanted,

=== Page 15 ===
Onward he went; the rushing streams
Heralded the coming spring.
Swayed in the stormy wind, the forest strangely was murmuring
Sounds as of churchbells chiming.
And then spake the king,
Spake as tho' dreaming:
Here the spot to found our kingdom!
Hell! these temple walls defy thee!
Hearts are swelling, souls are yearning,
God, to thee alone be glory.

Be my faith as yonder mountains,
Root as deeply, shine as purely;
And as these my faith strive upwards,
On to him, the All Creator.
Olav's prayer be ours to utter,
As we near the throne of mercy.
Hearts are swelling, souls are yearning,
God, to thee alone be glory.
    On to God! On to God!

THE LEGEND OF ST. ELIZABETH
(OF HUNGARY).
For Solo Voices, Chorus (S.A.T.B.) Organ & Orchestra,
BY
FRANZ LISZT.

S. ELIZABETH was specially composed by the Abbé Liszt at the instigation of the Grand Duke of Weimar for a Festival held at the Wartburg on the 28th of August, 1867, in commemoration of the eighth centenary of the founding and in honour of the restoration, then just completed, of that remarkable and

=== Page 16 ===
historically interesting relic of the middle ages. The legend of S. Elizabeth is a tolerably familiar one—at least to Roman Catholics. In the "Crusader Scene" to be performed this afternoon, the action presumably laid a Schmalkald on the borders of Thuringia—for it was to this place that Landgrave Ludwig went with Elizabeth and their family to meet the knights and nobles who were to accompany him to the Holy Land, represents the courtyard of a medieval castle, filled with troops on the point of departure and the friends who have come to bid them adieu. The troops, acknowledging Ludwig as their leader encourage each other in their resolve to fight for the Faith. Ludwig calls upon his assembled subjects to swear allegiance to him and to Elizabeth in his absence. After a sad but affectionate leave-taking of his wife and children, Ludwig places himself at the head of his troops, which now set out on their march to join the new crusade. The Gregorian "intonation" symbolical of the Cross, and as forming the key-note to its intent, appropriately forms the basis of the Crusaders' March and chorus. The "Trio" as it may be regarded, which occurs twice in the Crusaders' March, is derived from an old pilgrims' song dating from the time of the Crusaders.

![Portrait of a man](page_420_1042_420_320.png)

"The Crusaders' Scene."

Programme

PART I

Cantata "Harald's Bridal Voyage"
Heinrich Hofmann
(WITH ORCHESTRAL ACCOMPANIMENT)
Solos by Mr. A. H. Gee and Mr. Henry Rofe

Liedertafel

1.—The Departure

Up, up, and away, every sail widely spanned,
The anchor set free, and the yards all bemanned.
Yohio, yohi! wind, bear us a tide,
Guard us and the hero when storm billows ride.

High swells his heart, and he longs for the bride,
Her all of his soul and his life doth confide,
Beauteous will adorn her with purple and gold,
With gems and pearls as his queen enfold.

An island hides her in ocean afar,
There brightly she shines as a radiant star,
The Maid of the Sea, demons guard day and night,
But our hero will win her all valiant in might.

Yohio, yohi! wind, bear us a tide,
Guard us and the hero when storm billows ride.

=== Page 8 ===
2.—On the Strand

An Old Sailor:

Depart, farewell! thou'lt see this port aye never,
    Your fatherland greets ye the last to-day,
Soon raging storm as foam the ship shall sever,
    Ye all shall be of fish and fowl the prey.

    Storm birds I see are flying,
    The wolf to forest hieing;
    Signs these that hell aye keepeth,
    When low the eagle sweepeth.

These signs full oft I read descrying,
    But younger folk their doubt will cast,
High rolls the tide, the winds are sighing,
    What is to be, must be, at last.

    Shout then and revel,
    Soon thy song shall die away,
    The raven croaks, deep caverns yawn,
    Thy fatherland greets ye the last to-day.

3.—On the Sea

Beauteous prize our zeal engageth,
    Be thou gracious, seaman's fate!
Lead us safe though tempest rageth,
    Back to native port elate.

Where we wander, where abiding
    In the hand of God we are,
On, great ship, the waves dividing,
    Aye before goes God's fair star.

So we're full of valour daring,
    Fear naught deep nor storm award,
Joy all earthly treasure sharing,
    For the Lord our house doth guard.

=== Page 9 ===
Harald's Song:

From the sea all darkly flowing,
    High the sun ascends and higher,
Fills the mead with radiance glowing,
    Wakes the Nereidian choir.
Love's bright star is beck'ning me,
    O! I'll follow, follow thee!

Where the cooling springs are plying,
    Lone she waketh, dream-bedight,
There I'll listen for her sighing
    Through the love-enraptured night.
I will listen for her sighing
    Through the love-enraptured night.

Swell, ye sails, and call, ye billows,
    Roar and blow, ye strong winds wild,
That I with my warriors daring,
    Soon may reach the darling child.

Where the cooling springs are plying,
    Lone she waketh, dream-bedight,
There I'll listen for her sighing
    Through the love-enraptured night.

4.—The Storm

The God of Storms and the Demons of the South Sea:

Ye storms there on high,
    And fiends of the deep,
O tarry ye not,
    Where'er ye may sleep!

For battle prepared,
    Your God calleth ye,
Roll on as the thunder,
    And plough ye the sea.

=== Page 10 ===
O shiver the masts,
    Shake the bed of the sea,
Make known to them all
    Sons of hell ye be.

On the Ship:

Hark, storm-spirits dark are nighing,
    Threat'ning clouds all downward fly,
        For the storm spirit's nigh!
Reef the sails, the yards all lower,
    On the deck then every man.

Billow rises wild on billow,
    Piping raves the furious wind,
Is the anchor fast and steady?
    Still our hope to that we bind.

Woe! The mast broke, shrouds all shriven,
    Cleft the great ship's mighty bow,
Flash on flash red lightning driven
    Wraps in flame the anchor tow.

On and on the storm is waging,
    'Gainst the hellish rocks they dip.
See the furies, hear their raging,
    In the great deep sinks the ship.

The God of Storms:

To the deep she went down!
Come, O sun, here downward pour thee,
Ne'er that ship will sail before thee.

=== Page 11 ===
The Demons:

Victoria! That ship we sank for ever,
    Of shameless robbers quick revenge obtain
O'er us hath mortal had victory never,
    Ancient and mighty ocean race we reign.

Ill fares who seeks the prize 'tis ours to guard,
    And woe! shall sink in deepest wave.
Who his desire and hope our waves award,
    Earns for his daring bold an early grave.

5.—Closing Song

The Spirits of the Sea:

Slumber soft in deep sea lying,
    Lulled by billow-throng for aye.
Our ear heareth all your sighing,
    When ye plaint to plaint reply.

Calmly moon and stars are bending
    From high heaven unto the wave.
Far and wide night shadow blending,
    God doth guard your silent grave.

And the spirit choir are mourning
    With the nymphs thy fate's decree,
And the spirit choir are saying:
    Slumber soft in deepest sea!

Liedertafel and Orchestra

Why should we sigh, and mirth decry,
And why from content seek banishment?
With care why alloy the cup of joy,
To vainly repent o'er days misspent?
No! cherish the hours, while youth is ours;
And give not to care life's better share;
    But the sage old device
    Let us prize,
That this world's both good and fair!
Though in lane and street,
Oftsoe'er you meet
    Gloomy faces, sorrow's traces,
Think that evermore.
When the clouds pass o'er,
Lips will smile that smil'd before, Once more!
Ever thus sweet Spring
Weaves his flow'ry ring,
    Gladness wooing, world renewing;
And like airy sprite,
Ceaseless day and night,
Joy doth weave a new delight, With micht.
    Her shapes are manifold
    Her voices all untold,
    She dwells in ev'ry place
    Where pure hearts may follow
        Her fairy trace.
She roams on sunlit hills,
Or lurks by babbling rills,
Or rocks on ocean's breast,
    Or sings where the woodlands
        In shadow rest.

=== Page 16 ===
But, oh! sweet is the image of joy,
    In human face that dwells,
When love new-born, of its pure ecstasy
    In humid glances tells.

O'er joy-illumined eye
Night spreads no starless sky;
And love-filled heart can hear
    The chime of earth's joy-bells
        Sound far and near.

O ye, that look through a darkening veil,
And ye, faint souls, that life's sorrows bewail,
Look up! and trust to Nature's decree:
    Where life is, love can be.

Come, haste your dull doleful creed to forsake,
To brighter faiths let your spirits awake,
Nor doubt that towards a heaven-lov'd end
    All joyful things will tend.

Then silence not the voice
That would in glee rejoice,
Nor dim in darksome night
Eyes made to bask in light;
Hush not the silv'ry note
That falls from Mirth's gay throat,
But when the maid thou hast,
    O hold her fast!

No wanton sprite is she,
That would avoided be,
But in each guileless breast
A gladly harbour'd guest;
Love that hath such bridesmaid,
By her more lovely's made—
Blest, where in cot or hall,
    Joy's footsteps fall.

=== Page 17 ===
And oft, when adrift in thought's rudderless boat,
    Calmly we float
    From life's noise remote,
Across the still waters her bright glances beam,
And bathe all in sunlight our dream.
Or when at Humanity's glorious shrine
    Men's hearts entwine
    In love half-divine,
'Tis joy that her glow to our pulses imparts,
And throbs in our grateful hearts.
    O rejoice! Heart and voice
    Raise to heav'n above, laud the Source of Love.
    He is good, great and wise;
    Wraft from earth to skies
    Hymns of gratitude!
Now to the gay dance's rhythmical sound
See the golden-haired hours circle round,
While our thoughts in harmonious rhyme
To their soul-stirring cadence keep time!
Stealing us far from the sorrows of life,
Shedding balm o'er its heart-paining strife,
Guiding gently to sweet spots of rest
For the heart that with gladness is blest!
    Joy and song
    Be our theme life-long,
    And in jocund strain
    Sound again the refrain!
    Sing and laugh, laugh and sing—
    Come what fate may bring!
    Let joy's paeans rise
    In glad songs to the skies!
        Then sing, yes sing, O sing!

GOD SAVE THE QUEEN.

Part II.

CHORAL ODE—
From Goethe's "Helena"
(Faust, Part 2, Act 3.)
G. W. L. Marshall-Hall.

(Composed specially for and dedicated to the Melbourne Liedertafel.)

THE LIEDERTAFEL, LADIES' CHOIR
AND ORCHESTRA.

ALTO SOLO—MISS ADELAIDE BRUCE.

Life presented itself to the Greek mind as a series of manifestations of Power. Omnipotent, irresistible, irrevocable, first in the order of forces, loomed Fate, then the gods, the ancestral heroes, and the pre-eminent men of the times. Each State, surrounded by enemies, depended for its safety on the courage and power of its citizens, whom a reverse of war would convert into slaves with their wives and children. The actual experience of the Power and Tragedy of human existence, which to our modern comfortable plebian semi-vegetable life are almost unintelligible, lent an intensity to the moment which we can but faintly imagine. Power and its limitation were equally displayed in the sudden plunge from the height of prosperity to the depth of woe, and found expression in the never equalled strength and restraint of Greek art, imparting a reverential solemnity even to its most joyous utterances. This is the key note of their art, energetic power, and fate:

Fate, whose horizons, narrowing from afar
Within their blind abysmal night immerse
Both gods and men, and all things else that be
In irremediable catastrophe.

In the following ode from Goethe's masterpiece, these qualities are passionately felt by one who was himself a Greek at heart though born in a barbarian age. The music is an endeavour to complete and enforce the poet's intention. The serenity, not untinged with a certain noble sadness, of the first stanza, is contrasted with those following, in which the power and majesty and terrible presence of the gods is imaged, which succeeds the picture of limited fettered humanity.

MISS MARGUERITE HENDERSON.

I KNOW not what it betokens
That I am so sad at heart,
A legend from bygone ages
Will not from my mind depart.
The air is cool and it darkens,
And calmly flows the Rhine,
The mountain's far summit sparkles
In gentle evening shine.
A lovely lady sitteth
Thereby, entrancing fair,
Her golden raiment glistens,
She combs her golden hair.
She combs it with comb all golden,
And sings a song the while,
That has a soul-betwitching
Resistless melody.
The boatman, as onward he fareth,
It seizeth with anguish dread,
He sees not the rocks fast shoaling,
He looks ever up overhead.
Meseems the wavelets swallow
At last both boatman and boat,
And this with her fatal singing
The Loreley has wrought.

His horsemen hard behind us ride;
    Should they our steps discover,

Out spake the hardy highland wight,
    "I'll go, my chief, I'm ready!
It is not for your silver bright,

By this the storm grew loud apace,
    The water wraith was shrieking,

    Grew dark as they were speaking.
But still as wilder blew the wind,
    And as the night grew drearer,
Adown the glen rode armed men,
    Their tramping sounded nearer.
"Oh haste thee, haste!" the lady cries,
    "Though storms around us gather,
I'll meet the raging of the skies,
    But not an angry father."
The boat has left the stormy land,
    A stormy sea before her,
When, oh, too strong for human hand,
    The tempest gather'd o'er her.
And still they rowed amidst the roar
    Of waters fast prevailing:
Lord Ullin reached the fatal shore,
    His wrath was changed to wailing.
For sore dismayed, thro' storm and shade,
    He did his child discover:
One lovely arm she stretched for aid,
    And one was round her lover.
"Come back, come back!" he cried in grief
    Across the stormy water,
And I'll forgive your Highland chief,
    My daughter! oh, my daughter!"

PROGRAMME.

1. OVERTURE.

Die Meistersinger    Richard Wagner
THE ORCHESTRA.
No sooner do the first few bars of this masterly comedy sound than stern Time seems to flag, falter, turn tail, and run back a few centuries, and, like the worthy golosh-clad councillor of Hans Andersen, we wake up to find ourselves a hundred or two years younger, sauntering through the queer old streets of Nürnberg, in the company of those famous master-singers of whose quaint customs we have so often read. We seem to see it all—the various guilds in procession with banners flying! the impetuous, passionate idealist Walther, head-over-ears in love with Master Goldsmith Pogner's daughter; tender little Eva, who shyly returns his passion; the frolicsome apprentices, mimicking the somewhat pompous airs of their masters; and, as, in a dream, scenes the most diverse succeed one another without incongruity conjured up by the spell of music.

2. RECITATIVE AND ARIA—
Die Hochzeit des Figaro    Mozart
Miss KATE SAMUELS.
SUSANNA:—
At last the hour nears, when, O beloved! I shall possess thee entirely. Anxious doubts, begone! vanish for ever! disturb no more the joy of my heart! 'Ah! around me everything appears so gay: Hesperus looks down so smilingly, so smilingly upon my love! Come then, O my well-beloved! let the stillness of night watch over us. O finger no longer, beloved soul! thy friend waits for thee here, full of longing! The moon's silver torch not yet throws forth its light: stillness and peace reign in the fields. The murmur of the west-wind, and the gurgling brook attune every nerve to rapture; the flowers breathe o'er the glad meadows; all invites us to love, joy, and bliss. Come then, beloved! let me no longer await thee! Come that I may crown thy head with roses.

(Score and Orchestral Parts kindly lent by Herr Otto Linden.)

=== Page 6 ===
3. DRAMATIC BALLAD—

La Belle Dame sans Merci

G. W. L. Marshall-Hall

MR. JAMES WADE.

This wonderful poem represents in an ideal form the overpowering fascination which it is in the power of some women to exert over certain men—a fascination which makes or mars life. This the poets have pictured in "Antony and Cleopatra," "Launcelot and Guinevere," "Tristan and Isolde." The music is an attempt to realise the weird despair of the scene, and the strange irresistible magic of the love which usurps the man's whole being, with all its tender dreamy delight, of which the eighth stanza is the most marked instance, where the strange harmonic progressions seem to typify the "love-sleep" from which his life long he may never more awaken.

1.
Ah! what can ail thee, wretched wight,
Alone and palely loitering?
The sedge is withered from the lake,
And no birds sing.

2.
Ah! what can ail thee, wretched wight,
So haggard and so woe-begone?
The squirrel's granary is full,
And the harvest's done.

3.
I see a lily on thy brow,
With anguish moist and fever dew;
And on thy cheek a fading rose
Fast withereth, too.

4.
I met a lady in the meads,
Full beautiful—a fairy's child:
Her hair was long, her foot was light,
And her eyes were wild.

5.
I set her on my pacing steed,
And nothing else saw all day long:
For sideways would she lean, and sing
A faery's song.

6.
I made a garland for her head,
And bracelets, too, and fragrant zone;
She looked at me as she did love,
And made sweet moan.

7.
She found me roots of relish sweet,
And honey wild, and mamma dew;
And sure in language strange she said,
I love thee true.

8.
She took me to her elfin grot,
And there she gazed and sighed deep,
And there I shut her wild, sad eyes—
So kissed to sleep.

9.
And there we slumbered on the moss,
And there I dreamed, ah, woe beside!
The latest dream I ever dreamed,
On the cold hillside.

10.
I saw pale kings, and princes, too,
Pale warriors—death-pale were they all—
Who cried—"La Belle Dame sans Merci
Hath thee in thrall."

11.
I saw their starv'd lips in the gloom
With horrid warning gaped wide,
And I awoke, and found me here,
On the cold hillside.

12.
And this is why I sojourn here
Alone and palely loitering,
Though the sedge is withered from the lake,
And no birds sing.

(Keats.)

5. "A SONG OF DESTINY"
(Schicksalslied) Op. 54.
Johannes Brahms

LIEDERTAFEL AND ORCHESTRA.

Far in yon region of light, where pleasures fail not,
Wander the Spirits blest,
Breathed on by airs of glory, bright and divine,
Like a harp, when a master hand wakes it from silence;
Free from care, like a babe that is sleeping, are they in heaven that dwell:
Pure and lowly as half-open'd blossoms
In those fields of light they ever bloom;
And in bliss are their eyes still gazing on clearness calm and eternal.
But man may not linger, and nowhere finds he repose;
We stay not, but wander, we grief-laden mortals,
Blindly from one sad hour to another,
Like water from cliff unto cliff ever dropping
Blindly at last do we pass away.

Sig. ACHILLE REBOTARO.

"Get thee up! there, thy offspring I do permit thee to behold, in darkness and in silence; then awhile thy blushes and my shame be hidden."

"No, not on him, on you fragile existence, be my blows directed elsewhere I'll find that which shall wipe out my dishonour, 'tis e'en thy life's blood. From thy base heart my dagger ere long shall bid it swiftly flow—vengeance sternly exacting for all my woe."

And would'st thou thus have sullied a soul so pure,
In whose chasteness my spirit delighted.
Thou betray me, in whose love I felt all secure?
Of my days thou hast poisoned the stream.
Treacherous heart! is it thus he's requitted who the first in thy friendship, yes the first in thy friendship did seem?
O the pangs of a joy aye departed, of caresses that made life a heaven! when Adelia, an angel pure hearted, in my arms grew resplendent with love!
All is over; and hate's bitter leaven my widow'd heart only can move:
Oh the pangs of joy departed; Hope can buoy me no more.

THE ORCHESTRA.

He who can enter into the spirit of Shakespeare's "Midsummer Night's Dream," will need no other aid to throw himself into the mood in which this masterpiece is written. In delicacy of fancy it is unsurpassed, even by the great tragedian. The opening is delightful, where we hear the distant sound of Oberon's magic horn, and the following bars which so wonderfully depict the drowsy awakening of nature.

INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS, INC.

announces
THE
BRIAN D. BARNES
ONE MAN THEATRE
FESTIVAL

The art of one-man theatre takes a rare combination of artistry, technical skills and incredible feats of memory, to hold audiences at full-length performances, often without intervals, and move them through the whole range of human emotions, from laughter to tears. Brian D. Barnes has mastered the art superbly.

Four Different Programmes
3rd to 13th September, 1970
at the
San Miguel Auditorium
Makati, Rizal

1. BECKET: World Premiere in the Philippines. An adaptation from Alfred, Lord Tennyson's tragedy of Becket, with additional scenes and lines from The Chronicles.
2. PICKWICKIANS AT MANOR FARM: A new production, the script presents the happiest side of Charles Dickens' immortal Pickwick Papers, with Brian D. Barnes playing some 20 Dickensian characters.
3. UNDER MILK WOOD: First performed and highly-acclaimed in Manila in 1968. By popular demand a return of Dylan Thomas' modern classic, a play for over 36 voices.
4. RECITATION: Melodramas of poetry and prose set to the music of R. Strauss, Schubert, Schumann and Poulenc, originally composed for recitation with pianoforte. With REGALADO JOSE at the piano.

Galas: ₱20 & ₱15 — Matinees: ₱10 & ₱7

=== Page 6 ===
BECKET
World Premiere in the Philippines

This unprecedented cultural "first" in the Philippines is in commemoration of the Eight-Hundredth Anniversary of the death of Thomas Becket in 1170. The basis of this adaptation for Brian D. Barnes' One-Man Theatre is Alfred, Lord Tennyson's tragedy of Becket, with scenes and lines added from The Chronicles. The Encyclopaedia Britannica has this to say of Tennyson's Becket: "In the autumn of 1884, his tragedy of Becket was published, but the poet at last despaired of the stage and disclaimed any hope of 'meeting the exigencies of our modern theatre.' Curiously enough, after his death Becket was one of all his plays which enjoyed a great success on the boards." As such, it was one of the favourite roles of the distinguished English actor, Sir Henry Irving. Brian D. Barnes will perform "BECKET" without interval.

UNDER MILK WOOD

"It would be hard for any work of art to communicate more directly and funnily and lovingly what it is to be alive," writes poet-critic Randall Jarrell of Dylan Thomas' Under Milk Wood. Here, in the masterpiece completed just before his tragic death in 1953, Dylan Thomas gave fullest expression to his sense of the magnificent flavor and variety of life. The stage production of Under Milk Wood, given as an experiment at the Edinburgh Festival, was brought to London where it was the surprise success of the season, and then to Broadway. Enthusiastic audiences agreed with the critics who called it "probably the richest and certainly the earthiest theater experience of the season, and a dazzling combination of poetic fireworks and music-hall humor." Barnes' complete rendition of the over 36 different voices in Under Milk Wood has become a sturdy perennial in his ever-growing repertory, hailed wherever he has brought his One Man Theatre upon repeated invitation.

=== Page 7 ===
THE PICKWICKIANS AT MANOR FARM

This first presentation in Manila is commemorative of Charles Dickens' death one hundred years ago. The script presents the happiest side of Dickens' Pickwick Papers. The original intention was to build the situations centering around Mr. Winkle, but very quickly it became evident that he cannot be divorced from the rest of the club. The two visits at Manor Farm provide a continuity of story and character, thus comprising a certain wholeness to the episodes. Above all, it introduces the audience to some of the most immortal and beloved of Dickens' characters. Pickwick Papers achieved great success in the English-speaking world, as well as in translation. Pickwick hats, Pickwick coats, canes, cigars and all manner of fads were produced with a fervour rivalling the pop image of today for the then 25-year old author, who dressed "in the very height of the existing fashion, with long hair falling in silky masses over his temples."

RECITATION: MELODRAMA

Melody-drama . . . not to be confused with the 19th Century English theatre pieces also called melodramas. In the recitation-melodrama, the musical phrase and the spoken word must characterise each other, the phrases fit together and require careful timing. It does not enter into the area of improvisation as in the case of certain renditions of poetry and jazz. Many major composers wrote works as declamation or recitation to music for pianoforte, including Liszt, Schubert and Schumann. The same concept appears in some of Mozart's operatic works, in Beethoven's operas "Fidelio" and "Egmont," and Weber's "Der Freischutz." In the 20th Century there are examples by Janacek, Honegger, Searle, Copland, Stravinsky and Prokofiev.

AUSTRALIAN YOUTH ORCHESTRA

The Australian Youth Orchestra, comprising teenage musicians, recruited throughout Australia, is one of seven foreign symphony orchestras listed to perform at Osaka's Expo '70. It was founded 13 years ago by the National Music Camp Association.

The orchestra has been continuously revitalized with fresh and upcoming talent from the youth range. It has been engaged to play each year in one or another of Australian capital cities by the Australian Broadcasting Commission (ABC) or the organizers of the Adelaide Festival of Arts. Performances have been made in conjunction with visiting conductors and celebrity soloists such as Van Otterloo, Kentner, Barenboim, Atzmon, Anievas, etc., and at other times with outstanding young Australian instrumentalists under the orchestra's regular conductor, John Hopkins. It has featured in the ABC Youth series, has given concerts in schools, and in 1966 made a Royal Command Performance for the visiting Queen Mother at the Adelaide Festival of Arts.

The Osaka trip, sponsored jointly by the Australian Government and the Japan Association for the 1970 World Exposition, will be the orchestra's first overseas visit. In recent years a number of highly-rated youth orchestras of this kind have added an exciting splash of color to international music, and as the standards rise it becomes less necessary to stress that the best of them are able to stand comparison with all but the internationally famous big-name orchestras. This applies particularly in Britain, Europe, the United States, Japan and Australia, where serious orchestral music-making, under the guidance of trained music teachers and professionals, begins for many children at kindergarten age.

Australia was one of the first countries and remains one of the few to create a truly national young symphony orchestra. How good can this kind of youth orchestra be? How can youngsters, busy with so many other aspects of education and pleasure, match the skill, the precision and the musical insight of professionals? The answer is that even if they cannot always match the professionals, they bring a special quality of adventurous freshness plus youthful vitality and enthusiasm to the presentation of even the most difficult music.

When world-famed pianist, Hepzibah Menuhin played the Konzertstück of Weber with one of the young orchestras at a national summer Music Camp, she said: "This is so much more fun than playing with what are called the great orchestras. Here I feel really related, through music-making, to everybody on the platform and in the hall."

NOTE: The concert attire of the A.Y.O. was specially designed for their performances at Osaka Expo '70 and their Manila engagement.

JOHN HOPKINS, O.B.E.

Her Majesty the Queen of England has just honoured John Hopkins with the Order of the British Empire decoration, in recognition of his distinguished achievements in music.

John Hopkins has had a long and close association with the Australian Youth Orchestra, having conducted its concerts in five of the last eight years. Since 1963 he has regularly attended the National Music Camp each January to conduct the First Orchestra which consists mainly of Australian Youth Orchestra players.

Born in England in 1927, John Hopkins trained at the Royal Manchester College of Music, the Guildhall School of Music, London, and the Mozarteum, Salzburg. For eight years he was resident conductor with two B.B.C. orchestras before being appointed conductor of the National Orchestra of New Zealand Broadcasting Corporation in 1957, a position he held until 1963.

He has conducted extensively throughout Europe including the Soviet Union and Czechoslovakia, and has appeared in Asia and North America.

As ABC's Director of Music since 1963 he makes regular visits overseas to survey the musical scene, the last being in 1969 when he visited London, Paris, Brussels, Amsterdam, Cologne, Munich, Vienna, Bratislava, Dublin, Boston and Cleveland.

He attended the International Rostrum of Composers in Paris and the Tanglewood (Lenox) and Cleveland Festivals in the U.S.A.

Hopkins is the popular inaugurator and conductor of the successful Sydney Proms. Begun six years ago they now attract large and enthusiastic crowds, eager for new music in an informal atmosphere. This series of five concerts now sells out on the opening day each year.

1970 saw the establishment of the Melbourne Proms with the Melbourne Symphony Orchestra under Hopkins playing to capacity houses. He also regularly conducts ABC orchestras in other States and is a frequent visitor to the Composers' Workshop, an annual feature of the Festival of Perth.

TANYA HUNT

Young Melbourne cellist Tanya Hunt won the Commonwealth Finals of the ABC's Instrumental and Vocal Competitions last year. This was Tanya's first appearance in this competition.

At 18 she has been judged one of the finest young musicians in Australia today.

She began her musical studies with her mother at the age of seven and has since been the star pupil of several of Melbourne's leading cello teachers.

Tanya Hunt has attended the National Music Camp for the past five years and been a member of the Australian Youth Orchestra for the past three. She visited the Adelaide Festival in 1968 with the orchestra, and accompanied it last year when it gave concerts in Sydney.

She is at present a full-time student in the Concert Diploma Course at the Melbourne University Conservatorium and hopes to go overseas soon to study with André Navarra at the Paris Conservatoire.

In 1970, for the fourth successive year, she won first prize in the Chamber Music Section of the Dandenong Festival with her pianist sister.

Also this year she was soloist with the Sydney Symphony Orchestra conducted by John Hopkins at the Sydney Prom Concerts.

She has appeared recently as soloist with the Astra Chamber Orchestra and she has also played for the Musical Society of Victoria.

PROGRAMME NOTES

VARIATIONS AND FUGUE ON A THEME OF PURCELL, OP. 34 . . . BENJAMIN BRITTEN

Benjamin Britten is probably the most outstanding British composer of today.

This piece is subtitled "The Young Person's Guide to the Orchestra", and Britten wrote it in 1935, when he was in his early twenties, to accompany a film called The Instruments of the Orchestra. The film was composed and conducted by Sir Malcolm Sargent, and it has since been dubbed in fourteen different languages, so great is its popularity.

The work is a witty and ingenious composition illustrating the contribution each individual instrument makes to the orchestra and how each instrument fits into the orchestra as a whole. It consists of three main divisions: (a) a theme; (b) fourteen variations thereon; (c) a fugue.

The theme comes from Purcell's incidental music to Abdelazar (or "The Moor's Revenge"), written, probably, in 1695. This broad tune is at once announced by the full orchestra and is then repeated by the four sections of the orchestra (woodwind, strings, brass and percussion) in turn, followed by a full orchestral repeat.

Next we come to the interesting middle section (b)—fourteen variations—where each instrument (quickly accompanied sometimes) gives its own version of the opening tune. The instruments enter, section by section (the higher-pitched instruments first and the lower-pitched last) in the following order:—WOODWIND: (1) flute, (2) piccolo, (3) oboes, (4) clarinets, (5) bassoons; STRINGS: (6) violins, (7) violas, (8) cellos, (9) double basses, (10) harp; BRASS: (11) horns, (12) trumpets, (13) trombones and bass tuba; and finally, the PERCUSSION: (14) tympani, bass drum and cymbals, tambourine and triangle, side-drum and Chinese block, xylophone, castanets and gong and whip. All these fourteen variations differ from each other, and each is in a style characteristic of the instrument concerned.

CONCERTO FOR CELLO IN B FLAT MAJOR . . . LUIGI BOCCHERINI

Soloist: TANYA HUNT

Luigi Boccherini was born in Lucca, Italy, on the 19th February, 1743, and he died in Madrid in 1805. His life period was similar to that of Joseph Haydn (1732-1809) and his artistic ideals were almost identical. Haydn and Boccherini appear never to have met although they did exchange mutual regards by way of their publisher Artaria. When Boccherini's entire output is added together it comes to nearly 500 works, and includes 112 quartets for two violins, viola and two cellos, 91 string quartets, 48 trios for two violins and cello, 20 symphonies, and an opera, as well as a number of concertos—a tribute to his amazing facility.

When Boccherini was in his early twenties he toured with the violinist Filippo Manfredi, who was a pupil of Tartini. In 1768 they reached Paris where Boccherini's music, in particular his chamber music, was such a success that the Spanish Ambassador, a musical enthusiast, invited Boccherini to extend his concert tour to Madrid, which he did in the following winter. Unfortunately, neither the King nor the Prince of the Asturias took any notice of him, but he found a sympathetic friend in the King's brother the Infante Don Luis, to whom he dedicated six quartets. He stayed in Spain until 1785 when he was appointed chamber composer to the King of Prussia, who was a keen cellist. This appointment lasted for twelve years and when the King died Boccherini returned to Madrid where he spent the remaining years of his life until his death in 1805.

Writing of Boccherini, the well-known music writer Sondheim has this to say—"The technique of stringed instruments, which, in conformity with the demands of the development in style, progressed during the eighteenth century from almost primitive simplicity to all-embracing brilliance, was led on to its final stage by Boccherini. At the present day it may seem that the permanent artistic value of Boccherini's work is but small. His personality was indeed soon to be overshadowed by the classical masters, but, in the history of musical development at least, he deserves a place among the principal composers of all time."

Boccherini's Cello Concerto in B Flat is one of the best-known of his works for this instrument. There are three movements, the first in sonata form has many brilliant passages for the solo instrument. The slow movement is quite short but eloquent. The last movement is a Rondo on a straightforward theme. This melody is cleverly brought back each time, after episodes which exploit the whole range of the cello's capabilities.

MUSIC FOR JAPAN . . .

We are grateful to the composer for providing this programme note—

"Perhaps I should have called this work 'Music for Japan from Australia', because I want the Australian Youth Orchestra to take to Japan music that says something of my own country. If the view of desert and sea, bush and city seems to be a personal one, it's because I want also to send music that says something about me. Some of the most memorable times of my life have been in Australia and Japan.

Written especially for the Australian Youth Orchestra, Music for Japan is quite adventurous in its sonorities and in the means required

NOTE: The National Music Camp Association commissioned Mr. Sculthorpe to write a work for the A.Y.O. especially for its tour to Japan during Expo '70. The Australian Advisory Board of the Commonwealth Assistance to Australian Composers (Prime Minister's Department) kindly and generously assisted the Association with the honorarium to Mr. Sculthorpe.

SYMPHONY IN G MAJOR, NO. 8, OP. 88 . . . ANTONIN DVORAK

The simple, carefree mood of the G major Symphony long ago endeared it to concertgoers. Compositions often arouse widely contrasted feelings in listeners. The G major is not one of them. English critics in 1890 spoke of it as "pastoral", teeming with "rural sights and sounds", and stressed its freshness and charm. To an American critic writing in 1941, the score was "recolored of the Bohemian countryside, and marked by a decided charm and allure." The word "idyllic" occurs so often in references to the symphony that if a title were needed "Idyllic Symphony" would serve as well as any.

In the introduction of the opening movement (Allegro con brio, 4/4, G major) a lovely song of melancholy, in G minor, is uttered by cellos and horns. With the final cadence the mood changes to major and the flute brings in a bright theme which has been likened to the "chirping of a bird." A cadenza then leads to the first chief subject in the cellos. The strings chant part of the second theme, then taken up by clarinets and flutes. The woodwinds now usher in a delicate motif pianissimo, the whole orchestra soon shouting it fortissimo. The movement is remarkable for its wealth of full-fledged themes, which are set off in contrast rather than fully developed.

The second movement (Adagio, 2/4, C minor and major) begins with a somber phrase reiterated by the strings. This prefatory passage contains the melodic and rhythmic material of the first section.

to produce these. It might be called a 'sound piece', because, like my Sun Music series, it's made up of sound-impressions. Much as I enjoy writing melodies, in this work I've used no conventional melodic shapes, in order to get more fully an abstraction of my feelings.

Music for Japan is scored for a normal orchestra, with amplified percussion. Rather than provide a detailed programme note, I should like to say only that the work lasts for approximately twelve minutes; this may give the listener a sense of shape and flow within a certain period of time."

—Peter Sculthorpe.

PETER SCULTHORPE

Clarinets then discourse it in a minor-and-major exchange frequent in Dvorak's music. In the second section of the movement the strings and winds take turns at a staccato figure accompanying the main melody. The figure is used in building up a striking climax. After repetition, with changes in harmony, a brief coda ends the movement.

An odd device in the third movement (Allegretto grazioso, 3/8, G minor and major), is the "counterpoint of oboe and bassoon, in a virtual Cossack dance, to the theme of the coda, which changes from triple to duple time." With rapid staccati in the winds and counter-themes in the strings contrastingly marked, the effect was thought to be "thoroughly comical" in 1892. What would normally be the trio of a scherzo is taken up with a charmingly simple melody in folk style. It recalls like passages in Schubert's music.

A fanfare of trumpets ushers in the last movement (Allegro non troppo, 2/4, G major) as if heralding a brisk whirl of Bohemian folk dancing. Instead, the strings announce a stately subject in two eight-measure parts, which goes through four variations. Two new themes now appear, one a lyrical solo, the other for clarinets, against a drolly rumbling bass. The tempo speeds up with the return of the first subject. Echoes of the chief subject of the opening movement filter through as the finale mounts to a brilliant climax.
