=== Page 6 ===
Extract from the "Musical Times,"
1st June, 1891.

AMONGST the many College Concerts given in Oxford during the present term, that by the Eglesfield Musical Society, at Queen's College, on the 22nd ult., is deserving of special notice. This Society is one of the most enterprising in the University in the encouragement given to new works, and on this occasion a Ballad for men's voices and full orchestra entitled "Horatius" was performed. The composer, the Rev. J. H. Mee, conducted his work, which he had specially written for and dedicated to the society. The words are selected from the poem by Lord Macaulay, and are admirably suited for musical treatment. The composer divides his composition into five numbers: (1) "The Etruscan Muster," (2) "The Panic at Rome," (3) "The Captain of the Gate," (4) "The Keeping of the Bridge," and (5) the Epilogue. Each of these numbers has its special "point" and dramatic interest at the hands of the composer. It is really refreshing to find that (although restricted to men's voices) Dr. Mee has something new to say, and knows how to say it. The vocal parts throughout are well adapted for voices, and, consequently, effect is obtained by an easy and natural process. The instrumental parts, too, are by no means difficult, yet they give great dramatic colour to the work. The performance was one of great merit. It is impossible in a short notice like this to do more than single out a few places which seem to be of greatest interest. The opening number ("The Etruscan Muster") at once commends the attention of the musician, by the martial character of the first theme, led off by the strings in unison, and soon to be strengthened by the soft wind. The voices then take up the motive, firstly without accompaniment, and secondly with the addition of the orchestra, until a striking effect is obtained by the sustained harmony of the trombones and horns. Indeed, the entire number is rich in musical contrasts. In the second part ("The Panic at Rome") occurs a very effective melody with the full orchestra, where Horatius comes forward and declares his readiness to assist in defending "The Bridge" against the advance of the Tuscan army. This is followed by a pleasing melody for the tenor, in which at the words "And for the tender mother" is a beautiful accompaniment by the strings and horns, with an oboe obbligato. This second part concludes with a striking phrase for the full orchestra and voices, where Horatius and the two other volunteers set out in order to "keep the bridge." This phrase is evidently a favourite with the composer, for he reintroduces it in the last number (the Epilogue) no less than four times, and with it winds up his composition. Space forbids to enlarge on the remaining numbers further than to state that they are exceedingly vocal and effectively instrumented. There is no doubt that the work is a valuable addition to music for male voices. At the conclusion of the performance the composer was received with the greatest enthusiasm.

=== Page 7 ===
Programme

PART I

Cantata—"Horatius"                Dr. John H. Ree
Presented to the Society by John Eggleston, Esq., Member of R.M.L.
FIRST TIME IN AUSTRALIA
Liedertafel and Orchestra

No. 1.—THE ETRUSCAN MUSTER.

Lars Porsena of Clusium
    By the Nine Gods he swore,
That the great house of Tarquin
    Should suffer wrong no more.
By the Nine Gods he swore it,
    And named a trysting day,
And bade his messengers ride forth,
East and west and south and north,
    To summon his array.

East and west and south and north
    The messengers ride fast,
And tower and town and cottage
    Have heard the trumpet's blast.
Shame on the false Etruscan
    Who lingers in his home,
When Porsena of Clusium
    Is on the march for Rome.

The horsemen and the footmen
    Are pouring in amain
From many a stately market-place;
    From many a fruitful plain
From many a lonely hamlet,
    Which, hid by beech and pine,
Like an eagle's nest, hangs on the crest
    Of purple Apennine.

=== Page 8 ===
There be thirty chosen prophets,
    The wisest of the land,
Who alway by Lars Porsena
    Both morn and evening stand:
Evening and morn the Thirty
    Have turned the verses o'er,
Traced from the right on linen white
    By mighty seers of yore.
And with one voice the Thirty
    Have their glad answer given:
"Go forth, go forth, Lars Porsena;
    Go forth, beloved of Heaven;
Go, and return in glory
    To Clusium's royal dome;
And hang round Nurscia's altars
    The golden shields of Rome."
And now hath every city
    Sent up her tale of men;
The foot are fourscore thousand,
    The horse are thousands ten:
Before the gates of Sutrium
    Is met the great array.
A proud man was Lars Porsena
    Upon the trysting day.

NO. 2.—THE PANIC AT ROME.

But by the yellow Tiber
    Was tumult and affright:
From all the spacious champaign
    To Rome men took their flight.
A mile around the city,
    The throng stopped up the ways;
A fearful sight it was to see
    Through two long nights and days.
For aged folks on crutches,
    And women great with child,
And mothers sobbing over babes
    That clung to them and smiled.
And sick men borne on litters
    High on the necks of slaves,
And troops of sun-burned husbandmen
    With reaping-hooks and staves,
And droves of mules and asses
    Laden with skins of wine,
And endless flocks of goats and sheep,
    And endless herds of kine,

=== Page 9 ===
And endless trains of waggons
    That creaked beneath the weight
Of corn-sacks and of household goods,
    Choked every roaring gate.

The Fathers of the City,
    They sat all night and day,
For every hour some horseman came
    With tidings of dismay.
Out spake the Consul roundly:
    "The bridge must straight go down;
For, since Janiculum is lost,
    Nought else can save the town."

Just then a scout came flying,
    All wild with haste and fear;
"To arms! to arms! Sir Consul:
    Lars Porsena is here."
On the low hills to westward
    The Consul fixed his eye,
And saw the swarthy storm of dust
    Rise fast along the sky.

And nearer fast and nearer
    Doth the red whirlwind come;
And louder still and still more loud,
From underneath that rolling cloud,
Is heard the trumpet's war-note proud,
    The trampling and the hum.
And plainly and more plainly
    Now through the gloom appears,
Far to left and far to right,
In broken gleams of dark-blue light,
The long array of helmets bright,
    The long array of spears.

No. 3.—THE CAPTAIN OF THE GATE.

But the Consul's brow was sad,
    And the Consul's speech was low,
And darkly looked he at the wall,
    And darkly at the foe.
"Their van will be upon us
    Before the bridge goes down;
And if they once may win the bridge,
    What hope to save the town?"

Then out spake brave Horatius,
    The Captain of the Gate:
"To every man upon this earth
    Death cometh soon or late.

=== Page 10 ===
And how can man die better
Than facing fearful odds,
For the ashes of his fathers,
    And the temples of his gods,

"And for the tender mother
Who dandled him to rest,
And for the wife who nurses
    His baby at her breast,
And for the holy maidens
    Who feed the eternal flame,
To save them from false Sextus
    That wrought the deed of shame?

"Hew down the bridge, Sir Consul,
    With all the speed ye may;
I, with two more to help me,
    Will hold the foe in play.
In yon straight path a thousand
    May well be stopped by three.
Now who will stand on either hand,
    And keep the bridge with me?"

Then out spoke Spurius Lartius;
    A Ramnian proud was he:
"Lo, I will stand at thy right hand,
    And keep the bridge with thee."
And out spake strong Herminius;
    Of Titian blood was he:
"I will abide on thy left side
    And keep the bridge with thee."

"Horatius," quoth the Consul,
    "As thou sayest, so let it be,"
And straight against that great array
    Forth went the dauntless Three.
For Romans in Rome's quarrel
    Spared neither land nor gold,
Nor son nor wife, nor limb nor life,
    In the brave days of old.

No. 4.—The Keeping of the Bridge.

Meanwhile the Tuscan army,
    Right glorious to behold,
Came flashing back the noonday light,
    Rank behind rank like surges bright
Of a broad sea of gold.

=== Page 11 ===
Four hundred trumpets sounded
    A peal of warlike glee,
As that great host, with measured tread,
And spears advanced, and ensigns spread,
Rolled slowly towards the bridge's head,
    Where stood the dauntless Three.

And forth three chiefs came spurring
    Before that deep array;
To earth they sprang, their swords they drew,
And lifted high their shields, and flew
    To win the narrow way.

Stout Lartius hurled down Aunus
    Into the stream beneath:
Herminius struck at Seius,
    And clove him to the teeth:
At Picus brave Horatius
    Darted one fiery thrust;
And the proud Umbrian's gilded arms
    Clashed in the bloody dust.

Then Ocnus of Falerii
    Rushed on the Roman Three;
And Lausulus of Urgo
    The rover of the sea;
And Aruns of Volsinium,
    Who slew the great wild boar,
The great wild boar that had his den
Amidst the reeds of Cosa's fen,
And wasted fields, and slaughtered men,
    Along Albinia's shore.

Herminius smote down Aruns:
    Lartius laid Ocnus low:
Right to the heart of Lausulus
    Horatius sent a blow.
"Lie there," he cried, "fell pirate!
    No more, aghast and pale,
From Ostia's walls the crowd shall mark
The track of thy destroying bark,
    Thy thrice accursed sail."

But now no sound of laughter
    Was heard among the foes,
A wild and wrathful clamour
    From all the vanguard rose.
There lacked not men of prowess,
    Nor men of lordly race;
For all Etruria's noblest
    Were round the fatal place.

=== Page 12 ===
But all Etruria's noblest
    Felt their hearts sink to see
On the earth the bloody corpses,
    In the path the dauntless Three.

But meanwhile axe and lever
    Have manfully been plied;
And now the bridge hangs tottering
    Above the boiling tide.
"Come back, come back, Horatius!"
    Loud cried the Fathers all.
"Back, Lartius! back, Herminius!
    Back, ere the ruin fall!"

Back darted Spurius Lartius;
    Herminius darted back:
And, as they passed, beneath their feet
    They felt the timbers crack.
But when they turned their faces,
    And on the farther shore
Saw brave Horatius stand alone,
    They would have crossed once more.

But with a crash like thunder
    Fell every loosened beam,
And, like a dam, the mighty wreck
    Lay right athwart the stream.
And a long shout of triumph
    Rose from the walls of Rome,
As to the highest turret-tops
    Was splashed the yellow foam.
Alone stood brave Horatius,
    But constant still in mind;
Thrice thirty thousand foes before,
    And the broad flood behind.

"Down with him!" cried false Sextus
    With a smile on his pale face.
"Now yield thee," cried Lars Porsena,
    "Now yield thee to our grace."

Round turned he, as not deigning
    Those craven ranks to see;
Nought spake he to Lars Porsena,
    To Sextus nought spake he;
But he saw on Palatinus
    The white porch of his home;
And he spake to the noble river
    That rolls by the towers of Rome.

=== Page 13 ===
"Oh, Tiber! Father Tiber!
    To whom the Romans pray,
    A Roman's life, a Roman's arms,
        Take thou in charge this day!"
So he spake, and speaking sheathed
    The good sword by his side,
And with his harness on his back,
    Plunged headlong in the tide.

No sound of joy or sorrow
    Was heard from either bank;
But friends and foes in dumb surprise,
With parted lips and straining eyes,
    Stood gazing where he sank:
And when above the surges
    They saw his crest appear,
All Rome sent forth a rapturous cry,
And even the ranks of Tuscany
    Could scarce forbear to cheer.

But fiercely ran the current,
    Swollen high by months of rain:
And fast his blood was flowing;
    And he was sore in pain,
And heavy with his armour,
    And spent with changing blows:
And oft they thought him sinking,
    But still again he rose.

Never, I ween, did swimmer,
    In such an evil case,
Struggle through such a raging flood
    Safe to the landing-place.
    But his limbs were borne up bravely
By the brave heart within,
    And our good father Tiber
Bore bravely up his chin.

And now he feels the bottom;
    Now on dry earth he stands;
Now round him throng the Fathers
    To press his gory hands;
And now, with shouts and clapping,
    And noise of weeping loud,
He enters through the River-Gate,
    Borne by the joyous crowd.

    No. 5.—EPILOGUE.
They gave him of the corn-land,
    That was of public right,
As much as two strong oxen
    Could plough from morn till night;

=== Page 14 ===
And they made a molten image,
    And set it up on high,
And there it stands unto this day
    To witness if I lie.

It stands in the Comitium,
    Plain for all folks to see;
Horatius in his harness,
    Halting upon one knee:
And underneath is written,
    In letters all of gold,
How valiantly he kept the bridge
    In the brave days of old.

And still his name sounds stirring
    Unto the men of Rome,
As the trumpet-blast that cries to them
    To charge the Volscian home;
And wives still pray to Juno
    For boys with hearts as bold
As his who kept the bridge so well
    In the brave days of old.

And in the nights of winter,
    When the cold north winds blow,
And the long howling of the wolves
    Is heard amidst the snow;
When round the lonely cottage
    Roars loud the tempest's din,
And the good logs of Algidus
    Roar louder yet within;

When the oldest cask is opened,
    And the largest lamp is lit;
When the chestnuts glow in the embers,
    And the kid turns on the spit;
When young and old in circle
    Around the firebrands close;
When the girls are weaving baskets,
    And the lads are shaping bows;
When the goodman mends his armour,
    And trims his helmet's plume;
When the goodwife's shuttle merrily
    Goes flashing through the loom;
With weeping and with laughter
    Still is the story told,
How well Horatius kept the bridge
    In the brave days of old.

INTERVAL OF FIVE MINUTES.

=== Page 15 ===
PART II

Part Song—"The Better Land"  J. Kendall
(COMPOSED FOR THE SOCIETY)

Liedertafel

I hear thee speak of the Better Land,
Thou call'st its children a happy band;
Mother, where is that radiant shore?
Shall we not seek it and weep no more?
Is it where the flow'r of the orange blows,
And the fireflies dance thro' the myrtle boughs?
    Not there, not there, my child

Is it far away in some region old,
Where the rivers wander o'er sands of gold,
Where the burning rays of the ruby shine
And the diamond lights up the secret mine,
And the pearl gleams forth from the coral strand?
Is it there, sweet mother, that better land?
    Not there, not there, my child.

Eye hath not seen it, my gentle boy;
Ear hath not heard its sweet songs of joy;
Dreams cannot picture a world so fair;
Sorrow and death may not enter there;
Time doth not breath on its fadeless bloom;
Far beyond the clouds, beyond the tomb,
    It is there, my child, it is there.

Song—"Sing Sweet Bird"  Gans
Miss Marie Elster

=== Page 16 ===
Part Song—

(a) "Absence"                Hatton
(b) "Wine Galop"             Huntze

Liedertafel

(a) Tho' long years have passed away,
    And joyous summer left me;
Tho' autumn sings her plaintive lay,
    Yet art thou still dear to me.

Tho' far away, thy voice is ever near to me;
Absence but makes thee dearer to me;
No time can change my love for thee.

——

(b) Mine host, fill up!
What joy to drink of rosy wine!
    Fill the glass; drink it up!
Fill the goblet to the brim.
    Drink it off! Drink it off!
By the clink of glass,
By song and glee,
    Toujours fidèle.

When I kiss the foaming goblet,
    Dearest love, I think of thee.
When the landlord seeks his reckoning,
    Then I drink; love, to thee.
Mine host, this goblet fill with wine!
[SPOKEN—One! two! three!]    Hurrah!

Sweetheart, dearest sweetheart,
    Dearest love, I think of thee;
Dearest love, I daily pledge thee
    In the cup filled to thee.
Drink it up! My glass is gone!
    Mine host, fill up!

What joy to drink of rosy wine!
Boys, take another glass of wine,
That drives all sorrow from the heart of man.
Now drain the goblet! Quick the goblet drain!
[SPOKEN—One! two! three!]    Hurrah!

Song—"Dreams of thee"  A. E. Grimshaw

Graceful Dance  Sullivan
No. III.—From the Incidental Music to Shakespeare's "Henry VIII"
Melbourne Amateur Orchestral Society

Song—"Rocked in the Cradle of the Deep"  Blockley
Miss Clara Mongredien

Part Song—"Tyrolese Hunter's March"  Boschat
Liedertafel and Orchestra

HALLO! Hallo!
Now hunters come away, for early breaks the day;
With rifles prov'd and tried we range the mountain side;
Keep distance every man, each nook and covert scan,
From by the forest end to where the two ways blend.

Yoho, yoho, yoho!  There something crouches low;
What eyes can shine like that?  It is a mountain cat.
'Tis only so I fear: It is a crouching deer;
Surround it every way, before it steals away.

See now he springs and flies, and for the forest tries,
But there the hunters stand, with steady eye and hand.
And crack it goes, yoho!  the ball has laid him low;
A noble beast is he, and killed most manfully.

Here from the waterfall we send a hunter's call,
To glad the list'ning ear of wives and sweethearts dear,
So gently timid they, that if we shoot they say—
"Ah me! there's someone hurt to day."

=== Page 18 ===
O sweethearts in the vale, you from afar we hail,
With joyful notes that tell that all with us is well,
Yet here awhile we roam; and with the evening come
To seek our dear and quiet home.

Tra la, la la, la la! then here's hurrah, hurrah!
For such a bonny land, for vales and mountains grand.
And here's hurrah, hurrah! for wives and maidens true.
Sweethearts, we shout for you, hurrah!

An eye that never fails, a heart that never quails,
A cheek aglow with health, is more than idle wealth.
Hallo! hallo! hallo! a-hunting we will go:
By topmost crag and peak our timid prey we seek.
Hallo! hallo! hallo! a-hunting we will go:
Full quickly flies the day; Hallo, hallo, away!

GOD SAVE THE QUEEN

By Special Appointment To His Excellency the Governor-General.

Part Song

"Champagnerlied" Heinrich Hofmann
(Sele—Mr. JAMES WADE).

THE LIEDERTAFEL.

Pour the libation in fizzing champagne,
Leaping in silvery, swirling cascades;
Pour the libation in fizzing champagne,
Gushing in tremulous, prancing, proud courses.
Flowing in boiling and high foaming ardours,
Like to the olden-time streamlets and sources
Deeply in Ida's dun thickets concealed.

Mould there thy pearl drops from silvery foam;
Seething they climb from their specular home.
Mould there thy pearl drops from silvery foam.
There are the sharp infundibular goblets,
Sparkling and glistening like bubbling fountains,
Pour'd from the mouth of the broken sealed magnum
Deeply in Ida's dun thickets concealed.

Swaying and thinking in aureate room,
Clink now the glasses with resonant swing;
Rolling and swaying like zephyrs in spring-time.
Dance frolicsome genii of champagne:
Backward and forward enlacing departing,
Glistening, vanishing, lost in the crystal vase;
Brief as the day of youth's gay effervescence.

THE LIEDERTAFEL.

If thou art sleeping maiden,
Awake, awake and open thy door,
'Tis the break of day and we must away
O'er meadow and mount and moor.
Wait not to find the silken feet,
But come with thy silken feet,
We shall have to pass through the dewy grass
And the waters wide and fleet.

THE LIEDERTAFEL.

The Nation's glory into your hands is now given.
    Oh, guard it well.
To sink with you, or with you rise to heaven.
    The magic spell of heart and song
    Links all the worlds that roll along,
So may they ever blended be in richest harmony.
Her voice is like the dreadful thunder,
    Terrible in its might and anger;
It rises on victorious planks, and vengeance
    takes on foes and minions—
    Strikes terror to the tyrant's heart.
If truth to exile e'er be driven;
Then to her aid the Muse arisen
Shall find revenge in lofty music's song.
    Oh, freedom's soul of arise!
Lift up your head to beauty's throne,
And as with her you mount the skies,
All lesser crowns disown.
The thousand various ways unending
Of rich humanity explore,
Till from the summit's height extending,
Behold the vast eternal shore.

Part Song —
"Thou art my dream"
Gail Hofmann

THE LIEDERTAFEL.

THE drooping flowers their buds are closing.
The silver stars keep watch above!
The world in tranquil sleep reposing
My wakeful bosom yields to love.
While here in hopeless grief I languish,
Could I behold thy vision bright,
Then would I fondly breathe my anguish,
Thou art my dream thro' stilly night.

Tho' all unmoved by love's appealing,
No kindling passion lights thy brow?
No voice of love thy heart revealing,
Still, still, the silver stars above.
Bend softly down, ye golden tresses,
Beam kindly once, bright orbs of light;
List, lady, list to love's distresses—
Thou art my dream thro' stilly night.

Part Song —
"Die Post"
(Cornet Solo—Mr. ARTHUR HAIGH).
Schafer

THE LIEDERTAFEL.

THRO' forest deep at dead of night,
The mail is slowly borne;
While sleep the weary travellers,
The post-boy winds his horn.

The forest-ranger's dwelling
Within the wood is seen,
The horn a tale is telling—
What can its echoes mean?

Its tunes so soft and sweetly flow,
The mails, in passing by,
Pause at the open window,
And mingling with them fly.

Where sleeps the forest maiden,
While beams the moon above;
With love her dreams are laden—
With melody and love.

Part Song—

"Song of the Pirates"

Bruch

THE LIEDERTAFEL.

On land we find but scanty honour,
A vagrant folk without a home;
Exiles to-day on shore we wonder,
To-morrow monarchs of the foam!
    Clink again!
    Glasses drain!
    Drink amain!

When o'er the deep our sails are flying,
All things must bow to our control;
On every hand a tax we levy
And ocean's pride must pay us toll.
    Clink again!
    Glasses drain!
    Drink amain!

Our coats are good broad-cloth from England,
And heavy silk from Genoa;
Our scores we reckon with the grapnel,
And we receipt them with "Hurrah!"
    Clink again!
    Glasses drain!
    Drink amain!

Here's glorious beer! That comes from Hamburg!
Or is your taste for Spanish wine?
All climes are pledged to feed and clothe us,
All fill the cup when we would dine.
    Clink again!
    Glasses drain!
    Drink amain!

Gay go the hours with wine and singing,
A merry life beyond compare!
And when at last our skulls lay bleaching,
Why there's an end to further care.
    Clink again!
    Glasses drain!
    Drink amain!

=== Page 4 ===
曲目解説

モーツァルト Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart（1756—1791）
セレナーデ 二長調 K.250 "ハフナー"
セレナーデとは、本来"静かな夕べに恋人の窓の下で歌い奏でる夜の調べ"とされている。イタリア語のセレナータ serenata は、上記の"夜曲"の意味と、他に"晴朗な天気"の意味があるが、この語はもともと"静める"、"なだめる"という意味の他動詞と、"野宿する"という意味の自動詞セレナーレ serenare の女性分詞形であり、さらにこの語は、"夕方"、"夜"の意の名詞セラ sera に由来するものである。したがってセレナーデは、夕べに野外で演奏して、愛する人や尊敬する人物に捧げる音楽として、その名称は声楽と器楽に共通に用いられて来た。
夜半に恋する人の窓の下でマンドリンやギター等の運搬可能な楽器を弾きながら歌う場面は、モーツァルトの＜ドン・ジョヴァンニ＞、ロッシーニの＜セビリャの理髪師＞、ヴァーグナーの＜ニュルンベルクの名歌手＞等に見られる。また、セレナーデ本来の目的からは離れるが、やや通俗的な演奏会用歌曲としての作品も、シューベルトやブラームスをはじめ多くの作曲家によって書かれている。
器楽合奏曲としてのセレナーデは、18世紀後半から19世紀前半にかけて多数の作品が書かれた。これらの音楽は、ヤーン Otto Jahn が"愛する人、尊敬を寄せる人々の窓辺でセレナーデを奏でるという古来の習慣は、当時[18世紀後半]依然として行われていた"と指摘しているように、王侯貴族や富豪から依頼されて作曲された機会音楽である。その意味で、まだセレナーデ本来の目的を保っている楽曲ということができる。ハイドンやモーツァルトの少からぬ作品、ベートーヴェンの作品8と25、シューベルトの作品148等はこの種の音楽である。
こうしたセレナーデは、全曲が続けて演奏されるものではなかったために、交響曲や室内楽曲ほど固定化された形式はもたない。楽章の数と配置法はより自由なもので、古典的連関形式[ソナタ]と同様の3ないし4楽章構成のものから、8楽章もの長大なものにまでいたって
いる。
一方、楽器編成もさわめて自由で、小数の楽器のアンサンブルから、複数のオーケストラを用いたものまで多様多様である。
器楽用セレナーデは、楽章構成や楽器編成の自由さ、および機会音楽という目的の点でカッサシオンやディヴェルティメントと共通な音楽である。ただこれらの楽曲は、その用途と演奏される場所によって区別されたものと考えられる。実際に、2種以上の筆写譜ないしは印刷譜がのこっている作品で、その同一の楽曲を一方の資料では"カッサシオン"と記し、他方では"ディヴェルティメント"と題している場合がある[例えばハイドンのHob. II.9、Hob. II.20]。今日一般に、ディヴェルティメントは室内で、特に食事の席で演奏された、いわば"Tafelmusik[食卓の音楽]"であり、セレナーデとカッサシオンは野外で演奏された音楽と考えられている。しかし、カッサシオンに関しては、その名称の語源についても、また演奏される目的についてもセレナーデほど明確ではない[フランス語の"casatim一取り除く"に由来し、街頭で演奏された告別の音楽であろうとする推測がある]。
なおセレナーデは、19世紀後半にはその本来の目的を失い、軽い組曲風の演奏会用楽曲となった。ブラームスの作品11と16、ドヴォルザークの作品22と44、チャイコフスキーの作品48、リヒャルト・シュトラウスの作品7等は、そうした演奏会用のセレナーデである。
モーツァルトは、1767年にザルツブルクで最初のセレナーデ[K.100]を作曲して以来、合計13曲のセレナーデをこいた。それらは楽章構成の点でも、また楽器編成の点でもさまざまなである。
二長調 K.250 "ハフナー"[第7番]は、全13曲のセレナーデ中最も大規模であり、また二長調 K.320 "ポストホルン"[第9番]とともに、交響管弦楽用セレナーデの典型として、今日しばしば演奏されている。この曲は、1776年に、当時は故人であったザルツブルクの市長ジークムント・ハフナー Siegmund Haffner (1699-1772)の娘エリザベート Elisabeth (1753-1784)とフランツ・ザヴァー・アントン・シュペート Franz Xaver Anton Späth (1750-1808)との結婚を祝うために、エリザベートの兄（父と同名）の依頼で作曲された。そして、その旨はモーツァルトの自筆譜にもイタリア語で次のように明記されている。

=== Page 5 ===
Serenata per io sposalito del Sgr. Spattholla Sgra. Elisabetta Haffner…Luglio 1776 [スパート氏とエリザベッタ・ハフナー娘との結婚のためのセレナータ…1776年7月]
そして、演奏は結婚前夜の同年7月22日にハフナー一家で催された祝賀パーティーでおこなわれた。
全曲は Allegro maestoso、Allegro molto—Andante—Menuetto—Rondeau—Menuetto galante—Andante—Menuetto—Adagio、Allegro assaiの8楽章から成り、古典的交響曲の中間に、さらに5つの楽章を加えたような形をとっている。また、中間の第2、3、4楽章には独奏ヴァイオリンが用いられている点で、交響曲と協奏曲との混合形ともいえる。
楽器編成は、フルート、オーボエ、ファゴット、ホルン、トランペット各2本と弦楽合奏だが、フルートとオーボエが同時に用いられることなく、第1、5、6、8楽章にオーボエが、第2、3、4、7楽章にフルートが使用されている。このことは同一の奏者がフルートとオーボエを持ち替えて演奏したことを物語っている。18世紀においては、フルート、オーボエ、ブロックフレーテの3種の高音木管楽器を持ち替えて奏することは、ごく当然のことで、このように作曲された楽章は、パロック期のみならず、クリスティアン・バッハやモーツァルトの作品に少なくならず見出される。なお、トランペットも急速で力強い冒頭楽章と終楽章のみに使用されている。
ここでは、演奏所要時間の都合で、第1、2、7、8楽章の4つの楽章のみ演奏される。
第1楽章 Allegro maestoso—Allegro molto
ニ長調 4分の4拍子
導入部はもつソナタ形式で書かれているが、この導入部は通例の緩徐なものではなく、急速かつ荘重な曲で、これは行進曲ともとれる。しかし、ハフナー一家の結婚のために他にニ長調の行進曲K.249も書かれており、その間の事情は明らかではない。さらに、この導入部の動機は主部とも関わりをもっている。
第2楽章 Andante ト長調 4分の4拍子
展開部を省略した形の（短かい経過句で代用）ソナタ形式で書かれ、独奏ヴァイオリンが登場する。
第7楽章 Menuetto 二長調 4分の4拍子（第1トリオはト長調）
2つのトリオをもつメヌエットで、全体として小規模なロンドともみなし得る形式をとっている。
第8楽章 Adagio—Allegro assai 二長調 4分の4拍子
アダージョの荘重な導入部をもつソナタ形式だが、この主部は展開部の中程に別の新しい主題を配している点で、ロンド・ソナタ形式といえよう。
リスト Franz Liszt（1811—1886）
ピアノ協奏曲 第1番 変ホ長調
今日知られているリストのピアノ協奏曲は、第1番 変ホ長調と第2番 イ長調の2曲である。しかし、実際に彼が作曲したピアノ協奏曲の数は不明と言わなければならぬ。少なくとも、初期に属するスケッチの中には、さらに2曲の協奏曲が見出されるからである。
第1番 変ホ長調は、すでに1830年のスケッチの中に、明らかにその主題が記されている。しかし、その後長らく作曲にはとりかからず、1839年に協奏曲としてこの主題を扱いはじめた。リストはここで、多忙な演奏活動や女性関係のために再度作曲を中止し、結局本格的に作曲に従事したのは、1849年にロシア・ポーランドの貴族フオン・ザイン＝ヴィットゲンシュタイン公爵の夫人カロリーネ Carolyne von Sayn-Wittgensteinとワイマル近郊に同棲して以後のことであった。完成は、その1849年7月となっている。そして初演は、1852年2月17日にワイマルの宮廷演奏会において、リスト自身がピアノ独奏を受けもち、ベルリオーズの指揮でおこなわれた。
全曲は、切れ目なく続けて演奏するように書かれた4楽章構成で、さらに各楽章の主題は相互に無関係ではない。こうした手法がベルリオーズ、とりわけ彼の＜幻想交響曲＞作品14で確立された“idée fixe[固定楽想]”から影響を受けたであろうことは容易に推測しうる。また同時に、このピアノ協奏曲が、シューベルトの＜さららし人幻想曲＞の影響のもとに作曲されたということも、一般的指摘するところとなっている。実際にリストは、ピアノ協奏曲を完成する前年の1848年に、この＜さららし人幻想曲＞をピアノとオーケストラのための協奏風楽曲に編曲している。
作品はいうまでもなく、ピアノの名人芸の演奏技巧を前面にあらわすもので、ピアノのパートにオーケストラ

る。作曲の動機は、チェコの体育協会[ソーコル]から、

YAMAHA CONCERT GRAND PIANO CF

私たちがCFを「ピアノの芸術品」として自信をもっています。そのことは、世界の舞台でヤマハを選ぶピアニストが、年ごとに増えていることも証明されています。「ピアノは音の響きだけではだめだ。弾く人の嬉しい心、悲しい心まで表現できるものでなければならない。CFには心の感度がある。」鬼オスピヤトスラフ・リヒテルのこの言葉が、CFのすべてをあらわしています。

繊細な「心の感度」をうたいあげます。ときには激しく、またあるときは静かに。

=== Page 2 ===
博物館の歩み

武蔵野音楽大学楽器博物館は、当大学図書館の付属施設として、昭和42年10月に開設された。

昭和28年福井直弘学長は、学生たちの研究資料とするために、ドイツから一個のヴィオラ・ダモーレを持ち帰った。それが当博物館の第一号の資料となった。これに端を発して徐々に資料としての楽器が集められ、昭和35年には楽器陳列室が設けられた。

昭和41年、来学された伊丹市の邦楽器研究家故水野佐平氏は、邦楽器関係の資料の欠如を指摘されると共に、同氏の貴重な邦楽器コレクション寄贈の申し出をされ、これが契機となって陳列室は博物館として発足することになった。

所蔵品は、邦楽器、外国楽器、楽器付属品、音楽に関係した装置・器具類の4つの部分に大別でき、邦楽器部門には数々の逸品が、外国楽器部門にはヨーロッパの多くの名器の他アジア、アフリカなど世界の民族楽器が、楽器付属品部門にはヴァイオリンやチェロの名弓210本以上のコレクションが、そして装置器具類にはエジソンの蝋管器を含む蓄音機の歴史的蒐集がそれぞれ含まれており、その総数は2,000点に及びとんとしている。

=== Page 7 ===
WEDNESDAY & SATURDAY CONCERTS
（水曜コンサート・土曜コンサート）

The Wednesday and Saturday concert series, open to the public, is considered an integral part of the courses in music appreciation. Guest performers, members of the faculty, and selected students of the Musashino Academia Musicae take part in these concerts. On occasion it may be necessary to change the time and day of these concerts.

この一連のコンサートは、学生にすぐれた音楽作品ならびにその演奏を鑑賞させるため、授業の一環として企画運営されている。このコンサートの出演者は、選ばれた学生、本学教員および特に招聘された内外の演奏家である。

GRADUATE STUDENTS’ RECITALS
（大学院生による演奏会）

Every student enrolled in a graduate course leading to either a master’s degree or an artist’s diploma is required to give one recital during the course of each school year. For reasons of space, however, the programs of these concerts are not included in this booklet.

大学院に在籍する学生は、それぞれの学年度にリサイタルを開くことを義務づけられており、そのプログラムは、ジョイント・リサイタルの形で演奏したものである。スペースの都合上このプログラムは割愛する。

GROUP CONCERTS
（グループ・コンサート）

Group concerts are held during the course of the year in which students are given the opportunity to perform before their teachers and fellow students. For reasons of space, however, the programs of these concerts are not included in this booklet.

グループ・コンサートは、前期の終了時に全学生が参加し、各自の教師や学友の前で演奏の機会をあたえるべく企画されたものである。スペースの都合上このプログラムは割愛する。

FROM KEMBLE TO DONALD DUCK
A HUNDRED and thirty years ago The Times was engaged in open warfare with the theatres. The paper had adopted the novel practice of giving its readers genuine dramatic criticism. The theatrical managers of the day preferred the old system (not entirely extinct even now) of "puffing and plenty of tickets."
The Times won its fight, and it has jealously guarded ever since the tradition then established. Its treatment of the theatre is still anonymous, and independent alike of theatrical cliques and of "dining table amenities."
To-day the variety and scope of The Times Entertainments Page would astonish both the critic and the play-goer of a bygone age. Indeed, they may well surprise the modern reader who is not fully familiar with them.
The function of the page is to provide a complete guide for the modern play- or film- goer, as well as for the lover of music and the other arts. Every new play in London is reviewed at length on the morning after its first performance. Twice a week an account of forthcoming productions is given. But that is not all. The theatres of Paris and New York are regularly noticed, and special articles, which appear at frequent intervals, keep the interested reader in touch with the contemporary theatre throughout the world.
It is true that The Times has not yet found space for gossip about film stars. But the great figures of the cinema are discussed in relation to their art. Charlie Chaplin and Donald Duck have both been the subject of critical appreciation.
Music, too—opera, ballet, concerts and recitals, including important events in the provinces and abroad—is ably discussed in this daily Entertainments Page, and Art Exhibitions of all kinds are treated with the same authority.

INSTRUMENT FOR AN ARTISTE
WITH ALL BRITAIN FOR AN AUDIENCE

Music of the immortals springing to life beneath the fingers of an artiste . . . flung broadcast to the stars . . . caught and transmitted again into harmony, to delight the listening ear in a million homes . . . here is the very stuff of high romance, embodiment of the spirit of the artist and the craftsman. How fitting is it, then, that both should make contribution . . . the artist through his music, the craftsman through his instrument—Challen.

DAILY MIRROR

Who is the most outspokenly honest columnist writing in the daily papers to-day?
There can be only one answer—Cassandra of the Daily Mirror.
He abhors sham and hypocrisy.
He hates cruelty, oppression, injustice.
His views about world affairs are pungent, and he says just what he thinks.

IMPERIAL CANCER RESEARCH FUND

Patron: HIS MAJESTY THE KING.
President: The Rt. Hon. VISCOUNT HALIFAX, K.G., P.C., G.C.S.I., G.C.I.E.
Chairman of the Executive Committee: SIR HUMPHRY ROLLESTON, Bt., G.C.V.O., K.C.B.
Hon. Treasurer: SIR HOLBURT WARING, Bt., C.B.E., F.R.C.S.
Director: Dr. W. E. GYE.

Founded in 1902, under the direction of the Royal College of Physicians of London and the Royal College of Surgeons of England, as a centre for research and information on Cancer, the Imperial Cancer Research Fund is working unceasingly on the systematic investigation of the disease in man and animals. The work of this Fund and of other great centres of research has increased our knowledge of the origin and nature of Cancer and has so altered our outlook that the disease is now curable in increasing numbers. Our previous accommodation has become too limited, and we have recently built new modern laboratories to extend the scope of our investigations. The income from investments and the Endowment Fund is insufficient to cover the total annual expenditure, and help is urgently needed to meet the heavy additional cost of expansion.

Donations, Subscriptions and Legacies are earnestly solicited and should be sent to the Honorary Treasurer, Sir Holbert Waring, Bt., c/o Royal College of Surgeons of England, Lincoln's Inn Fields, London, W.C.2

FORM OF BEQUEST

I hereby bequeath the sum of £_________ to the Treasurer, Sir Holbert Waring, of the Imperial Cancer Research Fund, under the direction of the Royal College of Physicians of London and the Royal College of Surgeons of England, c/o Royal College of Surgeons of England, Lincoln's Inn Fields, W.C.2, for the purpose of Scientific Research, and I direct that his receipt shall be a good discharge for such legacy.

TRINITY COLLEGE of MUSIC (Instituted 1872)

President:
The Rt. Hon. Viscount Hailsham of Hailsham, P.C.

Chairman of the Corporation:
Sir Granville Bantock, M.A., Mus.D.

Principal:
E. Stanley Roper, M.V.O., M.A., Mus.B.

The College provides instruction and training during the day and evening in all departments of Music, and in Dramatic and Operatic Elocution. Students are received for single subjects at the rate of 4 guineas for 12 weekly lessons of 30 minutes for the recognised Teachers' Diploma, and Registration Course.

Teachers in Elementary, Central and Secondary Schools are catered for by a One Year's Course.

Fees and full particulars from the Secretary.

EXAMINATIONS FOR DIPLOMAS—
1. The College confers upon Examination the Professional Diplomas of Associate (A.T.C.L.), Licentiate (L.T.C.L.), and Fellow (F.T.C.L.).
2. The Subjects of Examination include Piano, Organ, Solo-singing, Orchestral Instruments and Elocution.
3. The College also confers upon Examination the Theoretical Diplomas of Association in Music (A.Mus.T.C.L.), and Licentiate in Music (L.Mus.T.C.L.).
4. The Royal Society of Teachers accepts the Licentiate (Practical) Diploma for the purpose of Registration of Teachers (M.R.S.T.).

Syllabus and full particulars from A. T. Rees, Secretary,

MANDEVILLE PLACE, LONDON, W.1

CHRISTMAS TERM—The Christmas Term will begin on Monday, September 18th, 1939. The Grading Examinations will be held on July 24th and September 13th, 1939. (New pupils are asked to state which of these dates they prefer.)

COMPLETE MUSICAL EDUCATION. The College offers a complete course of musical education to pupils of both sexes, both professional and amateur, by teachers of the highest eminence.

JUNIOR DEPARTMENT. Classes are held for pupils under 16, whose time is occupied also by their general education.

OPERATIC CLASSES. The College possesses a fully equipped College Opera Theatre for an audience of 600.

TERMS, FEES, etc. There are three terms in the year. The Tuition Fees are £16 16s. per Term, Entrance Fee, £2 2s. Students must continue at College for at least three terms. Female pupils requiring residence are accommodated at Queen Alexandra House, adjacent to the College, as far as the capacity of that Institution allows, on terms to be obtained from the Lady Superintendent.

SPECIAL CLASSES are held for Score Reading, Conducting, Training of Teachers, Musical Criticism and Ballet.

The Royal College of Music Patrons' Fund for the encouragement of British Composers and Executive Artists, and the S. Ernest Palmer Fund for Opera Study in the Royal College of Music (founded by Lord Palmer, F.R.C.M.). Syllabus and all particulars may be obtained from the Registrar.

SCHOLARSHIPS and EXHIBITIONS. Upwards of 70 scholarships and exhibitions are provided from a permanent endowment fund.

ENSEMBLE CLASSES. There are Vocal and Instrumental Ensemble Classes, and pupils sufficiently advanced in this work are given the opportunity of putting their knowledge into practice in College Concerts.

GRADUATE COURSE, G.R.S.M. (London). This Course is held jointly by the Royal College of Music and Royal Academy of Music for the Training of Teachers. The Diploma granted by Examination entitles successful Candidates to Graduate status (Burnham Scale), and to append to their names the letters "G.R.S.M. London" (Graduate of the Royal Schools of Music, London).

A.R.C.M. Examinations for Associateship of the College (A.R.C.M.), are held three times a year in September, December and April. Full particulars from the Registrar.

In performance a few words have been altered to bring the narrative into the present tense. The story of this Opera forms a part of Longfellow's "Song of Hiawatha." It is divided into three Acts: "Hiawatha's Wedding Feast," "The Death of Minnehaha," and "Hiawatha's Departure."

To understand the story it is necessary to know that it had been revealed to the Indian tribes by Gitche Manitou, the Great Spirit and Creator of all living things, that he would send to them from the land where there is no sin and no darkness, and where all is bathed in the glory of light and love, a great prophet who would teach them to adore the beauty of peace and who, after suffering with them the sorrows and privations of mankind, would lead them into the golden dawn of a new world.

In the fulness of time, Hiawatha was born, and became a great prophet, teacher and statesman. Under his influence five adjacent tribes buried the hatchet and welded themselves together as a powerful confederation which became allied to the British settlers and fought beside them against the Hurons and their allies, the French. Thus, Hiawatha played a considerable part in the history of the formation of the British Empire, in that he assisted to a great extent in the acquisition of Canada.

I.—HIAWATHA'S WEDDING FEAST

Hiawatha was a man as other men, and wooed and won sweet Laughing Water, Minnehaha from the land of the Dacotahs. The Opera opens with the festivities at their marriage, and gay are the guests as they offer their presents and receive the generous hospitality of their host. Quip and jest pass round, and Chibibabos, the singer of sweet songs, sounds the keynote of passionate love in the ears of his entranced listeners. Dance follows song, Pau-Puk-Keewis leaps and twines with the grace of a barbaric savage. The Medicine Man brews a Peyote plant potion, of which the guests partake, and through its magic visualize a dream ballet of childhood days. Then follows a thrilling totem dance, in which all the tribe take part, and give vent to their feeling in the hiss of the serpent, the bark of the fox, the shriek of the eagle or the bellow of the buffalo, according to the nature of their totem.

The Marriage Feast is over. Happy and joyous, the guests depart to their wigwams, and alone in the moonlight are Hiawatha and Minnehaha.

You shall hear how Pau-Puk-Keewis,
How the handsome Yenadizze,
Danced at Hiawatha's wedding;
How the gentle Chibibabos,
He the sweetest of musicians,
Sang his songs of love and longing,
How Iago, the great boaster,
He the marvellous storyteller,
Told his tales of strange adventure,
That the feast might be more joyous,
That the time might pass more gaily
And the guests be more contented.
Sumptuous was the feast Nokomis
Made at Hiawatha's wedding.
All the bowls were made of bass-wood
White and polished very smoothly,
All the spoons of horn of bison,
Black and polished very smoothly.

She had sent through all the village
Messengers with wands of willow,
As a sign of invitation,
As a token of the feasting;
And the wedding-guests assembled,
Clad in all their richest raiment,
Robes of fur and belts of wampum,
Splendid with their paint and plumage,
Beautiful with beads and tassels.
First they ate the sturgeon, Nahma,
And the pike, the Maskenoza,
Caught and cooked by old Nokomis,
Then on pemmican they feasted,
Pemmican and buffalo marrow,
Haunch of deer and hump of bison,
Yellow cakes of the Mondamin,
And the wild rice of the river.
But the gracious Hiawatha,

II.—THE DEATH OF MINNEHAHA

Summer is over, and Winter grips valley and mountain in its icy clutch. Fever and Famine stalked abroad. Clinging to each other for warmth, the stricken Indians cower and shiver beneath their blankets. And what of the lovely Minnehaha—"Minnehaha, Laughing Water, Loveliest of Dacotah women"? In the absence of Hiawatha—who has gone to seek vainly for food for his people, succour for his bride—she is sick unto death, and dread phantoms bend over her couch. Finally, with a wild cry of "Hiawatha! Hiawatha!" she dies in delirium. "Far away amid the forest, miles away among the mountains" the wanderer hears that cry. Homeward hurries Hiawatha. Passionately, despairingly, he flings himself beside the dead body of his beloved, and the old nurse Nokomis sobs out her anguish. The sorrowing Indians moan and wail forth their sorrow, and over the mountains falls the snow.

There is a pause to show the passage of seven days, and then the body of Minnehaha is borne away in stately procession, clothed in her richest garments, wrapped in her robes of ermine, ready for her journey to the Islands of the Blessed.

O the long and dreary Winter!
O the cold and cruel Winter!
Ever thicker, thicker, thicker.
Froze the ice on lake and river,
Ever deeper, deeper, deeper,
Fell the snow o'er all the landscape,
Fell the covering snow, and drifted
Through the forest, round the village.
Hardly from his buried wigwam
Could the hunter force a passage;
With his mittens and his snow-shoes
Vainly walked he through the forest,
Sought for bird or beast and found none,
Saw no track of deer or rabbit,
In the snow beheld no footprints,
In the ghastly, gleaming forest
Fell, and could not rise from weakness,
Perished there from cold and hunger.
O the famine and the fever!
O the wasting of the famine!
O the blasting of the fever!
O the wailing of the children!
O the anguish of the women!
All the earth was sick and famished,
Hungry was the air around them,
Hungry was the sky above them,
And the hungry stars in heaven
Like the eyes of wolves glared at them!

Into Hiawatha's wigwam
Came two silent guests and gloomy,
Waited not to be invited,
Did not parley at the doorway,
Sat there without word of welcome
In the seat of Laughing Water;
Looked with haggard eyes and hollow
At the face of Laughing Water.
And the foremost said, "Behold me!
I am Famine, Buckadawin!"
And the other said, "Behold me!
I am Fever, Akhosewin!"
And the lovely Minnehaha
Shuddered as they looked upon her,
Shuddered at the words they uttered,
Lay down on her bed in silence,
Hid her face, but made no answer;
Lay there trembling, freezing, burning
At the looks they cast upon her,
At the fearful words they uttered.
Forth into the empty forest
Rushed the maddened Hiawatha;
In his heart was deadly sorrow,
In his face a stony firmness;
On his brow the sweat of anguish
Started, but it froze, and fell not.
Wrapped in furs, and armed for hunting,
With his mighty bow of ash-tree,
With his quiver full of arrows,
With his mittens, Minjekahwun,
Into the vast and vacant forest
On his snow-shoes strode he forward.

"Gitche Manitou, the Mighty!"
Cried he with his face uplifted
In that bitter hour of anguish,
"Give your children food, O father!
Give us food, or we must perish!
Give me food for Minnehaha,
For my dying Minnehaha!"

Through the far-resounding forest,
Through the forest vast and vacant,
Rang the cry of desolation,
But there came no other answer
Than the echo of his crying,
Than the echo of the woodlands
"Minnehaha! Minnehaha!"
All day long roved Hiawatha
In than melancholy forest,
Through the shadow of whose thickets,
In the pleasant days of Summer,
Of that ne'er-forgotten Summer,
He had brought his young wife homeward,
From the land of the Dacotahs;
When the birds sang in the thickets,
And the streamlets laughed and glistened,
And the air was full of fragrance,

THE DEATH OF MINNEHAHA

And the lovely Laughing Water
Said, with voice that did not tremble,
"I will follow you, my husband!"
In the wigwam with Nokomis,
With those gloomy guests that watched her,
With the Famine and the Fever,
She was lying, the Beloved,
She the dying Minnehaha.
"Hark!" she said, "I hear a rushing,
Hear a roaring and a rushing,
Hear the Falls of Minnehaha
Calling to me from a distance!"
"No, my child!" said old Nokomis,
"'Tis the night-wind in the pine trees!"
"Look!" she said, "I see my father
Standing lonely at his doorway,
Beckoning to me from his wigwam,
In the land of the Dakotahs!"
"No, my child!" said old Nokomis,
"'Tis the smoke that waves and beckons!"
"Ah!" she said, "the eyes of Pauguk
Glare upon me in the darkness;
I can feel his icy fingers
Clasping mine amid the darkness!
Hiawatha! Hiawatha!"

And the desolate Hiawatha,
Far away amid the forest,
Miles away among the mountains,
Heard that sudden cry of anguish,
Heard the voice of Minnehaha
Calling to him in the darkness,
"Hiawatha! Hiawatha!"
Over snow-fields waste and pathless
Under snow-encumbered branches.
Homeward hurried Hiawatha,
Empty-handed, heavy-hearted,
Heard Nokomis, moaning wailing,
"Wahonomin! Wahonomin!
Would that I had perished for you,
Would that I were dead as you are!
Wahonomin! Wahonomin!"
And he rushed into the wigwam
Saw the old Nokomis slowly
Rocking to and fro and moaning,
Saw his lovely Minnehaha
Lying dead and cold before him
And his bursting heart within him
Uttered such a cry of anguish,
That the forest moaned and shuddered,
That the very stars in heaven
Shook and trembled with his anguish.

Then he sat down, still and speechless,
On the bed of Minnehaha,
At the feet of Laughing Water,
At those willing feet, that never
More would lightly run to meet him,
Never more would lightly follow.
With both hands his face he covered,
Seven long days and nights he sat there,
As if in a swoon he sat there,
Speechless, motionless, unconscious
Of the daylight or the darkness.

Then they buried Minnehaha:
In the snow a grave they made her,
In the forest deep and darksome,
Underneath the moaning hemlocks;
Clothed her in her richest garments,
Wrapped her in her robes of ermine,
Covered her with snow, like ermine;
Thus they buried Minnehaha.

And at night a fire was lighted,
On her grave four times was kindled,
For her soul upon its journey
To the Islands of the Blessed.
From his doorway Hiawatha
Saw it burning in the forest,
Lighting up the gloomy hemlocks;
From his sleepless bed uprising,
From the bed of Minnehaha,
Stood and watched it at the doorway,
That it might not be extinguished,
Might not leave her in the darkness.
"Farewell!" said he, "Minnehaha
Farewell, O my Laughing Water!
All my heart is buried with you,
All my thoughts go onward with you!
Come not back again to labour,
Come not back again to suffer,
Where the Famine and the Fever
Wear the heart and waste the body.
Soon my task will be completed,
Soon your footsteps I shall follow
To the Islands of the Blessed,
To the kingdom of Ponemah!
To the land of the Hereafter!"

III.—HIAWATHA'S DEPARTURE

Nature is eternally young. The Third Act opens with a Ballet of Spring, symbolizing life bursting forth throughout a rejuvenated world. Then Iago, the boaster, tells of how he had seen 100 warriors coming over a great water—"bitter so that none could drink it"—in a "great canoe with pinions." He is mocked at by the Indians. "Kaw?" they say, "what lies you tell us!" But Hiawatha declares that Iago speaks truth. The strangers are the coming White Race—traders, settlers and missionaries—bringing to the depths of the virgin forest civilization and the Faith and Hope of Christianity.

And presently this prophecy is fulfilled. The Black-Robe Chief, with the cross upon his bosom, accompanied by his guides and companions, lands on the sandy margin of the lake—bearing a message of Peace and Goodwill on earth.

Hiawatha's mission is at an end. Bidding his people cultivate friendship and unity, he steps into his magic canoe, and as it floats down the stream, the whole tribe raise their arms and their voices in final farewell. As their voices sound and swell and triumph, the vast crowd, the camp, valleys, trees and distant mountain peaks are mantled in solemn light, and in a blaze of sound and colour, Hiawatha westward passes away into the golden sunset. So ends the "Song of Hiawatha."

Spring had come with all its splendour
All its birds and all its blossoms,
All its flowers and leaves and grasses,
Sailing on the wind to northward,
Flying in great flocks, like arrows,
Like huge arrows shot through heaven,
Passed the swan, the Mahnahbezee,
Speaking almost as a man speaks;
And in long lines waving, bending
Like a bowstring snapped asunder,
The white goose, the Waw-be-wawa;
And in pairs, or singly flying,
Mahng the loon, with clangorous pinions,
The blue heron, the Shuh-shuh-gah,
And the grouse, the Mushkodasa.
In the thickets and the meadows
Piped the blue-bird, the Owaisa;
On the summit of the lodges
Sang the robin, the Opechee;
And the sorrowing Hiawatha,
Speechless in his infinite sorrow,
Heard their voices calling to him,
Went forth from his gloomy doorway,
Stood and gazed into the heaven,
Gazed upon the earth and waters.

From his wanderings far to eastward,
From the regions of the morning,
From the shining land of Wabun,
Homeward now returned Iago,
The great traveller, the great boaster,
Full of new and strange adventures,
Marvels many and many wonders.
And the people of the village
Listened to him as he told them
Of his marvellous adventures,
Laughing answered him in this wise:
"Ugh! it is indeed Iago:
No one else beholds such wonders!"

He had seen, he said, a water
Bigger than the Big-Sea-Water,
Broader than the Gitche Gumee,
Bitter so that none could drink it!
At each other looked the warriors,
Looked the women at each other,
Smiled, and said, "It cannot be so!
Kaw!" they said, "it cannot be so!"

O'er it, said he, o'er this water
A canoe with wings came flying,
Bigger than a grove of pine-trees,
Taller than the tallest tree-tops!
And the old men and the women
Looked and tittered at each other.
"Kaw!" they said, "we don't believe it!"

From its mouth, he said, to greet him,
Came Waywassimo, the lightning,
Came the thunder, Annemecekee!
And the warriors and the women
Laughed aloud at poor Iago;
"Kaw!" said they, "what tales you tell us!"

In the great canoe with pinions
Came, he said, a hundred warriors;
Painted white were all their faces,
And with hair their chins were covered!
And the warriors and the women
Laughed and shouted in derision,
Like the ravens on the tree-tops,
Like the crows upon the hemlocks.
"Kaw!" they said, "what lies you tell us!
Do not think that we believe them!"

Only Hiawatha laughed not,
But he gravely spake and answered
To their jeering and their jesting:

=== Page 43 ===
"True is all Iagoo tells us;
I have seen it in a vision,
Seen the great canoe with pinions,
Seen the people with white faces,
Seen the coming of this bearded
People of the wooden vessel,
From the regions of the morning,
From the shining land of Wabun.
"Gitche Manitou, the Mighty,
The Great Spirit, the Creator,
Sends them hither on his errand,
Sends them to us with his message.
Wheresoe'er they move, before them
Swarms the stinging fly, the Ahmo,
Swarms the bee, the honey-maker;
Wheresoe'er they tread, beneath them
Springs a flower unknown among us,
Springs the White-man's Foot in blossom.

"Let us welcome, then, the strangers,
Hail them as our friends and brothers,
And the heart's right hand of friendship
Give them when they come to see us.
Gitche Manitou, the Mighty,
Said this to me in my vision.

"I beheld, too, in that vision
All the secrets of the future,
Of the distant days that shall be.
I beheld the westward marches
Of the unknown, crowded nations.
All the land was full of people,
Restless, struggling, toiling, striving,
Speaking many tongues, yet feeling
But one heart-beat in their bosoms.
In the woodlands rang their axes,
Smoked their towns in all the valleys,
Over all the lakes and rivers
Rushed their great canoes of thunder.

"Then a darker, drearier vision
Passed before me, vague and cloud-like,
I beheld our nations scattered,
All forgetful of my counsels,
Weakened, warring with each other;
Saw the remnants of our people
Sweeping westward, wild and woeful,
Like the cloud-rack of a tempest,
Like the withered leaves of Autumn!"

By the shore of Gitche Gumee,
By the shining Big-Sea-Water,
At the doorway of his wigwam,
In the pleasant Summer morning
Hiawatha stood and waited.

All the air was full of freshness,
All the earth was bright and joyous,
And before him through the sunshine,
Westward toward the neighbouring forest
Passed in golden swarms the Ahmo,
Passed the bees, the honey-makers,
Burning, singing in the sunshine.

Bright above him shone the heavens,
Level spread the lake before him;
From its bosom leaped the sturgeon,
Sparkling, flashing in the sunshine,
On its margin the great forest
Stood reflected in the water,
Every tree-top had its shadow,
Motionless, beneath the water.

From the brow of Hiawatha
Gone was every trace of sorrow,
As a fog from off the water,
As the mist from off the meadow,
With a smile of joy and triumph,
With a look of exultation,
As of one who in a vision
Sees what is to be, but is not,
Stood and waited Hiawatha.

Towards the sun his hands were lifted,* Both the palms spread out against it,
And between the parted fingers
Fell the sunshine on his features,
Flecked with light his naked shoulders,
As it falls and flecks an oak-tree
Through the rifted leaves and branches.
O'er the water floating, flying,
Something in the hazy distance,
Something in the mists of morning,
Loomed and lifted from the water,
Now seemed floating, now seemed flying,
Coming nearer, nearer, nearer.

Was it Shingebis, the diver?
Was it the pelican, the Shada?
Or the heron, the Shuh-shuh-gah?
Or the white goose, Waw-be-wawa,
With the water dripping, flashing
From its glossy neck and feathers?

It was neither goose nor diver,
Neither pelican nor heron,
O'er the water floating, flying,
Through the shining mist of morning,
But a birch canoe with paddles,
Rising, sinking on the water,
Dripping, flashing in the sunshine.
And within it came a people
From the distant land of Wabun,
From the farthest realms of morning
Came the Black-Robe chief, the Prophet,
He the Priest of Prayer, the Pale-face,
With his guides and his companions.
And the noble Hiawatha,
With his hands aloft extended,
Held aloft in sign of welcome,
Waited, full of exultation,
Till the birch canoe with paddles
Grated on the shining pebbles,
Till the Black-Robe chief, the Pale-face,
With the cross upon his bosom,
Landed on the sandy margin.

* In this manner, and with such salutations, was Father Marquette received by the Illinois. See his Voyages et Découvertes, Section V.

=== Page 45 ===
HIAWATHA'S DEPARTURE

Then the joyous Hiawatha
Cried aloud, and spake in this wise:
"Beautiful is the sun, O strangers,
When you come so far to see us!
All our town in peace awaits you,
All our doors stand open for you:
You shall enter all our wigwams,
For the heart's right hand we give you.
"Never bloomed the earth so gaily,
Never shone the sun so brightly,
As to-day they shine and blossom,
When you come so far to see us!
Never was our lake so tranquil,
Nor so free from rocks and sand-bars;
For your birch canoe in passing
Has removed both rock and sand-bar!
"Never before had our tobacco
Such a sweet and pleasant flavour,
Never the broad leaves of our corn-fields
Were so beautiful to look on,
As they seem to us this morning,
When you come so far to see us!"

And the Black-Robe chief made answer,
Stammered in his speech a little,
Speaking words yet unfamiliar:
"Peace be with you, Hiawatha,
Peace be with you and your people,
Peace of prayer, and peace of pardon,
Peace of Christ, and joy of Mary!"

Then the generous Hiawatha
Led the strangers to his wigwam,
Seated them on skins of bison,
Seated them on skins of ermine,
And the careful old Nokomis
Brought them food in bowls of basswood,
Water brought in birchen dippers,
And the calumet, the peace-pipe,
Filled and lighted for their smoking.
All the old men of the village,
All the warriors of the nation,
All the Jossakeeds, the prophets,
The magicians, the Wabenos,
And the medicine-men, the Medas,
Came to bid the strangers welcome;
"It is well," they said, "O brothers,
That you come so far to see us!"
In a circle round the doorway,
With their pipes they sat in silence,
Waiting to behold the strangers,
Waiting to receive their message;
Till the Black-Robe chief, the Pale-face,
From the wigwam came to greet them.
Stammering in his speech a little,
Speaking words yet unfamiliar;
"It is well," they said, "O brother,
That you come so far to see us."

Then the Black-Robe chief, the prophet,
Told his message to the people,
Told the purport of his mission.
Told them of the Virgin Mary,
And her blessed Son, the Saviour:
How in distant lands and ages
He had lived on earth as we do;
How he fasted, prayed, and laboured;
How the Jews, the tribe accursed,
Mocked him, scourged him, crucified him;
How he rose from where they laid him,
Walked again with his disciples,
And ascended into heaven.

And the Chiefs made answer, saying:
"We have listened to your message,
We have heard your words of wisdom.
We will think on what you tell us.
It is well for us, O brothers,
That you come so far to see us!"

Then they rose up and departed
Each one homeward to his wigwam,
To the young men and the women
Told the story of the strangers
Whom the Master of Life had sent them
From the shining land of Wabun.

Heavy with the heat and silence
Grew the afternoon of summer;
With a drowsy sound the forest
Whispered round the sultry wigwam,
With a sound of sleep the water
Rippled on the beach below it;
From the cornfields shrill and ceaseless
Sang the grasshopper, Pah-puk-keena;
And the guests of Hiawatha,
Weary with the heat of Summer,
Slumbered in the sultry wigwam,
Slowly o'er the simmering landscape
Fell the evening's dusk and coolness.
And the long and level sunbeams
Shot their spears into the forest,
Breaking through its shields of shadow,
Rushed into each secret ambush,
Searched each thicket, dingle, hollow;
Still the guests of Hiawatha
Slumbered in the silent wigwam.

From his place rose Hiawatha,
Bade farewell to old Nokomis,
Spake in whispers, spake in this wise,
Did not wake the guests that slumbered:

"I am going, O Nokomis,
On a long and distant journey,
To the Portals of the Sunset,
To the regions of the home-wind.
But these guests I leave behind me,
In your watch and ward I leave them;
See that never harm comes near them,
See that never fear molests them,
Never danger nor suspicion,
Never want of food or shelter,
In the lodge of Hiawatha!"

HIAWATHA'S DEPARTURE

Forth into the village went he,
Bade farewell to all the warriors,
Bade farewell to all the young men,
Spake persuading, spake in this wise:

"I am going, O my people,
On a long and distant journey:
Many moons and many winters
Will have come, and will have vanished,
Ere I come again to see you.
But my guests I leave behind me;
Listen to their words of wisdom,
Listen to the truth they tell you,
For the Master of Life has sent them
From the land of light and morning!"

On the shore stood Hiawatha.
Turned and waved his hand at parting;
On the clear and luminous water,
Launched his birch canoe for sailing,
From the pebbles of the margin
Shoved it forth into the water;
Whispered to it, "Westward! westward!"
And with speed it darted forward.
And the evening sun descending
Set the clouds on fire with redness,
Burned the broad sky, like a prairie,
Left upon the level water
One long track and trail of splendour,
Down whose stream, as down a river,
Westward, westward Hiawatha
Sailed into the fiery sunset,
Sailed into the purple vapours,
Sailed into the dusk of evening.
And the people from the margin
Watched him floating, rising, sinking,
Till the birch canoe seemed lifted
High into that sea of splendour,
Till it sank into the vapours
Like the new moon, slowly, slowly
Sinking in the purple distance.

And they said, "Farewell for ever!"
Said, "Farewell, O Hiawatha!"
And the forests, dark and lonely,
Moved through all their depths of darkness
Sighed, "Farewell, O Hiawatha!"
And the waves upon the margin
Rising, rippling on the pebbles,
Sobbed, "Farewell, O Hiawatha!"
And the heron, the Shuh-shuh-gah,
From her haunts among the fenlands,
Screamed, "Farewell, O Hiawatha!"

Thus departed Hiawatha,
Hiawatha the Beloved,
In the glory of the sunset,
In the purple mists of evening,
To the regions of the home-wind,
Of the Northwest wind, Keewaydin,
To the Islands of the Blessed,
To the kingdom of Ponemah,
To the land of the Hereafter!

GLOSSARY

AH'MO, the stinging-fly.
ANNEMEE'KEE, the thunder.
CA'LUMET, a pipe; used as a symbol of peace, and as an evidence to strangers that they are welcome.
GITCHI GU'MEE, the Big-Sea-Water, Lake Superior.
GIT'CHE MAN'TO, the Great Spirit, the Master of Life.
HIAWA'THA, the prophet, the teacher; son of Mudjeheewis (the West Wind), and Wenonah (daughter of Nokomis).
IA'GOG, a great boaster and storyteller.
JOS'SAKES, a prophet.
KAW, no.
KEEWAY'DIN, the Northwest Wind; the Home Wind.
MAHNAHBE'ZEE, the swan.
MAHNG THE LOON, the northern diver (Urinator imber); an aquatic web-footed northern bird, noted for its expremess in diving and swimming under water.
ME'DA, a medicine man.
MUSHKODA'NA, the grouse.
NGOKO'MIS, the grandmother of Hiawatha; mother of Wenonah.
OME'NA, the pigeon.
OPECHEE', the robin.
OWAIS-SA, the blue bird; a small song bird (Sialia sialis), very common in the United States. It is related to the European robin.
PAH-PUK-KEE'NA, the grasshopper.
PONE MAH, hereafter.
SHA'DA, the pelican.
SHIN GEBIS, the diver or grebe; a swimming bird of the genus Colymbus, found in the northern parts of America.
SHUH'-SCH'-GAH, the blue heron.
UGH, yes.
WABE'NO, a magician.
WA'BUN, the East Wind.
WA-WB-WE'WA, the white goose.
WAYWAS'SIMO, the lightning.

=== Page 51 ===
SURFACE BEAUTY IS NOT ENOUGH

Prepare the UNDERSKIN today for loveliness tomorrow!

The underskin is a newly discovered element in beauty care. A very important element indeed. For the underskin today is your surface skin—your complexion beauty—tomorrow.

Modern skin specialists explain it thus. The complexion is a living thing, like a flower: and just like a flower it gradually, imperceptibly fades and dies. But a woman's complexion is really more wonderful than any flower. The fading tissue is constantly replaced—by an exquisite new skin underneath. That underskin is always living, always growing, always ready to come to the surface more beautiful tomorrow than today.

If your beauty care is modern . . . alive . . . vital . . . you'll cherish the underskin today, while it is still hidden. You will choose the cream designed by scientists specially to look after tomorrow's beauty! Potter & Moore's Powder-Cream not only gives your complexion a perfect matt powder finish, but it is the only known cream with the magic ingredient that nourishes, protects, beautifies the underskin before ever it comes to the surface.

Potter & Moore's Powder-Cream is obtainable everywhere in six flattering shades.

=== Page 6 ===
本学園では教育方針として音楽芸術の研鑽と併せ人間形成を強く掲げている。

音楽を専門として志すものの技術と芸術的創造力鍛錬への不屈の努力は、おのずから強く円満な人格の養成に通じるのである。このことから本学園ではここに学ぶ学生生徒諸君が、いたずらに技巧偏重に陥ることのないよう深い知識と幅広い教養を吸収し、建学の精神にもある“３Ｐ主義”（Propriety…礼儀、Purity…清潔、Punctuality…時間厳守）に象徴された“和”の心を養い、さらに人間的行動の基礎となる健康な身体を鍛えることに意を注いでいる。

優秀な指導者による個人授業はもとより、専門教科、一般教養、語学、保健体育、教職課程、外人教授による特別講座のすべてを重視しているのは、みな学生生徒諸君の芸術的と同時に人間的な成長を願ってのことである。さらに日々の秩序ある学園生活をとおし豊かな感受性を養い、健全な心身を育成するために清潔な校地校舎、整った運動施設、厚生施設、また豊富な参考図書、視聴覚資料、参考楽器など教育施設設備の整備にも力を重ねている。

一方近年江古田校地が都心の狭隘から制約を受けつつあり、また教育内容の拡充に伴ないその教育環境の根本的改善が望まれるところから、自然に恵まれた45万㎡の広大な入間校地に教室棟、研究室棟、練習室棟、研究所、図書館、体育館、総合運動場、学寮などの施設を逐次完成し現在その集大成としての講堂を建設中である。

本学園では今後多くの優秀な教授陣のもとで、この恵まれた江古田、入間両校地の教育環境を相互に充分活用し教育成果の一層の向上を期し、またわが国において音楽教育に占める私学の重要な役割と大きな責任を認識し、広く全国各地の音楽文化振興に貢献する所存である。

Educational Direction
教育方針

Musashino Academia Musicae strongly emphasizes both the pursuit of musical studies and the development of the student as a human being. For those whose aim is to specialize in music, their unceasing efforts to develop their skill and artistic creativity will result in their growth as human beings. Founded on the spirit of mutual friendship, the Academia emphasizes the study of music through purposeful activities, the goal being knowledge in depth. The Academia’s aim is to foster broad development of the mind and of the body through healthy, humanistic activities.

Emphasis on quality of instruction is to be found not only in the individual music lessons, but also in the professional, general education, foreign language and teacher’s qualification courses, as well as in physical education classes and in special lectures by foreign instructors. All areas aim for the artistic and human development of the student. The structured daily life on campus nurtures the students’ sensitivity. Every facility is provided for the development of a healthy mind and body.

We are very conscious of our responsibility as a private college of music, and are striving to play a vital role in contributing to music education in Japan. It is our aim to further interest in musical culture throughout the country.

=== Page 9 ===
The Founding of Musashino in Retrospect—The Spirit of Musashino
創立時の回顧・建学の精神

学校法人武蔵野音楽学園の前身である武蔵野音楽学校は昭和4年に創設され、昭和54年には学園創立50周年を迎えます。

創立者福井直秋は長く音楽教育に携っていたが、当初音楽学校を設立することなどは夢想もしていなかった。洋楽の普及度が低く官学万能の時代に、私立音楽学校を創設することは至難のわざであったからである。しかし多くの人々の要請を受けた創立者は、福蔵期にあったわが国音楽文化の向上に貢献しようとする情熱から意を決するに至った。とりあえず仮校舎を借りて授業を始め、創立者、教職員、学生が一体となった学校設立への努力が実って創立にこぎつけたが、この不可能とさえ思われたことを可能にしたエネルギーこそ創立者の唱えた“和”の精神であり、この建学の精神は在学生、同窓生、父兄、学園全職員の連帯と、“清潔”“礼儀”“時間厳守”の人間相互の理解と尊重を唱えた“3P主義”として、現在までも脈々と流れている。

昭和7年にはわが国唯一の、専門学校令による私立音楽学校へ昇格した。また幸い第2次大戦時および戦後の洋楽界にとって言語に絶する苦難の時代を、創立者以下関係者がこれによく対処して学校を維持しつづけ、これが今日学園が健在する基礎となったともいえる。

昭和26年財団法人武蔵野音楽学校は学校法人武蔵野音楽学園へ組織変更され、その後さらに音楽における一貫教育、早期教育の重要性の認識のもとに武蔵野高等学校、附設の4幼稚園が設置されたが、多くの関係の方々の理解と協力に支えられてますます発展の道を歩んでいることは、喜びに堪えないところである。

An accredited college, Musashino Academia Musicae was founded in 1929 as the Musashino Music School. In 1979 it will mark its 50th anniversary.

The school's founder, Naoaki Fukui, was long concerned with musical education, but at first he never dreamed that he would found a music school. But with the encouragement of many people, and with a desire to make a contribution to Japanese musical culture, then in its infancy, he made his decision. Fukui's efforts finally bore fruit. He attained his goal of establishing a school in which students and teachers work together in harmony. It was the boundless energy of this man that accomplished this difficult goal. Fukui's spirit of knowledge-seeking continues to be preserved today by past and present students and teachers, who strive for human respect and understanding according to the “3 Ps”: Purity, Propriety and Punctuality.

=== Page 18 ===
武蔵野音楽大学大学院は昭和39年4月設置された。
大学院の目的である専攻分野における研究能力または高度の専門性を要する職業等に必要な能力養成について不断の努力が続けられており、指導教授陣の充実、専攻科目の多岐化等深い研究に専念できるよう配慮されてい
る。
修了の要件は2年以上在学、30単位以上を修得し、か
つ研究指導を受けたうえ修士論文の審査及び試験に合格
することとなっており、修了者には芸術学修士の学位が
授与され、また音楽科について高等学校一級普通免許状
が取得できる。
なお本大学院は他大学の学部出身者にも開放されてお
り、外国や他大学からの入学者もすでに相当数を数えて
いる。

Graduate Musical Studies
大学院音楽研究科

Musashino Academia Musicae Graduate School was opened in April, 1964. The object of post-graduate study is to carry out research in special fields in order to develop professional skills, etc. Musashino's highly qualified teaching staff continues to explore better ways to provide guidance in various fields of study. Graduates receive the Master of Fine Arts degree.

・セミナー　A seminar

=== Page 19 ===
Undergraduate Department of Music
大学音楽学部

●授業　A lecture

The Music Department, by instilling knowledge of musical truths and by developing musical skills, seeks to produce good leaders of society. In a word, studies are oriented to character building.

All majors are to be completed in four years with a total of 124 credits. Graduates receive the Bachelor of Fine Arts Degree.

    <th>音楽教育

=== Page 23 ===
Short-Term Undergraduate Division
短期大学部

短期大学部は一般教育の知識を授けるとともに、音楽に関する実際的な学問技術を教授研究し、良き社会人としての品性と専門の職業的能力を養うことを目的としている。

短期大学部は第1部（音楽学科）、第2部（音楽教育学科）とに分かれ、修業年限はいずれも2年である。所定の62単位の外に教職課程を履修したものは、音楽科中学校教諭2級普通免許状を取得できる。

The short-term course of studies offers both general education and genuine musical scholarly studies. It aims to instill practical skills for professional employment and good citizenship as well. The short-term course of studies is divided into two departments: a full-time school for music, and an evening school for music education. Each course is to be completed in 2 years.

=== Page 24 ===
Undergraduate Majors
大学専攻科

大学専攻科は大学学部における一般的ならびに専門的基礎の上に、広い視野に立って音楽の専門分野を研究練磨し、精深な学識と高度な技術能力を修得展開することを目的としている。
専攻科はさらに作曲、声楽、器楽の3専攻に分かれ、いずれも専攻の外に音楽の専門科目を修得することとしている。

The various undergraduate departments have the common aim of broadening the student's mind and developing his skills through general education and major fields of study. One of three majors may be chosen: Composition, Voice or Instrumental Music. Each of these includes music major courses.

短期大学部専攻科

短期大学部卒業生がさらに深く勉学するためには、音楽学部第3年次に編入する以外に、1年課程の専攻科が設けられている。本専攻科は専門の職業能力を高度に展開せしめることを目的とし、修了単位は30単位である。

大学別科

音楽を教養として身につけたい人々が比較的容易に、そして自由な気持ちで音楽的雰囲気の中において、その技術を学びまた鑑賞力をたかめることを目的としている。1年課程である。

=== Page 32 ===
Musashino High School
武蔵野高等学校

●弦楽合奏 String ensemble

本学園では青少年の高潔な人格、円満な情操、健全な心身をはぐくむ教育環境として、45万㎡の美しい自然を誇る入間校地に理想的な教育施設の整備を進めてきたが、昭和48年に武蔵野高等学校音楽科を開設した。

この高等学校においても教育方針として、音楽芸術の研鑽とともに人間形成を掲げ、これを実現する手段として専門教科と一般教科との均衡、授業と教室内外の生活指導の一体化に重点を置いているが、本校が原則として全寮制を採用しているのもこの趣旨からである。

本校は大学との関連における一貫教育ならびに適切な早期教育の重要性を認識し、優れた専任教諭と武蔵野音楽大学からの指導陣を擁し、生徒の指導に万全を期している。

卒業生の大部分は武蔵野音楽大学への進学を希望するが、このうち学業、人物が特に優れたものには、同大学音楽学部(第一部)に推薦入学の特典が与えられる。

In order to provide an environment suitable for fostering well-rounded character development of young people, Musashino Academia Musicae has a 450,000 m^2 campus at Iruma that is rich in natural beauty and boasts superior facilities. In 1973, the Musashino High School of Music was opened on the campus. The high school aims at character building through a balance of general and specialized education and guidance inside and outside the classroom. For this purpose, all students at the Musashino High School live in the dormitories.

Recognizing the importance of consistency in musical education from an early age, the school provides an excellent all-round educational program, including teachers highly qualified in their respective specialities.

=== Page 37 ===
Kindergartens
幼稚園

幼児教育の重要性と地域社会への貢献を考え、本学園では次頁の４幼稚園を設置している。いずれも学校教育法に基づいて、４才児、５才児の２年保育を行う。
幼児期が基本的人格の形成に極めて重要、かつ音楽教育においても非常に大切な時期であることを認識し、幼児にふさわしい教育環境を整備して、人間形成の基礎を築くことを目指している。
この目的を達成するために学園と４幼稚園が協力、連繋して、幼稚園教育要領をもとに健康、社会、自然、言語、音楽リズム、絵画制作の６領域から適質、適量の教育内容を選択し、カリキュラムを編成している。
加えて音楽の基礎指導にカール・オルフのメソッドを、さらにヴァイオリンその他の楽器を採用して、大きな教育成果を挙げている。

To meet the need in certain localities for education of very young children, Musashino Academia Musicae offers four kindergartens. Each provides a 2-year program for children from the ages of 4 through 5 in accordance with education laws.
Realizing the importance of character building education during early childhood as well as the extreme importance of musical education during this period, these schools provide a suitable environment and facilities for these purposes.

武蔵野音楽大学附属音楽教室
主管/石黒 祥義
音楽教育においてとくに大切な幼少年期を正しく導き、その天分を豊かに伸ばす目的をもって本学園内に設置されている。指導者は外人教授を含め80名。本学園の充実した施設を活用し、個人レッスンのほかソルフェージュ、合唱、合奏などのクラス授業を全生徒に課し、技巧偏重を避けるとともに、音楽に対する歓びと広い視野を養い、また各生徒の適性に応じたきめこまかな指導を行なっている。授業は週2回。

This school is designed to provide guidance for children to bring out and develop their natural gifts. The teaching staff, including foreign instructors, consists of 80 people. Using the Academia's outstanding facilities, children are given individual lessons. In addition, classes are given in solfeggio, chorus and ensemble. Avoiding concentration on technique only, we strive to nurture an appreciation of the joy of music. Classes are held twice weekly.

=== Page 42 ===
Student Concerts
演奏会

●定時演奏会 Annual Concert
武蔵野音楽大学では、学生諸君が豊かな経験をとおして技術と創造性を練習し、同時にその実績を広く学外に紹介するために次のような演奏会を企画開催している。

●管弦楽団、合唱団演奏会
前期（7月）と後期（12月）の年2回、定期的に開催される演奏会。
7月は教職員と管・弦・打楽器専攻から選抜された学生で編成されるオーケストラによる演奏会で、古典から現代にいたる管弦楽曲や協奏曲がプログラムにとりあげられる。協奏曲の独奏者は全学から公募し、オーディションによって選出された学生が起用される。
12月にはこのオーケストラに声楽学生を主体とした混声合唱団が協演し、古今のレクイエム、パッション、オラトリオあるいはミサ曲などを上演するのが恒例である。
毎年全国各地または昭和52年度には西独に演奏旅行を行ない（別掲）大成功を収めている。

●オペラ公演
本大学では過去においてたびたびオペラを上演し好評を博してきたが、昭和48年度から新しい構想のもとに正規のカリキュラムに組込まれたオペラコースを発足させ、多くの外国人教授の協力、指導も得て、平素の歌唱、基礎演技の勉学をとおし、音楽大学におけるオペラ研究のあり方、上演の意義を追求している。従来毎年発表を行っているが、昭和53年度にはモーツァルト“コシ・ファン・トゥッテ”を上演した。

●管楽合奏団（ウィンドアンサンブル）演奏会
管楽器専攻学生によるウィンドアンサンブルは、古典から現代に至るオリジナル曲を中心に毎週練習に励んでおり、学内外で数多くの演奏の実績を誇っている。
毎年全国各地に演奏旅行を行っているが、昭和53年は東北地方での演奏が行なわれる。

●室内合奏団、室内合唱団、室内楽、ソロコンサート
それぞれ選抜された大学院生、学生が多くの指導者の指導を得て意欲的なプログラムと取組み、学内外で演奏会を開き好評を得ている。

●水曜、木曜、土曜コンサート
教職員、学生の研究発表、外来演奏家による演奏、あるいは邦楽鑑賞会など、学生に音楽全般にわたる広い知識と経験を与えるために、江古田校舎では水曜および土曜日にベートーヴェンホール、モーツァルトホールで、また入間校舎では木曜日に、カリキュラムの一環として企画開催される演奏会。

=== Page 43 ===
The following concerts are regularly scheduled at Musashino Academia:

Orchestra Concert/Choir Recital
These recitals are held twice yearly, once in the first semester (July), and once in the second semester (December). In July, students majoring in wind, string and percussion instruments are selected to make up an orchestra along with some instructors. Pieces performed range from classical to modern. Performers of solo parts are selected from among the entire student body through an open audition.
In December, this orchestra joins with a mixed chorus to perform a classic or modern requiem, passion, oratorio or mass.

Opera Performance
In 1973 for the first time, an opera course was included as a regular part of the curriculum. With the cooperation of many foreign instructors, performing and dramatic techniques are studied.

Wind Ensemble Recitals
Students majoring in wind instruments join to perform original pieces in modes ranging from classic to modern. It is recommended that practice sessions be held weekly. Many performances and concerts within and outside the Academia are successively held.

Chamber Ensembles, Chamber Choral Recitals, Chamber Music, Solo Concerts
Selected postgraduate and undergraduate students, under the direction of many teachers, put together various programs. These concerts have a very good reputation both within and outside the Academia.

Wednesday, Thursday and Saturday Concerts
Composed of teachers and students, these concerts exhibit the results of individual study, foreign performers or the work of groups like the Japanese Music Appreciation Society. As part of the regular curriculum, it provides an opportunity for a variety of experiences.

=== Page 44 ===
●海外演奏旅行● Overseas Performing Tour

昭和52年9月8日から約1ヶ月間、西独ボン市およびドイツ音楽協議会の主催になる、ベートーヴェン没後150年祭の公式行事に参加するとともに、同国13都市で演奏を行なった武蔵野音楽大学管弦楽団は、訪問地先々で大成功を収めた。

大統領府におけるシェール大統領への感激の対面、ベートーヴェンホールでの熱演、日・独・英の若人達の共演による「第9シンフォニー」、各都市における心温まる歓迎レセプション、民宿先でのドイツ人家族との交歓、史跡や音楽関係施設の見学など、この旅行が教育上または文化交流と国際親善に果した役割は大きい。

From September 8th, 1977, the Musashino Academia Musicae Orchestra toured 13 cities in West Germany for one month. Sponsored by the City of Bonn and the German Music Council, the tour was a highly successful event in honor of the 150th anniversary of Beethoven's death. This trip played an important role both in the students' education and in furthering international good will.

Special Lectures and Concerts
特別講座・特別演奏会

西洋音楽が数世の長い伝統に根ざしたものであり、日本の楽界が広く諸外国との交流を必要とする今日、本学園では“世界の中の武蔵野”の認識に立って常々教職員、卒業生の海外研修、留学を奨励する一方、海外から著名な音楽家、演奏家を客員教授として招聘、特別講座、特別演奏会を開催し、学生、生徒の芸術的才能を育成するよう努めてきた。これらの多くは公開され社会教育、音楽文化の啓蒙に資するところが大きい。この特別講座、演奏会は本学園の最も大きな特色の一つとなり、学園内には常に国際的な雰囲気が流れている。

近年の催しをふり返ってみても、年ごとに多くの著名な音楽家が講座や演奏会を行なっているが、今後もこれら意義ある催しを一層多彩なものとするべく、努力を重ねていく所存である。

Western Music, with its long tradition in Europe, America, and other countries, cannot be ignored by Japan's music world. Musashino Academia Musicae is ever conscious of its position in the world music community. As such, it encourages its students to study abroad on one hand, and on the other, invites renowned musicians and performers to come as visiting professors to give special lectures or concerts. These activities not only help realize the goal of developing the students' artistic abilities, but also make a positive contribution to the cultural uplifting of society.

=== Page 48 ===
Guidance
厚生補導

音楽大学ではその特長として、音楽実技の個人指導がそこでの教育の一つの中心をなしており、これがこと技術面だけでなく教師と学生との対話、相互信頼を保つものとして大きな意義を持っている。本大学においてもこのことが、カウンセリング制度、就職指導、奨学金制度などとともに、充実した厚生補導を支えているバックボーンであると言えよう。

The great advantage of the Academia as a college devoted to music is that it is centered around giving individual guidance in teaching musical skills. This direct dialogue between teacher and student is very important not only for the lesson content, but for the sake of mutual trust and understanding as well.

●カウンセリング制度
近年教育機関において特にカウンセリングの重要性が説かれているが、本大学でも専任教員数名が常時カウンセラーとして学生との相談に応じている。
カウンセラーの対象とする問題は勉学、健康、就職の相談から個人的な問題に至るまで広範囲にわたっている。
これは学生自身が種々の課題に立ち向かう意欲を生み出す環境をつくり、豊かな人間形成を助長し、日々の学園生活を快適で実りあるものとすることが目的である。

●就職指導
音楽大学の特殊性から、本学の学生は卒業後個人的に音楽活動を続けるものも多く、また就職希望職種も他の一般大学の傾向とは大変異なっている。本学園では就職指導を特に重視し、在学生全員にオリエンテーションの機会を設けると同時に就職の為の特別講座を開き、さらに個人的には関係教職員、特に就職問題専従のカウンセラーが、積極的に面接指導に当たっている。
近年学生の就職に対する熱意と関心は高く、就職者数と就職率が大幅に上昇していることは喜ばしい。

●奨学金制度
《福井直秋記念奨学金》
昭和41年、本学園創立者福井直秋先生からの寄付金などを基金として設けられた本学園独自の制度で、一切返済の義務がない。先生の遺志により大学院、大学、短大の学術優秀な学生に付与される。
毎年度約100名が採用されているが、今後の給付額の増額と奨学生の増員のため基金募集にも努力が払われている。
その他日本育英会、地方公共団体、民間財団法人などからの奨学金もある。

=== Page 49 ===
Counseling System
In recent years, more and more emphasis has been placed on the importance of counseling in schools. The Musashino staff includes several teachers whose extra job is to give students the counseling they need. The purpose of this service is to create an environment in which the students want to confront various subjects, to develop the students' characters and to make student life more pleasant.

Employment Guidance
As a school specializing in music, the types of employment its graduates seek greatly differ from those of students from other universities. Many students continue their music activities on an individual basis. Musashino places a great emphasis on employment guidance through positive individual counseling sessions.

Scholarship System
"The Naoaki Fukui Memorial Scholarship"
In 1961, Naoaki Fukui, the founder of Musashino Academia Musicae, made a contribution to help establish an independent scholarship fund that students needn't pay back. It was Fukui's wish that the scholarship be granted to outstanding students in the graduate, undergraduate and short-term divisions.

Activities of the Alumni Association
学友会活動

Musashino has an Alumni Association that encompasses all students in the undergraduate and short-term departments. Various activities and events are carried out to promote student welfare and amity. As the school's fundamental aim is character development, it actively promotes this kind of extracurricular activity.
