Yehudi Menuhin is one of those rare men who has become a legend in his own lifetime. He made his debut at the age of seven with the San Francisco Orchestra and shortly thereafter in Paris, Berlin, New York and London. Since then he has toured almost every country in the world and as his musicianship developed, so did the man, until he has become as well-known for his humanitarianism as for his glorious playing of the violin. A true citizen of the world, THE SCOTSMAN said of him: "Any investigator of British musical life keeps coming across the mixture of beneficence, idealism and common sense that informs the actions of Mr Menuhin – American's most valuable export to Britain since T S Eliot."

Born in New York in 1916 of Russian parents, Yehudi Menuhin began violin lessons at the age of five, his three teachers being Louis Persinger, Georges Enesco and Adolf Busch. Among others who left indelible impressions upon him as they made music together were Casals, Beecham, Bruno Walter, Furtwaengler, Kreisler, Toscanini, Schnabel, Weingartner, Fritz Bush and Kleiber.

In 1933 Yehudi and his sister, Hephzibah, gave the first of those piano and violin sonata evenings which still remain the memorable musical highlights of concert seasons wherever they appear; their first recordings together in 1932 won the national Prix du Disque in France.

During World War II Yehudi Menuhin gave more than 500 concerts for the Armed Forces, in recognition of which he was awarded the French Legion of Honour and Croix de Lorraine; the Belgium Ordre de la Couronne and Ordre Leopold; the Order of Merit from West Germany and the Order of the Phoenix from Greece. Other honours include the Royal Philharmonic Society's Gold Medal of 1962; the Cobbett Medal of the Worshipful Company of Musicians; the 1971 Sonning Prize (Copenhagen), and in 1974 the Artist/Teacher Award of the American String Teachers Association. He holds Honorary Degrees in eleven British Universities, including Oxford and Cambridge, is a Freeman of the Cities of Edinburgh and Bath and in 1966 was given an

=== Page 28 ===
Honorary Knighthood (KBE) by Queen Elizabeth. He was the first musician to be awarded in 1979 the Peace Prize of the Boersenverein des Deutschen Buchhandels.

Yehudi Menuhin has introduced to the public a number of new works commissioned by or dedicated to him by Bartok, Bloch, Enesco, Vaughan Williams, William Walton, Lennox Berkeley, Malcolm Williamson, Oedoon Partos, Priaulx Rainier, Jacob Gilboa and others. Such is his interest in every category of music that wherever he goes he seeks to discover that which is local and indigenous. Therefore, he was delighted to accept the invitation of the late Prime Minister Nehru to play in India, where in 1952 and 1954 he raised $74,000 for the Famine Fund. Other visits followed: in 1969 he inaugurated the Homi Bhabha Auditorium in Bombay, giving three concerts in memory of his friend, Dr Homi Bhabha, the great atomic scientist. In 1970 he received the Jawaharial Nehru Peace Award (1968) for his outstanding contribution to and promotion of international understanding, goodwill and friendship among the peoples of the world through the medium of music. He has given concerts for the United Nations in New York and elsewhere with Ravi Shankar, the well-known sitar player and their records have sold into the millions. Apart from his deep interest in Indian music, his latest excursion is into the jazz violinist world where, with that great exponent, Stephane Grappelli, he has appeared on BBC Television and at concerts and their joint recordings are also best sellers.

After ten years as Artistic Director of the Bath Festival, in 1969 he, with Ian Hunter, for four years directed the Festival of Windsor for which Her Majesty the Queen graciously permitted him the use of two of the great rooms of Windsor Castle. For twentyfour years he has been Artistic Director of the annual Yehudi Menuhin Festival in Gstaad, Switzerland, in recognition of which in 1970 the Swiss people bestowed upon him and his family Honorary Swiss Citizenship. In 1977 he gave his name to an International Music Academy in Gstaad where young graduate string players have the opportunity to both study and perform.

He founded the Bath Festival Orchestra, which continued under the name of the Menuhin Festival Orchestra and he travelled all over the world with them. He has conducted three Mozart operas, recorded all nine Schubert Symphonies and many other works with them and played in films and on television. In November 1969 Yehudi Menuhin was invited by the Prince of Wales to give a concert with the MFO at Buckingham Palace to mark His Royal Highness's twenty-first birthday. He has also conducted many orchestras of international renown.

Also in 1969, Yehudi Menuhin became President of the International Music Council of UNESCO and recently completed a third and final term of office; he continues, however, as Founding President of the Musicians' International Mutual Aid Fund of the IMC. For some years he has been Chairman of the City of Westminster Arts Council and in 1971 became President of Trinity College of Music.

He possesses an original, inquiring mind and deep sympathy for all people. He speaks German, Russian, French, Italian and Spanish fluently and finds the ideal form of exercise in the practice of Yoga. All his various pursuits and interests are shared by his wife (former dancer and actress, Diana Gould). His son, Gerard studied at Stanford University and Jeremy is a pianist. By his first marriage he has a daughter, Zamira, and a son, Krov, who has recently made three very successful nature films with his wife, Ann, for the BBC.

Yehudi Menuhin has published several books, including THE VIOLIN – SIX LESSONS WITH YEHUDI MENUHIN (Faber and Faber), THEME AND VARIATIONS (Heinemann) and Macdonald and Jane's have published a series of text books of the main musical instruments under his editorship, of which he has written those on the violin and viola. His autobiography, UNFINISHED JOURNEY, has been translated into many languages. He has contributed to newspapers and periodicals throughout the world, lectured widely on various subjects at the Royal Institution (London) and the Smithsonian Institution (Washington) and many other seats of learning. He has also conducted Master Classes in Colleges of Music and on television. The French film

THE WAY OF LIGHT on the life of Yehudi Menuhin has been widely shown throughout Europe as was a similar film on the Bell Telephone Hour in America. The BBC made an hour-long film on his life as a tribute on his sixtieth birthday. He has just completed a series of eight television programmes called MUSIC OF MAN for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation which will shortly be screened in North America and in Europe early next year. There is a book, published by Methuen, which accompanies the series.

In 1963, wishing to ensure continuance of the great art of violin playing, Yehudi Menuhin founded the Yehudi Menuhin School at Stoke d'Abernon in Surrey, England, a boarding school for young musical talent from the age of six. To celebrate the tenth Anniversary of the School, the pupils played for Her Majesty the Queen Mother at St. James's Palace and in 1973 the Ministry of Education and Science granted the School the same status as that accorded to the Royal Ballet School. The pupils have given concerts throughout Great Britain, in Switzerland, France and on two occasions toured the United States. They have won high awards, scholarships and bursaries on leaving the School at the age of sixteen or seventeen to pass on to music colleges in Britain, Belgium, France, Germany, America and Moscow. In 1976 they played at the British Embassy in Washington at the request of Her Majesty the Queen as part of the American Bicentennial celebrations.

In 1977 he founded LIVE MUSIC NOW in Britain, a charity which gives concert opportunities to young artists while at the same time bringing music beyond the confines of the concert hall to clubs, schools, old age homes, prisons and hospitals. This successful scheme has already expanded into France, Belgium and the Netherlands.

The Asian Youth Music Camp Association and the organisers of the 1979 Asian Youth Music Camp welcome Yehudi Menuhin to the Hong Kong Camp. His concert with the 1979 Asian Youth Orchestra will be a highlight in the history of the Asian Youth Music Camp movement and an encouragement to those taking part in the Camp.

=== Page 29 ===
曼紐軒是個一生充滿傳奇的人物。他七歲時就與三藩市樂團演出，其後到巴黎、柏林、紐約及倫敦獻技，足迹遍全球。他的音樂修養日漸增進，演奏小提琴達到爐火純青的地步，而亦以其仁厚之心馳名於世。蘇格蘭人報對他有如下的記載：「對英國音樂界留心的人可觀察到曼紐軒先生的活動包含了愛心、理想及常理，他是自 T. S. ELIOT 以來美國對英國的最珍貴輸出。」

曼紐軒一九一六年出生於紐約一個俄國家庭，五歲開始學習小提琴。曾師 LOUIS PER-SINGER 、GEORGES ENESCO 及 ADOLF BUSCH ，及與不少大音樂家合作過，每人都對他有不可磨滅的影響。

一九三三年曼紐軒首次與他的姊妹 HEPHZIBAH 合作演奏鋼琴與小提琴奏鳴曲，直到現在，他們的合作仍為各地樂季中的高潮；他們在一九三二年的第一次錄音贏得法國國家唱片大獎。

第二次世界大戰期間，曼紐軒爲軍隊作過超過五百場演奏，因此獲法國、比利時、西德及希臘各國頒發獎章。其他榮譽包括一九六二年之皇家愛樂協會金章、榮譽音樂家聯會的 COBBETT MEDAL 、一九七一年哥本哈根之 SONNING 獎和一九七四年美國絃樂教師協會的藝術家／教師獎。他擁有十一家英國大學（包括牛津及劍橋）的榮譽學位，是愛丁堡和巴芙的榮譽市民，一九六六年受勳為 K. B. E. 。一九七九年，成爲音樂界中獲 BOERSENVEREIN DES DEUTSCHEN BUCHHA-NDELS 和平獎的第一人。

不少名作曲家曾為曼紐軒特別作曲。他對每一類音樂都有興趣，每到一處地方都會去發掘當地的音樂。一九五二年和五四年，他應印度 尼克魯首相邀請為印度饑民救濟金籌款；又於一九六九年在孟買 HOMI BHABBA 音樂廳開幕時為紀念這位原子科學家作三場演奏。一九七○年他因以音樂促進國際間諒解和友好之突出貢獻而獲尼克魯和平獎。他與印度絃琴演奏家 RAVI SHANKAR 合作在紐約及其他地方演奏，他們的唱片銷售超過百萬張。除對印度音樂有興趣外，他最近向小提琴爵士樂方面進軍，與 STEPHANE GRA-PELLI 在 B B C 電視及音樂會中出現，而其唱片亦非常暢銷。

曼紐軒於擔任巴芙節藝術指導達十年後，在一九六九年開始和 IAN HUNTER 一起領導溫莎節，為此女皇特准二人使用溫莎堡中最大的兩房間。他任瑞士 GSTAAD 一年一度曼紐軒節的藝術指導達廿四年之久，於一九七○年他與家人獲瑞士榮譽市民之銜，一九七七年 GSTAAD 一間供年青絃樂學生深造及表演的國際音樂學院亦以他命名。

在巴芙節中成立的曼紐軒節日樂團與他一起到世界各地表演，他指揮樂團演出過三套莫扎特歌劇，將貝多芬的九首交響曲錄了音，又在電影和電視表演。一九六九年十一月威爾斯皇子廿一歲生辰時，曼紐軒與樂團受皇子之邀在白金漢宮表演。曼紐軒亦曾指揮多個國際知名的樂團。

一九六九年曼氏任聯合國國際音樂會會長，最近完成三任任期，不過他仍繼續擔任該會國際音樂家互助基金之首任會長。他是多屆西敏城藝行會主席，一九七一年任聖三一音樂學院院長。

他對任何人都真誠關心，能說六國語言。他家人在藝術界中都有很大的成就。

曼紐軒著有很多音樂書籍，他的自傳亦被翻譯成多種語言，他經常為世界各報章雜誌撰寫文章，又在各學院講學及主持大師班。他的一生被法國及美國人拍成電影。六十歲時， B B C 亦為其攝製了一部一小時長的電影。他剛為加拿大廣播公司完成了八集的 MUSIC OF MAN ，將於短期內在北美及歐洲播放，曼紐軒特為此片集寫了一本書。

曼氏於一九六三年在英格蘭 SUNNY 郡的 STOKE D 'ABERNON 設立曼紐軒學校教授小指琴，為訓練六歲起音樂天才的學校。今年該校十週年紀念，學生在 ST. JAMES 皇宮為皇太后演奏，該校於一九七三年已獲教育及科學部承認為與皇家芭蕾舞學校有同等地位，學生在英國各地瑞士、法國及美國舉行過音樂會，於十六、七歲離校時，都能取得獎學金往英國、比利時、法國、德國、美國及莫斯科的音樂學院深造。一九七六年美國建國二百週年紀念時，女皇特邀請該校學生往華盛頓英國大使館演奏。

一九七七年，曼紐軒在英國成立一個 LIVE MUSIC NOW 慈善團體，讓年青藝術家到音樂廳外的會所、學校、老人院、監獄及醫院演奏。此項計劃非常成功，現已擴大到法國、比利時及荷蘭等地。

曼紐軒今次到香港是為支持亞洲青年音樂營活動，乃亞洲青年音樂訓練發展史中的一盛事。

=== Page 30 ===
GARY KARR was born in Los Angles and is a seventh-generation bassist in a family of musicians. Acclaimed throughout the world as “a musician who has done more to expand the vocabulary of the double bass than any player alive”, Karr has given more than 500 recitals throughout the United States, Canada, Mexico and Europe and has performed as soloist with over 100 orchestras, including the New York Philharmonic, the Chamber Music Society of Lincoln Center, the Chicago Symphony, the Toronto Symphony, the English Chamber Orchestra, the BBC Symphony, the London Philharmonic and the Oslo Philharmonic. Karr’s awesome technique has inspired such leading composers as Hans Werner Henze, Gunther Schuller, Alec Wilder and Malcolm Arnold to write especially for him. He has made more than a dozen major recordings. He has been a faculty member of the Juilliard School, the New England Conservatory, the University of Wisconsin, and is now on the faculty of the Dalhousie University in Halifax.

DAVID C. STONE born of a musical family; Scholar of King’s College, Cambridge, a leading figure in London Chamber Music with the Martin Quartet, Trio Pro Musica, and as a conductor of the London Mozart Players, international recitalist, acknowledged interpreter of Delius (one of his discs was voted International Record of the Month in Britain), editor of 18th century music and Violin Pedagogy for Oxford University Press, Stone has particularly valued the privilege of working as a Principal of the Menuhin Festival Orchestra. Menuhin has said of him: “I have such a high regard for David Stone and treasure our long association.” With achievement in many areas of music, Stone brings to his work in the East a wealth of experience and far-ranging knowledge, tempered by an open mind.

As conductor and consultant, he has this year worked in Australia, Korea and South America: in all, he has performed in more than 30 countries. Instrumental in bringing the British Avon Youth Orchestra to Singapore, Hong Kong and Manila in 1978, and in the 1979 visit of the Hong Kong Youth Chinese and Western Orchestras to Britain and Paris, his concern for Youth and the Performing Arts has taken on wide dimensions. His work for Hong Kong, initiated by the 1977 Report, has a special meaning for him, as one of the most satisfying areas of creativity: the surge of development in both Asian and Western music and its exciting potential — of new works created by natural synthesis, of exchanges of performers, teachers and expertise, of refreshing contact with the roots of Ethnic Music, and of all the joy of shared cultural vitality.

The “Times of India” recently wrote of his performance “... as an example

=== Page 31 ===
of intense musical communication, it was one of the most thrilling things I have heard." These words well capture Stone's intrinsic quality, the gift of communication.

THOMAS Y.S. WANG was born in Shanghai. Before coming to Hong Kong in 1962, he was a violinist in the Shanghai Symphony Orchestra and a violin tutor in the Shanghai Conservatory.

In 1968, Wang was awarded violin diplomas of Fellow and Licentiate by the Trinity College of Music, London. Later in Switzerland, he was conferred a certificate for the Wolfgang Schneiderhan's Master Course by the Conservatory of Lucerne.

In 1974, he led the Hong Kong Festival strings to give a chamber orchestra concert in the second Hong Kong Arts Festival in conjunction with the famous Allegri Quartet of London. From 1973 to 1975, he conducted the University Orchestra of the Chinese University of Hong Kong. In September 1978 he joined the Music Administrator's Office as Senior Training Officer and in the same year led a group of students to participate in the Second Asian Youth Music Camp in Singapore.

Wang has also been directing the Diocesan Boys' School Orchestra for sixteen years with an outstanding record at the annual Hong Kong Schools Music Festival.

In August/September this year, Wang was Deputy Director of the tour of the Hong Kong Youth Symphony Orchestra and the Youth Chinese Orchestra in the United Kingdom and France.

TONG LEUNG-TAK was born in a family of musicians in Shanghai. He started playing various Chinese musical instruments as a child. He has played in several Chinese orchestras in Shanghai and Bei Jing, written and scored music for movies and has made recordings.

TONG came to Hong Kong in 1977 and joined the Hong Kong Chinese Orchestra. He was appointed the Training Officer (Chinese Instrumental Music) of the Music Administrator's Office, Hong Kong Government in September 1978. In August/September this year, he conducted the Hong Kong Youth Chinese Orchestra during its successful concert tour of the United Kingdom and France.

JOHN CHENG was educated in Macau. He received his music training in the United States and the United Kingdom, CHENG joined the Music Section of the Hong Kong Education Department in 1962. He led the Hong Kong delegation to the First Asian Youth Music Camp in the Philippines in 1977. In October of the same year, he joined the Music Administrator's Office as Training Officer for wind music. He is now the conductor of the Hong Kong Youth Symphonic Band.

KIM NAM-YUN, American-trained Korean violinist, started an early music career by winning many contests in Korea. At eighteen, she was sent for further studies at the Juilliard School of Music under Ivan Galamian. A consistent scholar, she continued to win many other awards including the Merriweather Post Competition in 1969 in Washington, D.C., the Tchaikowsky Concerto Competition in Juilliard; and the Tibor Varga International Violin Competition in Switzerland in 1974. She has made various appearances in recitals, chamber music concerts since 1967 in New York, Switzerland, West Germany and Korea.

WOON WEN KIN of Malaysia earned his violin training and musical experience as trombone player and conductor in London. He participated extensively in concerts and festivals, and was selected to represent the British Student Youth Symphony Orchestra in a UNESCO-sponsored tour of Austria in 1965 and of Paris in 1967. He also recorded for the BBC in London. Upon his return to Malaysia in 1968, he founded the Penang Philharmonic Society of which he is the present Vice-President and Director. He is also the conductor of the Penang Chung Hwa Brass Band. He still teaches violin and other instruments in Penang. He was also a Conductor and Assistant Director of the First and Second Malaysia National Music Camp.

SUTINSRINARONG (Thailand) plays the viola and holds a degree in teaching from the Chulalongkorn University. He was selected to represent Thailand at the Chamber Music Academy in Switzerland in the summer of 1972. He is at present teaching music at the Kasetsart University and conducts a group of young musicians. Under his competent and enthusiastic leadership, the group recently appeared on television to celebrate the birthday of the Queen of Thailand. Srinarong is most interested in the education of the young and in the formation of youth orchestra.

NA DUK SUNG, Korean cellist, finished his early music studies in Korea. He then proceeded to study further at the Musiklochschule in Cologne in 1972 as a scholar of Prof. Siegfried Palm. His noteworthy appearances as soloist has been with the National Symphony, the Seoul Philharmonic and the Taipei Symphony. He also has made a number of recitals in Seoul, in Cologne, in Salzburg, and participant of the World Symphony Orchestra held in New York and Washington, D.C. in 1971. At present, he is Asst. Professor of the Music Department of Kyung Hee University in Seoul, Korea.

GABOR REEVES, Hungarian clarinetist who migrated to

=== Page 32 ===
Australia, has filled the position of principal clarinet and lecturer on clarinet for several orchestras and music schools in Australia. Besides performances, he has conducted masterclasses in clarinet and has been active with the music camps movement in Australia.

GEOFF BAILEY is Lecturer in Brass at the N.S.W. Conservatorium of Music in Sydney. Before his appointment for this teaching stint, he worked for many years as a professional trombonist in all fields of performance in music symphonic, grand opera, music-comedy and cabaret. His intense interest in the development of music appreciation in school made him take the position of tutor for lower brass in the National Music Camp of Australia.

ROBERT E. JOHNSON is currently the principal French Horn player in the Singapore Symphony Orchestra. He studied the Horn with Michael Hatfield of the Cincinnati Symphony Orchestra and later with the great Philip Farkas of the Chicago Symphony. In the recent past he has been associated with the Aspen Music Festival in Colorado U.S.A., performing in the Festival, Chamber, Opera and Philharmonic orchestras. He was also involved in the Aspen Music Festival Conference on Contemporary Music. Early this year he served as Horn Clinician for the Cultural Center of the Philippines and was guest soloist with the Metro-Manila Symphony Orchestra. In Singapore besides his full time work in the S.S.O. he serves as a Music lecturer for the University of Singapore.

DICK SMITH, timpanist of the South Australian Symphony Orchestra has played solo on the xylophone, vibraphone, and marimba. He is teacher-lecturer for tympani and percussions at the University of Adelaide, Department of Further Education, and the college of advanced education. He plays and teaches the complete percussion and tympani.

DAVID HARMON LEWIS:
Harmon Lewis is a graduate in Organ from Millsaps College, Jackson, Mississippi, and holds a Masters degree in music from Indiana University. He is currently on the faculty of Dalhousie University as instructor in Organ and Harpsichord. As a member of the Karr-Lewis Duo, Harmon Lewis is an exponent of the almost forgotten art of accompaniments improvised directly from a figured bass. For the past summers he has been, with Gary Karr, a faculty member of the Shawnigan Lake Summer School of the Arts on Vancouver Island.

人物介紹

一九七八年九月任音樂事務統籌處高級訓練主任，並曾率領學生參加在新加坡舉行之第二屆亞洲青年音樂營。

汪氏還一直擔任拔萃男校管弦樂隊的指揮及教授小提琴。他的學生在歷屆校際音樂節中都取得很好的成績。

今年八、九月間，香港青年交響樂團及中樂團赴英、法演出，由汪氏任副團長。

湯良德原籍上海，出身於音樂世家，自幼學習各種民族樂器，曾於上海及北京各樂團演奏，並為電影作曲及配樂，灌有多張唱片。

湯氏於一九七七年來港，受聘於香港中樂團；一九七八年九月加入香港政府音樂事務統籌處任職中樂訓練主任，並指揮香港青年中樂團於本年八、九月間往英、法巡迴演出，非常成功。

DAVID HARMON LEWIS 畢業於密西西比傑克遜的MILLSAPS 學院，主修風琴，後於印第安那大學獲音樂碩士學位。現時則在HALIFAX 的DALHOUSIE 大學任教風琴及古鍵琴。

LEWIS 與嘉其理作二重奏時，為低音大提琴旋律加上即興伴奏，成爲這種幾已被遺忘的伴奏技巧的表表者。LEWIS 與嘉其理過去皆曾在溫哥華SHAWNIGAN LAKE 暑期藝術學校任教。

施東寧出自音樂世家，於劍橋大學英皇書院攻讀音樂及神學。施氏在倫敦音樂界大受歡迎，曾任曼紐軒節目樂團之主要者，備受樂界稱許。除演奏小提琴外

=== Page 33 ===
亦任指揮。施氏是唯一將戴流士全部小提琴與鋼琴作品錄奏的音樂家，奠定他成爲當代傑出的戴流士演奏者，牛津大學出版社曾出版他編寫的三冊有關小提琴的書籍。他是二十世紀的倡導者。施氏曾於三十多個國家演奏。施東寧常以指揮及顧問身份在世界各地工作，今年曾到澳洲、韓國及南美洲。他特別喜歡與青年音樂家合作。一九七八年他指揮英國雅樂郡青年樂團完成東南亞演出。一九七六年施氏應邀為香港政府教育署作一學校音樂教育的報告書。七七年一月報告書完成後，當局立即成立了音樂事務統籌處，委任施東寧為香港政府音樂顧問。一九七九年香港青年交響樂團赴英、法巡迴演出，由施氏擔任指揮，載譽而歸。

印度時報樂評對施氏演奏水平評價極高，譽為最深刻之音樂傳播媒介，從此可見施氏在音樂方面之成就及獨到之處。

金南潤乃韓國著名小提琴家，在美國接受訓練。

金氏早年已在韓國贏得多次比賽首獎。十八歲時被送往美國茱莉亞音樂學院事師 I VAN GALAMIAN。此後繼續多次得獎，包括一九六九年華盛頓MERRI WEATHER POST 比賽，茱莉亞音樂學院之柴可夫斯基協奏曲比賽及一九七四年瑞士TIBOR VARGA 國際小提琴比賽。

由一九六七年起，金氏一直在紐約、瑞士、西德及韓國舉行獨奏會及室樂音樂會。

GEOFF BAILEY（澳洲）現任雪梨新南威爾斯音樂學院之銅管樂講師。就任此教職前，他曾在多類音樂表演中，包括交響樂團、歌劇、音樂劇等，任職樂團號演奏家多年。

他對推廣學校音樂欣賞有濃厚興趣，在澳洲全國音樂營活動中，曾擔任低音銅管樂之導師。

GABOR REEVES（澳洲）乃匈牙利出生之單簧管演奏家，後移居澳洲，曾任數個樂團及音樂學校之首席單簧管及教授。

除演奏外，他尚曾主持多個單簧管大師班，在澳洲音樂營的推展活動中尤爲活躍。

NA DUK SUNG（韓國）乃大提琴演奏家，於韓國完成早期之音樂學習，一九七二年往科隆音樂學院隨 SIEGFRED PALM 教授繼續深造。

他與韓國國家交響樂團、漢城愛樂樂團及台北交響樂團合作演奏，皆獲稱讚，並曾在漢城、科隆及沙爾茲堡舉行獨奏會。

一九七一年，參加在紐約和華盛頓舉行之世界交響樂團。現任漢城KYUNG HEE 大學音樂系助理教授。

鄭繼祖早年於澳門就學，後赴美國及英國攻讀音樂。一九六三年加入香港教育司署音樂組，七七年帶領香港之代表參加在菲律賓舉行的第一屆亞洲青年音樂營，同年十月加入音樂事務統籌處任職管樂訓練主任，現為香港青年管樂團指揮。

DICK SMITH（澳洲）為南澳洲交響樂團之定音鼓手，曾獨奏多種敲擊樂器，現任阿德蘭（ADELAIDE）大學之定音鼓及敲擊樂講師。

SUTIN SRINARONG（泰國）乃中提琴演奏家，在CHULALONGKORN 大學獲教育學位。一九七二年夏天，他獲選代表泰國參加瑞士之室樂學院。他現時任教於KASETSART 大學，指揮一個青年音樂小組，在他的熱心領導下，該小組最近為祝泰國皇后生辰在電視表演。他對青年教育及組織青年樂團有濃厚興趣。

ROBERT E. JOHN-SON（新加坡）現任新加坡交響樂團首席法國號手。師承辛辛納第交響樂團之 MI CHAEL HATIFIELD，後隨芝加哥交響樂團 PHILIP FARKAS

曾在美國科羅拉多音樂節樂團演出，並參加ASPEN 音樂節之現代音樂研討會。本年初在菲律賓文化中心任圓號導師及為馬尼拉交響樂團擔任圓號獨奏。除在新加坡交響樂團全職工作外，亦為新加坡大學之音樂講師。

WOON WEN KIN（馬來西亞）於倫敦接受小提琴訓練，有指揮經驗，又曾擔任伸縮號之演奏。他多次參加音樂會及音樂節，並曾獲選由聯合國贊助的英國學生青年交響樂團團員於六五年訪奧大利及六七年訪巴黎演出。此外，尚曾於倫敦為英國廣播公司作海外錄音。

一九六八年，他返回馬來西亞，成立了檳城愛樂協會，現任該會副主席及總監。他又是檳城中華管樂團之指揮。現時仍在檳城教授小提琴及其他樂器。除此，他又曾任第一、二屆馬來西亞國家音樂營之指揮及副總監。

Programme

PART I

Part Song—"Consecration of Song"
Gustave Baldamus

SOLO—MR. J. GLADSTONE WRIGHT

Liedertafel

O'ER verdant meadows to the mountain height,
    In rays of morning do thou rise, O song,
And greet the sea and land, the day so bright,
    Rise to empyreal spheres where angels throng.

The solemn Sabbath bells intone the lay,
    That sweetly with the sylvan choir doth chime;
The brook doth gush, and thund'ring far away
    Roll hoary, crumbling rocks, e'en old as time.

Sublime, divine the pow'r of melodies
    That wakes the heart to worthiness and grace.
Sound forth o'er earth, ye wondrous harmonies,
    Resound in song throughout all time and space.

    Rejoice, O human-kind!
The pow'r of tone o'er life doth shed
    A happy ray of light.
Like sunshine spreading forth from zone to zone,
    So song shall quicken, waking pure delight.

Romanza—"Si tu Savais"    M. W. Balfe
Signor Attilio Buzzi

=== Page 8 ===
Cavatina—"Convien Partir"  Donizetti
(La Figlia del Reggimento)
Miss Juliet Flegeltaub

Cantata—"God and Fatherland" W. Tschirch
(TRANSLATED FROM THE GERMAN BY J. O. BROADLEY)

Liedertafel

From the clear blue arch of heaven
    Beams the sun with splendour bright.
Let our songs of praise be given
    To the God of life and light.
Great and wonderful art Thou!
Sovereign Lord, to Thee we bow.

Grand as organ nobly pealing,
    Let this vow to Heaven ascend;
Heart and voice the power revealing,
    Verse and harmony to blend.
Native country, native tongue,
Bind our hearts in union strong.

Word and weapon nobly plighted,
    To defend thee and to save;
We, thy children, stand united,
    Glorious shall thy banner wave.
Life we pledge at thy command,
O, thou dearest Fatherland.

Honour to the man who foldeth
    Truth and beauty to his breast;
But on him who sacred holdeth
    Woman's love let blessing rest.
Curse the dastard who doth prove
Traitor to a woman's love.

=== Page 9 ===
In full chorus now uniting,
    Pledged to love, be all agreed;
Friendship's sacred name now plighting,
    True to be in word and deed;
Swear by love to faithful stand;
Honour God and Fatherland.

Cello Solos—
    (a) "Nocturne"        Chopin
    (b) "Musette"        17th Century
Herr Theo. Liebe

Ballad—"Ever Thine"        Franz Abt
Mr. A. J. Chamberlin

Song—"I Love thee so" Sir W. C. F. Robinson
Miss Fannie Charlesworth

Part Song—"The Miller's Daughter" Hartel
Liedertafel

STREAM and mill, your murmurs cease,
Sounds, to silence all decline;
Now, ye woodbirds, rest in peace,
Or in this my burthen join,
She is mine, she is mine; she has said she is mine.

Lovely springtime, thee I welcome merrily,
All thy flowrets blooming smile so cheerily,
Now no more, with care o'ergrown,
Feels my beating heart alone.
She is mine, yes, the miller's daughter now is mine.

INTERVAL OF FIVE MINUTES.

=== Page 10 ===
PART II

Cantata—"To the Sons of Art" Mendelssohn
Liedertafel

O Sons of Art, man's dignity to you is given:
    Preserve it man!
It falls with you, with you ascends to heaven!
The hallowed themes of Magian dreams,
Founded in Wisdom's vast creation,
Gliding like rivers find their ocean,
    That great harmonious plan.

Eternal truth, tho' oft rejected,
Exists not ever unprotected;
She finds a refuge with the tuneful throng.
She there appears in all her glory,
Mighty when veil'd in mystic story;
She wakes the lay of lofty voices,
And over all her foes rejoices,
Her vengeance flashing, peals in song.

To your free mother homage render,
Boldly to gain her height aspire;
Enthron'd she dwells in radiant splendour
No other crown than hers desire.
While you her thousand paths are tracing
Press onward, keeping Truth in sight;
Come altogether, stand embracing
Before the Throne where paths unite!

=== Page 11 ===
9
Song—"Alla Stella Confidente" Bobaudi
(With Cello Obbligato by Herr Theo. Liebe)
Signor Buzzi

Part Song—"The Mariner's Return" Haeckler
Liedertafel

Pull away, boys, steer for the cove,
Yonder lie dreaming the hearts that we love.
Let us now banish all trouble and sorrow,
We shall have cause to be joyful to-morrow.
Glittering moonbeams bespangle the deep,
O'er the wide ocean the winds are asleep.

Storms are o'er, and land is in sight,
Calmly we glide thro' the waters to-night.
Many a heart will to-morrow be leaping,
Which in the bosom is quietly sleeping.
Rowing and singing we draw near the shore,
Where there are joys for us seamen in store.

Song—"The Three Wishes" Pinsuti
Miss Juliet Flegeltaub

=== Page 12 ===
Part Song—"Martyrs of the Arena" De Rille
Liedertafel

Great Caesar, with our dying breath,
    Thus we hail thee!
The body thou canst doom to death,
But the soul shall hold fast her faith.
O Caesar, with our dying breath,
    Thus we hail thee!
Great lord of life and death!

    See, the town keeps holiday to-day,
The circus in festive array!
Now raise a merry shout to the gods,
With cymbals clashing, and trumpets blowing.
Before them the stern lictors' rods
See the consuls in crimson glowing.
See the pale Vestals' white robes flowing,
All attend till great Caesar nods.

    And we, all amid the dread arena,
Naked, defenceless, in God our sole reliance,
We hear with calm defiance
The roaring lion and hyena,
Soon to be our living tomb.

    Heard ye that ringing cheer?
They open now the cage,
And the tiger and panther in their rage,
They come madly bounding along.
Brethren, be strong!
Lift up your heart in prayer and song.

    God of the martyr and the slave,
O Christ, who hast triumphed over death!
Come, oh come, thy suff'ring saints to save.
Now they draw their parting breath!

    'Tis the hour of joyful compensation,
Hark! it greets us from eternity.
Now comes the long-looked-for salvation,
Now dawns the day of liberty.

=== Page 13 ===
And when the life-blood is pouring,
And day is dark'ning into night,
O living God, to Thee our souls are soaring,
And death is the dawning of endless light.

Cello Solo—"Drinking Song" Dunkler
Herr Theo. Liebe

Part Song—
(a) "Mariner's Hymn to the Dioscuri" Schubert-Plumpton
(b) "Wanderer's Song" Schumann-Plumpton

Liedertafel

(a) Dioscuri! shining twin stars,
    Ye who light us o'er the ocean;
Mighty helpers, guide us safely,
    Still the waves to gentle motion.

Tho' with firm hearts, fear unknowing,
    Undismayed with storms contending,
We would see your mild rays beaming,
    Hope and courage to us lending.

This strong oar that bears us onward,
    O'er the waves your rule obeying,
At your shrine we then will offer,
    At your altar homage paying.

=== Page 14 ===
Again fill your glasses with bright sparkling wine,
Once more will I pledge ye, dear comrades of mine!
Farewell, hoary mountains and dear native home,
Farewell! to a far distant land I must roam.

The bright sun above us at rest does not stand,
His course he fulfils over ocean and land;
The billows disperse and recede from the shore,
The storm rushes onward its fury to pour.

With swift-speeding pinion the bird flies away,
Still singing and soaring it pours out its lay.
Thus youth's glowing visions will urge to the race,
Thus earth wanders on thro' regions of space.

The birds of his own land the wanderer greet,
Its flowr's meet his eye with their odour so sweet;
They bring to his heart thoughts of home and of love,
The meadow beneath and the blue sky above.

He dreams that once more he his fatherland sees,
And sweet scents of home life come borne on the breeze;
Thus love e'er will follow the lov'd one afar,
And shine through the distance his one guiding star.

GOD SAVE THE QUEEN

THE WASH
NATURE'S SOLUTION OF A 'PERMANENT' PROBLEM

For over 30 years a Father and Son went regularly to Lincoln to shoot wild fowl on the marsh land of the Wash; but this marsh land not only provided sport but also a great scientific discovery in two small rare plants. Mr. Rudolph persisted in careful research which revealed that these plants could provide invaluable formula for an entirely new method of Permanent Waving. By its use the hair is left in its natural condition. There is no possibility of breaking or of white hair turning yellow. The wave produced is strong, without fear of frizzing, and setting becomes easy and natural. In fact, this formula appears to reproduce the natural waves of the sea in the waves of the hair.

Mr. Rudolph has by personal investigation perfected his discovery, and the now famous "Vico Perm" is true testimony to the claims made for it.

Free consultations are welcomed, and test curlers taken free of charge.

VICO PERM
E. Rudolph 152 Sloane St. S.W.1.
PHONE: SLOANE 3744 FOR APPOINTMENT

ROYAL NORTHERN HOSPITAL
HOLLOWAY, N.7

IN 1935 the Royal Northern Group of Hospitals, which serves over a million people in an area of over seventy square miles of North London, dealt with the following cases:—

In-Patients received . 6,295
Out-Patients attendances 360,637
Casualty Attendances 53,676
Operations performed 6,254

The cost of treating these patients was £122,495, of which less than 4% is assured by endowments. There is a debt of £139,460.

St. David's Wing for private patients has been erected in Manor Gardens, N.7, providing 80 beds in private rooms completely equipped for the benefit of the middle classes. The fees range from 5 to 10 guineas per week.

There are also CUBICLED CONTRIBUTORY WARDS for those whose means do not permit of the use of the Private Hospital.

The Royal Northern Group of Hospitals consists of The Royal Northern Hospital, Holloway (220 beds), St. David's Wing, Manor Gardens, N.7, for private patients (80 beds), The Royal Chest Hospital, City Road (85 beds), Grovelands Hospital (Recovery), Old Southgate (60 beds), The Reckitt Convalescent Home, Clacton (35 beds), and The Maternity Nursing Association, Hynddalen Square, E.C.1, 235: Camden Road, N.7, and 2a, Howard Road, Southgate, N.15 (for District Midwifery Work with Ante-Natal and Infant Welfare Clinics), 480 beds in all.

Secretary: GILBERT G. PANTER

ROYAL ACADEMY OF MUSIC
YORK GATE, REGENT'S PARK, LONDON, N.W.1
Instituted 1822. Incorporated by Royal Charter 1830.
Patrons: HER MAJESTY QUEEN MARY
H.R.H. THE DUKE OF CONNAUGHT & STRATHARN, K.G.
President: H.R.H. THE DUKE OF CONNAUGHT & STRATHARN, K.G.
Principal: SIR JOHN McGELEN, M.A., D.Mus., L.D.
MICHAELMAS TERM BEGINS MONDAY, 21st SEPTEMBER, 1936.
ENTRANCE EXAMINATIONS FROM 10th SEPTEMBER.

STUDENTS' ORCHESTRA. Under the direction of SIR HENRY J. WOOD, D.Mus., F.R.A.M. Rehearsals, Tuesdays and Fridays, 2—5 p.m. during the term.

VACATION COURSE FOR TEACHERS. Pianoforte, Class Singing, Aural Training, Musical History and Appreciation, Elocution, 8th to 11th September, inclusive.

SPECIAL COURSES (Optional). Conducting, Art of Speech, School Music, Training of Teachers.

SCHOLARSHIPS. 78 Scholarships and Exhibitions in all branches of Music; 20 will be competed for in September next. Last day of entry, Monday, 31st August.

ENSEMBLE CLASSES. For the study of Vocal and Instrumental Ensemble.

GRADUATE COURSE (G.R.S.M. Lond.). Held jointly by the Royal Academy of Music and the Royal College of Music.

JUNIOR SCHOOL. Special curriculum for Junior Pupils. SUBJECTS TAUGHT (individual lessons): Pianoforte, Organ, Violin, Viola, Violoncello, Harp, Elocution, Dancing. SUBJECTS TAUGHT IN CLASS: Singing, Elements of Music, Aural Training, Harmony, Composition, Percussion Band, etc.

L.R.A.M. EXAMINATIONS. Held during the Summer, Christmas, and Easter Vacations. Last day of entry for the September Exam., 30th June, or with late fee (5/-) 12th July.

PROSPECTUSES, entry forms and all information on application.

L. GURNEY PARROTT, Secretary.

THE ROYAL COLLEGE OF MUSIC
PRINCE CONSORT ROAD, SOUTH KENSINGTON, LONDON, S.W.7
Patron: HIS MAJESTY THE KING
Director: SIR HUGH P. ALLEN, G.C.V.O., M.A., D.Mus., D.Litt.
Honorary Secretary: CHARLES MORLEY, F.R.C.M.
Registrar: BASIL C. ALLCHIN, M.A. (OXON.) F.R.C.M., F.R.C.O.

CHRISTMAS TERM
The Christmas Term will commence on Monday, Sept. 21st, 1936. Entrance Examination on or about Sept. 16th

COMPLETE MUSICAL EDUCATION. The College offers a complete course of musical education to pupils of both sexes, both professional and amateur, by teachers of the highest eminence.

JUNIOR DEPARTMENT. Classes are held for pupils under 16, whose time is occupied also by their general education.

OPERATIC CLASSES. The College possesses a fully equipped College Opera Theatre for an audience of 600.

TERMS, FEES, etc. There are three terms in the year. The Tuition Fees are £14 14s. and £12 12s. per Term. Entrance Fees are £12 12s. and may continue at College for at least three terms. Female Pupils requiring residence are accommodated at Queen Alexandra's House, adjacent to the College, as far as the capacity of that Institution allows on terms to be obtained from the Lady Superintendent.

THE ROYAL COLLEGE OF MUSIC PATRONS' FUND for the Ernest Palmer Fund for Opera Study in the Royal College of Music (Founded by Lord Palmer, F.R.C.M.). Syllabus and all particulars may be obtained from the Registrar.

SPECIAL CLASSES are held for score reading, conducting training of teachers, musical criticism and ballet.

SCHOLARSHIPS EXHIBITIONS. Upwards of 70 scholarships and exhibitions are provided from a permanent endowment fund.

ENSEMBLE CLASSES. There are Vocal and Instrumental Ensemble Classes, and Pupils sufficiently advanced in this work are given the opportunity of putting their knowledge into practice at College Concerts.

SCENES FROM THE SONG OF HIAWATHA

In performance a few words have been altered to bring the narrative into the present tense.

The story of this Opera forms a part of Longfellow's "Song of Hiawatha." It is divided into three Acts—"Hiawatha's Wedding Feast," "The Death of Minnehaha," and "Hiawatha's Departure."
To understand the story it is necessary to know that it had been revealed to the Indian tribes by Gitche Manitou, the Great Spirit and Creator of all living things, that he would send to them from the land where there is no sin and no darkness, and where all is bathed in the glory of light and love, a great prophet who would teach them to adore the beauty of peace and who, after suffering with them the sorrows and privations of mankind, would lead them into the golden dawn of a new world.

In the fulness of time, Hiawatha was born, and became a great prophet, teacher and statesman. Under his influence five adjacent tribes buried the hatchet and welded themselves together as a powerful confederation which became allied to the British settlers and fought beside them against the Hurons and their allies, the French. Thus, Hiawatha played a considerable part in the history of the formation of the British Empire, in that he assisted to a great extent in the acquisition of Canada.

I.—HIAWATHA'S WEDDING FEAST

Hiawatha was a man as other men, and wooed and won sweet Laughing Water, Minnehaha from the land of the Dacotahs. The Opera opens with the festivities at their marriage, and gay are the guests as they offer their presents and receive the generous hospitality of their host. Quip and jest pass round. Pau-Puk-Keewis leaps and twines in dance with the grace of a barbaric savage. The Medicine Man brews a Peyote plant potion, of which the guests partake, and through its magic visualise an ancient myth of a Young Chief who relinquishes his earthly body to seek his beloved in the Land of the Hereafter. He finds her, and soul meets soul in the Happy Hunting Grounds. Supreme happiness is his till he is reminded by Gitche Manitou, the Mighty, that he is mortal, and must return to fulfil his destiny on Earth. The return of the Young Chief to his people is celebrated by a thrilling totem dance, in which all the tribe takes part, and give vent to their feeling in the hiss of the serpent, the bark of the fox, the shriek of the eagle or the bellow of the buffalo, according to the nature of their totem. Song follows dance, and Chibabos, the singer of sweet songs, sounds the keynote of passionate love in the ears of his entranced listeners.

The Marriage Feast is over. Happy and joyous, the guests, led by Iagoo, the marvellous storyteller, depart to their wigwams, and alone in the moonlight are Hiawatha and Minnehaha.

You shall hear how Pau-Puk-Keewis,
How the handsome Yenadizze,
Danced at Hiawatha's wedding;
How the gentle Chibabos,
He the sweetest of musicians,
Sang his songs of love and longing,
How Iagoo, the great boaster,
He the marvellous storyteller,
Told his tales of strange adventure,
That the feast might be more joyous,
That the time might pass more gaily
And the guests be more contented.
Sumptuous was the feast Nokomis
Made at Hiawatha's wedding.
All the bowls were made of bass-wood
White and polished very smoothly,
All the spoons of horn of bison,
Black and polished very smoothly.

She had sent through all the village
Messengers with wands of willow,
As a sign of invitation,
As a token of the feasting;
And the wedding-guests assembled,
Clad in all their richest raiment,
Robes of fur and belts of wampum,
Splendid with their paint and plumage,
Beautiful with beads and tassels.
First they ate the sturgeon, Nahma,
And the pike, the Maskenoza,
Caught and cooked by old Nokomis,
Then on pemican they feasted,
Pemican and buffalo marrow,
Haunch of deer and hump of bison,
Yellow cakes of the Mondamin,
And the wild rice of the river.
But the gracious Hiawatha,

Skilled was he in sports and pastimes,

Skilled was he in games of hazard,

First he danced a solemn measure,
Very slow in step and gesture,
In and out among the pine trees,
Through the shadows and the sunshine,
Treading softly like a panther,
Then more swiftly and still swifter,
Whirling, spinning round in circles,
Leaping o'er the guests assembled,
Eddying round and round the wigwam,
Till the leaves went whirling with him,
Till the dust and wind together
Swept in eddies round about him.

Then along the sandy margin
Of the lake, the Big-Sea-Water,
On he sped with frenzied gestures,
Stamped upon the sand, and tossed it
Wildly in the air around him;
Till the wind became a whirlwind,
Till the sand was blown and sifted
Like great snowdrifts o'er the landscape,
Heaping all the shores with Sand Dunes,
Sand Hills of the Nagow Wudjoo!

Thus the merry Pau-Puk-Keewis
Danced his Beggar's Dance to please them,
And, returning, sat down laughing
There among the guests assembled,
Sat and fanned himself serenely
With his fan of turkey-feathers.

To the friend of Hiawatha,

In the Moon when leaves are falling.

"Does not all the blood within me
Leap to meet thee, leap to meet thee,
As the springs to meet the sunshine,
In the Moon when nights are brightest?

"Onaway! my heart sings to thee,
Sings with joy when thou art near me,

II.—THE DEATH OF MINNEHAHA

Summer is over, and Winter grips valley and mountain in its icy clutch. Fever and Famine stalk abroad. Clinging to each other for warmth, the stricken Indians cower and shiver beneath their blankets. And what of the lovely Minnehaha—"Minnehaha, Laughing Water, Loveliest of Dacotah women"? In the absence of Hiawatha—who has gone to seek vainly for food for his people, succour for his bride—she is sick unto death, and dread phantoms bend over her couch. Finally, with a wild cry "Hiawatha! Hiawatha!" she dies in delirium.

Far away amid the forest, miles away among the mountains" the wanderer hears that cry. Homeward hurries Hiawatha. Passionately, despairingly, he flings himself beside the dead body of his beloved, and the old nurse Nokomis sobs out her anguish. The sorrowing Indians moan and wail forth their sorrow, and over the mountains falls the snow.

There is a pause to show the passage of seven days, and then the body of Minnehaha is borne away in stately procession, clothed in her richest garments, wrapped in her robes of ermine, ready for her journey to the Islands of the Blessed.

O the long and dreary Winter!
O the cold and cruel Winter!
Ever thicker, thicker, thicker,
Froze the ice on lake and river,
Ever deeper, deeper, deeper,
Fell the snow o'er all the landscape,
Fell the covering snow, and drifted
Through the forest, round the village.
Hardly from his buried wigwam
Could the hunter force a passage;
With his mittens and his snow-shoes
Vainly walked he through the forest,
Sought for bird or beast and found none,
Saw no track of deer or rabbit,
In the snow beheld no footprints,
In the ghastly, gleaming forest
Fell, and could not rise from weakness,
Perished there from cold and hunger.
O the famine and the fever!
O the wasting of the famine!
O the blasting of the fever!
O the wailing of the children!
O the anguish of the women!
All the earth was sick and famished,
Hungry was the air around them,
Hungry was the sky above them,
And the hungry stars in heaven
Like the eyes of wolves glared at them!

Into Hiawatha's wigwam
Came two silent guests and gloomy,
Waited not to be invited,
Did not parley at the doorway,
Sat there without word of welcome
In the seat of Laughing Water;
Looked with haggard eyes and hollow
At the face of Laughing Water.
And the foremost said, "Behold me!
I am Famine, Buckadawin!"
And the other said, "Behold me!
I am Fever, Ahkosewin!"
And the lovely Minnehaha
Shuddered as they looked upon her,

Shuddered at the words they uttered,
Lay down on her bed in silence,
Hid her face, but made no answer;
Lay there trembling, freezing, burning
At the looks they cast upon her,
At the fearful words they uttered.
Forth into the empty forest
Rushed the maddened Hiawatha;
In his heart was deadly sorrow,
In his face a stony firmness;
On his brow the sweat of anguish
Started, but it froze, and fell not.
Wrapped in furs, and armed for hunting,
With his mighty bow of ash-tree,
With his quiver full of arrows,
With his mittens, Minjekahwun,
Into the vast and vacant forest
On his snow-shoes strode he forward.

"Gitche Manito, the Mighty!"
Cried he with his face uplifted
In that bitter hour of anguish,
"Give your children food, O father!
Give us food, or we must perish!
Give me food for Minnehaha,
For my dying Minnehaha!"

Through the far-resounding forest,
Through the forest vast and vacant,
Rang that cry of desolation,
But there came no other answer
Than the echo of his crying,
Than the echo of the woodlands,
"Minnehaha! Minnehaha!"
All day long roved Hiawatha
In that melancholy forest,
Through the shadow of whose thickets,
In the pleasant days of Summer,
Of that ne'er-forgotten Summer,
He had brought his young wife homeward,
From the land of the Dacotahs;
When the birds sang in the thickets,
And the streamlets laughed and glistened,
And the air was full of fragrance,

And the lovely Laughing Water
Said, with voice that did not tremble,
"I will follow you, my husband!"
In the wigwam with Nokomis,
With those gloomy guests that watched her,
With the Famine and the Fever,
She was lying, the Beloved,
She the dying Minnehaha.
"Hark!" she said, "I hear a rushing,

Hear the Falls of Minnehaha
Calling to me from a distance!"
"No, my child!" said old Nokomis,
"'Tis the night-wind in the pine-trees!"
"Look!" she said, "I see my father
Standing lonely at his doorway,
Beckoning to me from his wigwam,
In the land of the Dacotahs!"
"No, my child!" said old Nokomis,
"'Tis the smoke that waves and beckons!"
"Ah!" she said, "the eyes of Pauguk
Glare upon me in the darkness;
I can feel his icy fingers
Clasping mine amid the darkness!
Hiawatha! Hiawatha!"

And the desolate Hiawatha,
Far away amid the forest,
Miles away among the mountains,
Heard that sudden cry of anguish,
Heard the voice of Minnehaha
Calling to him in the darkness,
"Hiawatha! Hiawatha!"

Over snow-fields waste and pathless
Under snow-encumbered branches.
Homeward hurried Hiawatha,
Empty-handed, heavy-hearted,
Heard Nokomis moaning, wailing,
"Wahonomin! Wahonomin!
Would that I had perished for you,
Would that I were dead as you are!
Wahonomin! Wahonomin!"
And he rushed into the wigwam,
Saw the old Nokomis slowly
Rocking to and fro and moaning,
Saw his lovely Minnehaha
Lying dead and cold before him;
And his bursting heart within him
Uttered such a cry of anguish,
That the forest moaned and shuddered,
That the very stars in heaven
Shook and trembled with his anguish.

Then he sat down, still and speechless,
On the bed of Minnehaha,
At the feet of Laughing Water,
At those willing feet, that never
More would lightly run to meet him,
Never more would lightly follow.
With both hands his face he covered,
Seven long days and nights he sat there,
As if in a swoon he sat there,
Speechless, motionless, unconscious
Of the daylight or the darkness.

Then they buried Minnehaha:
In the snow a grave they made her,
In the forest deep and darksome,
Underneath the moaning hemlocks;
Clothed her in her richest garments,
Wrapped her in her robes of ermine,
Covered her with snow, like ermine;
Thus they buried Minnehaha.
And at night a fire was lighted,
On her grave four times was kindled,
For her soul upon its journey
To the Islands of the Blessed.
From his doorway Hiawatha
Saw it burning in the forest,
Lighting up the gloomy hemlocks;
From his sleepless bed uprising,
From the bed of Minnehaha,
Stood and watched it at the doorway,
That it might not be extinguished,
Might not leave her in the darkness.
"Farewell!" said he, "Minnehaha
Farewell, O my Laughing Water!
All my heart is buried with you,
All my thoughts go onward with you!
Come not back again to labour,
Come not back again to suffer,
Where the Famine and the Fever
Wear the heart and waste the body.
Soon my task will be completed,
Soon your footsteps I shall follow
To the Islands of the Blessed,
To the kingdom of Ponemah!
To the land of the Hereafter!"

III.—HIAWATHA'S DEPARTURE

Nature is eternally young. The Third Act opens with a Ballet of Spring, symbolising life bursting forth throughout a rejuvenated world. Then Iago, the boaster, tells of how he had seen 100 warriors coming over a great water—"bitter so that none could drink it"—in a "great canoe with pinions." He is mocked at by the Indians. "Kaw," they say, "what lies you tell us!" But Hiawatha declares that Iago speaks truth. The strangers are the coming White Race—traders, settlers and missionaries—bringing to the depths of the virgin forest civilisation and the Faith and Hope of Christianity.

And presently this prophecy is fulfilled. The Blackrobe Chief, with the cross upon his bosom, accompanied by his guides and companions, lands on the sandy margin of the lake—bearing a message of Peace and Goodwill on earth.

Hiawatha's mission is at an end. Bidding his people cultivate friendship and unity, he steps into his magic canoe, and as it floats down the stream, the whole tribe raise their arms and their voices in final farewell. As their voices sound and swell and triumph, the vast crowd, the camp, valleys, trees and distant mountain peaks are mantled in solemn light, and in a blaze of sound and colour, Hiawatha westward passes away into the golden sunset. So ends the "Song of Hiawatha."

Spring had come with all its splendour
All its birds and all its blossoms,
All its flowers and leaves and grasses,
Sailing on the wind to northward,
Flying in great flocks, like arrows,
Like huge arrows shot through heaven,
Passed the swan, the Mahnabhezee,
Speaking almost as a man speaks;
And in long lines waving, bending
Like a bowstring snapped asunder,
The white goose, the Waw-be-wawa;
And in pairs, or singly flying,
Mahng the loon, with clangorous pinions,
The blue heron, the Shuh-shuh-gah,
And the grouse, the Mushkodasa.
In the thickets and the meadows
Piped the blue-bird, the Owaisa;
On the summit of the lodges
Sang the robin, the Opechee;
And the sorrowing Hiawatha,
Speechless in his infinite sorrow,
Heard their voices calling to him,
Went forth from his gloomy doorway,
Stood and gazed into the heaven,
Gazed upon the earth and waters.

From his wanderings far to eastward,
From the regions of the morning,
From the shining land of Wabun,
Homeward now returned Iago,
The great traveller, the great boaster,
Full of new and strange adventures,
Marvels many and many wonders.
And the people of the village
Listened to him as he told them
Of his marvellous adventures,
Laughing answered him in this wise:
"Ugh! it is indeed Iago:
No one else beholds such wonders!"

He had seen, he said, a water
Bigger than the Big-Sea-Water,
Broader than the Gitche Gumee,
Bitter so that none could drink it!
At each other looked the warriors,
Looked the women at each other,
Smiled, and said, "It cannot be so!
Kaw!" they said, "it cannot be so!"

O'er it, said he, o'er this water
A canoe with wings came flying,
Bigger than a grove of pine-trees,
Taller than the tallest tree-tops!
And the old men and the women
Looked and tittered at each other.
"Kaw!" they said, "we don't believe it!"

From its mouth, he said, to greet him,
Came Waywassimo, the lightning,
Came the thunder, Annemeekie!
And the warriors and the women
Laughed aloud at poor Iago;
"Kaw!" said they, "what tales you tell us!"

In the great canoe with pinions
Came, he said, a hundred warriors;
Painted white were all their faces,
And with hair their chins were covered!
And the warriors and the women
Laughed and shouted in derision,
Like the ravens on the tree-tops,
Like the crows upon the hemlocks.
"Kaw!" they said, "what lies you tell us!
Do not think that we believe them!"

Only Hiawatha laughed not,
But he gravely spake and answered
To their jeering and their jesting:

"HIAWATHA'S DEPARTURE

"True is all Iagoo tells us;
I have seen it in a vision,
Seen the great canoe with pinions,
Seen the people with white faces,
Seen the coming of this bearded
People of the wooden vessel,
From the regions of the morning,
From the shining land of Wabun.

"Gitche Manito, the Mighty,
The Great Spirit, the Creator,
Sends them hither on his errand,
Sends them to us with his message.
Wheresoe'er they move, before them
Swarms the stinging fly, the Ahmo,
Swarms the bee, the honey-maker;
Wheresoe'er they tread, beneath them
Springs a flower unknown among us,
Springs the White-man's Foot in blossom.

"Let us welcome, then, the strangers,
Hail them as our friends and brothers,
And the heart's right hand of friendship
Give them when they come to see us.
Gitche Manito, the Mighty,
Said this to me in my vision.

"I beheld, too, in that vision
All the secrets of the future,
Of the distant days that shall be.
I beheld the westward marches
Of the unknown, crowded nations.
All the land was full of people,
Restless, struggling, toiling, striving,
Speaking many tongues, yet feeling
But one heart-beat in their bosoms.
In the woodlands rang their axes,
Smoked their towns in all the valleys,
Over all the lakes and rivers
Rushed their great canoes of thunder.

"Then a darker, drearier vision
Passed before me, vague and cloud-like,
I beheld our nations scattered,
All forgetful of my counsels,
Weakened, warring with each other;
Saw the remnants of our people
Sweeping westward, wild and woeful,
Like the cloud-rack of a tempest,
Like the withered leaves of Autumn!"

By the shore of Gitche Gumee,
By the shining Big-Sea-Water,
At the doorway of his wigwam,
In the pleasant Summer morning
Hiawatha stood and waited.

All the air was full of freshness,
All the earth was bright and joyous,
And before him through the sunshine,
Westward toward the neighbouring forest
Passed in golden swarms the Ahmo,
Passed the bees, the honey-makers,
Burning, singing in the sunshine.

Bright above him shone the heavens,
Level spread the lake before him;
From its bosom leaped the sturgeon,
Sparkling, flashing in the sunshine,
On its margin the great forest
Stood reflected in the water,
Every tree-top had its shadow,
Motionless, beneath the water.

From the brow of Hiawatha
Gone was every trace of sorrow,
As a fog from off the water,
As the mist from off the meadow,
With a smile of joy and triumph,
With a look of exultation,
As of one who in a vision
Sees what is to be, but is not,
Stood and waited Hiawatha.

Towards the sun his hands were lifted,* Both the palms spread out against it,
And between the parted fingers
Fell the sunshine on his features,
Flecked with light his naked shoulders,
As it falls and flecks an oak-tree
Through the rifted leaves and branches.
O'er the water floating, flying,
Something in the hazy distance,
Something in the mists of morning,
Loomed and lifted from the water,
Now seemed floating, now seemed flying,
Coming nearer, nearer, nearer.

Was it Shingebis, the diver?
Was it the pelican, the Shada?
Or the heron, the Shuh-shuh-gah?
Or the white goose, Waw-be-wawa,
With the water dripping, flashing
From its glossy neck and feathers?

It was neither goose nor diver,
Neither pelican nor heron,
O'er the water floating, flying,
Through the shining mist of morning,
But a birch canoe with paddles,
Rising, sinking on the water,
Dripping, flashing in the sunshine.
And within it came a people
From the distant land of Wabun,
From the farthest realms of morning
Came the Black-Robe chief, the Prophet,
He the Priest of Prayer, the Pale-face,
With his guides and his companions.
And the noble Hiawatha,
With his hands aloft extended,
Held aloft in sign of welcome,
Waited, full of exultation,
Till the birch canoe with paddles
Grated on the shining pebbles,
Till the Black-Robe chief, the Pale-face,
With the cross upon his bosom,
Landed on the sandy margin.

* In this manner, and with such salutations, was Father Marquette received by the Illinois. See his Voyages et Découvertes, Section V.

HOLLANDS IS DIFFERENT

MANUFACTURE

It must seem strange to anyone who stops to think about it that, in these days of Empire buying, there should still be a large demand for a Gin that comes from abroad when so many excellent home-made Gins are available. When one adds to this the facts that the Dutch article costs more, is not used in most pocket and bar drinks at all, and taste very attractive to drink, it is obvious that there must be in Hollands Gin some unique properties that distinguish it from all other Spirits. Yes, Hollands is different, and the object of this article and of the one in the adjoining column is to describe how it is made, and the uses for which it is so uniquely suited.

The remarkable qualities of Hollands are due to the materials of which it is composed and the way in which it is made. The basis is what is called in Holland, Moordwyn, a special distillery still set at a low stream which retains all the beneficial qualities of the blended grain. This is then twice again distilled with the actual berries of the Alpine Juniper—forming the true Spiritus Juniperi of the medical text books and a diuretic of considerable value and safety.

The best Hollands, like the finest of brandies, is made, or should be made, in pot stills, which, while they produce the finest of spirits, permit the curative ethers and higher alcohols to remain in the liquid. When one knows that in the case of the best Hollands, such as de Kuyper, the liquid passes not less than three times through their pot stills one can begin to get some slight idea of the care that is taken in its preparation.

The production of Hollands is in the care of specialists; in the case of De Kuyper the same family have given to it their unremitting attention for some 238 years, during which time they have constantly studied and improved the article which bears their name. It is not surprising, therefore, that the British public repay their devotion by putting their trust in them, and so acknowledge that Hollands has no rivals, no peers, and fills a place that nothing else can.

De Kuyper's Heart Label Hollands is available in miniatures, quarter, half, and full-size bottles, from all fully licensed houses, and many wine merchants. All sizes and prices are within everybody's reach.

IN USE

Many people are vaguely aware that Hollands is supposed to be good for them, without knowing precisely how it works and what it is good for. It is particularly what we may term a home medicine, especially for women throughout their life from adolescence to old age.

To start with, as a general pick-me-up it is a wonderful antidote for rheumatism, lumbago and many of its allied troubles. Hollands works directly on the Kidneys, enabling them to function properly and to eliminate injurious waste substances that affect the blood stream. In fact, it helps to do away with the conditions of internal poisoning that are so frequently the root causes of not only rheumatism, but also of many other allied complaints. Thus, it promotes a clear complexion, a healthy appetite and sound sleep and keeps weight down.

A regular dose of Hollands taken with warm water and lemon last thing every night is a priceless general tonic.

In addition to being a splendid general tonic, Hollands is invaluable in more specialised ways. Many women and girls today have to go to work whether they are feeling well or not. Periodic indisposition cannot be allowed to interfere with their regular duties, and at such times the full value of Hollands is experienced. It can be said without fear of contradiction that no other Gin approaches it in its beneficial results. In normal cases of feminine indisposition its effects is helpful and soothing, while for sluggish or congested conditions it acts definitely as a stimulant.

Again, women of middle age have learnt with reason to rely on de Kuyper's as their best friend in the troubles which come to them at that time.

HIAWATHA'S DEPARTURE

Then the joyous Hiawatha
Cried aloud, and spake in this wise:
"Beautiful is the sun, O strangers,
When you come so far to see us!
All our town in peace awaits you,
All our doors stand open for you:
You shall enter all our wigwams,
For the heart's right hand we give you.
"Never bloomed the earth so gaily,
Never shone the sun so brightly,
As to-day they shine and blossom,
When you come so far to see us!
Never was our lake so tranquil,
Nor so free from rocks and sand-bars;
For your birch canoe in passing
Has removed both rock and sand-bar!
"Never before had our tobacco
Such a sweet and pleasant flavour,
Never the broad leaves of our corn-fields
Were so beautiful to look on,
As they seem to us this morning,
When you come so far to see us!"

And the Black-Robe chief made answer,
Stammered in his speech a little,
Speaking words yet unfamiliar:
"Peace be with you, Hiawatha,
Peace be with you and your people,
Peace of prayer, and peace of pardon,
Peace of Christ, and joy of Mary!"

Then the generous Hiawatha
Led the strangers to his wigwam,
Seated them on skins of bison,
Seated them on skins of ermine,
And the careful old Nokomis
Brought them food in bowls of basswood,
Water brought in birchen dippers,
And the calumet, the peace-pipe,
Filled and lighted for their smoking.
All the old men of the village,
All the warriors of the nation,
All the Jossakeeds, the prophets,
The magicians, the Wabenos,
And the medicine-men, the Medas,
Came to bid the strangers welcome;
"It is well," they said, "O brothers,
That you come so far to see us!"

In a circle round the doorway,
With their pipes they sat in silence,
Waiting to behold the strangers,
Waiting to receive their message;
Till the Black-Robe chief, the Pale-face,
From the wigwam came to greet them.
Stammering in his speech a little,
Speaking words yet unfamiliar;
"It is well," they said, "O brother,
That you come so far to see us."

Then the Black-Robe chief, the prophet,
Told his message to the people,
Told the purport of his mission.
Told them of the Virgin Mary,
And her blessed Son, the Saviour:
How in distant lands and ages
He had lived on earth as we do;
How he fasted, prayed, and laboured;
How the Jews, the tribe accursed,
Mocked him, scourged him, crucified him;
How he rose from where they laid him,
Walked again with his disciples,
And ascended into heaven.

And the Chiefs made answer, saying:
"We have listened to your message,
We have heard your words of wisdom.
We will think on what you tell us.
It is well for us, O brothers,
That you come so far to see us!"

Then they rose up and departed
Each one homeward to his wigwam,
To the young men and the women
Told the story of the strangers
Whom the Master of Life had sent them
From the shining land of Wabun.

Heavy with the heat and silence
Grew the afternoon of summer;
With a drowsy sound the forest
Whispered round the sultry wigwam,
With a sound of sleep the water
Rippled on the beach below it;
From the cornfields shrill and ceaseless
Sang the grasshopper, Pah-puk-keena;
And the guests of Hiawatha,
Weary with the heat of Summer,
Slumbered in the sultry wigwam,
Slowly o'er the simmering landscape
Fell the evening's dusk and coolness.
And the long and level sunbeams
Shot their spears into the forest,
Breaking through its shields of shadow,
Rushed into each secret ambush,
Searched each thicket, dingle, hollow;
Still the guests of Hiawatha
Slumbered in the silent wigwam.

From his place rose Hiawatha,
Bade farewell to old Nokomis,
Spake in whispers, spake in this wise,
Did not wake the guests that slumbered:

"I am going, O Nokomis,
On a long and distant journey,
To the Portals of the Sunset,
To the regions of the home-wind.
But these guests I leave behind me,
In your watch and ward I leave them;
See that never harm comes near them,
See that never fear molests them,
Never danger nor suspicion,
Never want of food or shelter,
In the lodge of Hiawatha!"

HIAWATHA'S DEPARTURE

Forth into the village went he,
Bade farewell to all the warriors,
Bade farewell to all the young men,
Spake persuading, spake in this wise:

"I am going, O my people,
On a long and distant journey:
Many moons and many winters
Will have come, and will have vanished,
Ere I come again to see you.
But my guests I leave behind me;
Listen to their words of wisdom,
Listen to the truth they tell you,
For the Master of Life has sent them
From the land of light and morning!"

On the shore stood Hiawatha.
Turned and waved his hand at parting;
On the clear and luminous water,
Launched his birch canoe for sailing,
From the pebbles of the margin
Shoved it forth into the water;
Whispered to it, "Westward! westward!"
And with speed it darted forward.
And the evening sun descending
Set the clouds on fire with redness,
Burned the broad sky, like a prairie,
Left upon the level water
One long track and trail of splendour,
Down whose stream, as down a river,
Westward, westward Hiawatha
Sailed into the fiery sunset,
Sailed into the purple vapours,
Sailed into the dusk of evening.
And the people from the margin
Watched him floating, rising, sinking,
Till the birch canoe seemed lifted
High into that sea of splendour,
Till it sank into the vapours
Like the new moon, slowly, slowly
Sinking in the purple distance.

And they said, "Farewell for ever!"
Said, "Farewell, O Hiawatha!"
And the forests, dark and lonely,
Moved through all their depths of darkness,
Sighed, "Farewell, O Hiawatha!"
And the waves upon the margin
Rising, rippling on the pebbles,
Sobbed, "Farewell, O Hiawatha!"
And the heron, the Shuh-shuh-gah,
From her haunts among the fenlands,
Screamed, "Farewell, O Hiawatha!"

Thus departed Hiawatha,
Hiawatha the Beloved,
In the glory of the sunset,
In the purple mists of evening,
To the regions of the home-wind,
Of the Northwest wind, Keewaydin,
To the Islands of the Blessed,
To the kingdom of Ponemah,
To the land of the Hereafter!

Being an oriful and elegant reconstruction of the celebrated drama by Henning Nelms
Presented By
The Madang Dramatic Society
At The
HOTEL MADANG
With a distinguished cast of well loved stellar performers from all over, including:
* Mrs. Belle Meek   Mrs. Lorraine George   Mr. Gavin Miller   Mr. Noel Henderson
  Mrs. Shirley Richardson   Mrs. Caroline Crisp   Miss Rosemary Sutton *
Mr. Ron Gibbs has been employed to devise the action of the drama, which will be executed by the full strength of the company and the:
BARBER SHOP QUARTETTE.
Madang's choice illustrious vocalisers. Incidental solos by
Mr. Vin Smith,   Mr. Laurie Morgan   Mr. Ken Collier,   Mr. Trevor Parr
The scintillating and tuneful musical investiture has been composed and arranged in its entirety by Mrs. Elizabeth Brumby and will be conducted by her in person at each and every perform-ance in all its symphonic splendour.
The realistic stage presentation here tonight is due to the indefatigable efforts of Mr. Lloyd George
INTERMISSION
Patrons are asked to note that light refreshments will be available at the saloon during intervals
The management has gone to great pains to insure that the DRAMA is presented with ALL the effects that contributed so largely to its tremendous BROADWAY SUCCESS and have therefore engaged Mrs. Tessa Gibbs for props. and prompts.
The whole effect of the wonders of illumination has been achieved by the efforts of Mr. Len Burley with the sole use of ELECTRIC TY.

第2回 泛西現代音楽祭 開催を歓迎する

태평양을 함께 애워싼 이웃들이 모여 음악으로 화합하는 제2회 태평양 현대음악제가 우리 서울에서 열리게 된 것을 우리 서울 가족들은 대단히 기쁘게 생각합니다.
천만 시민을 대표하여 여러분을 환영합니다. 아시아 동쪽에 음악을 사랑하는 민족이 있고 그 민족은 매우 영국하고 고상한 품성을 지녔다고 말하던 이전의 중국의 哲人 공자였다고 합니다.
그 동쪽의 민족이란 말할 것도 없이 우리 민족을 듣는것이라고 들었습니다. 창의력이 뛰어나고 예술을 사랑하는 기질 때문에 마음이 트이고 악하지 않게 살아온 우리 한국인은, 언제 어디서나 음악을 즐기고 사랑합니다. 서울 음악회의 노래가 지구촌의 깊숙한 오지에도, 망망한 사막과 얼어붙은 동토에도 스며들어 오래오래 불리워지는 것은 우리의 마음이 깃들어 있기 때문입니다.
한국이 낳은 음악의 재능들은 세계무대를 누비고 있습니다. 국제적인 오페라좌를 이끌고 뛰어난 연주로 세계를 감동시키고, 음악을 경영하여 親和를 創出합니다.
미국에서 태평양 음악제를 설립 하신 우리의 김병곤 교수도 그런 업적을 남긴 분이라고 생각합니다. 다가오는 미래가 이곳 태평양권을 중심으로 펼쳐지리라는 예측은 세계가 공감하여 외심치 않는 일입니다. 창작예술의 中心軸이 태평양권으로 옮겨 온다는 것은 지극히 자연스런 당위입니다. 서울은 태평양시대의 핵심에 놓인 가장 자격있는 도시 입니다. 우아한 古都 그리고 신선한 현대 도시입니다. 정통과 활력으로 섬솟는 인재가 있고 이해력 깊은 청중이 있으며, 적당하고 빈곤하지 않은 시설이 있습니다. 富裕하지는 못해도 賦意가 있는 국력이 뒷받침 하고 있으며 언제나 정성을 다하려는 저희 서울 시가 있습니다. 그러한 우리의 자부심인 서울 시립 교향악단이 음악제를 빛내리라 확신 합니다. 성공적인 음악제를 시민 을 자랑스럽게 할 것입니다. 좋은 음악제를 위해 면길을 찾아오신 여러분들에게 만족한 마음을 느낄 수 있는 음악제가 되는 "서울 나들이"가 되기를 진심으로 기원합니다. 참가하신 모든분들의 노고를 치하드리며 도와주신 여러분께 감사드립니다.
고맙습니다.

1990. 6.
서울특별시장 高 健

Mayor's Welcome Message

We are honored to host the Pacific Contemporary Music Festival II, an event for which music lovers around the Pacific can get together as a family. I welcome you on behalf of our 10 million Seoul citizens.

Confucius, a saga of the ancient China, once said that there lived a people to the east of China who loved music and who was refined and intelligent. They must have meant our Korean people. Koreans today are open-minded and enjoy music anytime, any where, and because of their creative and music loving character, they have done no harm to other peoples. They hymn of the Seoul Olympics carrying our heart still echoes in the far away places, in the vast desert and in the frozen land around the globe.

Many young musicians of Korea are showing their talents all over the world. Leading international opera theater, some move the world with great performances, while some bring harmony to the world, organizing music festivals. I think Prof. Byong-kon Kim who founded the festival in America is a person.

The world of today foresees that in the near future the Pacific nations will play major roles in the world. It goes without speaking that these nations will also play major roles in the creative arts. Seoul, enjoying both ancient elegance and modern freshness, is the most qualified city in the center of the Pacific stage. There are people with tradition and liveliness, audience with deep understanding, and sufficient facilities. Seoul is not affluent, but is faithfully supported by the government, and the city of Seoul will do our best. I can assure you that Seoul Philharmonic Orchestra, the pride of our city, will add magnificence and grandeur to the Festival. And the citizens of Seoul will be proud of a successful festival.

I wish everyone a satisfying festival and a worthy trip to Seoul who came a long way for the festival. I thank all the participants who helped and put in so much efforts.

Thank you.

=== Page 4 ===
Welcoming to the Second Pacific Contemporary Music Fest!

It is my great honor to host the Second Pacific Contemporary Music Festival here in the City of Daegu. I share this delightful event together with all my citizens of Daegu whose concern in the exchanges of culture, especially in the field of contemporary music, is to great. It is my expectation that through the international exchanges of music cherishing its own country's traditions and characteristics will contribute to the promotion of mutual understanding and friendship between people as well as the nations concerned.

I, on behalf of the citizens of Daegu, send our warmest welcome to all the musicians concerned with this imminent event and look forward to meeting and sharing wonderful time with you. As we believe that music known as an international language has contributed so far to the promotion of happiness and harmony in this human world, we deem music to be a vital element in the life and we do not deny that music is indispensible whatever work we do and wherever we are.

We, people of Daegu, are very proud of that there have been so many good musicians in our city and they devoted themselves in the advancement of the excellence of performing arts in the educational institutions and in various fields of music. I trust this event will help them make close times with so many distinguished musicians from the Pacific countries, encouraging those our musicians toward the international trends of music.

I am sending to you our heart welcome again and hope that every person will have wonderful and unforgettable time here in Daegu.

Sung-Dal Park
Mayor,
City of Daegu

=== Page 5 ===
환영사

제2회 패시픽 현대음악제에 참가해주시는 여러분에게 환영의 인사말을 드리게 된 것을 무한한 기쁨으로 생각하며 또한 자랑스럽게 생각합니다.
캘리포니아주립대학교(로스앤젤레스)는 캘리포니아 남부지역의 복수문화예술에 있어서 급성장을 하고 있는 중심지입니다. 「패시픽 현대음악제」는 서로 현저하게 다른 문화를 가진 사람들 사이를 조명해 보기 위하여 다리를 놓으며, 동시에 혁신적인 예술적 실험을 맞이하는 본 대학교 최고의 위임기구들 중의 하나입니다.
김병곤 박사의 정력적인 리더십 아래, 본 센터는 30개국 이상의 작곡가들로 구성된계끔 성장을 하였으며, 이들 회원들은 학문연구, 창작예술의 시도, 그리고 훌륭한 음악연주에 참여하고 있습니다. 올해의 음악제는 전세계의 절반에 걸친 지역에서 참가하여, 본 대학교의 캠퍼스와, 한국의 서울, 대구 등지에서 음악회와 세미나를 개최하게 되었습니다.
우리는 여러분이, 이 음악제를 즐기시고 동시에 음악제 기간동안 펼쳐지는 풍부한 음악회와 학문의 행사에서 많은 것을 성취하시도록 뜨거운 마음으로 여러분을 초대합니다. 여러분의 참가로 인하여 모든 태평양 지역 국가들을 위한, 보다 큰 이해와 보다 나은 미래를 위한 많은 것들이 쌓아져리라 믿어지지 않습니다.

캘리포니아 주립대학교(로스앤젤레스)총장
제임스 로서 박사

WELCOME MESSAGE

It is with great pleasure and pride that I extend a warm welcome to the participants of the Pacific Contemporary Music Festival.

California State University, Los Angeles is a burgeoning center for the multicultural arts within Southern California. The Pacific Contemporary Music Center is one of the finest examples of the University's commitment to building bridges of illumination among peoples of widely different cultures while, at the same time, embracing innovative artistic experimentation.

Under Dr. Byong-kon Kim's dynamic leadership, the Center has grown to include composers from over 30 countries who participate in scholarly research, creative endeavors and exciting musical performances. This year's Music Festival spans half the globe, with concerts and seminars on the campus of Cal State L.A. and in Seoul and Daegu, Korea.

We invite you to enjoy and benefit from the rich array of music and scholarship presented during the Music Festival. Your participation in this event can build greater understanding of and a better future for all Pacific Rim nations.

Dr. James M. Rosser
President,
California State University, Los Angeles

패시픽 현대음악센터 (PCMC)

비영리적 단체인 「패시픽 현대음악센터」는 캘리포니아 주립대학교(로스엔젤레스)에서 이 학교의 작곡과 교수이고, 국제적인 명성을 얻고 있는 작곡가이며 지휘자, 또한 음악교육자인 김병곤 박사에 의하여 1986년 설립되었다. 본 센터는 환태평양지역 국가들의 작곡가들에 의한 현대음악작품의 연주, 교환, 이해를 촉진시키기 위하여 설립된 국제적인 기구이다. 이 기구는 연주가·메스미디어·학자들과의 연락업무도 담당하고 있으며, 작품·녹음·전기(傳記)·연주정보 등, 여러 분야와의 관계를 유지하고 있다.

위 원 회
김병곤 박사: 작곡가, 캘리포니아주립대학교(로스엔젤레스), PCMC 소장
올가 테르미니 박사: 음악학자, 캘리포니아주립대학교(로스엔젤레스), PCMC 부소장
이린 거어튼 박사: 음악이론가, 캘리포니아주립대학교(로스엔젤레스), PCMC 소장보
윌리엄 크래프트: 작곡가, 지휘자

마야실 비아로스키 박사: 작곡가, 캘리포니아주립대학교(도밍게즈 힐스)

PACIFIC CONTEMPORARY MUSIC CENTER

The Pacific Contemporary Music Center, a non-profit organization, was founded in 1986 at California State University, Los Angeles, by Dr. Byong-kon Kim, Professor of Composition and an internationally recognized composer, conductor and educator. The Center is an international organization established to encourage performance, exchange, and awareness of contemporary music by composers of the Pacific Rim countries. It serves as a liaison for performers, mass media, scholars, et al. It maintains a library of members: compositions, sound recordings, biographies and performance information.

베르나르도 펠드만은 멕시코 태생의 작곡가로 1982년 이후 캘리포니아에 살고 있다. 그의 작품은 실내악, 관현악곡, 테이프 음악, 전자음악등 다양하다. 그의 음악은 미국, 멕시코, 유럽, 이스라엘 등지에서 <Orquesta Filarmónica de la Ciudad de Mexico>, <Cal-Arts 20th Century Players>, <New London Contemporary Ensemble>, <New York North/South Consonance>등의 연주단에 의해 연주 되었다.

그는 1987년 로스엔젤레스 축제때 작품을 위촉 받은 바 있으며, 1989년 멕시코시에서 열린 <Foro Internacional de Música Contemporánea>에서도 작품 위촉을 받았다. 다른 분야의 예술가들과 공동작업한 작품중 타원한 것으로는 디즈니 유선방송을 위해 레이 페타가 제작한 <Cloud Dreamer>, Guillermo Gomez Pena의 <Orpheus and Euridice's Cumbia>를 위한 반주음악, 또 블록 연주자 주디 골드워터, 무용가 리 카밀로 등과 공동작업한 <A Tribute to Frida Kahlo>를 들 수 있다. 그는 <Churchill Films>회사를 위해 도큐멘터리 음악을 만든 바 있다. 펠드만은 <DAFCA>, <Ahmanson Foundation>, <ASCAP>, <Meet the Composer, Inc.>등으로부터 상을 받았다.

그는 California Institute of the Arts에서 가르쳐 왔으며, 현재 College of the Canyons의 음악과장으로 재직하고 있다. 또한 미국 전자 음향학회의 로스엔젤레스 지부장직도 맡고 있다.

ONIRICA: 현실세계에서는 이룩할 수 없는 많은 것들이 우리의 꿈속에서 이루어지니 꿈이란 얼마나 불가사의 하면서도 유익한 것인가? 꿈을 꾸는 사람은 현실세계에서의 이성적인 제약들을 초월하여 미지의 세계 속에서 현재와 과거의 벽을 넘나들며 여행하는 것이다.
눈을 감는 동시에 그녀는 결코 속이 더 큰 환상의 세계를 통과하며, 친숙한 얼굴과 낯선 얼굴들이 작가없는 연극의 주인공으로 둘러싸여 그녀를 현혹시킨다. 그녀는 아무도 쓰지않은 그 연극의 관객이자 동시에 주인공인 것이다. 그녀는 상처받고, 사랑받고, 모욕받는다. 그녀는 눈을 감아도 볼 수 있고, 귀가 없이도 들을 수 있다. 꿈에서 깨어남과 동시에 그녀는 자신이 꿈속에서 살았던 인생들에 대해 생각에 잠길지 모른다. 아니면 꿈속에서의 일들을 잊기로 하고 현실세계에서 자신에게 다가올 하루하루를 설계할지 모른다.

Bernardo Feldman is a Mexican composer who has lived in California since 1982. His works include music for chamber and symphonic ensembles as well as compositions for tape and live electronics. His music has been performed throughout the United States, Mexico, Europe and Israel by major ensembles such as the Orquesta Filarmónica de la Ciudad de Mexico, the Cal-Arts 20th Century Players, the New London Contemporary Ensemble and the New York North/South Consonance.

He has received commissions to write for the Los Angeles Festival in 1987 as well as for the Foro Internacional de Música Contemporánea in Mexico City in 1989. Prominent among his collaborations with artists of other media are Cloud Dreamer, an animated film for the Disney Cable Channel by Ray Huerta; the incidental music for Guillermo Gomez Pena's Orpheus and Euridic's Cumbia and A Tribute to Frida Kahlo with flutist Judy Goldwater and dancer Lee Carrillo. He has also scored several documentaries for Churchill Films.

Mr. Feldman has been the recipient of several awards from DAFCA, the Ahmanson Foundation, ASCAP, and Meet the Composer, Inc.

He has been a faculty member at the California Institute of the Arts and is currently head of the Music Department at College of the Canyons. He is also president of the Los Angeles Chapter of the United Society of Electro-Acoustic Music in the States (SEAMUS-L.A.).

ONIRICA: Nightmares and dreams possess wondrous advantages over reality; by transcending the constraints of reason, the dreamer travels beyond unforeseen places in which he confuses Now with a multitude of Yesterdays. As she closes her eyes, escaping through fantastic worlds that are larger on the inside than they are on the outside, hazy images of familiar and foreign faces dazzle her senses by transforming themselves into the characters of a play that nobody ever wrote and for which she is both audience and protagonist, all at once. She is hurt, loved or disdained. She can see and hear, although her eyes are shut and her ears slumber. Perhaps, as she awakes, she will wonder about the many lives she just lived or she may decide to forget them as they secretly continue to shape her days to come.

Kim Jong Gil (金正吉): 1962년 서울대학교 음악대학 작곡과를 졸업하고 1972년 서독의 Hannover Staatliche Hochschule für Musik의 미스터 클래스를 수료했다. 매우 활발한 작곡활동을 하고 있는 그는 수많은 음악제에서 작품이 위촉되어 연주되었다.

GO PUNG: The Wbang-jong, Eb, Choong-lyu, Ab, and Imjang, Bb, are often used as core-tones in both kinds of traditional Korean music: music for the Court, and folk music. These three notes assume a similar function in this composition. An extremely slow-moving melody with a harmonic ostinato reflects the peaceful and dignified mood of Court music in the first movement, Hyang-Hap (Incense Case). The second movement, Na-Mak Shin (Wooden Shoes), establishes a folkish mood with a minimalistically repeated rhythmic pattern derived from the "Taryong." The third movement, Ok-Bi-Nyo (Jade Hair Ornament), represents lyricism of the folk style with emotional density. The last movement, Mun-Pung-Gi (Paper Flap on a Door), expresses a strong national color with an abrupt introduction of new musical vocabulary.
